Hierarchy MUST NOT depend primarily on shadow, saturation, animation, or arbitrary font-size escalation.

A screen SHOULD have one dominant visual purpose.

Multiple elements MUST NOT compete simultaneously as the strongest object on the page unless the Pattern explicitly requires comparison.

Primary actions MUST be visually identifiable without making every action visually prominent.

Secondary and tertiary information SHOULD recede without becoming inaccessible or illegible.

Decorative elements MUST NOT outrank operational content.

---

## 2.3 Typography voice

Typography MUST communicate clarity first and brand character second.

Application typography SHOULD feel precise, compact enough for productive work, and neutral enough to support long sessions.

Marketing typography MAY be more editorial and expressive, provided recognisable brand characteristics remain intact.

### 2.3.1 Type roles

The system MUST define semantic typography roles rather than allowing arbitrary font-size selection.

At minimum, typography MUST distinguish:

- display;
- page title;
- section heading;
- subsection heading;
- body;
- compact body;
- label;
- metadata;
- caption;
- code or machine-readable values where applicable.

The actual font families, sizes, weights, tracking, and line heights MUST be encoded in Design Tokens.

### 2.3.2 Typography hierarchy

Heading hierarchy MUST reflect information hierarchy.

Font size MUST NOT be used to compensate for weak content structure.

Interfaces SHOULD normally use a restrained range of font weights.

Excessive semibold or bold text MUST NOT be used as a substitute for hierarchy.

Body text SHOULD maintain comfortable reading rhythm and MUST NOT be compressed to increase apparent information density beyond accessible limits.

Uppercase text SHOULD be reserved for short, deliberate labels or specialised notation. Long uppercase labels and paragraphs MUST NOT be used.

Letter spacing MUST NOT be manipulated decoratively in controls or body content where it impairs scanning.

### 2.3.3 Numeric and data typography

Financial values, measurements, identifiers, dates, table values, and other alignment-sensitive information SHOULD use appropriate numeric features where supported.

Tabular numerals SHOULD be used when changing values must remain visually aligned.

Monospace typography MAY be used for code, hashes, machine identifiers, technical paths, or similar technical material.

Monospace MUST NOT become the default visual language for ordinary application data merely to imply technical sophistication.

---

## 2.4 Colour semantics and emotional use

Colour MUST carry meaning intentionally.

Components MUST consume semantic colour tokens rather than raw palette values.

The semantic system MUST separate at least:

- canvas/background;
- foreground/content;
- muted content;
- surfaces;
- borders;
- primary/brand action;
- secondary action;
- focus;
- destructive/error;
- warning;
- success;
- informational;
- selected/active;
- data-visualisation categories where required.

A visual palette MAY contain more colours than the semantic system exposes, but application code MUST NOT depend directly on those palette values.

### 2.4.1 Brand colour

Brand colour SHOULD act as a recognisable signal, not as continuous decoration.

High-chroma brand colour SHOULD be concentrated in:

- primary action;
- selected states;
- meaningful highlights;
- signature marketing moments;
- small identity-bearing details.

Large quantities of saturated colour SHOULD NOT dominate operational workflows.

A brand colour MUST NOT be reused for warning, destructive, or success semantics where doing so creates ambiguity.

### 2.4.2 Semantic colour

Success, warning, destructive, and informational colours MUST have stable semantic meanings throughout the system.

The same colour MUST NOT indicate materially different states in different modules.

Semantic state MUST NOT be communicated through colour alone.

Icons, text, structure, labels, or other non-colour signals MUST accompany critical status differences.

### 2.4.3 Colour restraint

The default application experience SHOULD be predominantly neutral.

Neutral does not mean visually flat. Depth SHOULD arise from hierarchy, spacing, border treatment, typography, controlled contrast, and material transitions.

Screens SHOULD avoid simultaneously displaying numerous high-saturation colours unless the content itself requires categorical differentiation.

Decorative gradients MUST be controlled by approved tokens or assets.

Ad hoc gradients MUST NOT be introduced inside feature code.

---

## 2.5 Light and dark mood

Light and dark modes MUST represent the same visual system, not separate themes.

Semantic relationships MUST remain stable across modes.

Changing mode MUST NOT change:

- meaning;
- action priority;
- information architecture;
- component hierarchy;
- validation semantics;
- security semantics.

Dark mode MUST NOT be implemented as a simple inversion of light mode.

Dark surfaces SHOULD use controlled luminance separation rather than excessive shadow.

Pure black SHOULD NOT dominate large surfaces unless intentionally defined by the brand system.

Pure white SHOULD NOT be used indiscriminately for dark-mode foreground content.

High-saturation colours SHOULD generally be moderated for dark backgrounds to avoid vibration and disproportionate emphasis.

Images, logos, illustrations, charts, overlays, and maps MUST be reviewed in both modes.

Theme preference MUST follow the State Management standard. The visual layer MUST NOT create a separate unsynchronised theme state.

System preference SHOULD be supported.

User-selected preference SHOULD persist according to the canonical preference-state mechanism.

Theme hydration MUST NOT create avoidable flashes of the incorrect theme.

---

## 2.6 Whitespace rhythm and density

Whitespace is structural and MUST be intentional.

Spacing MUST be selected from canonical Design Tokens.

Arbitrary spacing values MUST NOT be introduced to visually repair individual screens.

Visual rhythm SHOULD use repeatable relationships between:

- page regions;
- sections;
- component groups;
- labels and controls;
- headings and content;
- related and unrelated objects.

Related elements MUST be visually closer than unrelated elements.

Large whitespace SHOULD signal hierarchy, change of context, or deliberate emphasis.

Whitespace MUST NOT be removed simply to make an interface appear more information-dense.

Conversely, operational interfaces MUST NOT use marketing-scale whitespace that forces unnecessary scrolling or separates controls from the data they govern.

### 2.6.1 Density modes

If products require compact and comfortable density variants, density MUST be implemented systematically through Design Tokens and Components.

Feature teams MUST NOT invent local compact modes.

Changing density MUST NOT reduce target sizes, focus visibility, legibility, or other accessibility requirements below the approved minimum.

---

## 2.7 Shape, radius, and geometry

Geometry SHOULD feel deliberate, restrained, and consistent.

Corner radius MUST derive from canonical radius tokens.

The system SHOULD use a small, coherent radius family.

Large rounded forms SHOULD be reserved for components where their geometry supports the product character.

Pill shapes SHOULD be reserved primarily for inherently compact or categorical objects such as badges, chips, segmented controls, or appropriate actions.

Containers MUST NOT become rounded cards merely because they contain content.

Nested rounded rectangles SHOULD be minimised.

A container SHOULD exist because it establishes grouping, interaction, clipping, separation, or elevation—not simply because visual decoration is desired.

---

## 2.8 Materials: opaque, translucent, and glass

Opaque surfaces MUST be the default material for operational UI.

Translucency MAY be used where background context remains useful, such as:

- overlays;
- floating navigation;
- selected immersive surfaces;
- media experiences;
- controlled marketing compositions.

Glass treatment MUST be exceptional rather than systemic.

Glass MUST NOT be used where it reduces text contrast, obscures boundaries, introduces visual noise, or weakens the user's understanding of layer order.

Critical forms, destructive confirmations, authentication, authorization, financial actions, and dense data surfaces SHOULD use stable opaque or near-opaque materials.

Backdrop blur MUST NOT be required to understand a hierarchy.

Interfaces MUST remain comprehensible when blur effects are unavailable or reduced.

Translucency MUST use approved material tokens and MUST NOT be recreated ad hoc through arbitrary alpha values.

---

## 2.9 Borders and separators

Borders SHOULD express structure quietly.

Border colour and strength MUST be semantic and tokenised.

Default containers SHOULD use the lightest boundary sufficient to communicate grouping.

Repeated heavy outlines MUST NOT become the primary means of structuring a page.

Separators SHOULD be preferred when the relationship is sequential.

Containment SHOULD be preferred when a group has independent behaviour, state, elevation, or identity.

Borders MUST NOT be removed from interactive controls where the resulting affordance becomes ambiguous.

---

## 2.10 Shadow and elevation character

Elevation MUST represent actual visual layering.

Shadow MUST NOT be used merely to make an element appear more polished.

The system SHOULD maintain a small elevation vocabulary, for example:

- base;
- raised;
- overlay;
- modal/top layer.

Exact values belong in Design Tokens.

Elevation SHOULD increase when an element physically or conceptually overlays another layer.

A static card inside the normal document flow SHOULD NOT receive strong floating elevation.

Menus, popovers, tooltips, sheets, dialogs, and other overlay components SHOULD express sufficient separation from the layer beneath them.

Shadows SHOULD be soft, controlled, and subordinate to content.

Large, dark, theatrical drop shadows MUST NOT be used in routine application UI.

Dark mode SHOULD rely more heavily on luminance and border separation because conventional dark shadows may have insufficient visual utility.

---

## 2.11 Imagery

Imagery MUST serve a communicative role.

Photography SHOULD feel credible, specific, and contextually relevant.

Generic stock imagery SHOULD NOT be used when it weakens trust or makes the product appear interchangeable.

Photography SHOULD favour natural composition, controlled colour, and sufficient negative space for the intended layout.

Image treatment SHOULD maintain a coherent:

- crop philosophy;
- tonal character;
- contrast range;
- saturation range;
- corner treatment;
- subject treatment.

Product screenshots used in marketing MUST represent plausible product states.

Screenshots MUST NOT expose credentials, private user information, confidential identifiers, API secrets, internal infrastructure details, or sensitive production data.

Any sample data shown in imagery MUST comply with Security and Data & Database standards.

Text rendered inside images SHOULD be avoided when semantic HTML text can provide the same information.

---

## 2.12 Illustration

Illustration MAY increase warmth, comprehension, identity, or narrative value where photography or interface imagery is inappropriate.

Illustration style MUST be coherent across the product family.

A product MUST NOT mix unrelated illustration languages such as:

- dimensional 3D objects;
- flat geometric vectors;
- hand-drawn sketches;
- photoreal AI imagery;
- cartoon characters;

unless an explicitly approved campaign or sub-brand system defines the relationship.

Illustration SHOULD use the same semantic colour philosophy as the interface.

Illustrations SHOULD NOT imitate interactive controls.

Decorative illustrations MUST NOT imply unavailable features, states, permissions, or outcomes.

Empty-state illustration SHOULD remain secondary to the explanation and next action.

---

## 2.13 Iconography

Icons MUST use the canonical icon family defined by the Design System.

Icons from unrelated families MUST NOT be mixed casually.

Icon size, stroke, optical weight, and alignment MUST be normalised by Components or Design Tokens.

Icons SHOULD communicate common actions or reinforce labels.

Unfamiliar icons MUST NOT replace clear text labels for important actions.

Icons MUST NOT be used as decorative noise inside every heading, card, or control.

Brand-specific icons MAY be introduced when they represent domain concepts not adequately covered by the baseline icon set.

New domain icons MUST match the optical language of the canonical family.

---

## 2.14 Motion personality

Motion SHOULD communicate continuity, causality, state change, hierarchy, or orientation.

Motion MUST NOT exist solely to demonstrate technical capability.

The motion personality SHOULD be:

**fast, controlled, quiet, and physically coherent.**

Routine interactions SHOULD feel responsive rather than cinematic.

### 2.14.1 Appropriate motion

Motion MAY clarify:

- enter and exit relationships;
- expansion and collapse;
- selection changes;
- overlay origin;
- drag relationships;
- progress;
- reordering;
- feedback following a deliberate action.

### 2.14.2 Prohibited motion

Routine UI MUST NOT use:

- decorative bouncing;
- continuous floating;
- gratuitous parallax;
- exaggerated spring effects;
- long page transitions;
- motion that delays task completion;
- multiple unrelated animations competing simultaneously.

Loading indicators MUST NOT create unnecessary visual activity when skeleton, progressive rendering, or stable progress feedback provides better information.

### 2.14.3 Reduced motion

Motion MUST respect applicable Accessibility requirements and user reduced-motion preferences.

Non-essential movement triggered by interaction SHOULD be disabled or substantially reduced when reduced motion is requested.

Removing motion MUST NOT remove information.

Opacity or immediate state changes MAY replace spatial movement where appropriate.

---

## 2.15 Interaction feedback

Every meaningful interaction MUST produce perceivable feedback.

Hover, focus, active, selected, loading, success, disabled, and error states MUST be visually intentional.

Hover styling MUST NOT be the only indicator that an element is interactive.

Keyboard focus MUST remain clearly visible and MUST follow the Accessibility standard.

Pressed or active feedback SHOULD feel immediate.

Optimistic interfaces MUST visually distinguish pending state where pretending completion could mislead the user.

Animation MUST NOT conceal API latency, validation latency, or processing state.

---

## 2.16 Forms and validation aesthetics

Forms MUST follow the canonical Forms & Validation standard.

Aesthetic treatment MUST reinforce rather than replace form semantics.

Labels MUST remain visually associated with their controls.

Placeholder text MUST NOT replace labels.

Required, optional, help, warning, and error information MUST have consistent visual treatment.

Error styling MUST NOT rely solely on red borders.

Validation feedback MUST identify:

- which field requires attention;
- what is wrong;
- what the user can do next.

Error messages SHOULD appear near the relevant control when possible.

Forms MUST NOT become visually unstable as validation messages appear.

Control height, label rhythm, help-text spacing, and error spacing SHOULD be designed as a coherent field system.

Destructive or irreversible actions MUST be visually distinct from normal primary actions in accordance with the relevant Pattern and Security standards.

---

## 2.17 Data-dense interfaces

Tables, dashboards, maps, analytics screens, and operational consoles MUST prioritise information comprehension over decoration.

Data regions SHOULD maximise signal-to-noise ratio.

Repeated cards SHOULD NOT be used where a table, list, definition structure, or grouped section communicates the information more effectively.

Colour in charts MUST follow semantic or categorical data-visualisation tokens.

Chart colour MUST NOT be borrowed arbitrarily from status colours.

Data visualisation MUST remain interpretable without relying solely on hue differences.

Decorative gradients, 3D charts, excessive gridlines, large shadows, and ornamental data ink SHOULD NOT be used.

Critical values SHOULD be emphasised through hierarchy and context rather than oversized typography alone.

---

## 2.18 Editorial versus utilitarian tone

The visual system MUST support two controlled presentation modes.

### 2.18.1 Utilitarian mode

Application workflows SHOULD default to utilitarian presentation.

Utilitarian presentation prioritises:

- clarity;
- density appropriate to the task;
- predictable controls;
- restrained colour;
- rapid scanning;
- stable placement;
- visible state.

Operational pages MUST NOT behave like marketing landing pages.

### 2.18.2 Editorial mode

Editorial treatment MAY be used for:

- marketing;
- onboarding;
- announcements;
- product education;
- reports;
- long-form documentation;
- feature storytelling;
- carefully designed empty or success moments.

Editorial presentation MAY use stronger typography, larger whitespace, photography, illustration, richer composition, and controlled motion.

Editorial treatment MUST NOT compromise navigation, semantic structure, accessibility, or task completion.

### 2.18.3 Transition between modes

A user moving from marketing into the application SHOULD recognise the same organisation.

The expressive intensity may change; the identity MUST NOT.

---

## 2.19 Brand expression rules

Brand identity MUST be built from repeatable signals rather than one-off decoration.

The system SHOULD maintain recognisable signatures across channels through a stable combination of:

- typography;
- semantic brand colour;
- geometry;
- icon character;
- image treatment;
- spacing rhythm;
- material treatment;
- motion character;
- writing and content hierarchy.

No single signature MUST carry the entire identity.

Removing a hero gradient, illustration, or large logo MUST NOT make the underlying product visually indistinguishable from an unrelated default template.

At the same time, brand expression MUST NOT override established usability conventions without a measurable benefit.

### 2.19.1 Logo use

Logos MUST use approved assets.

Logos MUST NOT be distorted, recoloured arbitrarily, reconstructed with text, or placed on insufficient-contrast backgrounds.

Logo scale SHOULD be proportionate to context.

Application chrome SHOULD favour product utility over repeated logo prominence.

### 2.19.2 Brand moments

High-expression brand treatment SHOULD be concentrated in deliberate moments, including:

- public marketing;
- first-run experiences;
- launch or campaign surfaces;
- selected success moments;
- reports and editorial content.

High-expression treatment SHOULD NOT surround every routine action.

Brand distinctiveness is stronger when contrast exists between expressive moments and calm operational surfaces.

---

## 2.20 Cross-channel consistency

Marketing, application UI, and email MUST share one visual identity while respecting the constraints of each medium.

### 2.20.1 Invariants

The following SHOULD remain recognisable across channels:

- typography character;
- brand colour relationships;
- logo treatment;
- hierarchy;
- geometry;
- image/illustration character;
- tone of emphasis;
- overall restraint.

### 2.20.2 Marketing

Marketing MAY use the broadest expressive range.

Marketing MAY introduce:

- larger typography;
- stronger composition;
- richer imagery;
- greater whitespace;
- controlled gradients;
- campaign-specific art direction;
- richer motion.

Marketing MUST still use canonical semantic and brand foundations.

Campaign expression MUST NOT silently redefine the product design system.

### 2.20.3 Application

The application MUST optimise for comprehension, predictability, and repeated use.

Application UI SHOULD use the least visual treatment needed to establish hierarchy and state.

Brand identity in the application SHOULD be evident through accumulated detail rather than constant visual emphasis.

### 2.20.4 Email

Email MUST preserve hierarchy, brand recognition, readable typography, semantic colour, and approved imagery while assuming restricted rendering capabilities.

Core email meaning MUST NOT depend on:

- backdrop blur;
- complex transparency;
- advanced animation;
- hover;
- JavaScript;
- custom web-font availability.

Email SHOULD degrade gracefully to robust typography, colour, spacing, and imagery.

Transactional email SHOULD be materially more utilitarian than promotional email.

Critical transactional information MUST remain readable when images are blocked.

---

## 2.21 Design Tokens relationship

Every reusable aesthetic value MUST ultimately resolve to a Design Token.

This includes recurring:

- colours;
- typography;
- spacing;
- radii;
- borders;
- shadows;
- opacity;
- motion duration;
- motion easing;
- layer/elevation values;
- material values.

Feature code MUST NOT establish a second token system through arbitrary utility values or local CSS variables.

Semantic tokens SHOULD be preferred over primitive tokens in component usage.

For example, components SHOULD consume concepts equivalent to `background`, `foreground`, `primary`, `muted`, `border`, `ring`, `destructive`, and their foreground relationships rather than literal palette coordinates.

Token names MUST describe role rather than aesthetic appearance wherever the value may vary by theme.

A token called `text-danger` is preferable to one whose contract is effectively `text-red-600`.

---

## 2.22 Component standard relationship

Components MUST embody this visual language by default.

Consumers SHOULD NOT need substantial styling to make a canonical component look canonical.

The Component standard MUST define the permitted:

- sizes;
- variants;
- states;
- slots;
- density options;
- composition boundaries.

Feature code MUST NOT create visual variants by repeatedly attaching custom class combinations to otherwise canonical components.

A repeated variation SHOULD be promoted to an approved Component variant or Pattern.

Component styling MUST NOT change the semantic behaviour established by the underlying accessible primitive.

---

## 2.23 Pattern standard relationship

Patterns define how components behave together.

Aesthetic consistency MUST NOT be achieved by forcing every workflow into the same composition.

Dialogs, sheets, inline editing, page forms, tables, cards, command interfaces, and navigation each have distinct structural purposes.

Teams MUST use the Pattern standard to select the appropriate interaction model before applying visual treatment.

Aesthetics MUST NOT be used to make an incorrect Pattern appear acceptable.

---

## 2.24 Accessibility relationship

Accessibility is a design input, not a final visual QA pass.

This visual language MUST operate within the canonical Accessibility standard.

At minimum, aesthetic choices MUST preserve:

- required contrast;
- visible focus;
- distinguishable interactive states;
- non-colour semantic cues;
- readable text;
- adequate target sizes;
- zoom and reflow;
- reduced-motion behaviour;
- meaningful content order;
- understandable error communication.

A visual treatment that cannot meet accessibility requirements MUST be changed.

Accessibility requirements MUST NOT be waived to protect a particular shade, opacity, font weight, animation, or decorative treatment.

---

## 2.25 Security relationship

Aesthetics MUST NOT obscure security-relevant meaning.

Authentication, authorization, destructive actions, sensitive settings, privilege changes, financial operations, and data-export actions MUST use clear language and unambiguous interaction states.

Visual similarity MUST NOT make a destructive action appear equivalent to a harmless action.

Security warnings MUST NOT be visually minimised to preserve a clean layout.

Marketing-style urgency MUST NOT be used around consent, permissions, authentication, payments, or security-sensitive actions.

The interface MUST NOT use visual dark patterns to:

- conceal consequences;
- pressure consent;
- disguise subscriptions or charges;
- make rejection materially harder than acceptance;
- blur the difference between optional and required permissions.

Sensitive information displayed visually MUST comply with masking, logging, screenshot, and exposure requirements in the Security standard.

---

## 2.26 Data & Database relationship

Presentation MUST reflect authoritative data semantics rather than inventing its own.

UI colour, labels, icons, and visual grouping MUST NOT redefine database or domain states independently.

If data has states such as pending, approved, rejected, expired, archived, or deleted, the canonical domain meaning MUST be established before aesthetic mappings are assigned.

Unknown, null, unavailable, zero, and empty MUST NOT be represented as interchangeable visual states.

The interface MUST distinguish these concepts when the domain distinguishes them.

Sample data used in marketing, demos, screenshots, storybooks, or visual regression fixtures MUST follow approved synthetic-data rules.

---

## 2.27 API relationship

Visual state MUST reflect actual API state.

Interfaces MUST distinguish where relevant:

- initial;
- loading;
- refreshing;
- successful;
- empty;
- partial;
- stale;
- offline;
- validation failure;
- authorization failure;
- server failure.

A loading animation MUST NOT falsely imply that a request has succeeded.

Success styling MUST NOT appear before the underlying operation reaches the success condition defined by the API and State Management standards.

API error detail MUST be transformed into safe, actionable user messaging according to the API, Security, and Error Handling standards.

Raw stack traces, infrastructure messages, database errors, internal identifiers, or sensitive API content MUST NOT be exposed merely because the visual error component can display arbitrary text.

---

## 2.28 State Management relationship

Visual state MUST derive from canonical application state.

Components MUST NOT independently maintain duplicate visual representations of domain state when a shared canonical source exists.

Theme, density, navigation expansion, modal visibility, pending interactions, selection, and similar UI states MUST follow the ownership rules in the State Management standard.

Temporary visual state SHOULD remain local when it has no wider semantic relevance.

Persisted preferences MUST NOT be inferred from arbitrary DOM classes where canonical state exists.

Animation state MUST NOT become an alternative business-state machine.

---

## 2.29 Loading, empty, error, and success aesthetics

System states MUST appear intentionally designed.

### Loading

Loading feedback SHOULD preserve spatial stability.

Skeletons SHOULD resemble the approximate structure of expected content without reproducing excessive decorative detail.

Skeletons MUST NOT be shown when the interface already has useful stale or cached content that should remain visible according to the relevant Pattern.

### Empty

Empty states MUST explain the absence of content.

Where an action is possible, the next appropriate action SHOULD be visible.

Illustration is optional.

An empty-state illustration MUST NOT outweigh the explanatory content.

### Error

Errors MUST clearly distinguish failure from normal emptiness.

Error presentation SHOULD match severity.

Recoverable errors SHOULD provide a recovery action where possible.

### Success

Routine success SHOULD normally be acknowledged with restrained feedback.

Large celebratory treatments SHOULD be reserved for genuinely meaningful milestones.

Confetti or similarly high-motion celebration MUST NOT be the standard success treatment for routine CRUD operations.

---

## 2.30 Responsive aesthetic behaviour

Responsive design MUST preserve hierarchy rather than merely scale dimensions.

Small screens MAY reduce decorative treatments before reducing content clarity.

Large display typography, decorative imagery, secondary panels, and expanded whitespace SHOULD collapse or simplify before core controls are compromised.

Mobile layouts MUST NOT preserve desktop aesthetics at the expense of usability.

Desktop layouts MUST NOT simply stretch mobile components across excess width.

The Layout standard owns responsive structure; this standard governs which visual characteristics are essential enough to survive those structural changes.

---

## 2.31 Performance and visual effects

Aesthetic effects MUST justify their runtime cost.

Large media, blur, filters, animation, video, custom fonts, and complex shadows SHOULD be budgeted against performance requirements.

Visual polish MUST NOT materially degrade:

- interaction latency;
- initial rendering;
- scrolling;
- battery consumption;
- memory usage;
- lower-powered device behaviour.

Decorative effects SHOULD be progressively enhanced where appropriate.

The usable baseline MUST remain visually coherent without optional effects.

---

## 2.32 Exceptions

A deviation from this standard MUST be intentional.

Exceptions SHOULD document:

- the rule being deviated from;
- why existing components or tokens are insufficient;
- accessibility impact;
- security impact where applicable;
- affected channels;
- whether the change should become a new reusable token, component, Pattern, or standard rule.

One-off visual exceptions SHOULD be treated as a design-system signal, not merely as local styling work.

Repeated exceptions MUST trigger design-system review.

---

# 3. Anti-patterns

The following are non-conformant unless explicitly covered by an approved Pattern or exception.

## 3.1 Default-template identity

A product consisting primarily of stock shadcn/ui components with unchanged visual defaults and no deliberate brand language.

shadcn/ui is the baseline, not the finished identity.

## 3.2 Ad hoc Tailwind design

Repeated arbitrary utilities such as ungoverned colours, shadows, radii, spacing, opacity, or animation values applied directly inside feature code.

Reusable visual decisions belong in tokens and components.

## 3.3 Card soup

Every section is placed inside a rounded, bordered, shadowed card regardless of semantic grouping.

## 3.4 Rainbow status design

Every state receives a bright colour, resulting in a screen where nothing has meaningful visual priority.

## 3.5 Brand-colour flooding

The primary brand colour is used across backgrounds, headings, borders, icons, controls, links, and decorative objects simultaneously.

## 3.6 Glass everywhere

Blurred translucent panels are used as the default material, including forms, tables, dialogs, and dense application surfaces.

## 3.7 Shadow as hierarchy

Elements receive progressively larger shadows because the underlying information hierarchy is weak.

## 3.8 Typography as decoration

Extreme display sizes, unnecessary weight variation, excessive letter spacing, or arbitrary font changes substitute for content hierarchy.

## 3.9 Invisible affordance

Controls look like ordinary text or decoration until hovered.

## 3.10 Colour-only meaning

State is differentiated only through red, green, yellow, or other hue.

## 3.11 Animation theatre

Routine navigation and CRUD interactions include long transitions, bouncing, parallax, staged reveals, or large spring movement.

## 3.12 Faux premium design

Heavy blur, metallic gradients, exaggerated glow, oversized shadows, excessive rounded geometry, and animated backgrounds are combined to manufacture perceived sophistication.

## 3.13 Marketing inside the workflow

Operational pages use hero sections, oversized slogans, decorative illustrations, excessive whitespace, or campaign-style calls to action where users need efficient task completion.

## 3.14 Dashboard by default

Information is split into cards and charts because a dashboard aesthetic is desired rather than because the underlying task benefits from summarisation.

## 3.15 Screenshot-driven product design

Feature UI is designed to produce impressive static screenshots while routine use, keyboard interaction, error states, loading states, density, or responsive behaviour remain weak.

## 3.16 Mode inversion

Dark mode is generated by mechanically reversing light colours without considering luminance, elevation, image treatment, or semantic emphasis.

## 3.17 Local component forks

Individual modules copy and modify canonical shadcn/ui components to achieve slightly different aesthetics instead of using the shared component system.

## 3.18 Raw-state styling

API values or database enum values are directly mapped to arbitrary colours inside feature code.

Domain semantics MUST be resolved before visual semantics.

## 3.19 Decorative accessibility regression

Focus rings, labels, borders, error text, contrast, or target sizes are weakened because they interfere with a desired minimalist aesthetic.

## 3.20 Artificial urgency

Colour, animation, countdowns, visual hierarchy, or button styling are used to pressure users into consent, payment, permission, or other consequential choices.

---

# 4. Checklist

A surface conforms to this standard only when the following can be answered **yes** where applicable.

### Identity and hierarchy

- [ ] The screen has a clear primary purpose.
- [ ] Visual hierarchy remains understandable without decorative effects.
- [ ] The surface is recognisably part of the product rather than an unchanged framework default.
- [ ] Brand expression is controlled rather than ubiquitous.
- [ ] Marketing, app, and email treatments retain common identity signals.

### Typography

- [ ] Typography uses canonical semantic roles.
- [ ] Heading hierarchy reflects content hierarchy.
- [ ] Weight is used deliberately.
- [ ] Body text remains comfortably readable.
- [ ] Technical or numeric typography is appropriate to the data.

### Colour

- [ ] Components use semantic tokens instead of raw palette values.
- [ ] Brand colour has a controlled purpose.
- [ ] Status colours have stable meanings.
- [ ] Meaning never depends on colour alone.
- [ ] Light and dark modes preserve the same semantics.

### Spacing and geometry

- [ ] Spacing resolves to canonical tokens.
- [ ] Related content is visually grouped correctly.
- [ ] Radius usage is coherent.
- [ ] Cards and containers exist for semantic reasons.
- [ ] Density suits the task.

### Materials and elevation

- [ ] Opaque surfaces are the default for operational content.
- [ ] Translucency has a specific reason.
- [ ] Glass does not reduce comprehension or contrast.
- [ ] Elevation corresponds to actual layering.
- [ ] Shadows are restrained and tokenised.

### Imagery and illustration

- [ ] Imagery has a communicative purpose.
- [ ] Image treatment is consistent with the brand system.
- [ ] Screenshots contain no sensitive information.
- [ ] Illustration uses the approved visual language.
- [ ] Decorative imagery does not compete with operational content.

### Motion

- [ ] Motion communicates state, relationship, or causality.
- [ ] Routine interactions remain fast.
- [ ] Decorative movement is limited.
- [ ] Reduced-motion preferences are supported.
- [ ] Removing animation does not remove meaning.

### Components and patterns

- [ ] The implementation begins with canonical shadcn/ui-based components.
- [ ] Component variants are approved and reusable.
- [ ] Feature code does not create a parallel aesthetic system.
- [ ] The correct interaction Pattern was selected before styling.
- [ ] Components retain accessible primitive behaviour.

### Forms and application state

- [ ] Labels, help, validation, and errors use canonical form treatment.
- [ ] Loading, empty, error, and success are visually distinct.
- [ ] Visual states correspond to real application/API states.
- [ ] Success is not shown prematurely.
- [ ] Domain states are mapped consistently to visual semantics.

### Accessibility and security

- [ ] Contrast meets the Accessibility standard.
- [ ] Focus remains clearly visible.
- [ ] Critical status is not colour-only.
- [ ] Security-relevant actions and consequences are visually unambiguous.
- [ ] No visual dark pattern is present.
- [ ] Sensitive content follows Security requirements.

### Cross-channel behaviour

- [ ] Marketing may be more expressive without redefining the core identity.
- [ ] Application UI remains efficient for repeated use.
- [ ] Email retains meaning without advanced CSS, animation, or images.
- [ ] Light, dark, mobile, desktop, and reduced-motion states have been reviewed.
- [ ] Optional visual effects can fail gracefully.

---

# 5. Canonical summary

The product MUST present a **precise, calm, contemporary, purposeful, and recognisable** visual identity.

Aesthetic decisions MUST begin with semantic intent and MUST be encoded through the canonical Design Token, Component, Pattern, and Layout systems.

**Typography MUST create hierarchy before decoration.**

**Colour MUST communicate semantics before emotion.**

**Whitespace MUST communicate structure rather than emptiness.**

**Opaque materials MUST be the operational default; glass and translucency MUST remain deliberate exceptions.**

**Elevation MUST represent layering rather than decoration.**

**Motion MUST explain change rather than attract attention.**

**Dark mode MUST be designed, not inverted.**

**Marketing MAY be expressive; application UI MUST remain task-oriented; email MUST preserve identity under constrained rendering.**

**shadcn/ui MUST provide the component baseline, but framework defaults MUST NOT become the product's visual identity.**

**Semantic Design Tokens MUST own reusable aesthetic values. Feature code MUST NOT create an independent visual language.**

**Accessibility, Security, domain correctness, API truth, State Management, and Forms & Validation requirements MUST take precedence over aesthetic preference.**

**Brand distinctiveness SHOULD emerge from a coherent combination of typography, colour, geometry, imagery, spacing, material, and motion—not from excessive effects or one-off decoration.**

The Gold Standard is achieved when the same product identity remains recognisable across **marketing, application, documentation, and email**, while each channel uses only the degree of visual expression appropriate to its purpose.

The 2026 shadcn-specific baseline above reflects the current project direction: Base UI is the default for new shadcn/ui projects, Radix remains supported, and semantic CSS-variable theming remains the recommended approach. citeturn360057search0turn360057search1turn360057search2 The reduced-motion requirements are also consistent with WCAG 2.2's treatment of interaction-triggered motion. citeturn360057search9


<!-- ===== states-catalogue | design | standards/design/09-states-catalogue.md ===== -->

Below is the canonical catalogue, structured for direct inclusion in the standards corpus.

# Empty, Loading and Error States Catalogue — Gold Standard 2026

**Canonical placement:** Components → States Catalogue → Patterns → Content & UX Writing  
**Status:** Canonical  
**Applies to:** Web applications, responsive web interfaces, authenticated products, administrative interfaces, dashboards, data-heavy workflows, forms, tables, dialogs, asynchronous actions, background synchronization, and offline-capable experiences  
**Component baseline:** shadcn/ui  
**Normative terms:** MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, MAY

---

# 1. Purpose

## 1.1 Objective

This standard defines the canonical UX, component, state-management, accessibility, layout, recovery, and content-writing requirements for:

1. loading states;
2. skeleton screens;
3. spinners;
4. determinate and indeterminate progress;
5. first-run empty states;
6. no-results states;
7. no-permission states;
8. intentionally cleared states;
9. inline errors;
10. page-level errors;
11. partial failures;
12. retry and recovery;
13. offline states;
14. degraded and stale-data states; and
15. accessible state announcements.

The purpose of a state UI is not merely to report that data is absent or an operation has failed. State UI MUST preserve the user's mental model of the application, explain what is happening at the correct scope, preserve recoverable work, expose meaningful recovery actions, and avoid representing one domain condition as another.

A loading state MUST NOT masquerade as an empty state. An authorization failure MUST NOT masquerade as missing data. A partial failure MUST NOT collapse an otherwise usable page. A background refresh MUST NOT regress usable content to a blocking loader.

## 1.2 Relationship to other standards

This catalogue MUST be implemented consistently with:

- **Security:** authorization boundaries, information disclosure, session expiry, safe error messaging, protected resource existence, sensitive caching, telemetry, and audit requirements;
- **Data & Database:** source-of-truth semantics, stale data, optimistic state, consistency, conflict handling, timestamps, and partial availability;
- **API:** HTTP semantics, error contracts, retryability, `Retry-After`, validation responses, idempotency, partial responses, and correlation identifiers;
- **State Management:** explicit state machines, derived state, server state versus client state, stale-while-revalidate behavior, cache retention, and mutation lifecycle;
- **Forms & Validation:** field errors, form-level summaries, preservation of entered values, async validation, submission state, and server-side validation;
- **Accessibility:** WCAG 2.2, keyboard operation, logical focus management, status messages, live regions, reduced motion, semantic progress, and non-color state communication;
- **Design Tokens:** semantic colors, spacing, typography, motion, borders, opacity, focus rings, icon sizing, and elevation;
- **Component standards:** Button, Alert, Empty, Skeleton, Spinner, Progress, Card, Table, Dialog, AlertDialog, and notification primitives;
- **Pattern standards:** page shells, tables, filters, search, CRUD workflows, forms, upload/download, authentication, permissions, and asynchronous background jobs; and
- **Content & UX Writing:** plain language, action-oriented recovery copy, specificity, consistent terminology, and prohibition on developer-facing implementation details.

WCAG 2.2 requires status messages such as loading, results, progress, and errors to be programmatically available to assistive technology without requiring an unnecessary focus change. `role="status"` provides a polite live-region mechanism; assertive alerts are intended for important, time-sensitive conditions and MUST therefore be used selectively. citeturn709403search2turn709403search4turn820345search6

## 1.3 shadcn/ui baseline

The canonical component baseline uses the current shadcn/ui primitives:

| State need | Baseline primitive |
|---|---|
| Shape-preserving loading | `Skeleton` |
| Small indeterminate activity | `Spinner` |
| Measurable or long-running progress | `Progress` |
| Empty/no-results/no-access presentation | `Empty` composition |
| In-flow warning or error | `Alert` |
| User decision that must interrupt work | `AlertDialog` |
| Recovery/action | `Button` |
| Structured state container | `Card`, page section, table region, dialog region |
| Transient supplementary feedback | Product notification/toast primitive |

shadcn/ui currently provides dedicated Skeleton, Spinner, Progress, Empty, Alert, and AlertDialog components; `Empty` is explicitly compositional with media, title, description, and content/action regions. citeturn709403search3turn709403search9turn820345search0turn820345search1turn820345search8

Applications MAY wrap these primitives in product-specific state components, but wrappers MUST preserve the accessibility contract and visual/token conventions of the canonical primitives.

---

# 2. Rules

## 2.1 Canonical state model

Applications MUST model asynchronous state explicitly. A single `isLoading` boolean is insufficient for any workflow that can distinguish initial loading, refreshing, success, empty success, failure, retry, offline operation, or stale data.

At minimum, data-driven interfaces MUST be able to represent:

```text
idle
pending
success:data
success:empty
error
```

Where applicable, the state model SHOULD additionally represent orthogonal conditions such as:

```text
refreshing
retrying
stale
offline
degraded
queued
optimistic
conflicted
```

The following distinctions are mandatory:

| Condition | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `pending` | No authoritative result for the current request is available yet |
| `success:data` | Request succeeded and meaningful content exists |
| `success:empty` | Request succeeded and the authoritative result is legitimately empty |
| `error` | The requested operation failed |
| `refreshing` | Existing usable content remains available while a new version is fetched |
| `stale` | Existing content is usable but may no longer represent the newest source state |
| `offline` | Required network connectivity is unavailable |
| `degraded` | Some dependency or capability is unavailable while the product remains partly usable |
| `queued` | A write has been accepted locally for later synchronization |
| `conflicted` | A write cannot safely complete because source state changed |

**Empty MUST only be entered after a successful authoritative result.**

A `401`, `403`, network failure, parse failure, timeout, or server failure MUST NOT produce a generic "No data" state.

Valid cached data MUST NOT be replaced by an initial-loading skeleton merely because a background refetch has started.

---

## 2.2 State scope

Every state MUST be rendered at the smallest scope capable of accurately representing the condition.

Examples:

- a failed table widget MUST show a table-level error rather than replacing the page;
- a failed profile avatar MAY show a media-level fallback;
- a failed page resource MAY use a page-level error;
- a failed form field MUST use a field-level error;
- a background synchronization problem SHOULD use a persistent but non-blocking status treatment;
- an application-wide outage MAY use a global degraded-service state.

A child failure MUST NOT unnecessarily destroy healthy parent content.

State scope MUST remain stable between loading, success, empty, and failure wherever practical so layout does not jump unpredictably.

---

## 2.3 Loading-state selection

The loading indicator MUST communicate the type and scope of waiting.

### 2.3.1 Selection rule

Use:

| Situation | Required pattern |
|---|---|
| Final content structure is known | Skeleton |
| Small atomic action with unknown duration | Spinner |
| Progress is meaningfully measurable | Determinate Progress |
| Long-running process without measurable progress | Indeterminate Progress plus status copy |
| Existing data is being refreshed | Preserve data; use subtle refresh state |
| Button-triggered mutation | Inline spinner/progress within triggering control |
| Page shell or navigation already exists | Preserve shell; load content region only |

A blank page plus centered spinner SHOULD NOT be used when the page structure is known.

Skeletons SHOULD be preferred for initial loading of cards, tables, lists, forms, and detail layouts because they preserve expected geometry.

Spinners SHOULD be reserved for compact or atomic operations where reproducing final geometry provides no value.

---

## 2.4 Loading timing

Loading indicators MUST be designed to minimize visual flashing without artificially delaying completed content.

Canonical timing defaults are:

| Duration | Treatment |
|---|---|
| `< 200 ms` | SHOULD normally show no loading indicator |
| `200 ms–1 s` | Local skeleton or compact spinner MAY appear |
| `> 1 s` | Loading purpose SHOULD be explicit in visible or accessible copy |
| `> 10 s` | The experience SHOULD expose meaningful progress, stage, explanation, cancellation, or continued-background behavior where technically possible |

The application MAY tune these thresholds using shared state/motion tokens, but different features MUST NOT invent arbitrary per-screen delays.

The product MUST NOT intentionally delay completed content merely to satisfy a minimum spinner duration.

Animation SHOULD appear after a short loading-delay token instead of immediately flashing on every fast request.

---

## 2.5 Skeleton screens

### 2.5.1 Anatomy

A skeleton MAY contain:

1. media placeholder;
2. title/text placeholders;
3. metadata placeholders;
4. control placeholders where the controls themselves cannot yet be used; and
5. repeating rows or cards representative of the expected content.

Skeletons MUST approximate the final layout sufficiently to reserve space and minimize cumulative layout shift.

### 2.5.2 Rules

Skeletons MUST:

- match the major geometry of the content being loaded;
- use Design Token spacing, radius, surface, and animation values;
- be visually subordinate to actual content;
- respect reduced-motion preferences;
- be non-interactive; and
- be hidden from the accessibility tree unless a specific semantic need requires otherwise.

The loading **region**, not every skeleton element, SHOULD carry the meaningful accessible loading state.

The parent region SHOULD use `aria-busy="true"` while materially updating and return to `false` when settled.

Skeletons MUST NOT:

- expose fake text to screen readers;
- imitate fully readable content;
- show controls that appear actionable;
- use random widths on every render;
- animate aggressively;
- replace usable cached data during routine refetch;
- display dozens of placeholder rows solely because the eventual collection could be large; or
- duplicate the entire application chrome when only one content region is loading.

### 2.5.3 Table skeletons

Table skeletons SHOULD preserve:

- column positions;
- header geometry when headers are already known;
- approximate row height;
- selection/action-column positions; and
- container height for the expected first viewport.

Table headers that are static SHOULD remain real rather than becoming skeletons.

---

## 2.6 Spinners

### 2.6.1 Anatomy

A spinner consists of:

1. animated visual indicator;
2. accessible label when it is the semantic loading indicator; and
3. optional visible activity text.

The shadcn/ui Spinner baseline exposes a loading status and label by default. citeturn709403search0

### 2.6.2 Rules

A semantic spinner MUST describe what is loading when "Loading" alone would be ambiguous.

Preferred labels include:

- "Loading projects";
- "Saving changes";
- "Checking availability";
- "Uploading file"; and
- "Refreshing results".

Multiple decorative spinners inside one semantic loading scope MUST NOT each be announced.

When a spinner is embedded in a button:

- the button MUST retain an accessible name;
- the spinner SHOULD be decorative if the button label already communicates the pending action;
- repeated activation MUST be prevented when duplicate execution is unsafe;
- focus MUST remain on the initiating control unless navigation or another explicit focus-management pattern requires otherwise; and
- the control SHOULD preserve its width to prevent layout movement.

Preferred button labels retain action context:

```text
Saving…
Uploading…
Deleting…
Sending…
```

Avoid replacing a descriptive button label with only "Loading…".

---

## 2.7 Progress indicators

Progress MUST be used when progress itself helps users understand or control a process.

### 2.7.1 Determinate progress

Use determinate progress when the application knows a meaningful completion ratio.

Examples:

- file upload;
- import;
- export generation with measurable stages;
- bulk processing;
- onboarding sequence; or
- installation/migration.

Determinate progress MUST expose its current value programmatically. A progress bar with a known value SHOULD show visible percentage or stage information for longer operations.

### 2.7.2 Indeterminate progress

Use indeterminate progress when completion cannot be meaningfully estimated.

An indeterminate progress bar MUST NOT fabricate a percentage.

For ARIA `progressbar`, `aria-valuenow` is expected for determinate progress and omitted for indeterminate progress. citeturn709403search5

### 2.7.3 Long-running processes

A process likely to exceed approximately 10 seconds SHOULD communicate at least one of:

- percentage;
- completed/total count;
- current stage;
- estimated scope;
- whether leaving the page is safe;
- whether processing continues in the background; or
- cancellation capability.

Copy MUST NOT claim an estimated completion time unless the estimate is backed by product logic that is sufficiently reliable.

"99%" MUST NOT be held indefinitely when the underlying job has no truthful mapping to 99%.

---

## 2.8 Background refresh

Existing valid data MUST remain visible during non-destructive refetch unless displaying it would be unsafe or misleading.

A background refresh SHOULD use one of:

- a subtle spinner adjacent to a refresh action;
- "Refreshing…" status copy;
- a stale timestamp;
- a lightweight progress treatment; or
- no visible loading indication for sufficiently fast automatic refresh.

The page MUST NOT regress to full skeletons solely because cached content is being validated.

Actions dependent on known-stale information SHOULD be disabled or qualified when using that information could cause an unsafe operation.

---

## 2.9 Empty states — general

An empty state represents a **successful absence of applicable content**.

Canonical anatomy is:

```text
Empty
├── Optional media/icon
├── Title
├── Description
├── Primary action, when applicable
├── Secondary action/help, when applicable
└── Optional contextual metadata
```

This aligns with the shadcn/ui `Empty` composition of `EmptyMedia`, `EmptyTitle`, `EmptyDescription`, and `EmptyContent`. citeturn709403search3

Empty states MUST:

- explain why the region is empty when that reason is actionable or meaningful;
- distinguish system state from user action;
- present the most likely next step;
- avoid developer terminology such as "null", "zero rows", or "API returned no records"; and
- occupy the same semantic region the content would normally occupy.

Empty states MUST NOT be used for failed requests.

---

## 2.10 First-run empty states

A first-run state occurs when the user has not yet created or acquired content.

### Anatomy

1. optional contextual icon or illustration;
2. outcome-oriented title;
3. short explanation of what belongs here;
4. one clear primary action;
5. optional secondary path such as import, documentation, or example data.

### Copy pattern

```text
{No items yet}

{Explain what the item enables or what will appear here.}

[Primary creation action]
[Optional secondary action]
```

Preferred:

```text
No projects yet

Create a project to organize your environments, members, and deployments.

[Create project]
[Import project]
```

Avoid:

```text
Nothing here!
Get started now!!!
```

First-run copy SHOULD communicate value before implementation detail.

The primary action SHOULD correspond directly to the action that resolves the empty state.

---

## 2.11 No-results states

A no-results state occurs when content exists in principle but the current search, filter, query, or scope returned none.

No-results states MUST preserve the controls that produced the result.

The state SHOULD identify the active constraint when practical.

### Copy pattern

```text
No {items} match your {search/filters}

Try changing your search or clearing one or more filters.

[Clear filters]
```

For search:

```text
No results for “{query}”

Check the spelling or try a different search.

[Clear search]
```

If filters are active, **Clear filters** SHOULD normally be the primary recovery action.

"Create new" SHOULD NOT be the default recovery for a filtered no-results state unless creating new content is genuinely likely to satisfy the user's intent.

Search terms entered by the user MUST NOT be discarded merely because there are no results.

---

## 2.12 No-permission states

No-permission is an authorization state, not an ordinary empty state.

It MAY use the visual `Empty` composition, but the state semantics and copy MUST identify an access restriction.

### Copy pattern

```text
You don't have access to {resource}

Ask an administrator for access, or return to {safe destination}.

[Request access]
[Go back]
```

Where product policy requires existence-hiding, the interface MUST use the approved Security standard response instead of revealing that a protected resource exists.

The interface MUST NOT expose:

- hidden resource metadata;
- owner identity when unauthorized;
- protected object names;
- access-policy internals;
- role mappings;
- raw permission IDs; or
- backend authorization details.

`403 Forbidden` SHOULD map to an access state where existence may safely be disclosed.

A security-approved `404 Not Found` MAY intentionally represent both absent and undisclosed resources.

Authentication expiry (`401`) MUST normally offer re-authentication rather than present "No permission".

---

## 2.13 Cleared or completed empty states

A cleared state represents an intentionally empty collection, completed queue, cleared inbox, empty trash, or other expected zero state after user activity.

This state SHOULD be lightweight and reassuring.

Examples:

```text
You're all caught up
There are no notifications requiring your attention.
```

```text
Trash is empty
Deleted items will appear here.
```

```text
No archived projects
Projects you archive will appear here.
```

A cleared state SHOULD NOT invent a call to action when no next action is necessary.

Celebratory treatment MAY be used for genuinely meaningful completion, but routine zero states MUST NOT become visually distracting.

---

## 2.14 Error-state classification

Errors MUST be classified by scope and recoverability.

The canonical hierarchy is:

| Type | Use when |
|---|---|
| Field error | One input is invalid |
| Form/action error | Submission or mutation failed |
| Inline/region error | One component or bounded region failed |
| Partial error | Some independent content failed while other content remains usable |
| Page-level error | Primary page resource cannot be used |
| Application/dependency error | Broad service capability is unavailable |

The UI MUST NOT escalate a local error to page-level unless the failure invalidates the page's primary purpose.

---

## 2.15 Inline errors

Inline errors belong immediately adjacent to the failing operation or region.

Examples:

- table widget failed to refresh;
- chart dependency failed;
- attachment upload failed;
- async selector could not retrieve options;
- field validation failed.

### Anatomy

1. error indicator;
2. concise description;
3. recovery action when recovery is available;
4. optional safe diagnostic reference.

### Copy pattern

```text
We couldn't load {content}.

[Try again]
```

For retained data:

```text
We couldn't refresh this data.
Showing the last available version from {time}.

[Try again]
```

For a mutation:

```text
We couldn't save your changes.
Your edits are still here.

[Try again]
```

Inline errors MUST NOT rely solely on a toast if the affected region remains in an error state.

---

## 2.16 Page-level errors

A page-level error is appropriate when the page's primary resource cannot be loaded and no meaningful page content can be used.

The global application shell SHOULD remain available when safe.

### Anatomy

1. clear page/state heading;
2. brief explanation;
3. primary recovery action;
4. secondary navigation action;
5. support or reference information only when useful.

### Copy pattern

```text
We couldn't load {resource}

Something went wrong while loading this page.

[Try again]
[Go back]
```

Where the reason is known and user-actionable, copy SHOULD be more specific:

```text
This link has expired

Request a new link to continue.

[Request new link]
```

Page-level errors MUST NOT expose stack traces, exception class names, SQL errors, internal service names, source paths, credentials, secrets, or infrastructure topology.

A correlation or support reference MAY be shown if it is safe for end-user disclosure.

---

## 2.17 Partial failures

Independent content SHOULD fail independently.

If a dashboard contains six widgets and one fails, the five healthy widgets MUST remain available unless the failed widget makes them materially misleading.

A partial error SHOULD:

- remain inside the affected region;
- identify only the failed capability;
- permit local retry;
- retain stale data when appropriate;
- expose a stale timestamp where relevant; and
- avoid presenting the entire page as unavailable.

Example:

```text
Revenue data is temporarily unavailable

Other dashboard data is still current.

[Retry]
```

If stale data remains visible:

```text
Couldn't refresh revenue
Showing data last updated at 10:42 AM.

[Try again]
```

---

## 2.18 Form submission failures

Form errors MUST comply with the Forms & Validation standard.

On failed submission:

- entered values MUST remain unless clearing them is explicitly required for security;
- invalid fields MUST identify their errors programmatically;
- a form-level summary SHOULD be provided for multiple errors;
- focus SHOULD follow the Forms standard rather than move unpredictably;
- server-side validation MUST be mapped to the relevant field where possible;
- general server failures MUST NOT be falsely represented as field validation;
- the submit control MUST return from pending to usable state if retry is possible.

Preferred mutation error:

```text
We couldn't save your changes.
Review the highlighted fields and try again.
```

For non-validation failures:

```text
We couldn't save your changes.
Your edits are still here. Try again.
```

---

## 2.19 API-to-UX error mapping

Frontend state MUST preserve meaningful API semantics.

Canonical mapping SHOULD follow:

| API condition | UX treatment |
|---|---|
| `400` malformed request | Product error or form error depending contract |
| `401` unauthenticated/session expired | Re-authentication flow |
| `403` forbidden | No-permission state if disclosure is allowed |
| `404` resource absent | Not-found state or security-preserving equivalent |
| `409` conflict | Conflict/review state; preserve user work |
| `422` semantic validation | Field/form validation |
| `429` rate limited | Retry guidance; honor server retry information |
| `5xx` | Recoverable service error where appropriate |
| network failure | Offline/connectivity state or generic network error |
| timeout | Retryable timeout state when operation is safe to repeat |

Applications MUST consume the canonical API error envelope rather than derive UX from arbitrary backend strings.

Raw API messages MUST NOT be shown directly unless they are explicitly authored, localized, security-reviewed, and designated as end-user-safe.

---

## 2.20 Retry rules

Retry MUST be based on operation semantics, not merely the existence of an error.

### Automatic retry

Automatic retry MAY be used for transient, idempotent reads.

Automatic retry SHOULD:

- use bounded exponential backoff;
- include jitter where appropriate;
- honor `Retry-After`;
- stop after the shared retry-policy maximum;
- terminate when the request is no longer relevant; and
- avoid duplicate status announcements.

Automatic retry MUST NOT normally be used for:

- validation failures;
- permission failures;
- authentication failures;
- confirmed not-found responses;
- business-rule conflicts;
- destructive mutations; or
- writes without idempotency guarantees.

### User-triggered retry

A visible **Try again** action MUST retry the failing scope only.

Retry MUST NOT reset unrelated state.

Retry MUST NOT discard entered form data.

Repeated retry failure SHOULD eventually provide an alternative recovery path where one exists, such as:

- reload;
- reconnect;
- return;
- save draft;
- download work;
- contact support; or
- continue with available data.

The application MUST avoid infinite retry loops.

---

## 2.21 Mutation recovery and idempotency

Write operations require stronger safeguards than reads.

A mutation MAY be automatically retried only when its API contract makes duplicate execution safe, for example through:

- idempotency keys;
- idempotent method semantics;
- transaction identifiers; or
- confirmed deduplication behavior.

The UI MUST NOT silently retry operations capable of:

- charging money twice;
- creating duplicate records;
- sending duplicate messages;
- triggering multiple approvals;
- deleting additional content; or
- invoking external side effects without idempotency protection.

When the final mutation outcome is uncertain, the interface SHOULD use an explicit uncertainty state such as:

```text
We couldn't confirm whether the payment completed.

Check the payment status before trying again.
```

It MUST NOT invite immediate repetition when duplicate side effects are possible.

---

## 2.22 Conflict recovery

A `409` or equivalent data conflict MUST preserve user work where technically possible.

Conflict copy SHOULD state:

1. what changed;
2. whether local edits are preserved;
3. what the user must decide next.

Example:

```text
This record changed while you were editing

Your edits are still available. Review the latest version before saving again.

[Review changes]
```

"Something went wrong" SHOULD NOT be used when the application knows the issue is a concurrency conflict.

---

## 2.23 Offline states

Offline is a capability state, not merely a visual banner.

The application MUST distinguish between:

- confirmed network request failure;
- browser/network hints;
- service outage;
- authentication failure; and
- application-specific API failure.

Browser connectivity signals SHOULD be treated as hints rather than the sole proof that a service is reachable.

### Offline with cached data

Preferred:

```text
You're offline

Showing saved data from {time}. Some actions are unavailable until you're back online.
```

The UI MUST identify stale or cached data when freshness materially affects decisions.

### Offline without cached data

Preferred:

```text
You're offline

Connect to the internet to load {content}.

[Try again]
```

### Offline writes

Every write-capable feature MUST explicitly choose one of three policies:

1. **Unavailable offline** — action disabled with explanation;
2. **Local draft** — data saved locally but not submitted;
3. **Queued sync** — operation queued for server synchronization.

The UI MUST NOT claim "Saved" when the operation is only stored locally unless the copy explicitly distinguishes local and server persistence.

Preferred queued copy:

```text
Saved on this device
We'll sync your changes when you're back online.
```

Sensitive information MUST NOT be persisted for offline use unless permitted by the Security and Data standards.

---

## 2.24 Reconnection

When connectivity returns, the application SHOULD recover without forcing a full reload where safe.

A reconnection state MAY announce:

```text
Back online
Refreshing your data.
```

Successful restoration SHOULD be communicated once:

```text
You're back online
Data is up to date.
```

The application MUST NOT repeatedly announce connectivity flapping if doing so creates excessive interruption.

Queued writes MUST expose unresolved conflicts or permanent failures rather than silently disappearing from the queue.

---

## 2.25 Degraded states

A degraded state occurs when the product remains usable but a capability, dependency, or data source is unavailable or delayed.

Examples:

- reporting unavailable while CRUD remains operational;
- search unavailable while direct navigation works;
- attachment service unavailable while form submission remains possible;
- one data source delayed while other sources are current;
- system operating read-only.

A degraded state MUST state the capability impact, not merely "Service degraded."

Preferred:

```text
File uploads are temporarily unavailable

You can continue editing and save the record without attachments.
```

or:

```text
Read-only mode

You can view current data, but changes cannot be saved right now.
```

Global degraded banners SHOULD remain persistent while the limitation is active and SHOULD disappear when the capability is restored.

Affected controls MAY be disabled, but the reason MUST be available to the user.

---

## 2.26 Stale data

Stale data MAY remain visible when it is safer and more useful than displaying no data.

Stale content MUST be identified when freshness materially affects user decisions.

Use specific timestamps where useful:

```text
Last updated 10:42 AM
```

or:

```text
Showing data from 21 September 2026
```

Avoid vague copy such as:

```text
Data may be old.
```

Staleness SHOULD be represented independently from error state so usable content remains available.

---

## 2.27 Accessible loading announcements

Dynamic state changes MUST satisfy the Accessibility standard and WCAG status-message requirements. citeturn709403search2turn709403search6

### Polite status

Use a `role="status"` or equivalent polite live region for non-critical changes such as:

- "Loading projects";
- "Searching";
- "18 results";
- "No results";
- "Saved";
- "Back online";
- "Retrying"; or
- completion of a background operation.

A status region SHOULD exist before its content changes when cross-assistive-technology reliability requires it.

### Assertive alert

Use `role="alert"` or equivalent assertive announcement only for important, time-sensitive errors or warnings requiring prompt awareness.

Routine loading messages MUST NOT use assertive announcements.

WAI-ARIA treats `alert` as an assertive live-region mechanism and advises that alerts should not move keyboard focus. citeturn820345search2turn820345search7

### De-duplication

The application MUST NOT announce:

- every skeleton element;
- every animated frame;
- every percentage increment;
- every automatic retry;
- both a spinner and identical live-region message independently.

Announcements SHOULD represent meaningful transitions rather than implementation events.

---

## 2.28 Accessible progress

Determinate progress MUST expose:

- progress semantics;
- an accessible name; and
- the current value.

For lengthy operations, visible textual progress SHOULD accompany visual progress.

For example:

```text
Uploading report.pdf — 64%
```

Assistive announcements SHOULD be throttled to meaningful increments rather than emitting every percentage change.

For long-running upload or processing progress, a polite live region MAY communicate milestone updates; W3C specifically documents live regions as a technique for communicating changing progress. citeturn709403search7

---

## 2.29 Focus management

Inline loading, success, warning, empty, and error states MUST NOT steal focus merely because they appear.

Focus MUST remain logically associated with the user's current operation.

Examples:

- a button retry keeps focus on the retry/action control where practical;
- an inline error does not move focus from an unrelated field;
- a background refresh does not move focus;
- an offline banner does not capture focus;
- a toast does not capture focus.

Page navigation and route-level state changes MUST follow the application's page-focus standard.

If an error requires immediate user action and is presented through a true modal decision, an accessible Dialog or AlertDialog pattern MUST be used.

Focus order MUST preserve meaning and operability. citeturn820345search9

---

## 2.30 Motion and animation

All loading animation MUST comply with the Design Tokens and Accessibility standards.

Skeleton shimmer, pulsing, rotating indicators, and progress animation SHOULD respect `prefers-reduced-motion`.

Reduced-motion mode MAY:

- remove shimmer;
- reduce pulse amplitude;
- use a static placeholder;
- use a low-motion spinner; or
- update progress without decorative interpolation.

Functionality and state comprehension MUST NOT depend on motion.

---

## 2.31 Color and iconography

Status meaning MUST NOT rely on color alone.

Error, warning, offline, degraded, loading, and success states SHOULD combine appropriate combinations of:

- text;
- iconography;
- shape;
- semantic component treatment; and
- programmatic semantics.

All colors MUST come from semantic Design Tokens.

Features MUST NOT introduce arbitrary red, amber, green, or gray values specifically for state UI.

Icons MUST use the product icon system and SHOULD be decorative when the adjacent text communicates equivalent meaning.

---

## 2.32 Layout rules

State layout MUST reflect its scope.

### Full-region states

When an Empty or page-level Error replaces an entire content region:

- content MAY be visually centered;
- the text column SHOULD remain compact;
- primary and secondary actions MUST be grouped with the state;
- the state MUST occupy sufficient region height to read as belonging to that region; and
- global navigation or shell UI SHOULD remain stable.

The content column SHOULD generally not exceed a comfortable reading width of approximately 28–32rem unless the Pattern standard specifies otherwise.

### Inline states

Inline and partial states SHOULD:

- align with surrounding content;
- remain left-aligned in dense data interfaces;
- use local spacing tokens;
- avoid oversized illustration treatment; and
- keep recovery actions near the failure.

### Tables and lists

A table-level Empty/Error MUST remain within the table's semantic/container boundary and MUST NOT appear as an unrelated floating card below the table.

Column headers and filters SHOULD remain visible when they remain meaningful.

### Dialogs and drawers

Loading inside an open Dialog or Sheet MUST remain inside the surface. The underlying page MUST NOT independently display the same operation state.

---

## 2.33 Action hierarchy

Each state SHOULD have no more than one visually dominant recovery action.

The primary action MUST represent the most likely next successful step.

Examples:

| State | Primary action |
|---|---|
| First run | Create |
| No results | Clear filters / modify search |
| No permission | Request access, where supported |
| Inline failure | Try again |
| Authentication expired | Sign in again |
| Conflict | Review changes |
| Offline | Try again after reconnection |
| Page failure | Try again |
| Irrecoverable removed resource | Return to parent/list |

Secondary actions SHOULD use lower emphasis.

A state MUST NOT present several equally prominent actions and force the user to diagnose the product's recovery strategy.

---

## 2.34 Copy principles

State copy MUST be:

- specific;
- concise;
- user-oriented;
- truthful;
- action-oriented where recovery exists;
- free from internal implementation terminology; and
- consistent with domain nouns used elsewhere in the product.

Copy SHOULD answer, where relevant:

1. What happened?
2. What remains safe or available?
3. What can the user do next?

### Loading

Preferred:

```text
Loading invoices…
Refreshing results…
Saving changes…
Uploading report.pdf — 64%
```

Avoid:

```text
Processing request…
Please wait…
Fetching API data…
Loading object…
```

"Please wait" SHOULD be omitted unless waiting itself carries a meaningful restriction.

### Errors

Preferred:

```text
We couldn't load invoices.
Try again.
```

Preferred where user work is safe:

```text
We couldn't save your changes.
Your edits are still here.
```

Avoid:

```text
Error!
Request failed.
Unexpected exception.
Something bad happened.
```

"Something went wrong" MAY be used only when no more useful user-safe diagnosis exists.

### Permissions

Preferred:

```text
You don't have access to this report.
```

Avoid:

```text
403 Forbidden.
Insufficient ACL privileges.
Authorization failure.
```

### No results

Preferred:

```text
No invoices match these filters.
```

Avoid:

```text
No data.
Nothing found.
0 records returned.
```

### Offline

Preferred:

```text
You're offline.
Showing saved data from 10:42 AM.
```

Avoid:

```text
Network Error 0.
Connection exception.
```

---

## 2.35 Error-detail disclosure

User-facing error copy MUST be separated from diagnostic detail.

Diagnostic systems MAY capture:

- HTTP status;
- API error code;
- service identifier;
- request/correlation ID;
- stack trace;
- retry count;
- connectivity condition; and
- technical context.

User-facing surfaces MUST only expose fields explicitly approved for display.

Secrets, tokens, database queries, internal file paths, credentials, PII, or sensitive authorization information MUST NOT appear in UI error messages, analytics events, or client logs contrary to Security policy.

---

## 2.36 Observability

Production state transitions SHOULD emit sufficient telemetry to diagnose systematic UX failures.

Recommended signals include:

- request duration;
- loader duration;
- error category;
- retry count;
- retry outcome;
- rate-limit occurrence;
- offline/online transitions;
- stale-data age;
- partial-failure rate;
- abandonment after error;
- repeated mutation attempts; and
- correlation IDs.

Telemetry MUST comply with Privacy, Security, and Observability standards.

UI copy itself SHOULD NOT be treated as the canonical machine-readable error code.

---

## 2.37 Component boundaries and reuse

Applications SHOULD provide shared state compositions such as:

```text
<LoadingState />
<EmptyState />
<NoResultsState />
<NoAccessState />
<ErrorState />
<OfflineState />
<DegradedState />
```

Shared components SHOULD standardize anatomy, accessibility, spacing, and action hierarchy while allowing domain-specific copy.

A generic component MUST NOT reduce every state to the same icon, title, description, and retry button when domain semantics differ.

Feature code MUST control domain meaning; shared state components MUST control presentation consistency.

---

## 2.38 Server rendering, hydration, and cached content

When authoritative content is already available from SSR, RSC, prefetch, or cache, the client MUST NOT replace it with a loading skeleton solely because client-side hydration is occurring.

Loading UI SHOULD represent genuine user-visible uncertainty, not framework lifecycle mechanics.

Valid previously rendered content SHOULD remain visible while client state reconnects unless displaying that content violates freshness or security rules.

Hydration mismatches MUST be fixed at the rendering/state layer rather than concealed with unnecessary loading states.

---

## 2.39 Destructive and irreversible operations

Errors related to destructive actions MUST preserve certainty about whether the action occurred.

If deletion definitively failed:

```text
We couldn't delete the project.
Nothing was removed.

[Try again]
```

If outcome is uncertain:

```text
We couldn't confirm whether the project was deleted.

Refresh the project list before trying again.
```

An `AlertDialog` MUST NOT be used simply to display a load error. It is appropriate when the user must make an important modal decision. shadcn/ui defines AlertDialog as an interruptive modal that expects a response. citeturn820345search8

---

## 2.40 Notifications and toasts

Transient notifications MAY supplement state feedback but MUST NOT replace persistent state UI when:

- the error continues to affect the region;
- recovery action remains necessary;
- the user needs the message to understand current content;
