Outside-pointer dismissal MUST be defined explicitly per pattern.

Typical policy:

| Pattern | Outside press |
|---|---|
| Tooltip | Not applicable as a primary dismissal action |
| Hover card | Usually closes when interaction leaves context |
| Popover | SHOULD normally dismiss |
| Standard dialog | MAY dismiss if no work can be lost |
| Form dialog with unsaved edits | SHOULD NOT silently dismiss |
| Alert dialog | SHOULD NOT rely on outside dismissal |
| Destructive confirmation | SHOULD require an explicit decision |
| Drawer/sheet | Depends on task and data-loss semantics |

Outside press MUST NOT:

- confirm destructive actions;
- submit a form;
- imply acceptance.

A backdrop click MUST NEVER mean “Yes”, “Delete”, “Pay”, “Send”, or another consequential affirmative action.

---

## 2.19 Dirty forms and dismissal

An overlay containing edited unsaved state MUST have an explicit dismissal policy.

If accidental dismissal could lose meaningful work:

- outside dismissal SHOULD be prevented;
- Escape SHOULD either be prevented or routed through an appropriate discard-confirmation flow;
- explicit close/cancel SHOULD communicate unsaved-state consequences where necessary.

Small reversible ephemeral inputs MAY dismiss without secondary confirmation.

Confirmation dialogs MUST NOT be added reflexively for trivial changes.

The cost of accidental loss SHOULD determine whether confirmation is warranted.

---

## 2.20 Form submission

A form inside an overlay MUST follow the canonical Forms & Validation and API standards.

Submission state MUST NOT depend on the overlay animation.

On successful submission, the overlay MAY close automatically when closure is an expected consequence.

On validation error, the overlay MUST remain open.

On server error, the overlay SHOULD remain open with entered data preserved unless the server contract makes that impossible.

Closing an overlay MUST NOT falsely imply successful persistence.

---

## 2.21 Pending operations

When a destructive or important operation is pending:

- the initiating action SHOULD communicate pending state;
- duplicate submission MUST be prevented;
- other safe controls MAY remain available.

The entire dialog MUST NOT automatically become inert because one request is pending unless interaction during that request would be unsafe.

An overlay MUST NOT close before a required successful server response merely to create a perception of speed, unless the workflow explicitly uses optimistic updates with valid rollback semantics.

---

## 2.22 Destructive confirmation

A destructive confirmation MUST identify:

- the action;
- the affected object or scope;
- whether the action is reversible;
- the consequence.

Prefer specific labels:

- `Delete project`;
- `Remove 12 members`;
- `Revoke access`;

over generic labels such as:

- `OK`;
- `Confirm`;
- `Yes`.

The safe action SHOULD be visually and structurally clear.

The destructive action MUST use the canonical destructive semantic token.

Colour MUST NOT be the only indication that an action is destructive.

---

## 2.23 Confirmation thresholds

A confirmation overlay SHOULD be used when an action is:

- irreversible;
- expensive to reverse;
- broad in scope;
- security-sensitive;
- likely to cause meaningful data loss.

A confirmation overlay SHOULD NOT be added to every delete-like action when robust undo provides a safer and less interruptive pattern.

For easily reversible operations, an immediate action with Undo MAY be superior.

For difficult-to-reverse actions, explicit pre-commit confirmation SHOULD be preferred.

---

## 2.24 High-risk confirmation

For unusually consequential actions, stronger confirmation MAY be appropriate.

Examples include:

- deleting an organization;
- destroying an environment;
- rotating a critical credential;
- permanently removing regulated records.

Stronger confirmation MAY require:

- typing an entity name;
- reauthentication;
- selecting an explicit acknowledgement.

Such friction MUST have a risk-based justification.

Security theatre MUST NOT be added merely to make an action feel important.

---

## 2.25 Scroll locking

A modal overlay SHOULD lock background document scrolling.

Scroll locking MUST NOT:

- move the page unexpectedly;
- reset the underlying scroll position;
- cause major horizontal layout shift;
- destroy fixed or sticky layout unexpectedly.

When the modal closes, the underlying document SHOULD return to the same scroll position.

The active overlay's own scrollable region MUST remain operable.

---

## 2.26 Non-modal scrolling

Non-modal popovers and hover cards MUST NOT normally lock document scroll.

A non-modal side panel MAY allow document scrolling when that is part of the intended interaction.

The implementation MUST NOT combine:

- visually non-modal presentation;
- arbitrary focus trapping;
- unexpected background scroll locking

without a documented interaction rationale.

shadcn/ui Drawer explicitly distinguishes non-modal operation and focus-trap configurations, reinforcing the need to choose these semantics intentionally. citeturn261455search4turn306571search7

---

## 2.27 Internal scrolling

Overlays taller than the usable viewport MUST provide a bounded internal scrolling strategy.

Header and footer MAY remain sticky where:

- the title must stay visible;
- primary actions must remain reachable.

The overlay MUST NOT place critical actions permanently below an unreachable scroll boundary.

Nested scroll containers SHOULD be minimized.

A scrollable modal inside another scrollable modal SHOULD NOT be created.

---

## 2.28 Mobile viewport behavior

Overlays MUST account for:

- dynamic browser chrome;
- software keyboards;
- safe areas;
- orientation changes;
- viewport resizing.

Critical controls MUST remain reachable when the virtual keyboard is open.

A focused field MUST NOT become permanently obscured by a fixed footer.

Mobile dialogs that become impractically narrow or tall SHOULD adapt to a Drawer, Sheet, or full-screen task where appropriate.

---

## 2.29 Portals

Overlay content SHOULD normally be portaled to a controlled application overlay root when required by the underlying component implementation.

Portals MUST preserve:

- logical accessible relationships;
- focus behaviour;
- form state;
- theme tokens;
- directionality;
- application context.

Portal placement MUST NOT be used to bypass authorization or state boundaries.

Overlay components MUST NOT create arbitrary portal roots per instance without a strong architectural reason.

---

## 2.30 Stacking contexts

Stacking behaviour MUST be deliberate.

Teams MUST understand that CSS `z-index` values are evaluated within stacking contexts.

A numerically large `z-index` inside a lower stacking context does not necessarily appear above a separate higher stacking context.

Unnecessary creation of new stacking contexts SHOULD be avoided on major application containers.

Properties such as transforms, opacity, isolation, positioned elements, and containment SHOULD be reviewed when overlay stacking behaves unexpectedly.

A stacking-context defect MUST NOT be “fixed” solely by increasing a random `z-index`.

---

## 2.31 Canonical z-index policy

Application layering MUST use semantic Design Tokens rather than arbitrary numbers.

The canonical conceptual stack is:

| Token | Default reference value | Purpose |
|---|---:|---|
| `z-base` | `0` | Normal content |
| `z-raised` | `10` | Raised local content |
| `z-sticky` | `100` | Sticky headers and local persistent controls |
| `z-dropdown` | `300` | Menus and select content |
| `z-popover` | `400` | Popovers and hover cards |
| `z-tooltip` | `500` | Tooltips |
| `z-overlay-backdrop` | `800` | Modal backdrop |
| `z-modal` | `900` | Dialog, modal sheet, modal drawer |
| `z-notification` | `1000` | Global notification/toast layer where appropriate |
| `z-critical` | `1100` | Reserved system-critical application surface |

Exact numeric values MAY be remapped centrally.

Feature code MUST NOT depend on the literal numeric gap between tokens.

Feature code MUST NOT introduce arbitrary values such as:

`z-index: 999999`.

---

## 2.32 Local versus global elevation

Not every raised element requires a global z-index token.

Local layering inside a component SHOULD use the smallest local context required.

Global z-index tokens MUST be reserved for surfaces that genuinely participate in application-wide layering.

A decorative icon above a card background MUST NOT consume the same global layer policy as a modal.

---

## 2.33 Backdrops

Modal overlays SHOULD use a backdrop where visual separation improves understanding.

Backdrop colour and opacity MUST come from Design Tokens.

The backdrop MUST indicate that background content is unavailable without reducing foreground contrast below accessibility requirements.

Backdrop styling MUST NOT be the only mechanism making outside content inert.

Blur MAY be used sparingly.

Heavy backdrop blur SHOULD NOT be relied on for privacy because sensitive content may remain perceptible and present in the DOM.

---

## 2.34 Overlay ordering

Only the topmost interactive overlay MUST receive input intended for that overlay stack.

A lower modal MUST NOT expose active controls through the topmost modal.

Visually obscured interactive elements MUST NOT remain keyboard reachable.

The overlay manager SHOULD track stacking order rather than relying on component mount order accidentally.

---

## 2.35 Nested overlays

Nested overlays SHOULD be avoided unless the child surface represents a genuine secondary interaction.

Reasonable compositions include:

- tooltip within dialog;
- select/menu/popover within dialog;
- date picker popover within dialog;
- confirmation alert dialog triggered from an editing dialog;
- nested drawer where the interaction model explicitly supports it.

shadcn/ui currently supports nested Drawer behavior, but capability alone MUST NOT be treated as justification for arbitrary nesting. citeturn261455search4

---

## 2.36 Nested modal limits

A workflow SHOULD normally have only one primary modal task.

Modal-on-modal interaction SHOULD be exceptional.

Three or more simultaneously active modal levels MUST NOT be used in ordinary product workflows.

If the design requires repeated nested dialogs, the workflow SHOULD be redesigned as:

- a multi-step dialog;
- dedicated page;
- internal view transition;
- inline confirmation.

Nested overlays MUST maintain an explicit parent-child relationship.

---

## 2.37 Nested focus restoration

When a child overlay closes:

- focus MUST return to the logical initiating element inside the parent overlay where that element still exists.

Focus MUST NOT return directly to the underlying page while the parent modal remains open.

When the parent subsequently closes, focus MUST follow the parent restoration policy.

Overlay focus management SHOULD therefore behave as a stack.

---

## 2.38 Nested Escape behavior

Escape MUST operate from the top of the overlay stack.

For:

`Dialog → Popover → Tooltip`

an Escape action MUST NOT close the parent Dialog merely because a Tooltip or Popover has active dismissal semantics.

Each layer MUST receive the opportunity to handle dismissal according to its type.

A child refusing dismissal MUST NOT accidentally propagate an Escape that closes its parent unless that propagation is explicitly intended.

---

## 2.39 Menus and select components inside overlays

Menus, comboboxes, select menus, and popovers inside modal overlays MUST remain within the effective modal interaction context.

Their portals MUST NOT create an accessibility escape route from the modal.

Keyboard focus MUST remain logically contained.

The overlay stack MUST account for these child surfaces even when they are rendered elsewhere in the DOM through portals.

---

## 2.40 Tooltip inside modal

Tooltips inside modal overlays MAY visually appear above the modal.

They MUST NOT create another focus trap.

The modal remains the focus-owning surface.

A tooltip z-index MAY exceed the modal content locally without becoming a separate modal layer.

---

## 2.41 Toasts and overlays

Global notifications SHOULD NOT steal focus from an active dialog merely because they visually appear above it.

Toasts MUST NOT obscure critical dialog actions.

A toast MUST NOT be the sole mechanism for reporting a validation error inside an active modal form.

Errors relevant to the modal task SHOULD appear within the task context.

---

## 2.42 Overlay state management

Overlay open state SHOULD have one canonical owner.

State MAY be:

- uncontrolled within a reusable local component;
- controlled by its owning workflow;
- encoded in route state when the overlay represents navigation.

The same overlay MUST NOT have competing independent sources of truth.

Animation state MUST remain subordinate to canonical open/closed state.

---

## 2.43 Route-backed overlays

An overlay MAY be route-backed when:

- it represents navigable content;
- deep linking is useful;
- browser history should represent opening and closing.

Examples include:

- record details;
- media viewer;
- item preview with dedicated canonical route.

Route-backed overlays MUST preserve correct behavior when loaded directly.

A directly loaded route MUST NOT assume an underlying page exists merely because normal navigation usually displays the route as an overlay.

Browser Back SHOULD close a route-backed overlay where opening it added the corresponding history entry.

---

## 2.44 URL state

Ephemeral overlay state SHOULD NOT automatically be placed in the URL.

URL state MAY be appropriate for:

- selected record;
- shareable detail view;
- navigation-level filters.

URL state SHOULD NOT normally represent:

- tooltip visibility;
- hover-card visibility;
- temporary menu state.

Sensitive information MUST NOT be serialized in overlay URLs merely to simplify state restoration.

---

## 2.45 Overlay forms

Forms inside overlays MUST use standard form components and validation behaviour.

Labels, descriptions, required state, field errors, and summary errors MUST remain accessible.

Validation MUST NOT close the overlay.

If validation fails:

- focus SHOULD move according to the canonical Forms & Validation error strategy;
- the invalid field MUST remain reachable;
- the dialog title MUST remain available as context.

Long forms SHOULD generally use a dedicated page or larger sheet rather than a small centered dialog.

---

## 2.46 Data persistence

Closing a presentation surface MUST NOT be confused with deleting or persisting domain state.

An overlay's visual lifecycle MUST remain separate from:

- API request lifecycle;
- transaction completion;
- cache invalidation;
- server persistence.

A close animation completing MUST NEVER be treated as confirmation that a mutation succeeded.

---

## 2.47 Security-sensitive overlays

Security-sensitive overlay content MUST follow ordinary authorization rules.

Opening a dialog MUST NOT fetch or reveal data that the user is unauthorized to access.

Sensitive underlying content MUST NOT remain exposed because a translucent backdrop visually obscures it.

Logout, permission loss, or session expiry MUST close or sanitize restricted overlay content immediately according to Security state.

Animation MUST NOT delay security-state enforcement.

---

## 2.48 Authentication overlays

Authentication or reauthentication MAY occur in an overlay where the security model permits it.

The user MUST be able to distinguish:

- application-controlled authentication UI;
- browser/platform authentication;
- third-party authentication contexts.

Credential entry MUST NOT occur in visually ambiguous hover or popover surfaces.

High-risk authentication SHOULD use a clear, focused dialog or dedicated route.

---

## 2.49 Sensitive confirmation

Security-sensitive confirmations MUST identify the requested action explicitly.

A permission escalation dialog MUST NOT use ambiguous language such as:

`Allow?`

Prefer:

`Allow Acme Reports to export customer records?`

where the domain context makes such detail appropriate.

Authorization decisions MUST NOT be accepted through outside click, backdrop interaction, or ambiguous dismissal.

---

## 2.50 Overlay accessibility

Every modal dialog MUST have an accessible name.

The accessible name SHOULD normally derive from the visible title.

WAI-ARIA requires dialogs to have an accessible name and recommends focus placement and management for modal dialogs. citeturn306571search0turn306571search3

Descriptions SHOULD be associated where concise explanatory text materially helps.

Complex dialog content MUST NOT be flattened into a long `aria-describedby` announcement when normal semantic navigation is more appropriate. WAI-ARIA APG explicitly notes that structured content can be easier to understand when users navigate its semantic structure directly. citeturn306571search2

---

## 2.51 Keyboard operability

Every overlay action MUST be keyboard operable.

Keyboard users MUST be able to:

- open the surface;
- operate required controls;
- dismiss it when dismissal is supported;
- move through content in logical order;
- return to the originating workflow.

WCAG requires keyboard navigation to avoid keyboard traps and requires sequential focus order to preserve meaning and operability. citeturn306571search1turn306571search5

A custom overlay MUST NOT capture keyboard input in a way that prevents expected browser or component behavior without a documented requirement.

---

## 2.52 No accidental keyboard traps

A modal dialog intentionally contains focus while active.

This is not permission to create an inescapable interface.

The user MUST retain an expected mechanism for resolving or dismissing the modal where dismissal is permitted.

Non-modal overlays MUST NOT accidentally trap keyboard focus.

Application-specific shortcuts MUST NOT prevent the user from reaching ordinary overlay controls.

---

## 2.53 Focus visibility

Focused controls inside overlays MUST have a visible focus indicator meeting the corpus Accessibility standard.

Backdrop, elevation, or overlay colour MUST NOT make the focus indicator imperceptible.

Focus indicators MUST remain visible inside:

- scrolled dialog regions;
- dark overlays;
- destructive surfaces;
- sheets and drawers.

---

## 2.54 Focus must not be obscured

Sticky overlay headers, footers, virtual keyboards, and nested surfaces MUST NOT obscure the focused control.

WCAG 2.2 includes focus-order requirements, and its enhanced guidance further emphasizes preventing focused components from being obscured by authored content. citeturn306571search1turn306571search5

Overlay scrolling SHOULD adjust as necessary to keep the active field or control visible.

---

## 2.55 Screen-reader reading order

Portal rendering MUST NOT produce a confusing logical sequence.

Dialog title and primary context MUST be available when focus first enters.

Critical explanatory text SHOULD appear before the action set in semantic reading order.

Destructive action controls MUST NOT be announced before users can understand what they affect.

---

## 2.56 Background content semantics

When a surface is truly modal, the underlying application MUST be unavailable to interaction and assistive-technology navigation according to the selected accessible primitive.

Developers SHOULD rely on the tested modality implementation provided by the component primitive rather than manually applying large trees of `aria-hidden`.

A surface MUST NOT mark itself `aria-modal="true"` while pointer or keyboard users can still interact freely with the underlying page. WAI-ARIA warns that this mismatch can have severe consequences for assistive-technology users. citeturn306571search2

---

## 2.57 Motion

Overlay movement MUST follow the Motion & Interaction standard.

Dialogs SHOULD use restrained opacity/scale or short positional movement.

Sheets and drawers MAY use directional movement because their edge relationship is meaningful.

Reduced-motion mode MUST remove or substantially reduce:

- large translations;
- spring movement;
- overshoot;
- substantial scaling.

Focus placement MUST NOT wait for decorative animation to finish unless immediate placement creates a verified accessibility defect.

---

## 2.58 Touch targets

Overlay controls MUST meet the corpus target-size requirements.

Close controls MUST NOT become tiny merely to reduce visual prominence.

Drawer handles MAY supplement swipe interactions but MUST NOT replace explicit accessible actions where those actions are required.

Touch dismissal regions MUST NOT overlap important controls.

---

## 2.59 Responsive action layout

Dialog action rows MAY become vertical on constrained widths.

The semantic action hierarchy MUST remain consistent across breakpoints.

Responsive layout MUST NOT reverse button meaning unexpectedly.

If the safest action is placed first in keyboard order, visual rearrangement MUST NOT create a contradictory or confusing reading order.

CSS visual order MUST NOT produce a focus order inconsistent with meaning.

---

## 2.60 Long content

Long content SHOULD generally not be forced into a small centered dialog.

Consider:

- larger Dialog;
- Sheet;
- Drawer;
- dedicated page.

If a long modal is justified:

- title SHOULD remain discoverable;
- scroll position SHOULD be clear;
- actions SHOULD remain reachable;
- keyboard focus MUST remain coherent.

The presence of scrollable-content support in a component library MUST NOT be treated as a reason to put entire pages inside dialogs.

---

## 2.61 Overlay performance

Opening an overlay SHOULD not require expensive synchronous work before the first visible response.

Large child content SHOULD load according to standard asynchronous patterns.

Portaled content MUST NOT repeatedly mount and unmount expensive global providers.

Overlay opening MUST NOT trigger unnecessary whole-page rerenders.

Large forms or data views MAY require lazy initialization, but essential title, close control, and state feedback SHOULD appear promptly.

---

## 2.62 Loading inside overlays

An overlay opened to perform a task SHOULD communicate loading within its established surface.

It SHOULD NOT repeatedly resize as loading states resolve.

Skeletons SHOULD preserve expected layout.

If loading fails:

- the overlay SHOULD show the relevant error;
- unaffected surrounding application content MUST remain valid.

A loading failure MUST NOT silently dismiss the overlay and lose task context.

---

## 2.63 Overlay testing

Overlay tests MUST verify behaviour, not only screenshots.

Tests SHOULD cover:

- open and close;
- initial focus;
- focus containment;
- focus restoration;
- Escape;
- outside press;
- close button;
- dirty forms;
- nested overlays;
- responsive substitution;
- loading;
- validation error;
- API error;
- destructive confirmation;
- reduced motion.

Accessibility testing MUST include actual keyboard navigation.

---

## 2.64 Stacking tests

Applications with multiple overlay types MUST test representative combinations such as:

- tooltip above dialog;
- popover inside dialog;
- select inside sheet;
- alert dialog above form dialog;
- toast while dialog is open;
- drawer containing a popover.

Tests MUST verify:

- visual order;
- pointer interaction;
- focus order;
- Escape order;
- scrolling;
- screen-reader semantics.

---

# 3. Anti-patterns

The following are non-conforming unless a documented requirement provides a stronger justification.

## 3.1 Wrong component choice

- Dialog for content that belongs inline.
- Tooltip containing buttons or a form.
- Hover card containing an essential workflow.
- Popover used as a multi-step application.
- Drawer used solely because it looks more modern.
- Alert dialog used for ordinary informational messages.
- Long primary workflows embedded inside small centered dialogs.

## 3.2 Focus

- Opening a modal without moving focus into it.
- Allowing `Tab` to reach the underlying page.
- Focusing the destructive action automatically without a safety rationale.
- Returning focus to `<body>` after close.
- Returning focus to the page while a parent modal remains open.
- Creating a non-modal popover that unexpectedly traps focus.
- Hiding a focused element underneath a newly opened overlay.

## 3.3 Dismissal

- Backdrop click performing an affirmative action.
- Escape closing multiple overlay levels.
- Disabling Escape merely to force a user decision.
- A form dialog silently closing on outside press and losing entered data.
- Swipe being the only way to close a drawer.
- Missing close/cancel mechanism in a dismissible dialog.

## 3.4 Destructive actions

- Generic `OK` for permanent deletion.
- Destructive confirmation without identifying what will be deleted.
- Making the destructive button the default focused action without reason.
- Using colour as the only warning.
- Confirmation dialog for every trivial reversible action.
- High-friction typed confirmation for low-risk changes.
- Closing before server failure can be communicated when success is required first.

## 3.5 Scroll

- Background page scrolling underneath a modal.
- Resetting page scroll to the top when a dialog closes.
- Three nested independent scroll containers.
- Sticky dialog footer covering focused fields.
- Popovers unnecessarily locking document scroll.
- Body-scroll hacks causing large horizontal layout shifts.

## 3.6 Layering

- `z-index: 999999`.
- Every feature inventing its own z-index scale.
- Increasing z-index repeatedly to compensate for misunderstood stacking contexts.
- A tooltip hidden behind its own parent dialog.
- Global navigation appearing above a modal accidentally.
- Lower modal controls remaining clickable through a child modal.
- Creating unnecessary stacking contexts on major layout roots.

## 3.7 Nested overlays

- Dialog inside dialog inside dialog.
- Modal picker opened merely to choose one small option inside another modal.
- Parent dialog closing when child popover receives Escape.
- Parent focus restoration running while child or parent overlay remains active.
- Unrelated overlays sharing one undifferentiated global Boolean such as `isOpen`.

## 3.8 Responsive behavior

- Small desktop dialog simply shrinking below usability on mobile.
- Switching Dialog to Drawer and losing form state.
- Mobile drawer requiring swipe gestures.
- Visual button reordering that contradicts keyboard order.
- Software keyboard obscuring the primary action.

## 3.9 Accessibility

- Dialog without an accessible name.
- Custom modal based only on a fixed `<div>`.
- Setting `aria-modal="true"` while background interaction remains available.
- Manually applying `aria-hidden` indiscriminately and hiding the dialog itself.
- Tooltip that works only on mouse hover.
- Close icon without an accessible name.
- Focus indicator invisible against overlay content.
- Modal that keyboard users cannot resolve or dismiss according to its workflow.

## 3.10 Forms and API state

- Closing a dialog because the submit button was clicked rather than because persistence succeeded.
- Losing form data after a validation or server error.
- Allowing duplicate destructive submission.
- Replacing the whole dialog with an unexplained spinner.
- Hiding API failure in a toast unrelated to the form context.

## 3.11 Security

- Using backdrop blur as protection for sensitive underlying information.
- Delaying permission removal until an exit transition finishes.
- Treating hidden dialog content as authorization.
- Passing secrets into URL-backed overlay state without need.
- Security approval dismissible through ambiguous outside interaction.

---

# 4. Checklist

## 4.1 Pattern selection

- [ ] The overlay has a reason to leave normal document flow.
- [ ] Inline expansion was considered first.
- [ ] Tooltip contains only brief supplementary information.
- [ ] Hover card is only a preview.
- [ ] Popover remains a bounded contextual interaction.
- [ ] Dialog represents a focused temporary task.
- [ ] Alert dialog is reserved for important decisions.
- [ ] Sheet/drawer usage follows viewport and spatial semantics.

## 4.2 Modality

- [ ] Modal versus non-modal behaviour is explicitly defined.
- [ ] Underlying content is truly inert when the surface is modal.
- [ ] A non-modal surface does not accidentally trap interaction.
- [ ] Accessibility semantics match actual modality.
- [ ] Only the topmost modal owns modal focus.

## 4.3 Focus

- [ ] Initial focus placement is intentional.
- [ ] Long dialogs can focus static introductory content.
- [ ] Destructive flows prefer safe initial focus.
- [ ] Modal focus is contained.
- [ ] Focus order preserves meaning.
- [ ] Focus returns to the logical trigger or next workflow target.
- [ ] Nested focus restoration behaves as a stack.
- [ ] Focus never falls arbitrarily to the page root.

## 4.4 Dismissal

- [ ] Escape behaviour is defined.
- [ ] Escape closes only the topmost appropriate layer.
- [ ] Explicit close/cancel exists where appropriate.
- [ ] Outside-press behaviour is intentional.
- [ ] Outside press never confirms an affirmative action.
- [ ] Unsaved data cannot be lost accidentally.
- [ ] Gesture dismissal has an accessible alternative.

## 4.5 Scrolling

- [ ] Modal background scroll is locked.
- [ ] Background scroll position is restored.
- [ ] Active overlay content can scroll when needed.
- [ ] Nested scroll containers are minimized.
- [ ] Focused fields remain visible.
- [ ] Software keyboard behaviour has been tested.
- [ ] Sticky actions do not obscure content.

## 4.6 Layering

- [ ] Global layers use Design Token z-index values.
- [ ] Feature code contains no arbitrary extreme z-index values.
- [ ] Stacking contexts are understood.
- [ ] Portals use a controlled overlay architecture.
- [ ] Tooltip/popover/modal ordering is intentional.
- [ ] Only the topmost active modal accepts modal input.
- [ ] Toasts do not obscure critical overlay actions.

## 4.7 Destructive confirmation

- [ ] The consequence is explicit.
- [ ] The affected entity/scope is identified.
- [ ] The action label is specific.
- [ ] Destructive styling uses semantic tokens.
- [ ] Colour is not the only warning.
- [ ] Confirmation friction is proportional to risk.
- [ ] Undo is considered for reversible operations.

## 4.8 Forms and APIs

- [ ] Form semantics follow Forms & Validation.
- [ ] Dirty-state dismissal is defined.
- [ ] Validation errors preserve entered state.
- [ ] Server errors preserve usable context.
- [ ] Duplicate requests are prevented.
- [ ] Visual closing is separate from persistence success.
- [ ] Pending state is explicit.

## 4.9 Responsive behavior

- [ ] Dialog-to-drawer/sheet adaptation is intentional where used.
- [ ] Semantic modality remains consistent.
- [ ] State survives responsive primitive changes.
- [ ] Mobile controls remain reachable.
- [ ] Touch targets remain adequate.
- [ ] Focus order remains logical after reflow.

## 4.10 Nested overlays

- [ ] Nesting is necessary.
- [ ] The parent-child relationship is explicit.
- [ ] No more modal levels exist than necessary.
- [ ] Child Escape does not incorrectly close the parent.
- [ ] Child close restores focus inside the parent.
- [ ] Portaled child controls remain inside the effective modal context.

## 4.11 Accessibility

- [ ] Every dialog has an accessible name.
- [ ] Descriptions are associated appropriately.
- [ ] Complex content is not flattened into an unusable announcement.
- [ ] Keyboard operation is complete.
- [ ] Focus is visible.
- [ ] Modal focus does not escape.
- [ ] Non-modal interfaces do not trap focus.
- [ ] Tooltips are available on focus.
- [ ] Close controls have accessible names.
- [ ] Reduced-motion behaviour follows the Motion standard.

## 4.12 Security

- [ ] Overlay visibility is not used as authorization.
- [ ] Sensitive content is removed according to security state.
- [ ] Backdrop styling is not treated as privacy protection.
- [ ] Authentication and authorization decisions require explicit interaction.
- [ ] Sensitive URL state is avoided.
- [ ] Security changes do not wait for animation completion.

## 4.13 Testing

- [ ] Keyboard-only flow has been tested.
- [ ] Initial focus is tested.
- [ ] Focus containment is tested.
- [ ] Focus restoration is tested.
- [ ] Escape is tested.
- [ ] Outside dismissal is tested.
- [ ] Nested layers are tested.
- [ ] Responsive variants are tested.
- [ ] Screen-reader semantics are tested.
- [ ] Unsaved forms and error states are tested.
- [ ] Layer ordering is tested with representative overlay combinations.

## 4.14 Corpus alignment

- [ ] shadcn/ui is the component baseline.
- [ ] Design Tokens own z-index, overlay, elevation, spacing and motion values.
- [ ] Motion standards govern enter/exit transitions.
- [ ] Forms & Validation governs forms inside overlays.
- [ ] State Management owns canonical open/task state.
- [ ] API state governs pending/success/error behaviour.
- [ ] Security state overrides visual overlay state.
- [ ] Accessibility governs focus, keyboard and semantic modality.
- [ ] Pattern standards govern destructive confirmation and disclosure.

---

# 5. Canonical summary

A Gold Standard 2026 overlay MUST be selected according to interaction semantics rather than appearance.

Inline expansion SHOULD be preferred when content belongs in normal flow.

Tooltips MUST contain only brief supplementary information and MUST work through keyboard focus as well as pointer interaction.

Hover cards MUST remain optional previews.

Popovers SHOULD provide bounded contextual interaction without unnecessarily making the application modal.

Dialogs SHOULD be used for focused temporary tasks. Alert dialogs MUST be reserved for important interruptive decisions. Sheets and drawers SHOULD represent meaningful side- or edge-oriented tasks and MAY adapt responsively according to device constraints.

Modality MUST be explicit. A modal surface MUST make underlying application content unavailable, move focus into the active surface, constrain focus appropriately, and restore focus when closed. A surface MUST NOT claim modal semantics while permitting ordinary interaction with the page beneath it. citeturn306571search2turn306571search3

Initial focus MUST reflect the task. Complex dialogs MAY focus structural introductory content, while difficult-to-reverse confirmation dialogs SHOULD generally favor the least destructive initial action. citeturn306571search2

Escape and outside-dismissal rules MUST be predictable. Escape SHOULD affect only the topmost applicable layer. Outside interaction MUST NEVER act as affirmative confirmation.

Unsaved work MUST NOT be silently discarded through incidental dismissal.

Modal overlays SHOULD lock background scroll while preserving the original page position. Non-modal surfaces SHOULD NOT impose modal scroll behaviour without a documented reason.

Layering MUST use centralized semantic z-index tokens. Arbitrarily escalating z-index values MUST NOT substitute for understanding CSS stacking contexts.

Nested overlays SHOULD be uncommon. Child tooltips, menus, selects, and popovers are valid where context requires them, but multiple primary modal tasks SHOULD be redesigned into a single coherent workflow whenever practical.

Destructive confirmation MUST state the consequence, affected scope, and action explicitly. Confirmation friction MUST be proportional to actual risk.

Overlay forms MUST preserve entered data on validation and recoverable API errors. Overlay visibility, mutation success, and persistence state MUST remain separate concepts.

Responsive implementation MAY substitute Dialog, Sheet, or Drawer while preserving interaction semantics and state. Current shadcn/ui supports responsive Dialog/Drawer composition and nested Drawer behaviour, but component capability does not override these architectural constraints. citeturn261455search4

Accessibility is part of overlay architecture. Keyboard users MUST be able to enter, operate, resolve, and leave overlay interactions with logical focus order and without unintended keyboard traps. citeturn306571search1turn306571search5

Security state MUST override presentation state. Sensitive information MUST NOT remain available merely because a close transition has not completed.

shadcn/ui is the canonical component baseline. Product overlays MUST extend its Dialog, AlertDialog, Sheet, Drawer, Popover, HoverCard, Tooltip, Accordion, and related primitives rather than creating incompatible local overlay systems.

**Canonical rule:** an overlay is conforming only when its purpose, modality, focus ownership, dismissal, layering, responsive behaviour, state lifecycle, and accessibility remain predictable regardless of pointer device, keyboard use, viewport size, nesting, animation, or asynchronous application state.

The z-index values in §2.31 are intentionally defined as **corpus reference tokens**, not intrinsic CSS or shadcn/ui requirements; the semantic ordering is the contract, and the literal values can be remapped centrally without changing feature code.


<!-- ===== feedback | design | standards/design/16-feedback.md ===== -->

# Feedback & Status — Gold Standard 2026

**Status:** Canonical  
**Standard level:** Gold Standard 2026  
**Canonical placement:** **Components → Feedback & Status → Patterns → Content & UX Writing**  
**Component baseline:** shadcn/ui  
**Applies to:** Application UI, forms, CRUD workflows, asynchronous operations, background jobs, uploads, exports, imports, payments, administrative actions, optimistic updates, validation, system notices, and operator-facing status surfaces.

Normative terms **MUST**, **MUST NOT**, **SHOULD**, and **SHOULD NOT** are requirements unless an approved exception is documented.

---

# 1. Purpose

## 1.1 Objective

This standard defines how the product MUST communicate:

- success;
- failure;
- warning;
- information;
- loading;
- progress;
- pending state;
- optimistic state;
- rollback;
- undo;
- background activity;
- degraded or unavailable state.

It governs:

- toast versus inline feedback;
- banners;
- field and section messages;
- persistent versus transient messaging;
- determinate and indeterminate progress;
- optimistic UI;
- rollback;
- undo;
- success acknowledgement;
- failure acknowledgement;
- notification fatigue;
- duplicate suppression;
- feedback timing;
- accessible live-region announcements.

This standard MUST be applied together with:

- Security;
- Data & Database;
- API;
- State Management;
- Forms & Validation;
- Accessibility;
- Design Tokens;
- Component;
- Pattern;
- Content & UX Writing;
- Observability standards.

Feedback is part of the interaction contract.

A system MUST NOT perform a meaningful action while leaving the user unable to determine whether the action:

1. started;
2. remains in progress;
3. succeeded;
4. failed;
5. requires further action.

---

## 1.2 Governing principle

Feedback MUST appear at the **smallest durable scope that fully explains the state**.

The preferred hierarchy is:

**field/control → component/section → page/workflow → transient toast → application/system banner**

A toast MUST NOT be selected merely because it is easy to implement.

Persistent problems SHOULD have persistent feedback.

Local problems SHOULD have local feedback.

Transient confirmation SHOULD be transient.

Critical interruption SHOULD be exceptional.

---

## 1.3 Feedback is not observability

User feedback and operational observability are different systems.

User-facing feedback MUST communicate what the user needs to know.

Logs, metrics, traces, error IDs, and incident telemetry MUST provide the technical detail required by operators.

A toast MUST NOT substitute for:

- error logging;
- failed-job monitoring;
- audit records;
- incident alerting;
- data reconciliation.

Conversely, the existence of logs MUST NOT excuse missing user-visible feedback.

---

# 2. Rules

## 2.1 Feedback-surface selection

The feedback surface MUST match the scope, persistence, and actionability of the message.

| Surface | Primary use | Persistence | Typical example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Field message** | State tied to one input | Until resolved or state changes | “Enter a valid email address.” |
| **Inline message** | State tied to one component, section, or action | Usually persistent while relevant | “This report could not be generated.” |
| **Inline banner / Alert** | Important state affecting a larger section or page | Persistent while relevant | “Some records could not be loaded.” |
| **Page/system banner** | Broad state affecting most or all of the experience | Persistent while relevant | “Service is temporarily unavailable.” |
| **Toast** | Brief acknowledgement not requiring continued context | Transient | “Copied to clipboard.” |
| **Dialog/Alert Dialog** | User decision is required before continuation | Until acted upon | Confirmation of irreversible action |
| **Progress UI** | A task is actively proceeding | Until completion/failure | Uploading 62% |

A message MUST NOT be promoted to a more interruptive surface merely to increase visibility.

A message MUST NOT be demoted to a transient surface if the user must retain or act on it.

---

## 2.2 Toast usage

Toasts SHOULD be used for brief, low-complexity acknowledgements that:

- do not block continuation;
- do not require sustained reading;
- are not needed to understand the current page;
- do not require a complex recovery workflow.

Appropriate examples include:

- copied to clipboard;
- preference updated;
- link created;
- minor background action completed;
- item moved where an immediate Undo action is available.

Toasts MUST NOT be the sole representation of:

- field validation errors;
- form submission errors requiring correction;
- persistent connection failure;
- authentication expiry requiring action;
- payment failure;
- unsaved work that remains at risk;
- security warnings;
- complex partial failure;
- long-running job state.

---

## 2.3 Canonical toast implementation

New shadcn/ui Base UI projects SHOULD use the current canonical shadcn Toast implementation behind the project-owned feedback abstraction.

Existing approved Sonner implementations MAY remain where they satisfy this standard.

Feature code SHOULD call a canonical application feedback API rather than importing a toast implementation directly.

The canonical abstraction SHOULD own:

- status type;
- duration;
- placement;
- stacking;
- duplicate suppression;
- accessibility behaviour;
- action layout;
- dismiss behaviour.

A feature team MUST NOT independently choose:

- toast library;
- placement;
- duration;
- animation;
- colours;
- stacking rules.

Migration between toast implementations MUST NOT require changes to domain/business logic.

---

## 2.4 Toast content

A toast SHOULD normally contain:

- one concise primary message;
- optional short supporting text;
- at most one primary inline action where appropriate.

Toast copy MUST describe the result or meaningful state.

Prefer:

**Report exported**

over:

**Success**

Prefer:

**Could not save changes**

over:

**Something went wrong**

when the operation is known.

Toasts SHOULD NOT contain:

- paragraphs of explanation;
- complex forms;
- multiple unrelated actions;
- raw technical errors;
- long lists of failed records.

Complex information belongs in persistent UI.

---

## 2.5 Toast duration

A transient message MUST remain visible long enough to be perceived and understood.

Duration SHOULD account for:

- message length;
- whether an action exists;
- severity;
- interaction method.

Very short automatic dismissal MUST NOT make meaningful content practically unreadable.

Actionable toasts SHOULD remain visible longer than simple acknowledgement toasts.

A toast containing an Undo action MUST remain available for the full supported undo interval or provide another persistent recovery mechanism.

Critical errors SHOULD NOT automatically disappear if disappearance would remove the user's only useful recovery information.

---

## 2.6 Toast stacking

The interface SHOULD minimise simultaneous toasts.

Repeated events SHOULD be:

- coalesced;
- updated in place;
- summarised;
- suppressed where redundant.

Routine batch operations MUST NOT produce one toast per record.

For example, deleting 50 selected records SHOULD produce one aggregate result rather than 50 success toasts.

Toast stacks SHOULD remain bounded.

When the bound is exceeded, older low-priority notifications SHOULD be removed or consolidated according to the canonical policy.

---

## 2.7 Inline messages

An inline message SHOULD be used when feedback is directly associated with nearby content or an action.

Inline messages SHOULD remain visible until:

- the condition is resolved;
- the user dismisses it where dismissal is appropriate;
- navigation makes it irrelevant.

Inline feedback SHOULD be positioned near the element whose state it explains.

A user SHOULD NOT have to remember a toast while searching the page for the affected control.

---

## 2.8 Field-level feedback

Validation and field state MUST follow the Forms & Validation standard.

Field errors MUST appear near the affected field.

A form submission MUST NOT communicate correctable field errors only through a toast.

A form-level summary MAY accompany field-level errors when:

- multiple fields fail;
- errors are distributed across a long form;
- accessibility requires a navigable summary;
- cross-field validation fails.

Field feedback MUST identify:

- what requires attention;
- why, where useful;
- how to correct it where not obvious.

---

## 2.9 Inline banners

An inline banner SHOULD communicate a condition affecting a logical region.

Examples include:

- partial data unavailable;
- read-only mode;
- imported data contains warnings;
- configuration is incomplete;
- connectivity affects one module.

The banner SHOULD appear inside or immediately before the affected region.

A section-level issue MUST NOT automatically become a global application banner.

---

## 2.10 Page and system banners

A page or system banner SHOULD be reserved for high-scope conditions.

Appropriate examples include:

- planned maintenance;
- system-wide outage;
- degraded service;
- account-level restriction;
- critical policy change;
- session-related state affecting the whole application.

Global banners MUST NOT become a general announcement area for low-priority product news.

Persistent system banners SHOULD be dismissible only if dismissal is compatible with the message's continued importance.

Critical unresolved state MUST NOT disappear permanently merely because the user dismissed its presentation.

---

## 2.11 Persistent versus transient messaging

Feedback MUST remain available for as long as the information remains operationally relevant.

### Transient feedback SHOULD be used when:

- the action completed;
- no follow-up is required;
- the current UI already reflects the result;
- the message only confirms what just occurred.

### Persistent feedback SHOULD be used when:

- the problem remains unresolved;
- the user must act;
- consequences continue;
- the state materially affects the current task;
- the user may need to refer back to the information.

A persistent condition MUST NOT be repeatedly resurfaced as transient toasts.

---

## 2.12 Feedback timing

Feedback SHOULD appear as close as practical to the triggering event.

The UI MUST acknowledge an interaction promptly when processing cannot finish immediately.

For synchronous-feeling interactions, the acknowledgement MAY be a visual pressed/pending state before explicit loading UI appears.

The system MUST NOT leave a control apparently idle after accepting an action that is still being processed.

Feedback MUST NOT falsely imply success before the authoritative success condition is met, except where an explicitly designed optimistic interaction is used.

---

## 2.13 Pending state

A control that has initiated an asynchronous action SHOULD expose a pending state when repeat activation would be confusing or unsafe.

Pending treatment MAY include:

- disabled/restricted repeat activation;
- loading indicator;
- changed label;
- nearby progress.

Pending state MUST NOT automatically disable unrelated page interaction.

A pending state MUST NOT conceal the action that is taking place.

Prefer a meaningful label such as:

**Saving…**

where it improves clarity over a spinner alone.

---

## 2.14 Preventing duplicate submission

Actions that are not safely repeatable MUST protect against accidental duplicate activation.

Protection MAY include:

- disabling repeat submission while pending;
- idempotency keys;
- deduplication;
- server-side operation locks.

Client disabling alone MUST NOT be considered sufficient protection for high-consequence operations.

The API remains responsible for appropriate idempotency or duplicate-control semantics.

---

## 2.15 Success acknowledgement

Success feedback SHOULD be proportional to the significance and visibility of the result.

Explicit success messaging MAY be unnecessary when the result is immediately obvious.

Examples:

- toggling a setting that visibly changes;
- adding an item that immediately appears in a list;
- closing a successfully submitted lightweight popover.

Redundant success toasts SHOULD be avoided where the changed UI already provides unmistakable confirmation.

Explicit success feedback SHOULD be used when:

- completion is otherwise invisible;
- the action occurred elsewhere;
- a long-running operation completed;
- the consequence is significant;
- users need confidence that the operation persisted.

---

## 2.16 Success intensity

Routine successful operations SHOULD use restrained acknowledgement.

Large positive animation, celebration, confetti, illustration, or modal interruption SHOULD be reserved for meaningful milestones.

Saving a record MUST NOT routinely trigger celebratory treatment.

Success colour SHOULD reinforce semantic meaning without dominating the interface.

Success status MUST NOT depend solely on green colour.

---

## 2.17 Failure acknowledgement

Failures MUST identify the failed operation when possible.

Prefer:

**Could not upload the document**

over:

**Error**

The message SHOULD distinguish, where useful:

- what failed;
- whether anything succeeded;
- whether user input was preserved;
- whether retry is possible;
- what the user should do next.

Failures MUST NOT imply that user data was saved when persistence is uncertain.

Ambiguous outcomes MUST be described honestly.

If an API call timed out after submission and the system cannot determine whether the operation completed, the UI MUST NOT confidently state either success or failure until the state is reconciled.

---

## 2.18 Recoverable errors

Recoverable errors SHOULD provide an appropriate recovery action.

Examples include:

- Retry;
- Reconnect;
- Reload;
- Fix highlighted fields;
- Choose another file;
- Contact support when no self-service recovery exists.

A generic **Try again** action SHOULD NOT be provided when retrying is known to be ineffective.

The system SHOULD preserve user work across recoverable failure wherever feasible.

---

## 2.19 Partial failure

Partial failure MUST be represented explicitly.

A bulk operation MUST NOT show complete success when some items failed.

Feedback SHOULD indicate:

- successful count;
- failed count;
- affected records or route to details;
- appropriate recovery action.

A toast MAY summarise partial failure, but detailed failures SHOULD be available in persistent UI when users need to act on them.

---

## 2.20 Warnings

Warnings SHOULD identify a condition that creates material risk or requires informed attention but does not yet represent failure.

Warnings MUST NOT be used as a generic visual emphasis style.

A warning MUST explain the consequence where the risk is not obvious.

Warning fatigue MUST be treated as a design defect.

If users routinely ignore the same warning, the system SHOULD reconsider:

- timing;
- targeting;
- severity;
- underlying workflow.

---

## 2.21 Informational status

Informational messages SHOULD provide useful context without implying risk.

Informational styling MUST NOT visually compete with warnings or errors.

Routine explanatory content SHOULD normally remain ordinary content rather than being placed inside an information banner.

A blue banner around normal instructions MUST NOT become the default content-layout pattern.

---

## 2.22 Loading versus progress

**Loading** means the system is waiting for content or operation state.

**Progress** means the system can communicate advancement toward completion.

The two MUST NOT be conflated.

A spinner indicates activity, not percentage completion.

A skeleton indicates anticipated structure, not work progress.

A progress bar MUST NOT advance artificially in a way that presents invented progress as authoritative.

---

## 2.23 Determinate progress

Determinate progress MUST be used when reliable measurable progress is available.

Examples include:

- bytes uploaded;
- records processed from a known total;
- completed steps from a fixed workflow;
- files processed from a known set.

Determinate progress SHOULD expose meaningful context such as:

- percentage;
- completed/total;
- current stage;
- estimated remaining quantity where reliable.

The displayed value MUST correspond to real progress.

The UI MUST NOT reach 100% before the operation's actual completion condition is satisfied.

---

## 2.24 Indeterminate progress

Indeterminate progress SHOULD be used when the remaining work cannot be quantified reliably.

Examples include:

- waiting for a remote service;
- unknown processing complexity;
- open-ended data preparation.

Indeterminate progress MUST NOT display a fictional percentage.

If the operation later becomes measurable, the UI MAY transition to determinate progress.

The transition MUST NOT imply that earlier progress was known.

---

## 2.25 Choosing a progress surface

Short operations MAY use local loading state.

Longer operations SHOULD provide a persistent progress surface.

Background tasks that survive navigation MUST NOT depend on a toast as their only status representation.

Where a job can continue beyond the current page, the product SHOULD provide an appropriate persistent location such as:

- activity centre;
- job list;
- export centre;
- notification centre;
- record-level status.

---

## 2.26 Long-running operations

A long-running operation MUST have an authoritative backend operation identity where its lifecycle exceeds the initiating request.

The UI SHOULD be able to recover status after:

- navigation;
- refresh;
- reconnect;
- device sleep where appropriate.

The browser MUST NOT be the sole owner of critical progress state.

A long-running API SHOULD normally return a job/operation resource rather than hold an interactive request open indefinitely.

---

## 2.27 Cancellation

Cancellation SHOULD be offered when:

- the operation is meaningfully cancellable;
- cancellation provides user value;
- partial completion can be handled safely.

A Cancel control MUST NOT be shown if the underlying system cannot actually cancel or safely stop the operation.

If cancellation is best-effort, the wording MUST reflect that semantic.

Cancellation MUST define what happens to partial output.

---

## 2.28 Optimistic UI

Optimistic UI MAY be used when the interface can safely predict the expected server result.

It SHOULD be considered when:

- success is highly probable;
- latency would otherwise materially reduce responsiveness;
- rollback is straightforward;
- temporary inconsistency has low consequence.

Examples MAY include:

- favouriting;
- simple preference toggles;
- lightweight ordering changes;
- reversible local classifications.

Optimistic UI SHOULD NOT be the default for high-consequence mutations.

---

## 2.29 Optimistic UI eligibility

Optimistic treatment SHOULD NOT be used when:

- server validation may commonly reject the change;
- authorization may change the outcome;
- money is transferred;
- inventory or scarce capacity is reserved;
- irreversible deletion occurs;
- compliance/security state changes;
- multiple dependent records must commit atomically;
- displaying unconfirmed success could materially mislead the user.

In these cases the UI SHOULD expose pending state until authoritative confirmation.

---

## 2.30 Optimistic state ownership

Optimistic state MUST be explicitly represented in State Management.

An optimistic value MUST NOT become indistinguishable internally from confirmed server state before reconciliation.

The implementation SHOULD track sufficient context to:

- confirm success;
- roll back;
- reconcile changed server values;
- handle concurrent updates.

The server remains authoritative.

---

## 2.31 Optimistic rollback

If an optimistic mutation fails, the UI MUST reconcile to an authoritative valid state.

Rollback MUST NOT silently remove user intent without explanation.

Failure feedback SHOULD explain that the change did not persist.

Where useful, the UI SHOULD offer:

- Retry;
- Reapply;
- another recovery path.

If subsequent user actions depend on the optimistic mutation, rollback behaviour MUST account for those dependent changes.

---

## 2.32 Optimistic concurrency

Optimistic UI MUST NOT be confused with optimistic concurrency control.

Where concurrent edits matter, the API/Data & Database standards SHOULD provide:

- version tokens;
- ETags;
- row versions;
- compare-and-set semantics;
- another approved conflict mechanism.

The UI MUST NOT overwrite a newer authoritative value merely because it previously displayed an optimistic local value.

---

## 2.33 Undo pattern

Undo SHOULD be used for reversible actions when it reduces unnecessary confirmation interruption.

Appropriate examples MAY include:

- move;
- archive;
- remove from a collection;
- dismiss;
- reversible deletion using a defined soft-delete/recovery period.

Undo MUST have a defined server/domain contract.

An Undo button MUST NOT merely reverse client appearance while the underlying operation remains irreversible.

---

## 2.34 Undo versus confirmation

Undo SHOULD be preferred over confirmation for frequent, low-risk, easily reversible actions.

Confirmation SHOULD be preferred when an action is:

- irreversible;
- high consequence;
- security-sensitive;
- financially consequential;
- legally consequential;
- difficult or expensive to reverse;
- likely to affect other users or systems immediately.

A destructive action MUST NOT skip appropriate confirmation merely because a toast can visually offer Undo.

---

## 2.35 Undo window

The supported undo interval MUST be explicit in implementation.

The user-facing presentation MAY omit the numeric duration if the behaviour remains understandable.

The backend MUST retain sufficient reversible state for at least the promised undo interval.

A toast MUST NOT show Undo after the backend can no longer honour it.

If Undo expires, invoking it MUST NOT silently fail.

---

## 2.36 Undo idempotency

Undo operations SHOULD be idempotent.

Retrying Undo MUST NOT corrupt state.

Undo MUST account for intervening state changes.

If another user or process has changed the resource such that reversal is no longer safe, the system MUST report the conflict rather than forcing an invalid historical state.

---

## 2.37 Offline and connectivity feedback

The interface SHOULD distinguish:

- offline;
- temporarily unreachable;
- request timeout;
- authenticated-but-service-unavailable;
- server rejection.

A transient network failure MUST NOT automatically be described as "offline."

Persistent offline state SHOULD use persistent feedback.

Repeated network failures MUST NOT create a toast on every failed polling request.

Background retry state SHOULD be communicated only at an appropriate frequency.

---

## 2.38 Reconnection

When connectivity returns, the system SHOULD reconcile authoritative state before announcing recovery where stale state is possible.

A **Back online** message MAY be used when useful.

Routine reconnection SHOULD NOT create unnecessary interruption if the user experienced no material degradation.

Queued offline mutations MUST have explicit conflict and failure behaviour.

---

## 2.39 Notification fatigue

The product MUST treat user attention as a limited resource.

Feedback SHOULD be omitted when:

- the result is self-evident;
- no user action is required;
- the message duplicates visible state;
- the event occurs too frequently to provide useful signal.

A system MUST NOT toast every successful API mutation.

A system MUST NOT announce every autosave if saves occur continuously and failures are the only actionable state.

---

## 2.40 Autosave feedback

Autosave SHOULD normally use low-intensity persistent or local status rather than repeated toasts.

Useful states MAY include:

- Saving…;
- Saved;
- Could not save.

Routine **Saved** state SHOULD fade or recede visually without requiring dismissal.

Autosave failure MUST remain visible while unsaved work remains at risk.

The interface MUST NOT falsely show **Saved** until the persistence condition required by the product is satisfied.

---

## 2.41 Duplicate suppression

Identical or equivalent feedback generated repeatedly within a short operational window SHOULD be deduplicated.

The canonical feedback layer SHOULD support:

- dedupe keys;
- update-in-place;
- aggregation;
- rate limits.

Repeated identical server failures MUST NOT create an ever-growing stack of identical alerts.

Deduplication MUST NOT hide materially distinct failures.

---

## 2.42 Feedback escalation

A condition MAY escalate from transient to persistent feedback when it continues.

For example:

1. one failed background refresh MAY remain subtle;
2. repeated failures MAY create inline degraded-state feedback;
3. sustained service failure MAY justify a page/system banner.

Escalation SHOULD be based on user impact and duration rather than raw error count alone.

---

## 2.43 Feedback de-escalation

Persistent feedback SHOULD be removed or downgraded when the underlying condition is resolved.

A stale warning MUST NOT remain visible after recovery.

Recovery MAY be announced briefly when users would otherwise remain uncertain.

The UI SHOULD avoid replacing one persistent outage banner with a persistent success banner unless that information continues to matter.

---

## 2.44 Notification priority

The Design System SHOULD define a restrained status vocabulary equivalent to:

- neutral/default;
- informational;
- success;
- warning;
- destructive/error;
- loading/pending.

Feature teams MUST NOT create additional semantic severities solely for visual variety.

Priority and colour semantics MUST follow Design Tokens and Aesthetic & Visual Language.

---

## 2.45 Visual status semantics

Semantic status colours MUST remain stable across components.

Success MUST NOT use the same semantic treatment as informational content.

Warning MUST NOT be used for ordinary information.

Destructive/error styling MUST be reserved for actual failure, danger, or destructive consequence.

Status MUST NOT depend on colour alone.

Where material, status SHOULD also use:

- icon;
- text;
- label;
- structural context.

---

## 2.46 Status icons

Status icons MUST follow the Iconography standard.

The canonical success, warning, informational, error, and loading metaphors MUST be used consistently.

A feature MUST NOT invent a new warning icon because it visually fits the layout better.

Loading icons MUST comply with reduced-motion requirements.

---

## 2.47 Accessible status messages

Status messages MUST be programmatically determinable where required so assistive technologies can announce them without forcing focus.

Routine advisory status SHOULD normally use semantics equivalent to `role="status"` or `aria-live="polite"`.

Important, time-sensitive failures or warnings MAY use `role="alert"` or an assertive live region.

Assertive announcements MUST be exceptional.

Routine success messages MUST NOT use assertive announcement merely to guarantee attention.

---

## 2.48 Live-region priority

The canonical priority SHOULD be:

**polite** for:

- success;
- routine completion;
- search result counts;
- non-critical background updates;
- ordinary progress milestones.

**assertive** for:

- immediately important errors;
- time-sensitive warnings;
- state requiring prompt awareness to avoid harm or task failure.

Feature teams MUST NOT choose live-region priority based on visual severity alone.

---

## 2.49 Focus and status messages

Ordinary status updates SHOULD be announced without moving keyboard focus.

A toast appearing MUST NOT steal focus.

An inline banner appearing MUST NOT automatically steal focus unless the workflow explicitly requires direct user action and the corresponding Pattern supports it.

Focus SHOULD move when the newly presented UI itself requires interaction, such as an alert dialog.

Validation submission MAY move focus to an error summary or first invalid control according to the Forms & Validation Pattern.

---

## 2.50 Live-region lifecycle

Live-region implementation MUST account for assistive-technology behaviour.

The canonical implementation SHOULD provide stable announcement regions rather than creating inaccessible ephemeral markup patterns.

Rapid updates SHOULD be throttled or summarised.

A live region MUST NOT announce every incremental technical state change.

Announcement content SHOULD reflect user-relevant meaning.

---

## 2.51 Progress accessibility

Determinate progress MUST expose:

- accessible name;
- current progress value;
- relevant minimum/maximum where not implicit.

Indeterminate progress MUST expose that work is in progress without inventing a current value.

For an ARIA progress bar, `aria-valuenow` MUST be omitted when progress is genuinely indeterminate.

Where a progress indicator describes a particular page region, the relationship SHOULD be programmatically available where appropriate.

Progress updates SHOULD NOT produce excessive spoken announcements.

---

## 2.52 Progress announcement frequency

Continuous visual progress MAY update frequently.

Assistive announcements SHOULD update less frequently.

A 1% visual increment MUST NOT automatically generate 100 live announcements.

Progress SHOULD be announced at meaningful intervals or stage changes.

Useful examples MAY include:

- started;
- 25%;
- halfway;
- 75%;
- complete;

or domain-relevant stages.

Exact announcement strategy MAY differ by operation length and importance.

---

## 2.53 `aria-busy`

A region whose content is being updated MAY use `aria-busy` or equivalent semantics where appropriate.

Busy state MUST NOT make usable existing content unnecessarily inaccessible.

The implementation MUST distinguish between:

- region actively updating;
- whole application unusable.

Global busy overlays SHOULD be avoided when only one region is pending.

---

## 2.54 Experimental announcement APIs

Experimental accessibility APIs MUST NOT be the sole mechanism for required feedback.

They MAY be used as progressive enhancement.

The product MUST retain a broadly supported fallback such as established live-region semantics until the Accessibility standard explicitly changes the baseline.

---

## 2.55 Reduced motion

Feedback animation MUST respect reduced-motion preferences.

Toasts, progress indicators, banners, and status transitions MUST NOT depend on large movement to convey meaning.

Indeterminate animation SHOULD have an appropriate reduced-motion treatment.

Removing animation MUST NOT remove the status itself.

---

## 2.56 Content & UX Writing relationship

Feedback copy MUST be concise, specific, and actionable.

Messages SHOULD use plain language.

The primary message SHOULD state:

- what happened;
- or what needs attention.

Supporting text SHOULD explain consequence or recovery only when necessary.

Technical implementation terminology SHOULD NOT appear in user-facing messages unless the audience requires it.

Avoid messages equivalent to:

- Error 500;
- Mutation failed;
- Invalid payload;
- SQL exception;
- Promise rejected.

---

## 2.57 Error copy

Error messages MUST avoid blaming the user.

Messages SHOULD identify incorrect input directly when validation is the cause.

Prefer:

**Enter a date after 1 January 2026**

over:

**You entered an invalid date**

when the requirement can be stated directly.

Generic language such as **Something went wrong** SHOULD be reserved for genuinely unknown failures.

Known failures SHOULD receive specific language.

---

## 2.58 Success copy

Success messages SHOULD use past-tense or completed-state language where appropriate.

Examples:

- **Changes saved**
- **Report created**
- **Invitation sent**

Redundant words such as **successfully** SHOULD usually be omitted when the status styling and completed verb already make success clear.

Prefer:

**Changes saved**

over:

**Changes saved successfully**

unless the distinction adds useful meaning.

---

## 2.59 Retry copy

Retry actions MUST be labelled according to what they do.

**Retry upload** MAY be clearer than generic **Retry** when multiple operations are visible.

A retry action MUST NOT imply the system will fix invalid user input automatically.

If intervention is required, copy SHOULD identify the required correction instead.

---

## 2.60 Security-sensitive feedback

Security feedback MUST avoid exposing information that creates enumeration or disclosure risk.

Authentication, password recovery, invitations, and account discovery MUST follow the Security standard.

The interface MUST NOT reveal sensitive existence/state information merely to make feedback more specific.

For example, account-recovery messaging MAY need deliberately equivalent responses for existing and non-existing identities.

Security requirements take precedence over ordinary feedback specificity.

---

## 2.61 Sensitive operation outcomes

High-consequence actions MUST communicate authoritative outcome clearly.

Examples include:

- payment;
- access changes;
- identity verification;
- data deletion;
- account closure;
- privilege changes;
- legal submissions.

Ambiguous transient confirmation MUST NOT be used where users may need evidence of completion.

The interface SHOULD provide a persistent receipt, record, audit entry, confirmation number, or equivalent where the domain requires durable proof.

---

## 2.62 Data & Database relationship

Feedback MUST reflect authoritative persistence semantics.

A database write queued for later processing MUST NOT be labelled **Saved** if the product contract defines saved as durable final persistence.

If the architecture distinguishes:

- locally cached;
- queued;
- persisted;
- processed;
- published;

the UI MUST use terminology consistent with the actual state where those distinctions matter.

Database rollback, constraint failure, conflict, or transaction failure MUST be propagated to an appropriate user outcome.

---

## 2.63 API relationship

The API MUST expose enough structured failure information for the UI to distinguish meaningful outcomes safely.

Client code SHOULD map machine-readable API errors to canonical feedback messages.

The UI MUST NOT display raw server exception text by default.

API status codes alone SHOULD NOT determine the complete user message.

A conflict response, for example, may require:

- reconciliation;
- reload;
- merge;
- specific explanatory feedback.

API request success MUST NOT automatically equal business-operation success where processing remains asynchronous.

---

## 2.64 State Management relationship

Feedback state MUST have an explicit owner.

Transient presentation state MAY live in the canonical feedback store/component.

Domain operation state MUST remain in the appropriate authoritative data/state layer.

A toast MUST NOT become the sole source of truth that an action completed.

Optimistic mutation state MUST be represented separately from authoritative server state.

Persistent feedback derived from domain state SHOULD be reproducible after rerender or navigation where relevant.

---

## 2.65 Forms & Validation relationship

Forms MUST use field and form feedback according to the Forms & Validation standard.

A toast MUST NOT replace validation.

Submission-level failures MAY use:

- form-level alert;
- inline summary;
- toast only as supplementary acknowledgement.

Values entered by the user SHOULD remain available after recoverable submission failure.

Success feedback SHOULD occur only after the form's defined persistence condition is met.

---

## 2.66 Accessibility relationship

Feedback MUST satisfy the Accessibility standard.

At minimum:

- meaning MUST NOT rely solely on colour;
- live updates MUST be programmatically discoverable where required;
- focus MUST NOT be stolen unnecessarily;
- interactive feedback controls MUST be keyboard operable;
- dismissal controls MUST have accessible names;
- progress MUST expose appropriate semantics;
- reduced-motion preferences MUST be respected.

Accessibility requirements take precedence over a desired minimal or silent interface.

---

## 2.67 Design Tokens relationship

Feedback presentation MUST use canonical semantic tokens.

This includes:

- success;
- warning;
- informational;
- destructive/error;
- neutral;
- pending;
- borders;
- foreground/background;
- status icons;
- animation;
- elevation.

Feature code MUST NOT create custom red/green/yellow feedback palettes.

Duration tokens MAY be defined for transient presentation, but duration MUST still account for content and accessibility requirements.

---

## 2.68 Component relationship

The Component standard SHOULD provide canonical components equivalent to:

- Alert;
- Toast;
- Progress;
- Skeleton;
- Spinner/loading indicator;
- Field message;
- Error summary;
- Badge/status indicator.

Components MUST encode default:

- semantics;
- icon treatment;
- spacing;
- status colour;
- accessibility behaviour.

Feature implementations SHOULD NOT rebuild feedback primitives from arbitrary containers.

---

## 2.69 Pattern relationship

Patterns MUST define complete workflow use of feedback.

Examples include:

- form submission;
- destructive action;
- async export;
- file upload;
- background job;
- optimistic mutation;
- bulk action;
- offline workflow;
- unsaved changes.

The Component provides the visual primitive.

The Pattern determines when and how that primitive is used.

---

## 2.70 Background jobs

Background jobs MUST have persistent status when completion may occur after the initiating context disappears.

A "Job started" toast MAY acknowledge initiation.

It MUST NOT be the only way to discover:

- whether the job remains running;
- whether it succeeded;
- whether it failed.

Completion MAY additionally trigger a toast or notification when useful.

Persistent job history SHOULD remain available according to domain requirements.

---

## 2.71 File uploads

Uploads SHOULD show determinate progress when reliable byte progress is available.

The UI SHOULD distinguish:

- uploading;
- uploaded;
- server processing;
- complete.

An upload reaching 100% transfer MUST NOT be labelled complete if server-side processing is still pending.

Failed individual files SHOULD remain identifiable and retryable where practical.

Multi-file uploads SHOULD aggregate progress without concealing per-file failures.

---

## 2.72 Imports and exports

Long-running imports and exports SHOULD use job-style persistent status.

A toast MAY acknowledge:

- export started;
- export ready.

The user SHOULD have a durable route to retrieve output if the job survives navigation.

Import feedback MUST distinguish:

- received;
- validating;
- processing;
- complete;
- complete with warnings;
- failed.

Partial data ingestion MUST NOT be represented as full success.

---

## 2.73 Bulk actions

Bulk feedback MUST report aggregate outcome truthfully.

For example:

**47 records updated. 3 could not be updated.**

Detailed failures SHOULD be inspectable where recovery is possible.

One toast per selected record MUST NOT be emitted.

Bulk optimistic UI SHOULD be used only when rollback and conflict handling remain tractable.

---

## 2.74 Navigation and feedback

Navigation MUST NOT unexpectedly destroy important feedback.

Persistent workflow errors SHOULD remain available on the relevant destination.

A successful redirect MAY carry one transient acknowledgement into the destination.

Flash-style success messaging MUST NOT repeatedly reappear after refresh or Back navigation unless the action genuinely occurred again.

---

## 2.75 Dismissal

Dismiss controls SHOULD be offered only where dismissal is meaningful.

A required unresolved error MUST NOT disappear permanently merely because a user clicked Close.

Dismissed informational notices MAY persist their dismissal according to State Management policy.

Dismissal preference SHOULD be scoped to the notice version when future materially different notices may need to appear.

---

## 2.76 Testing

Feedback behaviour SHOULD be tested for:

- immediate success;
- slow success;
- failure;
- timeout;
- ambiguous result;
- partial failure;
- duplicate activation;
- retry;
- rollback;
- undo;
- undo expiry;
- offline;
- reconnect;
- concurrent mutation;
- navigation during pending work;
- background completion.

Accessibility tests MUST include:

- keyboard interaction;
- focus preservation;
- live-region announcements;
- duplicate announcement behaviour;
- progress semantics;
- reduced motion.

Automated tests alone are insufficient for live-region behaviour.

Representative screen-reader testing SHOULD be performed for canonical feedback components and Patterns.

---

## 2.77 Exceptions

A deviation from this standard MUST document:

- affected workflow;
- standard rule being deviated from;
- rationale;
- user-impact risk;
- accessibility impact;
- Security impact;
- persistence/recovery implications.

Repeated exceptions MUST trigger Pattern or Design System review.

---

# 3. Anti-patterns

The following are non-conformant unless explicitly covered by an approved exception.

## 3.1 Toast everything

Every successful or failed API request creates a toast.

## 3.2 Toast validation

Field errors appear only in a toast while affected fields remain unexplained.

## 3.3 Persistent condition, transient message

An unresolved outage or permission problem disappears after a few seconds.

## 3.4 Global banner for local problem

One failed widget creates an application-wide alert.

## 3.5 Success redundancy

A visible state change, success icon, inline message, and toast all confirm the same routine action.

## 3.6 Generic success

Messages say only **Success!** without identifying what succeeded.

## 3.7 Generic failure

Known operations fail with only **Something went wrong**.

## 3.8 Raw backend error

Stack traces, SQL errors, internal service names, or exception messages are displayed directly.

## 3.9 Premature success

The UI announces success before the authoritative operation is complete.

## 3.10 Fake progress

A percentage is invented to make an unknown-duration operation feel determinate.

## 3.11 100% but not complete

The progress bar reaches 100% while significant server work remains without explaining the next stage.

## 3.12 Spinner forever

A long-running operation uses only an indefinite spinner and provides no persistent job state.

## 3.13 Browser-owned job

Closing or refreshing the browser destroys the only record of a critical long-running operation.
