Choose one model:

```text
design-first
```

or:

```text
code-first
```

Either can work.

Do not maintain two independently authoritative schemas.

---

# 174. OpenAPI Validation

OpenAPI definitions SHOULD be validated in CI.

Check:

```text
syntax
schema validity
broken references
breaking changes
```

where tooling supports it.

---

# 175. OpenAPI Version

Use an organization-approved current OpenAPI 3.x version supported by the relevant toolchain.

Do not upgrade specification versions before required:

```text
documentation
generation
validation
gateway
SDK
```

tools support them reliably.

---

# 176. Schema Reuse

Reuse schema components for concepts that are genuinely identical.

Do not create one gigantic universal schema hierarchy merely to eliminate repetition.

---

# 177. Request vs Response Models

Request and response models SHOULD be separate when their semantics differ.

Example:

```text
CreateUserRequest
UserResponse
UpdateUserRequest
```

Do not force one model to serve every context.

---

# 178. Persistence Models

Database entities MUST NOT automatically become API models.

Persistence and public contracts have different lifecycles.

---

# 179. Examples

API documentation SHOULD contain realistic examples.

Examples must conform to schemas.

Avoid examples that contain fake fields not actually supported.

---

# 180. Documentation

Every consumer-facing API SHOULD document:

```text
Purpose
Authentication
Authorization expectations
Endpoints/operations
Requests
Responses
Errors
Pagination
Filtering
Rate limits
Idempotency
Versioning
Examples
```

---

# 181. Documentation Generated From Contracts

Generate mechanical reference from OpenAPI where useful.

Human-written guides should complement generated reference.

---

# 182. API Tutorials

Provide task-oriented tutorials for important integration journeys.

Example:

```text
Authenticate
Create first project
Receive webhook
Handle pagination
```

Reference docs alone are insufficient for complex public APIs.

---

# 183. API Changelog

Public and broadly consumed APIs SHOULD maintain a consumer-focused changelog.

Document:

```text
new capability
behavior change
deprecation
security-relevant change
migration
```

---

# 184. SDKs

Provide SDKs when they materially reduce integration complexity.

SDKs SHOULD wrap protocol ergonomics—not hide the API so completely that debugging becomes impossible.

---

# 185. SDK Responsibilities

A high-quality SDK may provide:

```text
authentication setup
typed models
pagination helpers
retry behavior
error mapping
idempotency support
```

---

# 186. SDK Versioning

SDK versioning and API versioning are separate concerns.

Do not assume matching major numbers are always required.

---

# 187. SDK Generated Code

Generated SDK code SHOULD be clearly separated from hand-written ergonomic layers.

Do not hand-edit generated source.

---

# 188. SDK Retry Policy

SDKs MUST NOT blindly retry unsafe writes.

Retries should understand:

```text
method
idempotency
failure type
```

---

# 189. SDK Error Types

Expose structured errors.

Consumers should not parse strings to distinguish:

```text
authorization
validation
rate limit
conflict
```

---

# 190. Caching

HTTP APIs SHOULD use HTTP caching semantics where appropriate.

Possible mechanisms:

```text
Cache-Control
ETag
Last-Modified
```

---

# 191. Cache-Control

Public/static representations may be cacheable.

Sensitive/private responses MUST use appropriate cache directives.

Never accidentally cache personalized responses publicly.

---

# 192. Authorization and Caching

Cache keys must account for all security-sensitive context.

Do not serve one user's authorized representation to another user.

---

# 193. Conditional GET

Use conditional requests where they materially reduce transfer/load.

Example:

```text
If-None-Match
→ 304 Not Modified
```

---

# 194. Compression

Support appropriate HTTP compression for suitable response types.

Do not compress formats already highly compressed where unnecessary.

---

# 195. Response Size

Monitor large responses.

Prefer:

```text
pagination
field reduction
compression
streaming
```

over massive JSON payloads.

---

# 196. Streaming

Use streaming where:

- results are large;
- incremental delivery matters;
- the client can process incrementally.

Streaming changes failure semantics and must be designed deliberately.

---

# 197. SSE

Server-Sent Events may be appropriate for server-to-client realtime streams where one-direction communication is sufficient.

Define:

```text
reconnection
event identity
authorization
retention/replay
```

---

# 198. WebSockets

Use WebSockets when persistent bidirectional communication creates clear product value.

They require:

```text
connection authentication
subscription authorization
heartbeat
reconnection
backpressure
message limits
```

---

# 199. WebSocket Authorization

Authorization MUST apply to individual channels/resources, not only initial connection establishment.

---

# 200. Realtime Message Versioning

Realtime messages are contracts and require compatibility discipline.

---

# 201. BFF APIs

A Backend-for-Frontend may tailor APIs to:

```text
web
mobile
specialized client
```

when client requirements materially differ.

Do not create a BFF for every page.

---

# 202. BFF Ownership

BFFs SHOULD own composition/presentation adaptation.

Core domain rules remain in domain services/modules.

---

# 203. API Gateway

An API gateway MAY own cross-cutting concerns such as:

```text
TLS termination
routing
coarse rate limiting
authentication validation
request limits
```

Do not move all business authorization into the gateway.

---

# 204. Gateway Is Not Domain Authorization

Resource-level authorization still belongs near authoritative business resources.

---

# 205. API Aggregation

Aggregation endpoints MAY combine multiple underlying sources to prevent excessive client fan-out.

Avoid creating hidden distributed N+1 behavior.

---

# 206. Fan-Out

A single API request calling many downstream services synchronously creates latency and failure amplification.

Review large synchronous fan-out.

---

# 207. Dependency Failure

APIs MUST define behavior when dependencies fail.

Possible:

```text
fail request
return partial response
serve stale data
degrade optional capability
```

Choose intentionally.

---

# 208. Partial Responses

Use partial responses only where consumers can correctly interpret missing portions.

Never silently return incomplete data as complete success.

---

# 209. Resilience

External dependency calls SHOULD implement appropriate:

```text
timeout
retry
circuit breaking where warranted
fallback
observability
```

---

# 210. Circuit Breakers

Use circuit breakers where repeated failing calls would amplify outages.

Do not introduce them mechanically.

---

# 211. Load Shedding

Under severe load, low-priority API work MAY be rejected to protect core operations.

Priorities must be explicit.

---

# 212. Health Endpoints

Operational health APIs SHOULD distinguish where useful:

```text
liveness
readiness
```

Avoid exposing sensitive internal topology.

---

# 213. Health Endpoint Security

Health endpoints should reveal only information needed by operational systems.

Do not expose:

```text
credentials
database details
internal hostnames
stack traces
```

---

# 214. Metrics Endpoints

Internal metrics endpoints SHOULD be protected from public access unless intentionally exposed.

---

# 215. Observability

Every production API SHOULD provide sufficient telemetry for:

```text
traffic
latency
errors
saturation
dependency health
```

---

# 216. Structured Logs

Log structured API events.

Typical context:

```text
requestId
route
method
status
duration
tenant where safe
principal category
```

Do not log secrets.

---

# 217. Request IDs

Every request SHOULD have a correlation/request identifier.

Propagate appropriate correlation context across internal calls.

---

# 218. Distributed Tracing

Use tracing when request flow crosses enough boundaries to make ordinary logs insufficient.

---

# 219. Metrics

Useful API metrics include:

```text
request rate
error rate
latency
p50/p95/p99
rate-limit rejection
dependency latency
```

---

# 220. Route Cardinality

Metrics MUST use normalized route names rather than raw IDs.

Good:

```text
/projects/{projectId}
```

Bad metric label:

```text
/projects/123456
```

which creates high cardinality.

---

# 221. Logging Request Bodies

Do not routinely log complete request/response bodies.

They may contain:

```text
credentials
PII
financial data
large payloads
```

Log only what is operationally required.

---

# 222. Audit Logging

High-risk API actions SHOULD generate audit events.

Examples:

```text
permission changes
exports
API key changes
ownership transfers
administrative operations
```

---

# 223. Audit Identity

Audit records SHOULD capture:

```text
actor
action
target
tenant
timestamp
result
```

where applicable.

---

# 224. API Security Testing

Critical APIs SHOULD test:

```text
unauthenticated access
wrong role
wrong tenant
modified object ID
invalid input
oversized input
rate limits
replay
duplicate operation
```

---

# 225. Negative Authorization Tests

Every sensitive endpoint requires tests proving who **cannot** perform the operation.

Successful-path tests alone are insufficient.

---

# 226. Fuzz / Robustness Testing

High-risk parsers and public APIs MAY benefit from fuzz/property-based testing.

---

# 227. Contract Testing

Validate actual implementation against documented API schema.

Documentation that diverges from runtime behavior is a defect.

---

# 228. Schema Fuzzing

Generated schema examples and boundary values MAY be used to test:

```text
minimum
maximum
enum
nullability
malformed content
```

---

# 229. Performance Testing

High-traffic or expensive endpoints SHOULD be tested at realistic concurrency.

Measure:

```text
latency
database load
external calls
memory
response size
```

---

# 230. SLOs

Critical APIs SHOULD define service-level objectives where operational maturity warrants it.

Examples:

```text
availability
latency
error rate
```

---

# 231. Latency Budget

Critical request paths SHOULD have a latency budget distributed across:

```text
gateway
application
database
external dependencies
```

---

# 232. Public API Availability

Do not promise availability targets the architecture cannot sustain.

API contractual SLAs and engineering SLOs should be aligned.

---

# 233. API Ownership

Every API MUST have an owner.

Ownership includes:

```text
contract
security
documentation
operations
consumer support
versioning
deprecation
```

---

# 234. Endpoint Ownership

Large platforms MAY assign ownership at API/domain level rather than individual endpoints.

Ownership must remain discoverable.

---

# 235. API Catalog

Large organizations SHOULD maintain a catalog of significant APIs.

Useful metadata:

```text
name
purpose
owner
classification
base address
authentication
version
documentation
SLO
```

---

# 236. Shadow APIs

Avoid undocumented production APIs.

Every externally reachable endpoint should be intentional and owned.

---

# 237. Administrative APIs

Administrative APIs require stronger controls.

Consider:

```text
strong authentication
MFA
network restrictions
audit logs
narrow permissions
```

---

# 238. Debug APIs

Debug endpoints MUST NOT expose sensitive production internals.

Remove or protect them before production.

---

# 239. Internal-Only APIs

"Internal" MUST be enforced by architecture, not merely naming.

Use:

```text
network policy
identity
authorization
gateway rules
```

as appropriate.

---

# 240. API Discovery

Clients should know where authoritative API documentation and schemas live.

Do not require reading source code to discover supported endpoints.

---

# 241. API Base URL

Use stable environment-specific base addresses.

Example:

```text
api.example.com
```

Do not encode transient infrastructure details into consumer contracts.

---

# 242. Environments

Clearly distinguish:

```text
production
sandbox
test
```

where public integration workflows require them.

---

# 243. Sandbox

Public/partner APIs SHOULD provide a sandbox where integration risk justifies it.

Sandbox behavior should approximate production semantics without production data.

---

# 244. Sandbox Credentials

Sandbox credentials MUST NOT work against production.

---

# 245. Test Resources

Avoid mixing obvious development endpoints into production APIs.

Bad:

```text
/test-charge
/debug-create-user
```

unless explicitly secured operational tools.

---

# 246. API Secrets in URLs

Never send secrets through query strings when safer headers/body mechanisms are available.

URLs may appear in:

```text
logs
history
referrers
analytics
```

---

# 247. Sensitive Query Data

Avoid sensitive personal information in URL paths/query parameters for the same reason.

---

# 248. Header Usage

Use headers for protocol metadata.

Use bodies for domain payload.

Do not move arbitrary business fields into custom headers.

---

# 249. Custom Headers

Custom headers should have clear semantics and documentation.

Avoid creating dozens of organization-specific headers when ordinary HTTP mechanisms suffice.

---

# 250. User-Agent / Client Identification

SDKs and API consumers MAY identify client/version where this materially improves support and analytics.

Do not rely on client identity as authorization.

---

# 251. Locale

If API-generated human text is localized, define locale selection.

Machine identifiers MUST remain locale-independent.

---

# 252. Internationalization

APIs dealing with:

```text
currency
dates
time zones
addresses
names
phone numbers
```

must not assume one locale.

---

# 253. Time Zone Semantics

API contracts MUST distinguish:

```text
instant
calendar date
local time
timezone
```

---

# 254. Geographic Data

Coordinates must document:

```text
coordinate order
unit
reference system
```

where relevant.

---

# 255. Units

Never return ambiguous measurement units.

Prefer explicit naming:

```text
weightKg
distanceMeters
durationSeconds
```

or a structured quantity model.

---

# 256. IDs and Enumeration

Unpredictable IDs can reduce accidental enumeration but do not provide authorization.

Always enforce access control.

---

# 257. Resource Existence Leakage

For sensitive resources, consider whether:

```text
403
```

vs:

```text
404
```

should expose existence.

Apply consistently.

---

# 258. Data Minimization

Return only information required for the consumer's use case.

Do not expose internal fields merely because they exist.

---

# 259. Sensitive Fields

Fields such as:

```text
passwordHash
internalRiskScore
secretToken
providerCredential
```

MUST never be included in ordinary API serialization.

---

# 260. Serializer Allowlist

Prefer explicit response mapping.

Do not automatically serialize complete ORM/database objects.

---

# 261. Field-Level Authorization

Some resources require field-level restrictions.

Example:

```text
basic member
→ name

admin
→ name + email + audit details
```

Apply server-side.

---

# 262. Overposting

Request DTOs SHOULD expose only fields consumers are permitted to change.

Never reuse database/entity models blindly for updates.

---

# 263. Optimistic UI Support

APIs MAY provide semantics enabling optimistic interfaces.

Examples:

```text
stable IDs
idempotency
version numbers
predictable validation
```

---

# 264. Resource Creation IDs

Where useful, clients MAY provide idempotent resource IDs.

Otherwise server-generated IDs remain the common default.

---

# 265. Create Response

Creation SHOULD generally return enough information for the client to identify/use the new resource.

---

# 266. Update Response

Choose one convention:

```text
return updated representation
```

or:

```text
204 + client re-fetch
```

based on product needs.

Use consistently.

---

# 267. Delete Response

Deletion behavior should clarify whether:

```text
resource immediately disappears
cleanup is asynchronous
recovery remains possible
```

---

# 268. Soft Delete API Semantics

Do not expose implementation terms like `deleted_at` unless part of the public domain contract.

Expose meaningful states such as:

```text
archived
trashed
```

when relevant.

---

# 269. Restore

If deletion is reversible, expose restoration as an intentional operation rather than database implementation leakage.

---

# 270. State Transitions

Domain state transitions SHOULD have clear API semantics.

Example:

```text
POST /invoices/{id}/approve
```

can be preferable to:

```json
PATCH /invoices/{id}

{
  "status": "approved"
}
```

when approval has distinct authorization/business effects.

---

# 271. Actions

Resource actions are acceptable when they represent domain commands.

Examples:

```text
approve
cancel
publish
archive
restore
```

Use predictable conventions.

---

# 272. Do Not CRUD Complex Workflows Blindly

If changing a field invokes:

```text
permissions
payments
notifications
side effects
audit
```

represent the business operation explicitly.

---

# 273. Command Result

Domain command responses SHOULD make outcome clear.

Avoid exposing implementation workflow steps unless consumers need them.

---

# 274. Transactions and APIs

An API operation should define the atomic business boundary.

Clients should not need to orchestrate low-level calls to maintain server invariants where the server can own that transaction.

---

# 275. Chatty APIs

Avoid requiring clients to make many sequential calls for one common business task.

Provide appropriately coarse operations.

---

# 276. Fine-Grained APIs

Do not make APIs so coarse that they become generic:

```text
/doEverything
```

Balance network efficiency with semantic clarity.

---

# 277. N+1 API Calls

Watch for clients doing:

```text
GET list
↓
GET each item separately
```

to assemble common views.

Consider:

```text
expansion
batch retrieval
aggregation
```

where appropriate.

---

# 278. Batch Retrieval

Batch lookup MAY use:

```text
POST /projects/batch-get
```

or another canonical convention when query length/complexity makes GET impractical.

Document read semantics.

---

# 279. URL Length

Do not depend on arbitrarily long query URLs.

For complex queries, a POST-based query endpoint MAY be appropriate when semantics justify it.

---

# 280. Query APIs

Complex read-only domain queries MAY use command-like POST endpoints when the request structure cannot reasonably fit ordinary GET semantics.

Document that the operation is read-only.

---

# 281. API Evolution

Prefer:

```text
add
deprecate
migrate
remove
```

over:

```text
break
notify later
```

---

# 282. Strangler Migration

When replacing an API:

```text
old contract
↓
adapter/migration
↓
new implementation
↓
consumer migration
↓
old retirement
```

is often safer than simultaneous replacement.

---

# 283. Adapter Compatibility

Temporary compatibility adapters MUST have:

```text
owner
purpose
removal plan
```

Do not allow legacy translation layers to become permanent accidentally.

---

# 284. Third-Party API Consumption

External APIs are unreliable dependencies from your application's perspective.

Wrap important providers when this provides:

```text
timeouts
retry policy
auth configuration
error translation
observability
provider isolation
```

---

# 285. External API Schema

Validate external responses when incorrect/malformed data could affect correctness or security.

Do not blindly trust third-party JSON.

---

# 286. Provider Changes

Third-party providers may change behavior.

Monitor:

```text
deprecation notices
API versions
SDK versions
error rates
```

for critical providers.

---

# 287. External API Credentials

Provider credentials MUST use the secret-management standard.

Never ship server credentials to clients.

---

# 288. Provider Sandbox

Use provider sandbox/test environments where available.

Do not test destructive integrations against production by default.

---

# 289. API Testing Layers

Use:

```text
Unit
→ domain/validation

Integration
→ actual API + data boundary

Contract
→ API schema compatibility

E2E
→ critical consumer journeys
```

---

# 290. Endpoint Integration Tests

Important endpoints SHOULD test:

```text
success
validation failure
unauthenticated
unauthorized
not found
conflict
dependency failure
```

as applicable.

---

# 291. Pagination Tests

Test:

```text
first page
next page
empty page
boundary values
stable ordering
invalid cursor
```

---

# 292. Idempotency Tests

Critical idempotent operations SHOULD verify:

```text
same key + same request
→ same effective result

same key + different request
→ rejected or documented behavior
```

---

# 293. Rate-Limit Tests

Verify rate limits do not accidentally:

```text
block unrelated tenants
allow easy bypass
return unsafe errors
```

---

# 294. API Documentation Tests

Examples SHOULD be executable or schema-validated where practical.

---

# 295. Backward Compatibility Tests

API CI SHOULD detect accidental:

```text
field removal
type change
required-field change
path removal
operation removal
```

for stable APIs.

---

# 296. Production Monitoring

Every critical API route should be diagnosable from production telemetry.

Operators should be able to answer:

```text
Is it failing?
Is it slow?
Which dependency?
Which version?
Which clients?
```

---

# 297. API Dashboards

Critical APIs SHOULD have dashboards for relevant:

```text
traffic
latency
errors
rate limits
dependency failures
```

---

# 298. API Alerts

Alerts SHOULD reflect meaningful user/service impact.

Do not alert on every individual 4xx client error.

---

# 299. 4xx vs 5xx Monitoring

Distinguish client-driven failures from server failures.

Unexpected growth in either may reveal:

```text
client regression
attack
deployment defect
contract mismatch
```

---

# 300. Deprecation Metrics

Measure usage of deprecated APIs.

Do not remove a deprecated API without knowing whether important consumers remain where measurement is feasible.

---

# 301. API Cost

Expensive endpoints SHOULD understand resource cost.

Examples:

```text
database work
external API cost
compute
AI tokens
large exports
```

---

# 302. Cost Abuse

Where operations directly incur financial cost, enforce:

```text
authorization
quota
rate limit
budget
```

as appropriate.

---

# 303. AI API Endpoints

AI-backed API endpoints require additional controls for:

```text
input size
token limits
model cost
tool permissions
output validation
prompt injection
PII
timeouts
```

---

# 304. AI Output

AI-generated content MUST be treated as untrusted.

Do not allow an LLM response directly to become:

```text
SQL
shell command
permission decision
financial transaction
privileged API call
```

without controls.

---

# 305. AI Structured Output

Where downstream software consumes AI output, use structured schema validation.

Do not rely solely on prose instructions to guarantee format.

---

# 306. API Gateway Authentication

Gateway-level authentication can reject invalid credentials early.

Resource-level authorization remains mandatory downstream.

---

# 307. mTLS

Mutual TLS MAY be appropriate for high-assurance service-to-service or partner integrations.

It does not replace application authorization.

---

# 308. IP Allowlisting

IP allowlists MAY provide defense in depth.

They MUST NOT be the sole authorization mechanism for sensitive APIs.

---

# 309. Signature Authentication

Signed request schemes MAY be suitable where integrity/replay protection is important.

Use established protocols where possible.

Avoid inventing custom cryptography.

---

# 310. Replay Protection

High-risk signed requests SHOULD define:

```text
timestamp
nonce/event ID
allowed time skew
deduplication
```

as appropriate.

---

# 311. API Enumeration

APIs SHOULD minimize unnecessary information leakage during:

```text
authentication
resource lookup
password recovery
invitation
```

where enumeration creates security risk.

---

# 312. Sensitive Errors

Security errors should provide enough information for legitimate recovery without providing attackers unnecessary detail.

---

# 313. API Input Encoding

Normalize and validate:

```text
Unicode
filenames
URLs
identifiers
```

where ambiguous encoding could create security or correctness issues.

---

# 314. URL Inputs

Server-side URL fetch APIs MUST consider SSRF.

Validate destination and network behavior according to the Security Gold Standard.

---

# 315. Redirect Inputs

Redirect parameters such as:

```text
next
returnTo
redirectUri
```

must be validated.

Prevent open redirects.

---

# 316. API File Names

Do not trust client filenames as storage paths.

Treat them as metadata.

---

# 317. Content Disposition

File-download endpoints SHOULD set safe content behavior appropriate to file type.

Do not allow dangerous content to execute in trusted product origins accidentally.

---

# 318. API Compression Bombs

Compressed/uploaded data processing must enforce expanded-size/resource limits where relevant.

---

# 319. API Serialization Security

Serialization libraries MUST NOT instantiate arbitrary executable types from untrusted data.

Use data-oriented serialization formats.

---

# 320. API Lifecycle

Every significant API goes through:

```text
Design
↓
Review
↓
Implement
↓
Validate
↓
Publish
↓
Observe
↓
Evolve
↓
Deprecate
↓
Retire
```

---

# 321. API Design Review

Significant APIs SHOULD undergo design review before consumers exist.

Review:

```text
resource model
security
schema
naming
errors
pagination
versioning
operability
```

It is cheaper to fix a contract before adoption.

---

# 322. Public API Review

Public APIs require stronger review because mistakes have higher long-term compatibility cost.

---

# 323. Security Review Trigger

Security review is warranted for:

```text
new public API
new authentication method
new privileged operation
new file processing
new webhook
new partner integration
new tenant boundary
```

---

# 324. API Governance

The organization SHOULD define ownership for:

```text
API design standard
OpenAPI tooling
gateway
security baseline
version policy
deprecation policy
SDK conventions
```

---

# 325. API Exception Process

Deviations from the standard SHOULD document why the standard cannot reasonably satisfy the requirement.

Do not create feature-level conventions casually.

---

# 326. API Design Checklist

Before implementing:

```text
□ Consumer identified
□ API classification identified
□ Resource/action model clear
□ Naming follows standard
□ HTTP method appropriate
□ Authentication defined
□ Authorization defined
□ Tenant scope defined
□ Request schema defined
□ Response schema defined
□ Error model defined
□ Pagination defined where needed
□ Filtering/sorting defined
□ Idempotency considered
□ Concurrency considered
□ Rate limits considered
□ Resource limits considered
□ Version impact considered
□ Observability considered
□ OpenAPI ownership defined
```

---

# 327. Endpoint Review Checklist

```text
□ Path canonical
□ Method semantic
□ Request bounded
□ Runtime validation present
□ Unknown-field behavior defined
□ Authentication enforced
□ Object authorization enforced
□ Tenant isolation enforced
□ Mass assignment prevented
□ Response fields minimized
□ Sensitive fields excluded
□ Status codes correct
□ Problem/error format consistent
□ Expected errors tested
□ Unexpected errors safe
□ Database queries bounded
□ Timeout defined for dependencies
□ Retry behavior safe
□ Audit event added where needed
```

---

# 328. Public API Release Checklist

```text
□ OpenAPI published
□ Documentation published
□ Authentication guide published
□ Examples verified
□ Errors documented
□ Pagination documented
□ Rate limits documented
□ Idempotency documented
□ Changelog initialized
□ Version policy published
□ Deprecation policy published
□ SDKs tested where provided
□ Security assessment complete
□ Monitoring operational
□ Support ownership defined
```

---

# 329. Webhook Checklist

```text
□ Stable event name
□ Unique event ID
□ Timestamp
□ Schema documented
□ Signature validation documented
□ Replay considerations defined
□ Duplicate delivery expected
□ Ordering semantics documented
□ Retry policy documented
□ Consumer acknowledgement behavior documented
□ Test mechanism provided where appropriate
```

---

# 330. API Definition of Done

An API operation is complete only when:

```text
✓ Contract is explicit
✓ Schema validated
✓ Authentication enforced where required
✓ Authorization enforced
✓ Tenant isolation verified
✓ Validation implemented
✓ Error model implemented
✓ Status codes appropriate
✓ Result sizes bounded
✓ Idempotency handled where required
✓ Concurrency considered
✓ External calls bounded by timeout
✓ Retries safe
✓ Logs/metrics available
✓ Tests cover positive and negative behavior
✓ OpenAPI/reference updated
✓ Documentation updated
```

---

# 331. API Anti-Patterns

Avoid:

```text
POST /getUsers
```

for ordinary resource retrieval.

Avoid:

```text
GET /deleteUser?id=123
```

for mutation.

Avoid:

```text
200 OK
{
  "error": true
}
```

for ordinary protocol failures.

Avoid:

```text
/api/doEverything
```

generic mega-endpoints.

Avoid:

```text
request.body
→ ORM update
```

mass assignment.

Avoid:

```text
client sends tenantId
→ trusted automatically
```

Avoid:

```text
SELECT *
→ serialize entire row
```

Avoid:

```text
unbounded collection response
```

Avoid:

```text
random custom error format per endpoint
```

Avoid:

```text
string error message as machine contract
```

Avoid:

```text
access token in URL
```

Avoid:

```text
retry every failure
```

Avoid:

```text
no timeout
```

Avoid:

```text
non-idempotent payment retry
```

without an idempotency mechanism.

Avoid:

```text
API v2
```

solely because implementation was rewritten.

Avoid:

```text
database schema = public API
```

Avoid:

```text
public API without owner
```

Avoid:

```text
internal API therefore no auth
```

Avoid:

```text
Swagger/OpenAPI document manually drifting from implementation
```

Avoid:

```text
webhook assumes exactly-once delivery
```

Avoid:

```text
rate limiting by IP only
```

when authenticated/tenant-aware abuse requires better scope.

---

# 332. AI API Rules

AI coding agents MUST inspect existing API conventions before creating endpoints.

Inspect:

```text
routes
OpenAPI
authentication
authorization
error format
pagination
query conventions
validation
API clients
tests
```

---

# 333. AI Existing-Contract Rule

AI MUST NOT invent a new API convention when an established one exists.

Consistency takes precedence over local preference.

---

# 334. AI Endpoint Rule

Before creating an endpoint, AI must identify:

```text
Who calls it?
What resource/action does it represent?
Why is HTTP needed?
What security boundary exists?
```

Do not create internal HTTP endpoints unnecessarily.

---

# 335. AI Method Rule

AI MUST choose HTTP methods according to operation semantics.

It MUST NOT use GET for destructive changes.

---

# 336. AI Validation Rule

AI-generated endpoints MUST validate runtime input.

Type annotations alone are insufficient.

---

# 337. AI Authorization Rule

For every protected operation, AI must answer:

```text
Who is the principal?
Which tenant?
Which resource?
Which action?
Where is authorization enforced?
```

---

# 338. AI Serialization Rule

AI MUST NOT serialize database models directly by default.

Create explicit response representations.

---

# 339. AI Error Rule

AI SHOULD reuse the canonical API error/problem model.

Do not create endpoint-specific ad hoc envelopes.

---

# 340. AI Pagination Rule

AI MUST add bounded pagination to collections capable of meaningful growth.

It SHOULD NOT generate `findMany()`-style unlimited public endpoints.

---

# 341. AI Idempotency Rule

Before generating:

```text
payment
order
invitation
provisioning
webhook processing
```

AI MUST evaluate duplicate execution.

---

# 342. AI Retry Rule

AI MUST NOT add retries without identifying:

```text
failure class
operation idempotency
attempt limit
backoff
```

---

# 343. AI Timeout Rule

AI-generated outbound HTTP calls require bounded timeouts where the platform supports them.

---

# 344. AI OpenAPI Rule

When an API contract changes, AI SHOULD update the authoritative OpenAPI definition in the same change.

---

# 345. AI Compatibility Rule

AI MUST evaluate whether an API modification breaks active consumers.

Do not casually:

```text
rename fields
remove fields
change types
change status codes
tighten required input
```

---

# 346. AI Security Rule

AI MUST apply the Security Gold Standard to:

```text
public APIs
Route Handlers
Server Functions exposed to clients
webhooks
service APIs
```

---

# 347. AI Rate-Limit Rule

AI SHOULD consider rate/resource limiting for abuse-sensitive endpoints.

Do not mechanically rate-limit every internal operation.

---

# 348. AI Webhook Rule

AI-generated webhook handlers MUST consider:

```text
signature verification
replay
duplicate delivery
idempotency
fast acknowledgement
```

---

# 349. AI Documentation Rule

AI-generated APIs are incomplete without updated:

```text
schema
examples
error documentation
consumer documentation
```

where the API is consumer-facing.

---

# 350. AI Gold Rule

When uncertain:

```text
Stable semantics
>
Explicit contracts
>
Correct authorization
>
Backward compatibility
>
Convenience
```

---

# 351. Golden API Rules

**1. APIs are contracts.**

**2. Design the contract before allowing implementation details to define it.**

**3. Use HTTP semantics correctly.**

**4. Prefer nouns for REST resources.**

**5. Use explicit domain actions when CRUD would hide important behavior.**

**6. One API surface uses one consistent naming convention.**

**7. Validate every untrusted request at runtime.**

**8. Authentication proves identity; authorization grants access.**

**9. Authorize the specific object and action.**

**10. Tenant IDs supplied by clients are claims, not authority.**

**11. Prevent mass assignment.**

**12. Return only required fields.**

**13. Never expose persistence models automatically.**

**14. Use standard HTTP status codes.**

**15. Use one predictable machine-readable error model.**

**16. Do not make clients parse error strings.**

**17. Paginate collections that can grow.**

**18. Bound request and response sizes.**

**19. Use deterministic pagination ordering.**

**20. Protect repeatable high-impact writes with idempotency.**

**21. External calls have timeouts.**

**22. Retries are bounded and semantics-aware.**

**23. Webhooks may be duplicated, delayed, and reordered.**

**24. Version only when compatibility cannot reasonably be preserved.**

**25. Prefer additive evolution.**

**26. Deprecate before removing.**

**27. OpenAPI is part of the API contract.**

**28. Documentation changes with the contract.**

**29. Public APIs have explicit owners.**

**30. Internal APIs still require engineering discipline.**

**31. Observe every critical production API.**

**32. Test forbidden behavior, not only successful behavior.**

**33. Security, rate limits, and resource limits are API design concerns.**

**34. Database schema is not automatically API schema.**

**35. Consumer experience is part of API quality.**

---

# 352. Canonical API Standard

The organizational standard is:

> **APIs are designed and maintained as stable product contracts. HTTP APIs use standard protocol semantics, resource-oriented structures where appropriate, explicit domain actions where CRUD semantics would obscure business behavior, runtime schema validation, server-side authentication and authorization, bounded resource consumption, consistent machine-readable errors, and deliberate compatibility management. Database and internal implementation models are never exposed automatically as public contracts.**

> **Collections are paginated when they can grow, high-impact repeatable operations use idempotency where required, external dependencies have bounded timeouts and safe retry policies, multi-tenant operations enforce tenant isolation, and sensitive data is minimized in requests, responses, logs, and URLs. Webhooks are designed for authenticated, duplicate, delayed, and potentially out-of-order delivery.**

> **Meaningful HTTP APIs maintain an authoritative OpenAPI contract, consumer-facing documentation, tests, observability, explicit ownership, and a controlled lifecycle from design through deprecation and retirement. Breaking changes are avoided through additive evolution wherever practical and introduced only through intentional versioning and migration.**

A production-grade API should make it easy to answer:

```text
Who consumes this API?
Who owns it?
What resource or action does it represent?
How is the caller authenticated?
What exactly are they authorized to do?
Which tenant owns the resource?
What input is accepted?
What output is guaranteed?
How are errors represented?
How large can requests/results become?
How is pagination performed?
Can the request be retried?
Is it idempotent?
What happens when a dependency fails?
What is the rate limit?
How does the contract evolve?
Where is its authoritative schema?
How do we know it is healthy?
How do consumers migrate away from deprecated behavior?
```

If those questions cannot be answered from the contract and its documentation, the API is not yet production-grade.

For the standards baseline: as of **September 22, 2026**, OpenAPI lists **3.2.1**, published September 10, 2026, as its latest specification. Its purpose is specifically to provide a language-agnostic description of HTTP APIs usable by documentation, client/server generation, and testing tooling. citeturn232342search0turn232342search1

For errors, **RFC 9457** is the current IETF Problem Details standard and supersedes RFC 7807. It standardizes the `application/problem+json` model and supports stable problem types plus extensions for cases such as field-level validation errors. citeturn705625search0

In the master standard, the sequence now becomes:

**Foundations → Architecture → Framework → Security → Auth/AuthZ → Data & Database → API → Routes → State Management → Design Tokens → Layouts → Facade → Components → Forms → Patterns → Reusability → Testing → Performance → Observability → Infrastructure → Documentation → Governance.**


<!-- ===== state-management | engineering | standards/engineering/07-state-management.md ===== -->

# State Management Guidelines — Gold Standard

## 1. Purpose

These guidelines define the canonical standard for application state.

They govern:

- server state;
- URL state;
- form state;
- local component state;
- shared context;
- global client stores;
- derived state;
- persisted state;
- cached state;
- optimistic state;
- realtime state;
- synchronization;
- invalidation;
- hydration;
- state ownership.

The objective is to make state:

- predictable;
- minimal;
- correctly owned;
- recoverable;
- shareable where necessary;
- easy to invalidate;
- resistant to synchronization bugs.

The core principle is:

> **Every piece of state should have one authoritative owner. Everything else should be derived, projected, cached, or synchronized deliberately.**

---

# 2. State Is an Ownership Problem

Before choosing a library, ask:

```text
Who owns this value?
Where is its source of truth?
Who needs it?
How long should it live?
Should it survive refresh?
Should it be shareable?
Can it become stale?
```

State-management tools come after these decisions.

---

# 3. Canonical State Categories

Every application state SHOULD be classified into one of these categories:

```text
Server state
URL state
Form state
Local UI state
Contextual state
Global client state
Derived state
Persisted client state
Realtime state
```

Do not treat all state as one generic category.

---

# 4. State Selection Order

When deciding where state belongs, evaluate in this order:

```text
Can it be derived?
    ↓ yes
Do not store it.

Is the server authoritative?
    ↓ yes
Server state.

Does navigation/shareability define it?
    ↓ yes
URL state.

Is it unsaved user input?
    ↓ yes
Form state.

Does one component/subtree own it?
    ↓ yes
Local state.

Does a bounded subtree need it?
    ↓ yes
Context.

Does unrelated client UI require shared ephemeral state?
    ↓ yes
Global store.

Does it need persistence?
    ↓ yes
Persist only the minimum necessary state.
```

---

# 5. Golden State Hierarchy

Prefer:

```text
Derived
↓
Server
↓
URL
↓
Form
↓
Local
↓
Context
↓
Global store
↓
Persistent global store
```

The further down this hierarchy you go, the stronger the justification should be.

---

# 6. Minimize State

State creates:

- synchronization;
- lifecycle;
- invalidation;
- debugging;
- persistence;
- concurrency;

obligations.

Therefore:

> **The best state is often state you do not store.**

---

# 7. Single Source of Truth

Every important fact MUST have one authoritative source.

Bad:

```text
server user
+
global-store user
+
context user
+
local user
```

all independently mutable.

Good:

```text
server/user cache
→ authoritative remote representation

local components
→ consume derived projection
```

---

# 8. Duplicate State

Duplicate state is allowed only when explicitly treated as:

```text
cache
snapshot
draft
projection
optimistic representation
```

Its relationship to the source of truth MUST be clear.

---

# 9. Derived State

If a value can be calculated reliably from existing authoritative state, derive it.

Example:

```ts
const fullName = `${firstName} ${lastName}`
```

Do not store:

```text
firstName
lastName
fullName
```

and manually synchronize all three.

---

# 10. Derived Collections

Prefer:

```text
items
+
filter
→ filteredItems
```

rather than storing:

```text
items
filteredItems
```

independently.

---

# 11. Derived Counts

Prefer:

```text
items.length
```

rather than separately storing:

```text
itemCount
```

unless count comes from an independent server query or has different semantics.

---

# 12. Derived Booleans

Prefer:

```text
status === "loading"
```

rather than:

```text
status
isLoading
```

if one is fully derivable from the other.

---

# 13. Illegal State Combinations

Avoid:

```text
isLoading
isSuccess
isError
```

when combinations can contradict one another.

Prefer:

```text
status =
idle
loading
success
error
```

---

# 14. Server State

Server state is data whose authoritative source lives remotely.

Examples:

```text
User account
Projects
Invoices
Permissions
Notifications
Search results
Subscription state
```

The client does not own this data.

It holds a representation of it.

---

# 15. Server State Principle

Treat server state as:

```text
remote
potentially stale
shared
asynchronous
authoritative elsewhere
```

This makes it fundamentally different from local UI state.

---

# 16. Server-First Default

For server-rendered applications, initial server data SHOULD generally be obtained on the server where practical.

Prefer:

```text
Server Component
→ data layer
→ database/API
```

over:

```text
render empty page
→ useEffect
→ fetch
→ loading spinner
```

for initial data.

---

# 17. Do Not Copy Server State Into a Global Store

Avoid:

```text
fetch projects
↓
copy into global Zustand/Redux
↓
manually synchronize
```

unless the global store genuinely becomes an intentional application state machine.

Remote data should normally remain server/cache state.

---

# 18. Server State Cache

A client/server-state library MAY maintain a local cache.

That cache remains:

```text
cache
```

not independent product truth.

The server remains authoritative.

---

# 19. Server State Questions

For every server state query define:

```text
Query key
Freshness
Cache scope
Invalidation
Authorization
Error behavior
Loading behavior
```

---

# 20. Server State Freshness

Not all data needs the same freshness.

Examples:

```text
Permissions
→ correctness-sensitive

Billing balance
→ freshness-sensitive

Country list
→ highly cacheable

Activity feed
→ moderately stale acceptable
```

---

# 21. Avoid Arbitrary Refetching

Do not repeatedly fetch remote state simply because a component rendered.

Data fetching must have an intentional lifecycle.

---

# 22. Server State Deduplication

Equivalent concurrent requests SHOULD be deduplicated where platform/cache support makes this practical.

Avoid multiple components independently fetching the same canonical data unnecessarily.

---

# 23. Server State Ownership

Fetch data at the narrowest meaningful server ownership boundary.

Avoid giant page loaders returning unrelated data to every child.

---

# 24. Server State Mutations

A mutation should generally follow:

```text
Validate
↓
Authenticate
↓
Authorize
↓
Perform operation
↓
Persist
↓
Invalidate/update affected state
↓
Render/return result
```

---

# 25. Mutation Is Not State Assignment

Do not treat remote mutation as:

```text
globalStore.user.name = ...
```

The actual operation happens against the authoritative source.

The client representation is updated afterward.

---

# 26. Server State Invalidation

Every mutation MUST determine what existing remote representations became stale.

Examples:

```text
Create project
→ project collection stale

Rename project
→ project detail stale
→ relevant lists potentially stale

Delete project
→ project list stale
→ project detail no longer valid
```

---

# 27. Invalidate Narrowly

Prefer:

```text
invalidate affected project
invalidate affected project list
```

over:

```text
invalidate everything
```

when safe.

---

# 28. Avoid Fragile Manual Cache Mutation

Manual cache updates are appropriate when semantics are clear.

Do not manually reproduce complex backend state transitions across many cached queries if revalidation is safer.

---

# 29. Mutation Result Reuse

If a mutation returns the canonical updated resource, the client MAY update its cache directly.

Example:

```text
PATCH project
→ returns current Project
→ update project cache
```

---

# 30. Revalidation

Revalidate when:

- server performs additional transformations;
- multiple records may change;
- permissions influence result;
- computed values are difficult to reproduce safely.

---

# 31. Optimistic State

Optimistic updates represent expected future server state before confirmation.

Use them only when:

```text
success probability is high
rollback is understandable
user benefit is meaningful
```

---

# 32. Good Optimistic Operations

Typical candidates:

```text
Like
Toggle
Simple reorder
Minor label change
Low-risk preference
```

---

# 33. Risky Optimistic Operations

Be cautious with:

```text
Payments
Permission changes
Account deletion
Inventory reservation
Complex workflows
```

where failure has consequential meaning.

---

# 34. Optimistic Rollback

Every optimistic update MUST define:

```text
success reconciliation
failure rollback
concurrent update behavior
```

---

# 35. Optimistic State Is Temporary

Once the authoritative result returns:

```text
optimistic representation
→ reconcile with server truth
```

Do not keep an independent client version indefinitely.

---

# 36. URL State

URL state represents navigational/shareable application state.

Examples:

```text
Search query
Filters
Sorting
Pagination
Selected resource
Meaningful tab
Date range
View mode
```

---

# 37. URL State Principle

Use URL state when the user should reasonably expect:

```text
Refresh
Share
Bookmark
Back
Forward
```

to preserve the state.

---

# 38. Search State

Prefer:

```text
/projects?search=acme
```

over only:

```text
localSearchState = "acme"
```

when search results are a navigational state.

---

# 39. Filter State

Data-page filters SHOULD normally be URL-backed when users benefit from sharing or refreshing the filtered view.

---

# 40. Sort State

Sorting SHOULD generally be URL-backed on meaningful collection pages.

---

# 41. Pagination State

Pagination usually belongs in the URL.

Example:

```text
?page=3
```

or cursor representation where appropriate.

---

# 42. Meaningful Tabs

If selecting a tab changes meaningful page content and should be deep-linkable:

```text
URL state
```

is appropriate.

---

# 43. Cosmetic Tabs

If a tab is purely transient presentation with no value on refresh/share:

```text
local state
```

may be sufficient.

---

# 44. URL vs Local Test

Ask:

> If I send this URL to another user with equivalent access, should they see the same view?

If yes, URL state is likely appropriate.

---

# 45. Do Not Duplicate URL State

Bad:

```text
URL:
?status=active

Global store:
status = "pending"
```

Avoid competing sources of truth.

If the URL owns the state, derive UI from the URL.

---

# 46. URL Normalization

Invalid URL state SHOULD:

- fall back safely;
- be normalized;
- or be rejected predictably.

Never allow malformed query state to crash the page.

---

# 47. URL Serialization

Define one convention for:

```text
arrays
booleans
dates
enums
ranges
```

Do not let features invent independent encodings.

---

# 48. Sensitive State in URLs

Never store:

```text
passwords
session tokens
API keys
private secrets
sensitive personal data
```

in navigational URLs.

---

# 49. Form State

Form state represents user input not yet committed to authoritative state.

Examples:

```text
Input values
Touched state
Validation errors
Dirty state
Submission state
Draft changes
```

---

# 50. Form State Has Different Semantics

A form may intentionally diverge from server state.

Example:

```text
server name:
"Acme"

form draft:
"Acme International"
```

This divergence is correct until submission/cancellation.

---

# 51. Form Ownership

The form owns its unsaved input.

Do not update server/global canonical state for every keystroke unless the product intentionally implements autosave.

---

# 52. Server Data → Form Initial Values

Use remote data to initialize form state.

After initialization, clearly define whether later remote updates should:

```text
replace draft
merge
warn
be ignored
```

Do not reset user input unexpectedly.

---

# 53. Avoid Form Mirroring

Bad:

```text
form library
+
local useState for every field
+
global store copy
```

Choose one form-state owner.

---

# 54. Form Validation

Client-side validation is part of form UX.

Server-side validation remains authoritative.

Do not assume valid client form state means valid mutation input.

---

# 55. Field Errors

Field errors belong to form submission/validation state.

They should not become global application state.

---

# 56. Form Submission State

Form state MAY include:

```text
idle
submitting
success
error
```

Do not rely solely on global loading state.

---

# 57. Dirty State

Track dirty state when it influences:

- unsaved-change warning;
- save button;
- autosave;
- reset.

Do not compute complex dirty state independently if the form framework already owns it.

---

# 58. Draft Persistence

Persist form drafts only where losing them would materially harm the user.

Examples:

```text
Long application form
Long article editor
Complex workflow
```

Do not persist every two-field dialog.

---

# 59. Draft Keying

Persisted drafts MUST be scoped appropriately.

Example:

```text
user
resource
form version
```

Avoid one global key such as:

```text
draft
```

---

# 60. Draft Versioning

Persisted form structures may outlive deployments.

Include versioning/migration or safe discard behavior.

---

# 61. Draft Security

Do not persist sensitive form values in browser storage unnecessarily.

Examples:

```text
password
payment credentials
government ID
```

require strong scrutiny.

---

# 62. Autosave

Autosave requires explicit state:

```text
dirty
saving
saved
error
conflict
```

Users should understand whether changes are durable.

---

# 63. Autosave Debouncing

Debounce or batch autosave where appropriate.

Do not create a network mutation for every keystroke without need.

---

# 64. Autosave Conflict

Collaborative or multi-tab editing requires conflict semantics.

Do not silently overwrite newer server data.

---

# 65. Local Component State

Local state is the default for transient state owned by one component or tightly coupled subtree.

Examples:

```text
Dropdown open
Accordion expanded
Hovered item
Temporary selection
Local panel state
```

---

# 66. Keep State Local

If only one component needs state:

> Keep it there.

Do not move it into context/global store for theoretical reuse.

---

# 67. Lift State Only When Necessary

Move state upward when multiple sibling components need to coordinate around the same state.

Do not lift state to the application root prematurely.

---

# 68. Colocation

State SHOULD live near the code that owns its behavior.

Colocation improves:

- readability;
- deletion;
- refactoring;
- debugging.

---

# 69. Transient UI State

Typical local state:

```text
popover open
menu open
selected row during interaction
hovered chart item
```

Do not persist or globalize by default.

---

# 70. Modal State

Simple modal visibility usually belongs locally.

Example:

```text
isDeleteDialogOpen
```

unless modal state is route-backed or shared through a centralized workflow.

---

# 71. Route-Backed Modal

If a modal represents a meaningful deep-linkable destination:

```text
route/URL state
```

may be more appropriate than local modal state.

---

# 72. Controlled Components

Use controlled state when the parent needs to own or coordinate the value.

Example:

```text
value
onValueChange
```

---

# 73. Uncontrolled Components

Use internal/uncontrolled state when the state is genuinely encapsulated.

Do not expose control props automatically for every component.

---

# 74. Controlled/Uncontrolled Ambiguity

A component MUST NOT unpredictably switch between controlled and uncontrolled state.

The contract should be clear.

---

# 75. Context

Context is appropriate for bounded cross-tree state or dependencies.

Good examples:

```text
Theme
Compound component state
Editor context
Workspace UI context
Form sub-context
```

---

# 76. Context Is Not Automatically Global State

Context solves propagation.

It does not automatically solve:

- caching;
- selectors;
- persistence;
- complex updates;
- synchronization.

---

# 77. Context Scope

Providers SHOULD be placed at the lowest meaningful common ancestor.

Avoid putting feature-specific providers around the entire application.

---

# 78. Root Provider Discipline

Keep the application root provider tree small.

Avoid:

```text
<AuthProvider>
  <ProjectProvider>
    <BillingProvider>
      <SearchProvider>
        <ModalProvider>
          ...
```

when those concerns can remain route/feature scoped.

---

# 79. Context Update Cost

Large frequently-changing context values may trigger excessive rerenders.

Split contexts or use selectors/store architecture where actual performance requires it.

---

# 80. Stable Context Values

Avoid unnecessarily recreating complex provider values every render when identity stability matters.

Do not cargo-cult memoization when it does not.

---

# 81. Context for Dependencies

Context MAY provide stable runtime dependencies such as:

```text
locale
feature configuration
editor controller
```

when prop passing would be inappropriate.

---

# 82. Global Client State

Global client state is justified when unrelated parts of the client need to coordinate around shared ephemeral state.

Examples may include:

```text
Complex editor session
Realtime collaborative state
Cross-route draft workflow
Client-only desktop-like workspace state
```

---

# 83. Global Store Is Last Resort, Not First Choice

Do not create global stores for:

```text
server data
URL filters
simple form state
one modal
one component selection
```

without strong reason.

---

# 84. Global Store Qualification Test

Before creating a global store, verify:

```text
Multiple distant consumers exist.
State is genuinely client-owned.
URL is not the right owner.
Server is not the right owner.
Context alone is insufficient.
Persistence semantics are understood.
```

---

# 85. Store Boundaries

Prefer domain/feature-specific stores.

Example:

```text
editorStore
```

over:

```text
appStore
```

containing every application value.

---

# 86. Avoid Mega Stores

Avoid:

```text
user
projects
forms
filters
modals
notifications
theme
permissions
```

all inside one universal store.

Separate ownership.

---

# 87. Store Shape

Store canonical values.

Derive secondary values through selectors.

Avoid storing every derived representation.

---

# 88. Store Selectors

Consumers SHOULD subscribe only to state they need when the store system supports selectors.

This reduces unnecessary coupling and rerendering.

---

# 89. Store Actions

Complex global stores SHOULD expose meaningful operations.

Prefer:

```text
openDocument()
selectNode()
resetWorkspace()
```

over exposing arbitrary unrestricted mutation.

---

# 90. Store Invariants

If store state has valid transitions, centralize those transitions.

Do not let every component mutate low-level fields independently.

---

# 91. Global Store Serialization

If state is persisted, distinguish serializable durable state from runtime-only state.

Do not attempt to persist:

```text
DOM nodes
functions
connections
AbortController
service instances
```

---

# 92. Store Reset

Global stores SHOULD have a clear reset lifecycle.

Examples:

```text
logout
tenant switch
session expiration
```

must not leave stale state from the previous user/tenant.

---

# 93. Tenant Switching

On tenant/workspace change, explicitly reset or re-scope:

```text
client stores
queries
drafts
caches
subscriptions
```

where tenant-specific.

---

# 94. User Switching

Never allow persistent state from user A to leak into user B's session on shared devices or long-lived browser state.

---

# 95. Persistent Client State

Persistence means state survives page refresh or browser restarts.

Possible mechanisms:

```text
URL
cookie
localStorage
IndexedDB
server
```

Choose based on semantics.

---

# 96. Persist Only What Must Survive

Do not persist merely because it is easy.

Every persisted state introduces:

- migration;
- stale data;
- security;
- cleanup;
- synchronization.

---

# 97. Persistence Decision

Ask:

```text
Should this survive reload?
Should it survive browser restart?
Should it follow the user across devices?
Is it sensitive?
```

Answers determine storage location.

---

# 98. Cross-Device State

If state should follow the user across devices:

```text
server
```

is usually the correct owner.

Browser storage is device-specific.

---

# 99. Browser Preference State

Local persistence is appropriate for some device/browser preferences.

Examples:

```text
sidebar collapsed
table density
dismissed local hint
```

when server sync is unnecessary.

---

# 100. User Preferences

Important user preferences SHOULD generally be persisted server-side if they should:

- follow account;
- work on multiple devices;
- participate in backup.

---

# 101. Theme Preference

Theme may be:

```text
system
light
dark
```

and persisted via cookie/local preference depending on rendering requirements.

Avoid hydration flashes by making server/client theme strategy coherent.

---

# 102. LocalStorage

Use `localStorage` only for non-sensitive browser-owned persistence.

Remember:

```text
available to client JavaScript
not server-authoritative
not cross-device
```

---

# 103. IndexedDB

Use IndexedDB for larger structured offline/client datasets where requirements justify it.

Do not introduce it for trivial preferences.

---

# 104. Cookies

Cookies are appropriate for request-relevant server-visible state.

Examples:

```text
session
locale
theme hint
```

Apply Security Gold Standard attributes.

---

# 105. Sensitive State

Do not persist sensitive state in browser storage unless architecture explicitly accepts the risk.

Never treat local storage as a secure credential vault.

---

# 106. Persistent State Versioning

Persisted client state MUST be treated like a schema.

Define:

```text
version
migration
fallback/reset
```

for state likely to outlive deployments.

---

# 107. Stale Persisted State

On load, persisted state may no longer be valid.

Validate before use.

Do not assume yesterday's browser state matches today's application contract.

---

# 108. Persistence Expiration

Some persisted values SHOULD expire.

Examples:

```text
temporary drafts
recent search
wizard state
```

Define TTL where stale state creates confusion.

---

# 109. Hydration

Hydration bridges server-rendered output and client state.

Initial client state MUST be compatible with server-rendered UI.

---

# 110. Hydration Mismatch

Do not render one value on the server and a different immediate client value without intentional handling.

Typical causes:

```text
localStorage
current time
random values
browser dimensions
```

---

# 111. Persisted State Hydration

If client-only persisted state is required, design a loading/initialization strategy that avoids incorrect initial UI.

Do not globally suppress hydration warnings.

---

# 112. Server-to-Client Initial State

Pass only the minimum client state required.

Do not serialize complete server caches or sensitive resources automatically.

---

# 113. Client-to-Server State

Any value sent from the client is untrusted.

State-management architecture does not provide security.

Server MUST validate and authorize mutations.

---

# 114. State and Authentication

Authentication session state has a server/security owner.

Client UI may derive:

```text
signed in
signed out
loading
```

but must not independently create authorization truth.

---

# 115. Permissions

Permissions SHOULD be authoritative on the server.

Client-side permission state exists for UX only.

Never rely on:

```text
canDelete === false
```

in client state as the security boundary.

---

# 116. Permission Caching

Permission representations may be cached but should be invalidated appropriately after:

```text
role changes
membership changes
ownership changes
```

---

# 117. Realtime State

Realtime state represents server state delivered through subscriptions.

Examples:

```text
presence
chat
live metrics
collaborative changes
```

---

# 118. Realtime Source of Truth

Determine whether realtime messages are:

```text
authoritative events
cache updates
notifications to refetch
```

Do not treat every event payload as authoritative full state automatically.

---

# 119. Realtime Reconciliation

A safe pattern may be:

```text
event received
↓
update known cache
or
invalidate/refetch
```

depending on event semantics.

---

# 120. Realtime Duplication

Realtime messages may arrive:

```text
twice
late
out of order
```

State logic must tolerate this where protocol permits it.

---

# 121. Presence State

Presence is usually ephemeral.

Do not persist indefinitely as durable business state.

---

# 122. Multi-Tab State

Browser tabs may represent multiple concurrent client sessions.

If state needs synchronization across tabs, define it explicitly.

Possible mechanisms:

```text
BroadcastChannel
storage events
service worker
server realtime
```

---

# 123. Multi-Tab Auth

Logout/session invalidation SHOULD eventually propagate to other open tabs.

Do not leave stale privileged UI indefinitely.

---

# 124. Cross-Tab Drafts

Be cautious synchronizing drafts automatically.

Two tabs editing the same resource can create data loss.

Define conflict behavior.

---

# 125. State Machines

Use explicit state machines for interaction/workflow states with meaningful transitions.

Examples:

```text
upload
checkout
onboarding
approval
connection
```

---

# 126. State Machine Example

Prefer:

```text
idle
↓
uploading
↓
processing
↓
complete
```

with explicit failure transitions.

Avoid many independent booleans.

---

# 127. State Transition Validation

Only valid transitions should be possible.

Example:

```text
processing
→ complete

complete
→ uploading
```

may be invalid unless explicitly restarted.

---

# 128. Async State

Async operations SHOULD distinguish:

```text
idle
pending
success
error
```

or an equivalent model.

Do not interpret `data === undefined` as every possible loading/error state.

---

# 129. Previous Data

Some UI should retain previous successful data while a new request loads.

Example:

```text
filter change
→ keep table
→ indicate refreshing
```

This differs from initial loading.

---

# 130. Initial Loading vs Refreshing

Distinguish:

```text
no data yet + loading
```

from:

```text
existing data + refreshing
```

They usually deserve different UX.

---

# 131. Error State

Errors SHOULD live at the narrowest scope capable of recovering appropriately.

Do not put every request error into one global error string.

---

# 132. Global Errors

Global error state is appropriate only for truly application-global incidents.

Examples:

```text
session invalidated
application offline
critical configuration failure
```

---

# 133. Toasts Are Not State Ownership

A toast is feedback.

It should not become the only representation of persistent failure state.

Important errors belong near the failed operation.

---

# 134. Loading Indicators Are Derived

Avoid manually storing:

```text
isSaving
```

when the mutation framework already exposes pending state.

Derive from operation state.

---

# 135. Global Loading Spinner

Avoid one global application loading flag for unrelated operations.

Example:

```text
global.isLoading
```

cannot meaningfully represent simultaneous independent requests.

---

# 136. Operation-Specific Pending State

Prefer:

```text
createProjectPending
deleteMemberPending
```

or mutation-instance state where relevant.

---

# 137. Concurrent Operations

State architecture must support multiple simultaneous operations.

Do not assume:

```text
one request at a time
```

in modern applications.

---

# 138. Request Identity

For concurrent requests, state may require request/resource identity.

Avoid one shared result slot for multiple active resources.

---

# 139. Race Conditions

Common race:

```text
search "a" starts
search "ab" starts
"ab" finishes
"a" finishes
old result overwrites new
```

Prevent stale-response overwrite.

---

# 140. Request Cancellation

Cancel obsolete requests where practical.

Alternatively ensure stale results are ignored.

---

# 141. Debounced State

Debounce effects, not necessarily the visible input value.

Preferred:

```text
input state updates immediately
↓
debounced query changes later
```

This preserves responsive typing.

---

# 142. Throttled State

Use throttling for high-frequency signals where full fidelity is unnecessary.

Examples:

```text
scroll
resize
pointer movement
```

Do not make business state eventually update by throttling without careful semantics.

---

# 143. Undo

Undo architecture requires intentional history.

Possible models:

```text
local operation history
command history
server compensating operation
```

Do not implement undo by retaining arbitrary uncontrolled snapshots.

---

# 144. Redo

Redo is usually meaningful only when state transitions are deterministic and history is well modeled.

---

# 145. Selection State

Transient list selection MAY remain local.

If selection drives:

```text
bulk operations
URL navigation
cross-panel coordination
```

scope it accordingly.

---

# 146. Table State

Possible table state categories:

```text
Pagination → URL
Filters → URL
Sort → URL
Row selection → local
Column visibility → local/user preference
Column width → local/user preference
Server rows → server state
```

Do not place all table state into one generic store automatically.

---

# 147. Dashboard State

Dashboard widgets may combine:

```text
server data
URL filters
local expansion state
user preferences
```

Keep these sources distinct.

---

# 148. Wizard State

Wizard state may involve:

```text
route/current step
form draft
server-created resource
```

Model these separately.

Avoid one massive wizard object unless it is genuinely the domain draft.

---

# 149. Wizard URL

If steps should support refresh/back/deep linking, step identity SHOULD be route/URL state.

---

# 150. Onboarding State

Distinguish:

```text
server-completed onboarding milestones
```

from:

```text
current temporary UI step
```

Do not confuse durable account state with navigation.

---

# 151. Feature Flags

Feature flags come from an authoritative configuration service/server.

The client may consume their result.

Do not treat client-modifiable feature state as authority.

---

# 152. Experiment State

Experiment assignment should have one authoritative allocation strategy.

Avoid reassigning randomly on every render.

---

# 153. Locale State

Locale may be owned by:

```text
URL
account preference
cookie/request context
```

according to internationalization architecture.

Choose one canonical priority.

---

# 154. Responsive State

Do not store viewport width in global state merely to style layouts.

Prefer CSS media/container queries.

Use JavaScript state only when behavioral differences genuinely require it.

---

# 155. Online/Offline State

Connectivity state is advisory.

`navigator.onLine` or equivalent does not guarantee server reachability.

Design offline behavior around actual operations.

---

# 156. Offline State

Offline-first applications require explicit architecture for:

```text
local persistence
queueing writes
conflict resolution
sync
schema migration
```

Do not add offline storage casually.

---

# 157. Offline Mutation Queue

If writes are queued offline, define:

```text
operation identity
ordering
retry
idempotency
conflict behavior
expiration
```

---

# 158. Conflict Resolution

Offline/collaborative systems may use:

```text
last-write-wins
optimistic concurrency
merge
CRDT
manual conflict resolution
```

Choose according to domain semantics.

---

# 159. Do Not Use LWW Automatically

Last-write-wins can silently destroy valid work.

Use only when this tradeoff is acceptable.

---

# 160. State Normalization

Large interconnected client stores MAY normalize entities by identity.

Do not normalize small/simple state automatically.

Normalization creates its own complexity.

---

# 161. Normalized Server Cache

If a data library handles normalized or keyed server caching, do not duplicate another normalization layer unless needed.

---

# 162. State Denormalization

UI-oriented projections MAY be denormalized for convenient rendering.

They should remain derived from canonical state.

---

# 163. Memoization

Memoization is not state management.

Do not store values purely to avoid calculation when memoization/derivation is sufficient.

---

# 164. Memoization Rule

Use memoization when:

- computation is materially expensive;
- reference identity matters;
- measurement supports it.

Do not memoize every derived value.

---

# 165. Effects

Effects synchronize React/client state with external systems.

Examples:

```text
subscription
browser API
imperative third-party widget
```

They are not a general-purpose state pipeline.

---

# 166. Avoid Effect-Based Derivation

Bad:

```text
state A changes
↓
useEffect
↓
set state B
```

when B can be calculated during render.

---

# 167. Avoid Effect Chains

Avoid:

```text
A changes
→ effect updates B
→ effect updates C
→ effect updates D
```

This produces fragile temporal coupling.

Model the source state better.

---

# 168. Event-Driven Updates

User-driven state changes SHOULD occur directly in event handlers or store actions when possible.

Do not detect a button action later through effects unnecessarily.

---

# 169. Initialization

State initialization SHOULD be deterministic.

Avoid complex effects whose only purpose is to initialize values that could be calculated at construction/render time.

---

# 170. Reset Semantics

Every complex stateful feature SHOULD define reset behavior.

Examples:

```text
close dialog
cancel edit
change resource
logout
switch tenant
```

---

# 171. State Leakage

Component reuse must not accidentally retain old state for a new resource.

Use stable resource identity and component keys intentionally where reset semantics require them.

---

# 172. React Keys

Keys identify component state ownership.

Changing the key intentionally resets component-local state.

Use this deliberately, not as a random rendering fix.

---

# 173. State and Navigation

Decide whether navigating between resources should:

```text
preserve local state
reset local state
restore history state
```

according to UX expectations.

---

# 174. Back Navigation

Browser back SHOULD restore meaningful URL-driven state.

This is a major reason not to hide navigational state in global stores.

---

# 175. Scroll State

Browser/framework scroll restoration SHOULD be preferred.

Store custom scroll position only when application architecture requires it.

---

# 176. Local Persistence and Privacy

Persisted state can reveal user behavior on shared devices.

Do not persist:

```text
recent sensitive searches
private resource names
sensitive drafts
```

without considering privacy.

---

# 177. Store Encryption

Client-side encryption cannot make browser-controlled state fully trusted.

Do not treat encrypted local storage as equivalent to server-side secret storage.

---

# 178. State Cleanup

Persistent and global state requires cleanup.

Define cleanup for:

```text
logout
expiration
resource deletion
tenant deletion
version migration
```

---

# 179. Resource Deletion

When a resource is deleted:

```text
server cache
URL
selection
drafts
global store references
realtime subscriptions
```

must no longer assume it exists.

---

# 180. Cache Keys

Server-state cache keys SHOULD encode all state that changes the result.

Examples:

```text
resource ID
tenant
filters
sort
page
locale
permission-relevant scope
```

---

# 181. Cache-Key Consistency

Centralize key construction where complexity warrants it.

Avoid slightly different representations of the same query.

---

# 182. Cache Authorization

Never allow caches to cross authorization boundaries.

A cache hit must not bypass current permission checks where security requires fresh authorization.

---

# 183. Cache Staleness

Explicitly distinguish:

```text
fresh
stale but usable
invalid
```

where state-management library semantics support it.

---

# 184. Stale-While-Revalidate

Stale-while-revalidate is useful when temporary staleness is acceptable.

Example:

```text
render cached value
↓
refresh in background
↓
replace when current result arrives
```

---

# 185. Freshness Is Domain-Specific

Do not choose one universal stale time.

A configuration page and live trading price have different freshness requirements.

---

# 186. Cache Expiry Is Not Invalidation

TTL answers:

> How long may this representation remain cached?

Invalidation answers:

> What known change makes it incorrect now?

Use both where necessary.

---

# 187. Mutation Invalidation Map

For important domains, know relationships such as:

```text
createProject
→ projects list
→ dashboard project count

updateProject
→ project detail
→ projects list

deleteProject
→ project detail
→ projects list
→ search result
```

---

# 188. Avoid Manual Synchronization Explosion

If every mutation requires manually modifying 12 client collections, state architecture is probably too duplicated.

Prefer canonical cache/invalidation patterns.

---

# 189. Query Keys Are Contracts

Changing query-key structure can break cache behavior.

Treat central cache-key conventions intentionally.

---

# 190. State Persistence vs Cache Persistence

Do not confuse:

```text
persisted application state
```

with:

```text
persisted remote cache
```

A persisted cache can be stale immediately when reopened.

---

# 191. Persisted Server Cache

If server cache is persisted client-side:

```text
validate age
scope to user
scope to tenant
clear on logout
```

and treat it as untrusted stale data.

---

# 192. SSR Cache Isolation

Server-side request caches MUST NOT accidentally share user-specific data across users.

Understand request/process/global cache scope.

---

# 193. State Security

State location does not create authorization.

Anything in:

```text
URL
local state
context
global store
localStorage
IndexedDB
```

is client-controlled.

---

# 194. Hidden State Is Not Secure

Do not assume state is secure because:

```text
not shown in UI
not exposed in URL
stored in Redux
encoded
```

Client environments are inspectable.

---

# 195. Sensitive Server State

Sensitive state should remain server-side whenever client knowledge is unnecessary.

---

# 196. Global Store and Secrets

Never store server secrets in global client state.

---

# 197. State Observability

Complex state systems SHOULD be debuggable.

Useful capabilities include:

```text
action logging
state inspection
query inspection
request IDs
realtime event tracing
```

in development.

---

# 198. Production State Logging

Do not dump entire state trees into production logs.

They may contain:

```text
PII
tokens
draft content
sensitive resource data
```

---

# 199. Store DevTools

Development tools MAY be used for debugging.

Ensure production exposure does not leak sensitive data or create unsafe mutation capabilities.

---

# 200. State Testing

Test state behavior according to ownership.

```text
Derived state
→ unit tests where logic is complex

Form state
→ interaction tests

Server state
→ integration tests

URL state
→ navigation tests

Global state
→ store/state-machine tests

Persistence
→ reload/migration tests
```

---

# 201. Test User Outcomes

Prefer tests such as:

```text
user applies filter
URL updates
results update
back restores previous filter
```

over tests tightly coupled to implementation details such as a specific store action name.

---

# 202. Invalidation Tests

Important mutations SHOULD verify affected views eventually reflect authoritative state.

---

# 203. Optimistic Tests

Test:

```text
optimistic success
optimistic failure
rollback
concurrent mutation
```

where optimistic UI is used.

---

# 204. Persistence Tests

Persisted state SHOULD test:

```text
reload
old version
corrupt value
logout
tenant switch
```

where relevant.

---

# 205. Multi-Tab Tests

Security-sensitive or collaboration-heavy applications SHOULD test multi-tab scenarios.

---

# 206. Realtime Tests

Test:

```text
duplicate event
out-of-order event
disconnect
reconnect
missed events
```

where protocol requires resilience.

---

# 207. State Performance

Performance problems can arise from:

```text
oversized providers
global rerenders
large store subscriptions
expensive derived selectors
high-frequency events
```

Measure before redesigning.

---

# 208. Rerendering Is Not Automatically a Problem

Do not create architectural complexity merely to eliminate harmless rerenders.

Optimize when user-visible or measured cost exists.

---

# 209. Selector Granularity

Use narrow selectors when large global stores create unnecessary rerendering.

---

# 210. High-Frequency State

High-frequency values such as:

```text
pointer position
animation values
scroll
```

should not necessarily flow through ordinary application-global state.

Use appropriate specialized mechanisms.

---

# 211. Animation State

Visual animation state SHOULD generally remain close to the visual system.

Do not persist or globalize ephemeral animation progress.

---

# 212. Server State Libraries
