# 200. Browser Storage

Large synchronous browser-storage operations can block execution.

Use appropriate storage mechanisms for large data.

---

# 201. Hydration Mismatch Workarounds

Do not defer huge parts of the application to client-only rendering merely to avoid hydration design problems.

Fix ownership/rendering architecture.

---

# 202. Initial Render

Prioritize content users need immediately.

Secondary UI may load progressively.

---

# 203. Above-the-Fold Principle

Do not equate above-the-fold with "download everything immediately."

Only genuinely critical content receives priority.

---

# 204. Lazy Routes

Large independent application routes SHOULD load only their required code where framework routing supports this naturally.

---

# 205. Admin Code

Do not ship large admin-only functionality to ordinary users when it can remain route-separated.

---

# 206. Role-Based Code Loading

Security must remain server-side, but client bundles MAY avoid loading large privileged-only interfaces unnecessarily.

---

# 207. Feature Flags

Disabled heavy features SHOULD ideally not impose substantial client bundle/runtime cost where build/runtime architecture allows avoidance.

---

# 208. Locale Bundles

Do not ship all translations to all users if routing/build architecture can load only required locale data.

---

# 209. Charting Libraries

Charts can be expensive.

Load chart code only where needed.

---

# 210. Editors

Rich text/code editors are strong candidates for lazy loading.

---

# 211. PDF / Document Tools

Heavy document tooling SHOULD load on demand.

---

# 212. Maps

Interactive map SDKs are often large third-party dependencies.

Use lightweight placeholders/facades until interaction if appropriate.

---

# 213. Bundle Analysis

Frontend projects SHOULD support bundle inspection.

Use it to identify:

```text
large modules
duplicate libraries
unexpected client dependencies
```

---

# 214. Bundle Regression

Significant bundle-size regressions SHOULD be visible in CI/review.

---

# 215. Bundle Budget

Set budgets by route/chunk where useful.

Avoid only one global number that hides large route regressions.

---

# 216. Duplicate Dependencies

Detect multiple versions/copies of heavy libraries where consolidation is practical.

---

# 217. Tree Shaking

Libraries intended for frontend reuse SHOULD support effective dead-code elimination where possible.

---

# 218. Import Discipline

Prefer targeted imports where package architecture requires them.

Avoid import patterns known to pull unnecessary modules.

---

# 219. Client/Server Boundary Imports

Server-only libraries MUST NOT leak into browser bundles.

Use architectural import restrictions.

---

# 220. Source Maps

Source maps improve production diagnosis but should be delivered/configured in a way that does not create unnecessary user payload or sensitive exposure.

---

# 221. Profiling

Performance optimization workflow:

```text
Observe
↓
Measure
↓
Profile
↓
Identify bottleneck
↓
Change
↓
Measure again
```

---

# 222. Never Optimize Without Re-Measurement

Every meaningful optimization should verify:

```text
Did it improve the target metric?
Did another metric regress?
```

---

# 223. CPU Profiling

Use CPU profiles for:

```text
slow JS
server compute
serialization
expensive render
```

---

# 224. Memory Profiling

Use memory profiles for:

```text
leaks
large retention
high allocation churn
```

---

# 225. Network Profiling

Inspect:

```text
request waterfall
connection reuse
resource priority
cache status
payload size
```

---

# 226. Database Profiling

Use:

```text
slow query logs
EXPLAIN / execution plans
lock monitoring
connection metrics
```

---

# 227. Distributed Tracing

Tracing is useful for identifying latency across:

```text
gateway
service
database
provider
queue
```

---

# 228. Trace Sampling

Use an appropriate tracing sample strategy.

Do not generate more telemetry than the system can economically retain.

---

# 229. RUM

Production web applications SHOULD collect Real User Monitoring where privacy and architecture allow it.

---

# 230. RUM Context

Useful dimensions may include:

```text
route
device class
network
application version
```

without high-cardinality sensitive labels.

---

# 231. Synthetic Monitoring

Use controlled synthetic navigation to detect regressions even when production traffic is low.

---

# 232. Lighthouse / Lab Tools

Lab tools MAY be used for:

```text
development
CI
diagnosis
baseline comparison
```

They do not replace field data.

---

# 233. Benchmark Environment

Performance benchmarks require stable:

```text
hardware
runtime
dataset
configuration
```

for meaningful comparison.

---

# 234. Benchmark Noise

Do not fail builds on insignificant variations inside normal measurement noise.

---

# 235. Baseline

Performance changes SHOULD compare against a known baseline.

---

# 236. Regression Threshold

Define what constitutes a significant regression.

Examples:

```text
bundle +X%
latency +Y%
query count +N
```

according to project risk.

---

# 237. CI Performance Gates

CI SHOULD enforce stable mechanical budgets such as:

```text
bundle size
query count
asset size
```

where reliable.

---

# 238. CI Latency Benchmarks

Latency benchmarks MAY run in CI when environment variance can be controlled sufficiently.

---

# 239. Performance Test Tiering

Potential tiers:

```text
PR
→ quick budget checks

Main/nightly
→ broader benchmarks

Pre-release
→ load/performance testing

Production
→ RUM
```

---

# 240. Query Regression Tests

Critical paths MAY assert query-count ceilings.

Use as regression guardrails, not universal dogma.

---

# 241. Load Testing

Load testing verifies behavior at expected concurrency.

It should answer:

```text
capacity
latency
error rate
resource saturation
```

---

# 242. Load Test Model

Use realistic workload distributions.

Do not test only:

```text
one endpoint
constant request rate
perfect cache hits
```

if production is more complex.

---

# 243. Expected Peak

Test expected peak load with margin.

---

# 244. Stress Testing

Stress testing determines behavior beyond expected capacity.

Identify:

```text
saturation point
failure behavior
recovery
```

---

# 245. Spike Testing

Spike tests evaluate abrupt traffic changes.

Useful for products with bursty traffic.

---

# 246. Soak Testing

Long-duration testing detects:

```text
memory leaks
connection leaks
resource buildup
queue growth
```

---

# 247. Performance Under Failure

Performance testing SHOULD include degraded dependencies where resilience matters.

Retries and timeouts can drastically alter latency under outage.

---

# 248. Cache-Warm vs Cold

Measure both where relevant:

```text
cold cache
warm cache
```

Do not publish only best-case warmed results.

---

# 249. Cold Start vs Warm

Serverless/elastic environments should measure both paths.

---

# 250. Database Dataset Size

Performance tests must use representative data scale.

A query fast on 100 rows may fail at 100 million.

---

# 251. Cardinality

Representative data should model realistic:

```text
tenant sizes
relationship counts
distribution
skew
```

---

# 252. Hot Tenants

Large tenants may require separate performance analysis from typical tenants.

---

# 253. Multi-Tenant Fairness

One tenant SHOULD NOT consume unbounded shared resources.

Apply:

```text
quotas
concurrency controls
rate limits
```

where needed.

---

# 254. Noisy Neighbor

Monitor tenant workloads capable of degrading others.

---

# 255. Rate Limiting

Rate limits can protect capacity but should not substitute for fixing inefficient architecture.

---

# 256. Backpressure

Systems SHOULD slow/reject work before uncontrolled overload causes collapse.

---

# 257. Load Shedding

Low-priority operations MAY be shed during extreme capacity pressure.

Protect critical paths.

---

# 258. Graceful Degradation

Performance degradation under load should remain understandable.

Better:

```text
recommendations disabled
```

than:

```text
entire checkout unavailable
```

where dependencies are optional.

---

# 259. Capacity Planning

Track:

```text
traffic growth
storage growth
CPU
memory
connections
queue depth
provider quotas
```

before reaching limits.

---

# 260. Headroom

Production systems SHOULD maintain capacity headroom appropriate to scaling architecture.

Running continuously at maximum capacity is fragile.

---

# 261. Autoscaling

Autoscaling should use signals aligned with actual bottlenecks.

Examples:

```text
CPU
concurrency
queue depth
requests
```

---

# 262. Scaling Delay

Account for the time required to add capacity.

Reactive autoscaling may not handle instant spikes without baseline headroom.

---

# 263. Vertical Scaling

Vertical scaling is often the simplest performance improvement.

Do not dismiss it merely because horizontal scaling appears more sophisticated.

---

# 264. Horizontal Scaling

Use horizontal scaling when workload supports it and availability/capacity requirements justify it.

---

# 265. Database Scaling Order

Before sharding, evaluate:

```text
query optimization
indexes
better schema
vertical scale
read replicas
archival
partitioning
```

---

# 266. Sharding

Sharding SHOULD require demonstrated scale need.

It introduces significant query and operational complexity.

---

# 267. Read Replicas

Use read replicas for workloads that tolerate replication lag.

---

# 268. Read-After-Write

Do not route freshness-sensitive reads to stale replicas blindly.

---

# 269. Compression Tradeoff

Higher compression may reduce bytes while increasing CPU.

Choose appropriate compression level for:

```text
dynamic
static
edge-cached
```

resources.

---

# 270. Static Asset Precompression

Build/CDN infrastructure SHOULD precompress static assets where supported.

---

# 271. HTTP Versions

Use modern HTTP protocol support provided by infrastructure.

Do not build application architecture around assumptions from old connection limits unnecessarily.

---

# 272. Connection Reuse

Avoid repeatedly establishing expensive connections where pooling/reuse is appropriate.

---

# 273. Keep-Alive

Use appropriate persistent connection behavior for:

```text
database
HTTP dependencies
```

according to client/server architecture.

---

# 274. DNS

Excessive third-party origins create DNS/TLS/connection overhead.

Minimize unnecessary origins.

---

# 275. Origin Consolidation

Do not split static assets across many domains without measured benefit.

---

# 276. Request Count

Request count remains useful, but payload and CPU cost matter more than simplistic "fewest requests" rules under modern HTTP.

---

# 277. Payload Budget

Large API payloads SHOULD have explicit review.

---

# 278. GraphQL Performance

GraphQL APIs MUST guard against:

```text
unbounded query complexity
N+1
deep nesting
large result sets
```

---

# 279. GraphQL DataLoader

Batching/caching mechanisms MAY solve repeated backend lookups where appropriate.

---

# 280. REST Performance

REST collection endpoints must remain:

```text
paginated
bounded
filterable
```

rather than requiring clients to download everything.

---

# 281. API Compression

Large JSON responses SHOULD be compressed where infrastructure supports it.

---

# 282. Mobile Performance

Mobile performance must consider:

```text
slower CPU
limited memory
battery
cellular latency
bandwidth
```

---

# 283. Develop on Representative Devices

Do not use a high-end development machine as the only performance test device.

---

# 284. Network Throttling

Use network throttling for diagnosis.

Remember simulated throttling is not identical to real-world mobile conditions.

---

# 285. Low-End Device Testing

Consumer-facing products SHOULD periodically test representative lower-performance devices.

---

# 286. Battery and Power

Avoid unnecessary:

```text
polling
animation
background work
repeated network calls
```

on mobile.

---

# 287. Polling

Polling intervals SHOULD reflect actual freshness needs.

Do not poll every second for data that changes once an hour.

---

# 288. Visibility-Aware Polling

Pause/reduce appropriate polling when pages are backgrounded or inactive.

---

# 289. Realtime vs Polling

Choose realtime connections when latency requirements justify persistent infrastructure.

Polling may be simpler and cheaper.

---

# 290. WebSockets

Realtime systems should monitor:

```text
connection count
message rate
reconnect storms
backpressure
```

---

# 291. Reconnect Jitter

Use backoff/jitter for mass reconnect after outage.

---

# 292. Performance and Accessibility

Do not sacrifice accessibility for micro-performance gains.

Native semantic controls are often both accessible and efficient.

---

# 293. Performance and Security

Do not weaken:

```text
authorization
encryption
validation
security headers
```

to improve benchmarks.

---

# 294. Performance and Correctness

Correctness outranks speed.

An instant wrong answer is not an optimization.

---

# 295. Performance and Maintainability

Avoid obscure micro-optimizations without measured user benefit.

Readable maintainable code is usually preferable until profiling demonstrates a hotspot.

---

# 296. Premature Optimization

Do not introduce:

```text
cache
sharding
worker
custom memory pool
complex memoization
```

without a demonstrated need.

---

# 297. Performance Debt

Known performance compromises SHOULD document:

```text
impact
affected users
owner
trigger for remediation
```

---

# 298. Performance Incident

Severe sustained latency degradation can be an operational incident even when requests still technically succeed.

---

# 299. Performance Alerting

Alert on meaningful:

```text
latency
saturation
queue age
database contention
```

before complete failure where possible.

---

# 300. Performance Review Triggers

Performance review SHOULD occur for:

```text
new heavy dependency
new dashboard
new large table
new image-heavy experience
new provider
new background pipeline
new high-volume query
major framework change
```

---

# 301. Frontend Performance Checklist

```text
□ CWV targets defined
□ LCP resource identified
□ LCP image not lazy-loaded
□ Below-fold images lazy-loaded
□ Image dimensions reserved
□ Responsive images used
□ Font families/weights bounded
□ JavaScript budget reviewed
□ Heavy features code-split
□ Unnecessary client boundaries avoided
□ Third-party scripts reviewed
□ Layout shifts checked
□ Interaction responsiveness checked
□ Bundle analysis reviewed
```

---

# 302. Server Performance Checklist

```text
□ Endpoint latency measured
□ p50/p95 tracked
□ Latency budget defined
□ Blocking work minimized
□ External calls bounded
□ Independent calls parallelized where safe
□ CPU profile available for hotspots
□ Serialization size reviewed
□ Memory behavior understood
```

---

# 303. Database Performance Checklist

```text
□ Query count understood
□ Slow queries identified
□ Query plans inspected
□ N+1 absent
□ Appropriate indexes exist
□ Rows returned bounded
□ Pagination appropriate
□ Connection pool sized
□ Lock contention monitored
□ Dataset scale realistic
```

---

# 304. Caching Checklist

```text
□ Cache provides measured value
□ Source of truth known
□ Cache key correct
□ Tenant/auth scope correct
□ TTL defined
□ Invalidation defined
□ Stampede considered
□ Hit rate measured
□ Outage behavior defined
```

---

# 305. Image Checklist

```text
□ Correct dimensions
□ Correct format
□ Compressed
□ Responsive source
□ Width/height/aspect ratio
□ Correct loading priority
□ LCP image eager
□ Off-screen image lazy
□ Long-lived caching where versioned
```

---

# 306. Font Checklist

```text
□ Families minimized
□ Weights minimized
□ Font files optimized
□ Subsetting considered
□ Display behavior defined
□ Critical preload limited
□ Long caching enabled
□ Fallback layout checked
```

---

# 307. Bundle Checklist

```text
□ Route bundle analyzed
□ Heavy dependencies justified
□ Duplicate packages checked
□ Server-only modules excluded from client
□ Heavy optional UI lazily loaded
□ Locale/admin code separated where useful
□ Regression budget enforced
```

---

# 308. Streaming Checklist

```text
□ Streaming improves user-visible result
□ Critical content arrives first
□ Slow regions isolated
□ Too many loaders avoided
□ Partial stream failure handled
□ Cancellation considered
```

---

# 309. Performance Test Checklist

```text
□ Representative workload
□ Representative dataset
□ Cold/warm behavior considered
□ p50/p95/p99 where relevant
□ CPU/memory observed
□ Database observed
□ Failure behavior observed
□ Result compared with baseline
```

---

# 310. Performance Definition of Done

A significant feature is performance-ready when:

```text
✓ Critical user path identified
✓ Performance budget considered
✓ No obvious request waterfalls
✓ Query behavior bounded
✓ Payloads bounded
✓ Images/media optimized
✓ Client JS justified
✓ Third-party costs understood
✓ Loading behavior intentional
✓ Interaction remains responsive
✓ Production measurement available where relevant
✓ No known severe regression
```

---

# 311. Performance Anti-Patterns

Avoid:

```text
Optimize without profiling.
```

Avoid:

```text
Ship all JavaScript to every route.
```

Avoid:

```text
Turn entire server-first app into client components.
```

Avoid:

```text
Fetch initial page data only after client mount without reason.
```

Avoid:

```text
Lazy-load hero/LCP image.
```

Avoid:

```text
Preload every resource.
```

Avoid:

```text
Prefetch the entire application.
```

Avoid:

```text
Load all font weights.
```

Avoid:

```text
Serve original 10 MB image as thumbnail.
```

Avoid:

```text
No image dimensions.
```

Avoid:

```text
100-row list
→ 101 database queries
```

Avoid:

```text
SELECT *
```

for every API.

Avoid:

```text
No pagination.
```

Avoid:

```text
Add Redis before measuring DB.
```

Avoid:

```text
Cache with no invalidation.
```

Avoid:

```text
One-hour cache for permission decisions without revocation strategy.
```

Avoid:

```text
Promise.all on thousands of expensive tasks.
```

Avoid:

```text
Optional analytics in checkout critical path.
```

Avoid:

```text
Every UI component memoized.
```

Avoid:

```text
Virtualize every list.
```

Avoid:

```text
Microservice because function is slow.
```

Avoid:

```text
Edge deployment while database remains half the world away.
```

Avoid:

```text
Average latency is good, therefore performance is good.
```

Avoid:

```text
Lighthouse score = complete performance strategy.
```

---

# 312. AI Performance Rules

AI coding agents MUST consider performance as part of design, but MUST NOT prematurely optimize without evidence.

---

# 313. AI Measurement Rule

Before making a non-obvious optimization, AI SHOULD identify:

```text
metric
bottleneck
baseline
expected improvement
```

---

# 314. AI Server-First Rule

AI SHOULD avoid unnecessary client-side JavaScript when server rendering can satisfy the requirement.

---

# 315. AI Client Boundary Rule

AI MUST NOT add broad `"use client"`-style boundaries merely because one descendant requires interaction.

Use the smallest appropriate client boundary.

---

# 316. AI Fetch Rule

AI SHOULD identify independent requests and avoid avoidable sequential waterfalls.

---

# 317. AI Query Rule

AI MUST inspect database access for:

```text
N+1
unbounded retrieval
missing pagination
unnecessary fields
```

when implementing data-heavy features.

---

# 318. AI Index Rule

AI MUST NOT add indexes merely from intuition.

Indexes should correspond to known query patterns and be verified where performance matters.

---

# 319. AI Cache Rule

AI MUST NOT introduce caching without defining:

```text
source of truth
key
scope
freshness
TTL
invalidation
```

---

# 320. AI Image Rule

AI-generated image usage SHOULD include:

```text
appropriate dimensions
responsive sizing
aspect ratio
loading priority
```

---

# 321. AI LCP Rule

AI MUST NOT lazy-load a likely LCP/hero image by default.

---

# 322. AI Lazy-Loading Rule

AI SHOULD lazy-load heavy noncritical resources where delayed loading improves initial experience.

---

# 323. AI Dependency Rule

Before adding a heavy browser dependency, AI SHOULD inspect whether:

```text
native browser feature
existing dependency
smaller implementation
server-side alternative
```

already solves the requirement.

---

# 324. AI Bundle Rule

AI MUST avoid importing server-only dependencies into client code.

---

# 325. AI Third-Party Rule

AI SHOULD treat new third-party scripts as a performance dependency requiring justification.

---

# 326. AI Streaming Rule

AI SHOULD use streaming/Suspense-style boundaries only when meaningful independent content can render earlier.

---

# 327. AI Memoization Rule

AI MUST NOT automatically wrap every:

```text
function
component
derived value
```

in memoization.

Profile or demonstrate reason.

---

# 328. AI Virtualization Rule

AI SHOULD introduce virtualization only when collection size and measured rendering cost justify it.

---

# 329. AI Timeout Rule

AI-generated external network calls MUST remain bounded according to the Error & Resilience Standard.

---

# 330. AI Background Rule

AI SHOULD move noncritical expensive side effects out of synchronous request paths when durability/semantics allow.

---

# 331. AI Budget Rule

AI SHOULD preserve established:

```text
bundle
query
latency
asset
```

budgets.

If a change exceeds a budget, it should explain the tradeoff rather than silently bypassing the limit.

---

# 332. AI Performance-Test Rule

Performance-sensitive changes SHOULD include appropriate regression protection where measurement is deterministic enough.

---

# 333. AI Optimization Rule

AI SHOULD prefer removing work over making unnecessary work marginally faster.

Priority:

```text
Do less
↓
Do later
↓
Do concurrently
↓
Cache
↓
Optimize implementation
```

where semantics allow.

---

# 334. AI Gold Rule

When uncertain:

```text
Correctness
>
Security
>
Measured user experience
>
Simplicity
>
Micro-optimization
```

---

# 335. Golden Performance Rules

**1. Performance is a product requirement.**

**2. Measure before optimizing.**

**3. Optimize user-visible bottlenecks.**

**4. Define performance budgets.**

**5. Track percentiles, not averages alone.**

**6. Measure real users as well as lab environments.**

**7. Meet Core Web Vitals at the required population percentile.**

**8. Leave margin below performance thresholds.**

**9. Identify and optimize the actual LCP resource.**

**10. Never lazy-load likely LCP content by default.**

**11. Protect the main thread to preserve INP.**

**12. Reserve layout space to protect CLS.**

**13. Minimize JavaScript shipped to browsers.**

**14. Prefer server rendering for noninteractive content.**

**15. Keep client boundaries narrow.**

**16. Avoid data-fetch waterfalls.**

**17. Parallelize independent work.**

**18. Bound concurrency for large work.**

**19. Move noncritical work outside the synchronous request path.**

**20. Every large collection is bounded.**

**21. Eliminate harmful N+1 patterns.**

**22. Inspect query plans for slow queries.**

**23. Index real access patterns.**

**24. Treat query count and query latency separately.**

**25. Cache only when it solves a measured problem.**

**26. Every cache has invalidation semantics.**

**27. HTTP/browser/CDN caching should be preferred where appropriate.**

**28. Optimize image dimensions, format, compression, and priority.**

**29. Load only necessary font families and weights.**

**30. Lazy-load noncritical heavy content.**

**31. Do not over-prefetch or over-preload.**

**32. Third-party scripts require performance justification.**

**33. Streaming improves perceived latency but does not excuse slow backends.**

**34. Use representative devices, networks, and datasets.**

**35. Test cold and warm behavior where both occur in production.**

**36. Protect critical paths from noisy neighbors and overload.**

**37. Maintain capacity headroom.**

**38. Performance regressions should be visible before production where practical.**

**39. Profile after identifying a bottleneck and measure again after changing it.**

**40. Remove unnecessary work before optimizing necessary work.**

---

# 336. Canonical Performance Standard

The organizational standard is:

> **Performance is designed and measured across the complete user journey, from network connection and server processing through database access, resource delivery, browser rendering, hydration, and interaction. Critical user journeys maintain explicit performance budgets, and production performance is evaluated using field telemetry and percentile distributions rather than averages or laboratory scores alone. Web experiences target current Core Web Vitals good thresholds for the applicable user population, with engineering margin below those thresholds.**

> **Applications minimize work on critical paths. Initial content is rendered server-first where practical, client-side JavaScript is restricted to functionality that requires it, critical resources are prioritized, noncritical resources are deferred, independent data requests are parallelized, and expensive non-user-blocking operations move to durable asynchronous processing. Images, fonts, CSS, JavaScript, third-party scripts, API payloads, and database queries are treated as budgeted resources.**

> **Database performance is managed through bounded queries, suitable pagination, elimination of harmful N+1 patterns, appropriate indexes, execution-plan analysis, connection-pool management, and workload isolation. Caches are introduced only where measured benefit justifies their consistency complexity, with explicit key, scope, freshness, TTL, invalidation, and failure semantics.**

> **Performance optimization is evidence-driven. Teams observe production behavior, profile the actual bottleneck, make the smallest effective architectural or implementation change, and measure again. Complex caching, sharding, virtualization, memoization, edge execution, multi-region deployment, and other optimization mechanisms are adopted only when simpler approaches cannot satisfy demonstrated requirements.**

A production-grade performance architecture should make it easy to answer:

```text
What is the critical user journey?
What metric represents its performance?
What is its budget?
What do real users experience at p75/p95?
What is the LCP element?
What blocks interaction?
What causes layout shift?
How much JavaScript is shipped?
Which resources are critical?
Which resources can load later?
How many database queries occur?
Which query dominates latency?
Are result sizes bounded?
What is cached?
How is the cache invalidated?
Which dependency dominates server latency?
Can independent work execute concurrently?
Can noncritical work move to background processing?
How does performance behave on low-end devices?
How does it behave under load?
How do we detect a regression?
What measurement proves an optimization worked?
```

If those questions cannot be answered, performance is being managed reactively rather than engineered.

Two implementation details behind the standard are worth making explicit. Google’s current guidance says **INP should be ≤200 ms**, **LCP ≤2.5 s**, and **CLS ≤0.1**, judged at p75; INP also covers responsiveness throughout the page lifecycle, not merely initial load. citeturn441053search2turn441053search5

For loading policy, off-screen images and iframes are strong lazy-loading candidates, but likely above-the-fold/LCP images should **not** be lazy-loaded because doing so delays their discovery. citeturn208388search0turn208388search5 For versioned immutable static resources, long HTTP caching is appropriate; HTTP also provides `stale-while-revalidate` and `stale-if-error` semantics when the content’s freshness model permits them. citeturn208388search6

In the master hierarchy, **Performance** should sit immediately after Testing and before Observability:

**Architecture → Framework → Security → Authentication & Authorization → Data & Database → API → Routes → State Management → Forms & Validation → Error Handling & Resilience → Testing → Performance → Observability → Infrastructure & Deployment → Documentation → Governance.**

# Accessibility Guidelines — Gold Standard 2026

## 1. Purpose

These guidelines define the canonical accessibility standard for all product interfaces.

They apply to:

- web applications;
- public websites;
- internal applications;
- admin systems;
- mobile-responsive web interfaces;
- forms;
- navigation;
- dialogs;
- menus;
- tables;
- charts;
- dashboards;
- data visualizations;
- realtime interfaces;
- media;
- documents generated by the product;
- design-system components.

The organizational baseline is:

```text
WCAG 2.2
Level AA
```

unless a stronger contractual, regulatory, customer, or jurisdiction-specific requirement applies.

The core principle is:

> **Accessibility is a correctness requirement of the product, not an optional visual enhancement.**

---

# 2. Normative Language

- **MUST** — mandatory.
- **MUST NOT** — prohibited.
- **SHOULD** — expected unless a documented reason exists.
- **SHOULD NOT** — generally avoided unless justified.
- **MAY** — optional.

Accessibility exceptions SHOULD document:

```text
Affected functionality
Barrier
User impact
WCAG criterion where applicable
Reason
Compensating alternative
Owner
Remediation plan
Review date
```

---

# 3. Compliance Floor

All user-facing interfaces MUST target:

```text
WCAG 2.2 AA
```

as the minimum organizational accessibility baseline.

AAA criteria MAY inform internal best practices even where full AAA conformance is not required.

---

# 4. Compliance Is Not the Goal by Itself

A technically conforming interface can still be difficult to use.

Teams SHOULD optimize for:

```text
Perceivable
Operable
Understandable
Robust
+
Actually usable
```

rather than checklist completion alone.

---

# 5. Accessibility Is Cross-Functional

Accessibility responsibility spans:

```text
Design
Engineering
Content
QA
Product
Documentation
```

It is not delegated solely to accessibility specialists.

---

# 6. Accessibility by Default

The design system SHOULD make accessible implementation the path of least resistance.

A developer using canonical components correctly should receive:

```text
semantics
keyboard support
focus behavior
accessible states
contrast-aware tokens
```

without rebuilding these concerns feature by feature.

---

# 7. Native HTML First

Prefer native semantic HTML before ARIA.

Examples:

```html
<button>
<a>
<input>
<select>
<textarea>
<table>
<dialog>
<nav>
<main>
```

are generally preferable to recreating equivalent behavior with generic elements.

---

# 8. The First Rule of ARIA

If native HTML already provides the required semantics and interaction:

> **Use the native element.**

Do not add ARIA simply because an interface is "accessible."

---

# 9. ARIA Does Not Add Behavior

ARIA can describe semantics.

ARIA does not automatically provide:

```text
keyboard behavior
focus management
selection logic
interaction
```

Custom widgets require implementation of those behaviors.

---

# 10. Accessibility Tree

Interfaces MUST expose meaningful:

```text
role
name
state
value
relationships
```

to accessibility APIs where relevant.

---

# 11. Semantic Structure

HTML structure SHOULD communicate document meaning independently of visual styling.

Examples:

```text
heading
paragraph
list
navigation
article
table
form
button
```

should remain identifiable programmatically.

---

# 12. Visual Appearance Is Not Semantics

A styled `<div>` that visually resembles a button is still not a button.

Likewise:

```text
bold text
```

is not automatically a heading.

Use semantic elements.

---

# 13. DOM Order

DOM order SHOULD reflect:

```text
reading order
focus order
logical workflow
```

Visual CSS rearrangement MUST NOT create a misleading sequence.

---

# 14. Landmarks

Major application regions SHOULD use appropriate landmarks.

Typical page structure:

```text
header
nav
main
aside where applicable
footer
```

---

# 15. Main Landmark

Each page SHOULD normally contain one primary:

```html
<main>
```

representing its main content.

---

# 16. Multiple Navigation Regions

If multiple navigation landmarks exist, give them distinguishing accessible names.

Example:

```text
Primary navigation
Project navigation
Footer navigation
```

---

# 17. Skip Link

Pages with repeated navigation SHOULD provide a keyboard-accessible mechanism to bypass it.

Common pattern:

```text
Skip to main content
```

---

# 18. Skip Link Visibility

Skip links MAY remain visually hidden until focused.

They MUST become clearly visible when keyboard focus reaches them.

---

# 19. Headings

Headings MUST represent meaningful content hierarchy.

Use:

```text
h1
h2
h3
...
```

according to structure, not desired font size.

---

# 20. Heading Levels

Avoid skipping levels merely for styling.

Preferred:

```text
h1
  h2
    h3
```

rather than:

```text
h1
  h4
```

without semantic reason.

---

# 21. Page Heading

Application pages SHOULD normally expose a clear programmatic page heading.

---

# 22. Heading Styling

Visual appearance and heading level are independent.

Use design tokens/classes to style semantic headings appropriately.

---

# 23. Lists

Use semantic lists when content represents a list.

```html
<ul>
<ol>
<li>
```

provides information that generic repeated `<div>` elements do not.

---

# 24. Description Lists

Use description lists when representing term/value relationships where appropriate.

---

# 25. Links

Use links for navigation.

Use buttons for actions.

---

# 26. Link vs Button

Canonical distinction:

```text
Navigate
→ Link

Perform action
→ Button
```

Do not choose based solely on visual appearance.

---

# 27. Link Destination

Link text SHOULD give meaningful destination context.

Prefer:

```text
View invoice
```

over repetitive:

```text
Click here
```

---

# 28. Duplicate Link Text

Repeated generic link labels MAY require contextual accessible names.

Example:

```text
View invoice INV-1042
```

for assistive technology.

---

# 29. New Window Behavior

Opening a new tab/window SHOULD be deliberate.

Avoid forcing new windows where ordinary navigation is sufficient.

Communicate unexpected context changes where necessary.

---

# 30. Buttons

Use native `<button>` elements for actions wherever possible.

---

# 31. Button Accessible Name

Every button MUST have an accessible name.

Icon-only buttons require an accessible name such as:

```text
Close
Delete project
Open navigation
```

---

# 32. Icon-Only Buttons

The icon's visual meaning is not sufficient by itself.

Provide a programmatically determinable name.

---

# 33. Button Text

Visible button labels SHOULD clearly describe actions.

Prefer:

```text
Save changes
Delete workspace
Send invitation
```

over:

```text
OK
Submit
Yes
```

when the action can be named explicitly.

---

# 34. Disabled Controls

Disabled controls SHOULD still leave users able to understand why an action is unavailable when that information is necessary.

Do not create inaccessible dead ends.

---

# 35. Disabled vs Hidden

Do not hide an unavailable action if users need to understand that it exists but cannot currently be used.

Choose deliberately.

---

# 36. Keyboard Accessibility

All functionality that can be operated with a pointer MUST also be operable through a keyboard where the function is not inherently pointer-specific.

---

# 37. Keyboard-Only Completion

A keyboard-only user MUST be able to complete all essential workflows.

This includes:

```text
navigation
forms
dialogs
menus
tables
file selection
settings
checkout
administration
```

---

# 38. Standard Keyboard Conventions

Custom controls SHOULD follow established platform/APG keyboard conventions.

Users should not need to learn arbitrary keys for ordinary widgets.

---

# 39. Tab

`Tab` and `Shift+Tab` SHOULD move between logical interactive components.

---

# 40. Composite Widgets

Within composite widgets such as:

```text
menu
tablist
radio group
tree
grid
```

arrow-key navigation MAY be appropriate instead of placing every child in the page Tab sequence.

Follow the canonical accessible pattern.

---

# 41. Enter

Enter SHOULD activate controls where expected.

Links and buttons should retain native behavior.

---

# 42. Space

Space SHOULD activate controls where native/platform conventions require it.

Do not remove expected keyboard behavior.

---

# 43. Escape

Escape SHOULD dismiss temporary interfaces where established conventions apply.

Examples:

```text
dialog
popover
menu
combobox popup
```

provided doing so does not cause data loss without appropriate handling.

---

# 44. Arrow Keys

Arrow-key navigation SHOULD follow standard interaction patterns for:

```text
radio groups
menus
tabs
listboxes
grids
sliders
```

---

# 45. Custom Keyboard Shortcuts

Custom keyboard shortcuts SHOULD be introduced sparingly.

They MUST avoid conflicts with:

```text
browser
OS
assistive technology
```

commands.

---

# 46. Shortcut Discoverability

Keyboard shortcuts SHOULD be discoverable if they are important to efficient operation.

---

# 47. Single-Character Shortcuts

Avoid single-character shortcuts that unexpectedly trigger when focus or speech-input context changes unless the applicable WCAG safeguards are implemented.

---

# 48. Keyboard Traps

Keyboard focus MUST NOT become trapped in a component unless trapping is intentional for a modal interaction and users can exit through an expected mechanism.

---

# 49. Focus Is State

Keyboard focus is application state with UX consequences.

Treat focus movement intentionally.

---

# 50. Visible Focus

Every keyboard-operable component MUST expose visible keyboard focus.

Never globally remove:

```css
outline: none;
```

without providing an equivalent or stronger indicator.

---

# 51. Focus Ring

The design system SHOULD provide one canonical focus-ring treatment.

It must remain visible against relevant backgrounds.

---

# 52. Focus Contrast

Author-created focus indication SHOULD achieve strong visible contrast against adjacent colors.

A minimum 3:1 contrast for the meaningful non-text indication is the baseline.

---

# 53. Focus Appearance

Although WCAG's detailed Focus Appearance criterion is AAA, the organizational design system SHOULD target a clearly visible focus indicator at least equivalent to a substantial perimeter/ring rather than a subtle color shift.

---

# 54. Focus and Hover

Focus appearance MUST NOT depend on hover.

Keyboard users may never trigger hover.

---

# 55. Focus and Selection

Do not confuse:

```text
focused
selected
active
```

states.

They can be different simultaneously.

---

# 56. Focus Not Obscured

When a component receives keyboard focus, author-created content MUST NOT completely hide it.

---

# 57. Sticky Headers

Sticky headers must not hide focused elements when users Tab or navigate anchors.

Use appropriate:

```text
scroll margin
layout
focus management
```

where necessary.

---

# 58. Sticky Footers

Sticky action bars MUST NOT obscure:

```text
focused controls
form errors
content
```

especially at high zoom.

---

# 59. Focus Order

Focus order MUST follow the meaningful workflow.

Avoid positive `tabindex` values as a mechanism to repair incorrect DOM structure.

---

# 60. tabindex

Preferred usage:

```text
tabindex="0"
→ include custom element in natural focus order when necessary

tabindex="-1"
→ programmatic focus target
```

Positive values SHOULD generally be avoided.

---

# 61. Programmatic Focus

Move focus programmatically only when a meaningful context change requires it.

---

# 62. Route Changes

Single-page applications SHOULD manage route-transition focus intentionally.

A user navigating to a new page should be able to understand that navigation occurred and begin at an appropriate point.

---

# 63. Page Navigation Focus

After client-side route navigation, a common strategy is to move focus to:

```text
page heading
main region
```

depending on product architecture.

---

# 64. Do Not Steal Focus

Background refreshes, toasts, and minor updates MUST NOT unexpectedly steal keyboard focus.

---

# 65. Focus Restoration

Temporary interfaces SHOULD restore focus to a logical location after closure.

Usually:

```text
trigger that opened the interface
```

unless the workflow created/removed something requiring a different destination.

---

# 66. Removed Focus Target

If the triggering element no longer exists after an operation, focus should move to a logical nearby target.

---

# 67. Semantic Controls

Prefer native controls because browsers provide established:

```text
keyboard behavior
focusability
state exposure
form behavior
```

automatically.

---

# 68. ARIA Roles

ARIA roles MUST match actual implemented behavior.

Do not write:

```html
<div role="button">
```

unless the element genuinely behaves like a button.

---

# 69. ARIA State

Dynamic state MUST be kept synchronized.

Examples:

```text
aria-expanded
aria-selected
aria-checked
aria-disabled
aria-pressed
```

must reflect actual UI state.

---

# 70. Invalid ARIA

Incorrect ARIA can create a worse experience than no ARIA.

Do not add roles/states without understanding their semantics.

---

# 71. Redundant ARIA

Avoid redundant roles on native elements unless a specific interoperability requirement justifies them.

---

# 72. Accessible Names

Every interactive component MUST have an appropriate accessible name.

Accessible naming SHOULD preferably derive from visible text where possible.

---

# 73. Visible Label Alignment

The accessible name SHOULD contain or closely correspond to visible label wording.

This supports speech-input users as well as screen-reader users.

---

# 74. aria-label

Use `aria-label` when an appropriate visible label cannot reasonably provide the accessible name.

Do not use it to replace useful visible text.

---

# 75. aria-labelledby

Use `aria-labelledby` where an existing visible element provides the appropriate name.

---

# 76. Accessible Description

Additional help/context MAY use:

```text
aria-describedby
```

or the equivalent relationship.

Descriptions should supplement names, not replace them.

---

# 77. Hidden Text

Visually hidden text MAY provide additional accessible context.

It must remain available to assistive technologies.

---

# 78. Hidden Content

Content intentionally hidden from everyone should generally not remain exposed to accessibility APIs.

---

# 79. aria-hidden

Never place:

```text
aria-hidden="true"
```

on a focusable element or an ancestor containing active focusable controls.

---

# 80. Decorative Icons

Purely decorative icons SHOULD be hidden from the accessibility tree.

Their adjacent text provides meaning.

---

# 81. Functional Icons

Icons conveying functionality without visible text need accessible naming.

---

# 82. Status Icons

Do not communicate:

```text
success
warning
error
status
```

through an icon or color alone.

Provide text or another equivalent cue.

---

# 83. Images

Meaningful images require appropriate text alternatives.

---

# 84. Informative Images

Alt text SHOULD communicate the information or function relevant to the surrounding context.

Do not mechanically describe every visual detail.

---

# 85. Decorative Images

Decorative images SHOULD use an empty text alternative where appropriate.

They should not create screen-reader noise.

---

# 86. Functional Images

If an image acts as a control, its accessible name should communicate the action rather than merely describe the image.

---

# 87. Complex Images

Complex diagrams, charts, and infographics may require:

```text
short text alternative
+
longer textual explanation/data representation
```

---

# 88. Images of Text

Avoid images containing text when normal text can provide the same presentation.

Text must remain selectable, resizable, translatable, and adaptable.

---

# 89. Contrast Baseline

Normal text MUST meet at least:

```text
4.5 : 1
```

contrast against its background.

---

# 90. Large Text Contrast

Large text MAY use the WCAG AA minimum:

```text
3 : 1
```

according to WCAG's large-text definition.

---

# 91. Avoid Threshold Design

Do not intentionally design every color combination exactly on the minimum ratio.

Rendering, anti-aliasing, themes, and displays vary.

Maintain practical margin.

---

# 92. Non-Text Contrast

Meaningful visual information required to identify:

```text
controls
states
graphical objects
focus
```

MUST meet the applicable 3:1 contrast requirement against adjacent colors.

---

# 93. Input Borders

If a visible border is required to identify an input, that border must have sufficient non-text contrast.

---

# 94. Placeholder Contrast

Placeholder text SHOULD remain readable.

It MUST NOT be the only label.

---

# 95. Disabled Contrast

WCAG contrast rules contain exceptions for inactive controls, but disabled states SHOULD still remain understandable and not disappear into the interface.

---

# 96. Color Is Not Enough

Color MUST NOT be the only means of conveying information.

Bad:

```text
green = passed
red = failed
```

without another indication.

---

# 97. Status Encoding

Use combinations such as:

```text
color
+
icon
+
text
```

for critical status.

---

# 98. Links Within Text

Inline links MUST be identifiable without relying only on color unless the applicable contrast and state behavior satisfy the accessibility requirement.

Underlines are usually the clearest convention.

---

# 99. Error States

Form errors require textual indication.

A red border alone is insufficient.

---

# 100. Required Fields

Required state must not rely only on color or an unexplained symbol.

---

# 101. Charts and Color

Chart series MUST remain distinguishable without color perception alone.

Possible distinctions:

```text
line style
marker shape
labels
pattern
direct annotation
```

---

# 102. Dark Mode

Dark mode MUST meet the same accessibility requirements as light mode.

It is not exempt because it is optional.

---

# 103. High Contrast

Interfaces SHOULD remain usable with operating-system/browser high-contrast or forced-colors modes where supported.

---

# 104. Forced Colors

Do not remove essential borders/icons/state indicators merely because custom CSS colors disappear in forced-color environments.

---

# 105. User Styles

Avoid author styles that unnecessarily prevent users from applying their own:

```text
font sizes
colors
spacing
zoom
```

---

# 106. Zoom

Interfaces MUST remain usable at increased browser zoom.

---

# 107. Text Resize

Text MUST remain usable when resized to:

```text
200%
```

without loss of content or functionality.

---

# 108. Reflow

At the equivalent of:

```text
320 CSS px
```

for vertically scrolling content, users MUST NOT generally need two-dimensional scrolling to read or operate content.

Exceptions exist where two-dimensional layout is genuinely essential.

---

# 109. 400% Zoom Test

A practical desktop test SHOULD include:

```text
1280 px viewport
+
400% browser zoom
```

which approximates the WCAG 320-CSS-pixel reflow condition.

---

# 110. Horizontal Scrolling

Ordinary:

```text
text
forms
settings
cards
navigation
```

should not require horizontal scrolling at narrow/reflowed widths.

---

# 111. Legitimate Two-Dimensional Content

Some content may genuinely require horizontal and vertical navigation.

Examples:

```text
large data table
map
diagram
canvas
timeline
```

Contain the scrolling to that region where practical.

---

# 112. Fixed Heights

Avoid fixed-height text containers that clip content when:

```text
zoom
translation
user font settings
```

increase text size.

---

# 113. Text Truncation

Do not truncate information required to complete a task without a way to access the full value.

---

# 114. Ellipsis

If ellipsis is used, users SHOULD have an accessible method to obtain complete content when it matters.

---

# 115. Responsive Accessibility

Responsive layout changes MUST preserve:

```text
content
functionality
semantics
focus order
```

not merely visual appearance.

---

# 116. Mobile Recomposition

Desktop multi-column interfaces SHOULD recompose into readable mobile structures rather than shrink unusably.

---

# 117. Orientation

Do not lock content to one device orientation unless orientation is essential to functionality.

---

# 118. Touch Targets

WCAG 2.2 AA minimum pointer-target sizing MUST be satisfied.

The baseline target is:

```text
24 × 24 CSS px
```

subject to WCAG-defined exceptions.

---

# 119. Preferred Touch Target

For ordinary product controls, the internal design-system target SHOULD generally be larger than the WCAG minimum.

Preferred target for important touch actions:

```text
≈ 44 × 44 CSS px
```

where layout permits.

---

# 120. Small Icons

A 16 px icon MAY sit inside a larger interactive hit area.

Visual size and target size are different concepts.

---

# 121. Target Spacing

Closely packed small controls increase accidental activation.

Use adequate spacing, especially for:

```text
delete
close
pagination
table row actions
```

---

# 122. Destructive Touch Targets

Destructive actions SHOULD NOT be placed immediately beside common primary actions with tiny separation.

---

# 123. Pointer Gestures

Functionality requiring complex pointer gestures SHOULD have a simpler single-pointer alternative unless the gesture is essential.

---

# 124. Drag and Drop

Drag-and-drop MUST NOT be the only way to perform an essential operation.

Provide alternatives such as:

```text
Move up/down
Select destination
File picker
```

---

# 125. Motion

Motion SHOULD support understanding rather than decoration alone.

---

# 126. Reduced Motion

The application MUST honor:

```css
prefers-reduced-motion
```

for nonessential motion as an organizational standard.

This requirement intentionally goes beyond relying only on the minimum AA set.

---

# 127. Reduced-Motion Behavior

When reduced motion is requested, remove or substantially reduce:

```text
large translations
parallax
zoom effects
continuous movement
decorative animation
```

that is not essential.

---

# 128. Essential Motion

If movement communicates necessary information, provide a reduced alternative that preserves meaning.

---

# 129. Opacity Transitions

Simple low-impact opacity transitions may remain appropriate under reduced-motion mode if they do not cause motion-related harm.

Use judgment.

---

# 130. Auto-Playing Motion

Avoid automatically playing distracting movement.

Users SHOULD be able to pause, stop, or hide moving content where applicable.

---

# 131. Continuous Animation

Decorative continuous animation SHOULD stop under reduced-motion preferences.

---

# 132. Parallax

Parallax SHOULD be disabled under reduced motion.

---

# 133. Scroll-Linked Motion

Avoid large scroll-linked transformations as essential navigation.

---

# 134. Flashing Content

Content MUST NOT flash in ways that create seizure risk.

Do not produce content exceeding applicable WCAG flash thresholds.

---

# 135. Animation Timing

Do not make functionality dependent on users completing actions during brief animation windows.

---

# 136. Time Limits

Avoid time limits unless necessary.

Where time limits exist, provide applicable:

```text
warning
extension
adjustment
```

mechanisms.

---

# 137. Session Timeout

Users SHOULD receive advance warning before session expiry when unsaved work or interruption is likely.

---

# 138. Authentication Timeout

Security session timeouts remain legitimate.

Accessibility requires making the process understandable and recoverable without weakening security.

---

# 139. Auto-Advancing Content

Carousels/slides SHOULD NOT auto-advance in a way users cannot control.

---

# 140. Pause Controls

Moving/auto-updating content requiring user attention SHOULD expose suitable pause/stop controls.

---

# 141. Screen Readers

Interfaces MUST expose sufficient semantics for screen-reader users to understand:

```text
structure
controls
states
relationships
updates
```

---

# 142. Screen Reader ≠ Linear Visual Description

Do not attempt to narrate every visual detail.

Expose semantic meaning.

---

# 143. Source Order

Screen readers generally consume semantic DOM order.

CSS positioning MUST NOT produce a contradictory reading sequence.

---

# 144. Name, Role, Value

Interactive components MUST expose appropriate:

```text
name
role
value/state
```

to assistive technology.

---

# 145. Dynamic Updates

Important dynamic content changes SHOULD be communicated appropriately when they occur without moving focus.

---

# 146. Live Regions

Use live regions for status information that users need to hear without navigating to it.

---

# 147. aria-live

Choose:

```text
polite
assertive
```

according to urgency.

Most product updates should use `polite`.

---

# 148. Assertive Announcements

Reserve assertive announcements for urgent information.

Overuse can interrupt screen-reader users repeatedly.

---

# 149. Do Not Announce Everything

Frequent data updates SHOULD NOT all become live announcements.

This creates unusable noise.

---

# 150. Status Messages

Examples appropriate for accessible status messaging:

```text
Changes saved
3 results found
Upload completed
Connection lost
```

---

# 151. Loading Announcements

Long-running transitions MAY communicate:

```text
Loading…
```

where the loading state is not otherwise apparent.

Do not announce tiny background requests.

---

# 152. Error Announcements

Submission errors SHOULD become discoverable to screen-reader users.

Use:

```text
focus management
error summary
associated field messages
live status
```

appropriately.

---

# 153. Notifications

Toasts MUST NOT require visual observation alone.

Important notifications should be exposed to assistive technologies.

---

# 154. Toast Timing

Do not disappear critical messages before users can perceive or interact with them.

---

# 155. Interactive Toasts

If a toast contains:

```text
Undo
Retry
View
```

the control must be keyboard accessible.

---

# 156. Forms

Forms MUST follow the Forms & Validation Gold Standard and WCAG 2.2 AA requirements.

---

# 157. Form Labels

Every user-input control MUST have an accessible label.

---

# 158. Visible Form Labels

Visible persistent labels SHOULD be used for ordinary form fields.

Placeholder-only fields are prohibited.

---

# 159. Label Association

Labels must be programmatically associated with controls.

Use:

```html
<label for>
```

or equivalent native/design-system relationships.

---

# 160. Grouped Controls

Related controls such as radio/checkbox groups SHOULD use:

```html
<fieldset>
<legend>
```

where appropriate.

---

# 161. Form Instructions

Required formats or important instructions SHOULD be provided before users encounter predictable errors.

---

# 162. Required Status

Required fields need accessible and visible indication.

---

# 163. Autocomplete

Use recognized autocomplete attributes where appropriate.

This particularly helps users with:

```text
motor
cognitive
memory
```

limitations.

---

# 164. Input Purpose

Common personal-data inputs SHOULD expose machine-determinable purpose where applicable.

---

# 165. Form Errors

Automatically detected errors MUST identify the affected item and describe the error in text.

---

# 166. Error Recovery

Errors SHOULD explain how to fix the issue.

Prefer:

```text
Enter an email address in the format name@example.com.
```

over:

```text
Invalid value.
```

---

# 167. Error Summary

Long forms SHOULD consider an accessible error summary.

---

# 168. Error Summary Links

Error summaries MAY link users directly to problematic controls.

---

# 169. Error Focus

After failed submission, focus SHOULD move to:

```text
error summary
```

or the first invalid control according to the established pattern.

---

# 170. Error Preservation

Do not erase valid entered data after validation failure.

---

# 171. Color and Forms

Error/success/required states cannot rely solely on:

```text
red
green
yellow
```

color.

---

# 172. Form Descriptions

Help text and error text should be programmatically associated with controls.

---

# 173. Disabled Submit

Avoid permanently disabled submit controls that provide no explanation for users who cannot determine why submission is unavailable.

---

# 174. Pending Submission

Pending form state should be perceivable to:

```text
visual
keyboard
screen-reader
```

users where meaningful.

---

# 175. Accessible Authentication

Authentication must support:

```text
password managers
paste
autocomplete
passkeys
keyboard
zoom
```

where applicable.

---

# 176. CAPTCHA

CAPTCHA mechanisms require accessible alternatives.

Avoid introducing CAPTCHA unless abuse risk justifies it.

---

# 177. OTP

One-time-code fields SHOULD support:

```text
paste
autocomplete
keyboard entry
```

and avoid unnecessary multi-field complexity.

---

# 178. File Uploads

File uploading must be operable without drag-and-drop.

Provide a standard file-picker mechanism.

---

# 179. Upload Status

Upload progress and errors must not be communicated visually alone.

---

# 180. Dialogs

Modal dialogs MUST follow an established accessible dialog pattern.

---

# 181. Dialog Role

Modal dialog containers require appropriate dialog semantics.

---

# 182. Dialog Name

Every dialog MUST have an accessible name.

Usually derived from a visible title.

---

# 183. aria-modal

A truly modal ARIA dialog should expose appropriate modal semantics.

Do not mark a dialog modal while allowing interaction with the background.

---

# 184. Dialog Initial Focus

When a dialog opens, focus MUST move inside it.

The correct initial target depends on dialog content.

---

# 185. Initial Focus — Simple Dialog

For a simple confirm dialog, focus may move to the first appropriate interactive control.

---

# 186. Initial Focus — Structured Content

For large or structured dialog content, initial focus MAY move to a semantic static element such as the heading using:

```text
tabindex="-1"
```

so users can perceive the content from its beginning.

---

# 187. Dialog Focus Containment

While a modal dialog is active:

```text
Tab
Shift+Tab
```

must not move into inert background content.

---

# 188. Background Inertness

Users must not be able to interact with content behind a modal dialog.

---

# 189. Dialog Escape

Escape SHOULD close ordinary modal dialogs unless doing so would create an unsafe or ambiguous operation.

---

# 190. Dialog Close Control

Dialogs SHOULD contain a visible keyboard-operable method for closing/cancelling.

---

# 191. Dialog Focus Restoration

On close, return focus to:

```text
trigger
```

or another logical target when the workflow changed the page.

---

# 192. Confirmation Dialogs

Destructive dialogs must state:

```text
resource
consequence
reversibility
```

rather than only:

```text
Are you sure?
```

---

# 193. Alert Dialog

Use alert-dialog semantics only for urgent modal information that truly requires immediate attention.

Do not use alert dialogs for ordinary notifications.

---

# 194. Popovers

Nonmodal popovers require intentional:

```text
focus
dismissal
keyboard
trigger state
```

behavior.

---

# 195. Disclosure

Simple show/hide content SHOULD generally use disclosure/button semantics.

The trigger should expose:

```text
aria-expanded
```

where applicable.

---

# 196. Menus

Use menu semantics for actual application-style command menus.

Do not use ARIA menus for ordinary site navigation solely because it visually resembles a menu.

---

# 197. Navigation Menus

Standard website/app navigation is usually better represented through links inside `<nav>` than ARIA menu widgets.

---

# 198. Menu Keyboard Model

True ARIA menus require expected arrow-key interaction and focus management.

---

# 199. Tabs

Tabs SHOULD follow established tab semantics.

Expose:

```text
tablist
tab
tabpanel
selected state
relationships
```

appropriately.

---

# 200. Tab Keyboard Behavior

Tabbed interfaces SHOULD support established:

```text
Arrow keys
Home/End where applicable
Tab into panel
```

behavior.

---

# 201. Automatic vs Manual Tab Activation

Choose automatic or manual tab activation deliberately.

Automatic activation is appropriate when panel switching is effectively instantaneous.

---

# 202. Accordions

Accordion triggers should be real buttons and expose expanded/collapsed state.

---

# 203. Tooltips

Tooltips are supplementary information.

Do not place essential task information only in a hover-only tooltip.

---

# 204. Tooltip Trigger

Tooltip information should be available to:

```text
keyboard focus
pointer hover
```

as appropriate.

---

# 205. Tooltip Dismissal

Users should be able to dismiss hover/focus content where required by accessibility criteria.

---

# 206. Hover Content

Content triggered by hover must also work for keyboard focus when applicable.

---

# 207. Comboboxes

Comboboxes MUST follow a tested accessible interaction pattern.

They are not simply:

```text
input + random div dropdown
```

---

# 208. Combobox Keyboard

Expected behavior may include:

```text
typing
ArrowDown / ArrowUp
Enter
Escape
```

according to the chosen pattern.

---

# 209. Combobox State

Expose:

```text
expanded state
active option
selected value
popup relationship
```

correctly.

---

# 210. Listboxes

Use listbox semantics only when the interaction genuinely behaves as a listbox.

---

# 211. Native Select

Prefer native `<select>` where its capabilities satisfy the product requirement.

---

# 212. Custom Select

A custom select incurs substantial accessibility responsibility.

Use the canonical design-system primitive rather than feature-specific recreation.

---

# 213. Checkbox

Use native checkbox semantics for independent binary selections.

---

# 214. Radio Groups

Radio groups represent mutually exclusive choices.

Keyboard behavior should remain native or follow established patterns.

---

# 215. Switch

Switches represent immediate binary on/off state.

Ensure:

```text
name
state
```

are programmatically available.

---

# 216. Slider

Custom sliders require complete keyboard support and accessible:

```text
minimum
maximum
current value
name
```

---

# 217. Range Controls

Where possible, use native range inputs or tested canonical primitives.

---

# 218. Date Pickers

Date picker dialogs require careful:

```text
grid semantics
keyboard navigation
focus
current date
selected date
month navigation
```

behavior.

Prefer proven accessible components.

---

# 219. Calendar Input Alternative

Users SHOULD be able to enter dates efficiently without being forced to operate a complex visual calendar where practical.

---

# 220. Tables

Use semantic HTML tables for tabular data whenever practical.

---

# 221. Tables Are Not Layout Tools

Do not use tables for general application layout.

---

# 222. Table Headers

Data tables MUST identify relevant row/column headers programmatically.

Use:

```html
<th>
```

with appropriate relationships.

---

# 223. Simple Tables

For simple tables:

```text
header row
+
data rows
```

native HTML semantics are usually sufficient.

---

# 224. Complex Tables

Complex multi-level headers may require explicit:

```text
scope
headers/id
```

relationships.

---

# 225. Table Caption

Provide a caption or equivalent accessible context when users need to understand the table's purpose.

---

# 226. Table Sorting

Sortable headers MUST expose:

```text
control
current sort direction
```

accessibly.

---

# 227. Sort Button

A sortable header SHOULD contain an actual button or equivalent accessible interaction rather than click handling on a passive `<th>`.

---

# 228. aria-sort

Use the appropriate sort-state semantics where applicable.

---

# 229. Table Selection

Selectable rows require explicit selectable-control semantics.

Do not make the row itself an ambiguous invisible checkbox.

---

# 230. Row Actions

Row actions MUST be keyboard reachable.

Avoid hover-only controls.

---

# 231. Responsive Tables

Do not destroy header relationships when adapting tables to smaller screens.

---

# 232. Table Horizontal Scroll

Data tables are legitimate cases where horizontal scrolling MAY be necessary.

Scrolling should be contained to the table region rather than the entire page where possible.

---

# 233. Interactive Grid

Use ARIA grid behavior only when the interface behaves like an application grid.

A normal data table with links/buttons is not automatically a grid.

---

# 234. Grid Complexity

Grid widgets require sophisticated:

```text
keyboard navigation
focus management
row/column semantics
selection
```

and should use proven components.

---

# 235. Virtualized Tables

Virtualized tabular interfaces require additional attention to exposing:

```text
row count
column count
row/column indices
```

when the DOM contains only a subset.

---

# 236. Charts

Charts MUST NOT be the sole representation of critical information when a reasonable text/data alternative can be provided.

---

# 237. Chart Accessible Name

Each meaningful chart SHOULD have a clear accessible:

```text
title/name
purpose
```

---

# 238. Chart Summary

Provide a concise textual summary of the key information or trend.

Example:

```text
Revenue increased from January through May, then declined in June.
```

---

# 239. Chart Data Alternative

When users may need exact values, provide an accessible alternative such as:

```text
data table
structured list
downloadable accessible data
```

---

# 240. Chart Color

Do not encode series exclusively through color.

---

# 241. Chart Contrast

Meaningful graphical elements required to understand the chart MUST meet applicable non-text contrast requirements.

---

# 242. Direct Labels

Directly labeling lines/bars/regions can improve accessibility compared with relying exclusively on a color legend.

---

# 243. Chart Tooltips

Hover tooltips MUST NOT be the only mechanism for accessing important values.

---

# 244. Keyboard Charts

Interactive chart data points SHOULD be keyboard accessible if interaction with individual points is part of the product requirement.

---

# 245. Chart Screen Reader Strategy

Do not expose hundreds of meaningless SVG paths individually.

Expose useful:

```text
summary
structure
data
controls
```

instead.

---

# 246. SVG Charts

SVG requires intentional accessible naming/description where it communicates meaningful content.

---

# 247. Canvas

Canvas content requires an accessible alternative if it contains required information or functionality.

---

# 248. Maps

Maps SHOULD provide textual/location alternatives for required tasks.

Do not require precise pointer interaction as the only way to select a location.

---

# 249. Data Visualization Interaction

Zoom, pan, hover, and brush interactions should have accessible alternatives where those actions are required to obtain information.

---

# 250. Dashboards

Dashboards should expose:

```text
meaningful headings
region names where useful
accessible metrics
chart alternatives
logical navigation order
```

---

# 251. KPI Cards

A metric card should expose meaning, not merely:

```text
42
+7%
```

without context.

---

# 252. Status Badges

Badges MUST include understandable text where the status is meaningful.

Color alone is insufficient.

---

# 253. Progress Indicators

Progress bars should expose:

```text
name
current value
minimum/maximum where applicable
```

---

# 254. Indeterminate Progress

Use appropriate indeterminate/busy semantics when completion percentage is unknown.

---

# 255. Spinners

A visual spinner by itself is not sufficient status communication for significant loading.

---

# 256. Skeletons

Skeleton loaders are visual presentation.

Screen-reader users should receive useful:

```text
busy/loading
```

state rather than dozens of meaningless skeleton elements.

---

# 257. aria-busy

Regions undergoing meaningful asynchronous update MAY expose busy state appropriately.

---

# 258. Empty States

Empty states should communicate:

```text
what is empty
why where useful
what action is available
```

without relying solely on illustration.

---

# 259. Error States

Error states must remain distinguishable from legitimate empty data.

---

# 260. Navigation

Navigation MUST be keyboard and screen-reader understandable.

---

# 261. Current Location

Navigation SHOULD expose the current item/page programmatically where useful.

---

# 262. Breadcrumbs

Breadcrumb navigation should:

```text
use nav landmark
have accessible label
identify current page
```

---

# 263. Sidebar Navigation

Collapsed sidebars must preserve accessible names for icon-only navigation.

---

# 264. Mobile Navigation

Mobile navigation controls need:

```text
accessible name
expanded state
focus behavior
dismissal
```

---

# 265. Focus in Mobile Drawer

A modal navigation drawer should follow modal focus-management behavior when it blocks the underlying page.

---

# 266. Search

Search regions SHOULD expose clear labels and structure.

---

# 267. Search Suggestions

Autocomplete search requires accessible combobox/listbox behavior rather than a visual suggestions list alone.

---

# 268. Pagination

Pagination links/buttons require meaningful accessible names.

Example:

```text
Go to page 3
Next page
Previous page
```

---

# 269. Current Page

Current pagination state SHOULD be exposed programmatically.

---

# 270. Infinite Scroll

Infinite scrolling requires care for:

```text
keyboard position
screen-reader context
back navigation
footer access
```

Pagination or explicit Load More may provide a more robust experience.

---

# 271. Load More

Load More controls SHOULD preserve focus/context after new content is inserted.

---

# 272. Realtime Feeds

Realtime feeds should avoid constantly changing the user's reading position.

---

# 273. Auto-Prepending

Do not automatically prepend content above the user's current reading/focus position in a disruptive way.

---

# 274. Chat

Chat interfaces SHOULD expose new messages appropriately without announcing excessive history.

---

# 275. Chat History

Conversation history should remain semantically navigable.

---

# 276. Chat Composer

Message composer controls require visible labels/accessibility names and predictable keyboard semantics.

---

# 277. Editors

Rich-text/code editors are complex accessibility surfaces.

Use mature editors with documented accessibility support.

---

# 278. Editor Toolbar

Editor toolbars SHOULD use appropriate toolbar/composite keyboard patterns.

---

# 279. Markdown

Markdown authoring SHOULD provide discoverable syntax/help or preview options where necessary.

---

# 280. Code Blocks

Code examples should remain keyboard-selectable and readable at zoom.

---

# 281. Copy Buttons

Copy-code controls need accessible names such as:

```text
Copy code
```

and should announce success appropriately.

---

# 282. Media

Audio/video content requires accessible alternatives according to content type and WCAG requirements.

---

# 283. Captions

Prerecorded synchronized video containing meaningful audio requires captions according to the applicable WCAG requirement.

---

# 284. Audio Description

Provide audio description or equivalent media alternatives where visual information essential to understanding is not otherwise available.

---

# 285. Transcripts

Transcripts can substantially improve access to audio/video information and SHOULD be provided where appropriate.

---

# 286. Media Controls

Media controls MUST be keyboard operable and screen-reader accessible.

---

# 287. Autoplay Audio

Do not automatically play audio without user control.

---

# 288. Background Video

Decorative video should not create accessibility barriers.

It SHOULD:

```text
not contain unique information
respect reduced motion
provide pause where applicable
```

---

# 289. Language

Set the document's primary language programmatically.

---

# 290. Language Changes

Substantial passages in another language SHOULD identify the language programmatically where applicable.

---

# 291. Plain Language

Content SHOULD use direct, understandable language appropriate to its audience.

Accessibility includes cognitive load.

---

# 292. Jargon

Use domain jargon only where users are expected to understand it.

Explain uncommon terms where necessary.

---

# 293. Instructions

Do not rely exclusively on sensory descriptions such as:

```text
Click the green button on the right.
```

Prefer:

```text
Select Save changes.
```

---

# 294. Consistency

Repeated components/navigation SHOULD behave and be identified consistently.

---

# 295. Predictability

Focus, input, or selection SHOULD NOT trigger unexpected major context changes without warning.

---

# 296. Auto-Submission

Changing a select/field SHOULD NOT unexpectedly submit or navigate unless that behavior is clear and appropriate.

---

# 297. Cognitive Load

Avoid unnecessary:

```text
motion
dense layouts
ambiguous icons
long unstructured forms
competing actions
```

that increase cognitive effort.

---

# 298. Reading Width

Long-form content SHOULD use readable line lengths rather than stretching across the entire viewport.

---

# 299. Text Alignment

Avoid full justification for ordinary long-form content.

Uneven spacing can reduce readability.

---

# 300. Line Height

Typography SHOULD provide sufficient line spacing for comfortable reading.

Avoid tightly packed body text.

---

# 301. Paragraph Spacing

Use consistent spacing between paragraphs and sections.

---

# 302. All Caps

Avoid long passages of uppercase text.

Use capitalization according to content rather than visual emphasis alone.

---

# 303. Decorative Fonts

Decorative typography SHOULD NOT reduce readability of primary content.

---

# 304. Icons + Labels

Use text labels alongside unfamiliar or consequential icons.

Do not assume every user knows product-specific icon meaning.

---

# 305. Responsive Text

Do not prevent browser text scaling.

---

# 306. Fixed Font Sizes

CSS pixels are scalable under browser zoom, but layouts must not depend on fixed dimensions that prevent content from accommodating enlarged text.

---

# 307. Content Clipping

Do not use:

```text
overflow: hidden
fixed height
```

in ways that clip meaningful enlarged text.

---

# 308. Sticky UI at Zoom

At high zoom, reduce or recompose sticky regions if they consume too much viewport space.

---

# 309. Keyboard + Zoom

Test keyboard workflows at high zoom.

An interface may technically reflow but still hide focused controls behind sticky elements.

---

# 310. Mobile Screen Readers

Responsive experiences SHOULD be tested with representative mobile screen-reader behavior for critical workflows where product usage warrants it.

---

# 311. Pointer Hover

Essential functionality MUST NOT depend on hover.

Touch users may have no hover state.

---

# 312. Hover and Focus Parity

Information revealed by hover should generally also be available through keyboard focus.

---

# 313. Persistent Hover Content

Hover/focus content must satisfy applicable requirements around:

```text
dismissibility
hoverability
persistence
```

---

# 314. Context Menus

Custom context menus require keyboard alternatives.

Right-click alone is insufficient for essential actions.

---

# 315. Long Press

Long-press interactions require an alternative where they provide essential functionality.

---

# 316. Voice Input

Visible labels and accessible names should align so speech-input users can refer to controls by the words they see.

---

# 317. Error Prevention

For legal, financial, or data-changing submissions with serious consequences, provide appropriate mechanisms to:

```text
review
confirm
correct
reverse
```

according to WCAG requirements and product risk.

---

# 318. Destructive Actions

High-impact destructive actions should identify:

```text
target
consequence
reversibility
```

clearly before commitment.

---

# 319. Undo

Reversible low-risk actions MAY use Undo instead of modal confirmation when this improves usability.

Undo itself must be accessible.

---

# 320. Authentication Accessibility

Security MUST NOT depend on inaccessible cognitive puzzles or mechanisms without alternatives.

---

# 321. Passkeys

Passkey/WebAuthn flows SHOULD use native browser/platform dialogs rather than recreating inaccessible authentication interfaces.

---

# 322. MFA

MFA flows should support:

```text
paste
password managers where applicable
keyboard
screen readers
sufficient timing
```

without weakening authentication.

---

# 323. QR Codes

A QR code MUST NOT be the sole mechanism where users may need an accessible text/manual alternative.

---

# 324. Recovery

Account-recovery information and controls must be operable with assistive technology.

---

# 325. Accessible Names and Security

Do not hide critical authentication semantics from assistive technology in an attempt to increase security.

Accessibility and secure implementation are compatible.

---

# 326. Notifications of Security Events

Security notices SHOULD use clear text and accessible action controls.

---

# 327. Tables vs Cards

Do not convert a semantically tabular dataset into unrelated visual cards solely for responsiveness if doing so destroys meaningful relationships.

---

# 328. Cards

Card collections SHOULD have semantic structure appropriate to their content.

Do not make every card an unlabeled generic region.

---

# 329. Clickable Cards

Avoid making an entire complex card one ambiguous nested interactive target when it also contains buttons/links.

---

# 330. Nested Interactive Controls

Do not place interactive controls inside other interactive controls.

Example:

```html
<button>
  ...
  <button>...</button>
</button>
```

is invalid and creates unpredictable behavior.

---

# 331. Toolbars

Command toolbars SHOULD use established toolbar keyboard interaction if implemented as an ARIA toolbar.

---

# 332. Command Palettes

Command palettes are dialog/combobox-like interfaces and require:

```text
accessible name
focus containment
search semantics
keyboard selection
escape
```

---

# 333. Drag Reordering

Reorderable lists MUST provide a keyboard-accessible mechanism.

---

# 334. Reordering Feedback

After a reorder action, communicate the resulting position where useful.

Example:

```text
Moved item to position 3 of 8.
```

---

# 335. Resizable Panels

Resizable split panes need keyboard-operable resizing where resizing is necessary to access functionality.

---

# 336. Resize Handles

Resize handles require appropriate accessible:

```text
role
orientation
value/state
keyboard controls
```

if implemented as interactive controls.

---

# 337. Carousels

Carousels SHOULD:

```text
not auto-advance by default where avoidable
expose next/previous controls
support keyboard
identify slide position
```

---

# 338. Carousel Rotation

If automatic rotation exists, users must have an appropriate pause mechanism.

---

# 339. Breadcrumb Separators

Decorative breadcrumb separators should not create unnecessary screen-reader speech.

---

# 340. Icons in Text

Decorative icons adjacent to equivalent visible text should be hidden from the accessibility tree.

---

# 341. Loading Buttons

When a button enters loading state:

