Generation and tool status SHOULD use an appropriate accessible status mechanism.

`role="status"` or an equivalent polite status mechanism MAY be used for ordinary asynchronous status changes. W3C documents `role="status"` as a technique for notifying assistive technology without moving focus. citeturn919553search2

Urgent `alert` semantics MUST NOT be used for routine:

- token updates;
- thinking state;
- progress;
- completed generation.

---

## 2.58 Completed responses SHOULD be discoverable without forced focus

Completion of a generated answer SHOULD NOT automatically move keyboard focus into the response unless that context change is required.

The interface SHOULD:

- announce completion appropriately;
- provide a stable way to navigate to the response.

A screen-reader user MUST NOT lose their composer position merely because generation completed.

---

## 2.59 Conversation semantics

Conversation interfaces SHOULD expose coherent semantic structure.

Each turn SHOULD make it possible to determine:

- author or role;
- content;
- relevant controls.

Repeated decorative labels SHOULD not create excessive screen-reader verbosity.

A generated response SHOULD be navigable using semantic headings, landmarks, message grouping, or another appropriate structure.

---

## 2.60 Generated content MUST preserve semantic markup

When generated content contains:

- headings;
- paragraphs;
- lists;
- tables;
- code;
- quotations

the rendered result SHOULD use the corresponding semantic HTML.

Visual Markdown styling without semantic elements MUST NOT be the standard rendering approach.

Heading levels SHOULD fit the surrounding document hierarchy rather than blindly reproducing model-provided heading numbers.

---

## 2.61 Generated tables MUST remain accessible

Generated tables MUST use semantic table markup where they represent tabular relationships.

Tables MUST NOT be rendered as images or monospaced ASCII solely because the model emitted text in that form when structured rendering is available.

Large generated tables SHOULD provide:

- horizontal accessibility strategy;
- responsive handling;
- downloadable structured data where useful.

---

## 2.62 Generated code MUST remain operable

Code blocks SHOULD expose:

- language where known;
- copy control;
- horizontal scrolling where necessary.

Copy controls MUST have accessible names.

Code highlighting MUST NOT reduce text contrast below Accessibility requirements.

Screen-reader users MUST be able to reach code without navigating decorative token spans individually.

---

## 2.63 Generated mathematics requires semantic access

Mathematical output SHOULD use an accessible math rendering strategy when supported.

Important equations MUST NOT exist only as raster images.

Generated explanations SHOULD provide textual context for complex notation where needed.

---

## 2.64 Generated images require accessible treatment

AI-generated images MUST follow the corpus image accessibility standard.

Where an image conveys meaningful content, appropriate alternative text or another equivalent representation MUST be available.

The alt text SHOULD describe the useful content, not merely:

`AI-generated image`.

AI provenance MAY be communicated separately.

---

## 2.65 Citations MUST remain accessible inside generated content

Interactive citation controls MUST not disrupt reading order.

Citation markers SHOULD remain compact visually while exposing descriptive accessible names.

Opening citation details MUST follow Overlay standards for:

- focus;
- dismissal;
- keyboard access.

---

## 2.66 Copy behavior MUST be predictable

Users SHOULD be able to copy generated output without accidentally copying:

- hidden status messages;
- control labels;
- citation implementation metadata;
- invisible accessibility text unrelated to the copied artifact.

Where citations are copied, the product SHOULD define whether the copied result includes:

- inline citation markers;
- source list;
- links.

---

## 2.67 Editing generated content

Generated content intended for downstream use SHOULD be editable where the workflow permits.

Users MUST be able to distinguish:

- regenerated content;
- manually edited content

where that distinction matters for audit or collaboration.

Regeneration MUST NOT overwrite manual edits without warning.

---

## 2.68 AI-generated form suggestions

AI suggestions in forms MUST remain suggestions until accepted when automatic application could materially change user intent.

Suggested values SHOULD be visually distinguishable before acceptance.

Acceptance MUST produce ordinary validated form state.

Rejecting a suggestion MUST NOT repeatedly reinsert it without a new trigger.

---

## 2.69 Autocomplete and inline generation

Inline AI completion MUST NOT interfere with ordinary text editing.

Suggested text SHOULD be distinguishable from committed text.

Users MUST have predictable controls to:

- accept;
- ignore;
- dismiss.

Screen readers MUST NOT repeatedly announce long speculative completions during ordinary typing.

---

## 2.70 Loading personality

AI loading states SHOULD be calm and factual.

Loading copy MAY communicate the current operation.

The product SHOULD NOT use fabricated activity such as:

- `Checking every possibility…`;
- `Almost done!`

unless that statement reflects actual system state.

Personality MUST NOT compromise status accuracy.

---

## 2.71 Latency messaging

A long-running request SHOULD provide meaningful state rather than an indefinitely animated spinner.

If execution duration becomes unusual, the product SHOULD communicate:

- that work is still active;
- relevant phase where known;
- cancellation options.

The product MUST NOT provide invented completion-time estimates.

---

## 2.72 Background or asynchronous execution

If the product genuinely supports background execution, the UI MUST distinguish:

- active foreground generation;
- queued work;
- background task;
- completed task.

A system that cannot continue work after the current interaction MUST NOT claim that it will complete something later.

Notification semantics MUST reflect actual background infrastructure.

---

## 2.73 Empty state

An AI surface empty state SHOULD explain:

- what the system can help with;
- what input is expected;
- important capability boundaries where useful.

Empty-state suggestions SHOULD be representative prompts, not claims that all shown tasks are guaranteed to succeed.

Sensitive information SHOULD NOT be solicited casually through example prompts.

---

## 2.74 Prompt input

The prompt composer is a form and MUST follow Forms & Validation.

It MUST support:

- keyboard input;
- multiline input where appropriate;
- predictable submission;
- accessible label.

Submission shortcuts MUST NOT make multiline authoring inaccessible.

The product MUST clearly distinguish:

- Enter to submit;
- Shift+Enter or equivalent to insert a new line

where keyboard conventions depend on that distinction.

---

## 2.75 Attachments

Attachment state MUST be explicit.

Users SHOULD be able to determine whether a file is:

- selected;
- uploading;
- uploaded;
- processed;
- failed.

The model MUST NOT imply it read an attachment that failed processing.

Removing an attachment before submission MUST remove it from the generation context.

---

## 2.76 File processing status

For long document-processing operations, the interface SHOULD distinguish:

- upload;
- parsing/indexing;
- ready;
- failure.

`Uploaded` MUST NOT be treated as equivalent to `available to the model` unless that is actually true.

---

## 2.77 Source and context boundaries

When a response uses a constrained source set, the UI SHOULD communicate that context where it affects interpretation.

Examples include:

- `Answering from uploaded files`;
- `Using company knowledge base`;
- `Web sources enabled`.

The system MUST NOT imply comprehensive external research when it used only a narrow context.

---

## 2.78 Conversation context limits

If earlier content is no longer available to the model because of architectural context limits, the product SHOULD avoid implying perfect recall.

Where loss of earlier context materially affects the task, the interface SHOULD communicate or mitigate it.

The system MUST NOT invent recollection of content that is no longer accessible.

---

## 2.79 User feedback

Feedback controls MAY collect quality signals such as:

- helpful;
- not helpful;
- incorrect citation;
- unsafe;
- formatting problem.

Feedback MUST NOT interrupt normal reading.

Feedback categories SHOULD be actionable.

Submitting feedback MUST follow applicable privacy and telemetry standards.

---

## 2.80 shadcn/ui baseline

shadcn/ui MUST be the component baseline for AI application UI.

Current shadcn/ui includes conventional primitives as well as message-oriented components such as `Message`, `Message Scroller`, `Bubble`, `Attachment`, plus `Progress`, `Skeleton`, `Alert`, `Tooltip`, `Textarea`, and related primitives. citeturn324584search4

Preferred mappings include:

| Concern | shadcn/ui baseline |
|---|---|
| Prompt input | `Textarea`, `Input Group` |
| Primary actions | `Button`, `Button Group` |
| Conversation message | `Message` / application message abstraction |
| Scrollable conversation | `Message Scroller` or canonical scroll pattern |
| Attachments | `Attachment` / application attachment abstraction |
| Processing state | `Spinner`, `Progress`, `Skeleton` as appropriate |
| Error or warning | `Alert` |
| Citation preview | `Popover`, `Hover Card`, `Sheet` depending complexity |
| Details / reasoning summary | `Collapsible`, `Accordion` |
| Memory/settings controls | `Dialog`, `Sheet`, standard form controls |
| Model selection | `Select`, `Combobox`, `Dropdown Menu` |
| Cost explanation | `Tooltip`, `Popover` for supplementary detail |
| Retry/regenerate/stop | `Button`, `Button Group` |

shadcn/ui `Progress` supports labelled progress composition, while `Skeleton` is explicitly intended as a loading placeholder. citeturn324584search0turn324584search5

Product teams SHOULD build AI-specific abstractions from these primitives rather than introduce an unrelated component system.

---

## 2.81 Design tokens

AI UX MUST use shared semantic tokens.

Relevant concepts SHOULD include:

- AI-generated content;
- user content;
- source/citation;
- pending;
- success;
- warning;
- error;
- refused;
- selected;
- uncertain;
- memory/personalization indicator where visually required.

Tokens MUST describe semantic purpose rather than model vendor or literal colour.

Prefer:

`--ai-source`

over:

`--ai-purple`.

AI identity colour MUST NOT override established semantic warning, destructive, or success colours.

---

## 2.82 AI styling MUST NOT imply authority

Generated responses MUST NOT use visual styling that makes them indistinguishable from:

- legal system notices;
- verified database records;
- official human approval;
- validated medical or financial results

unless the underlying content actually has that status.

Typography, badges, and colour SHOULD preserve the distinction between generated advice and authoritative application state.

---

## 2.83 Security state overrides generated content

If authorization changes, restricted generated or retrieved content MUST be removed or protected according to Security policy.

A generated response MUST NOT retain access to restricted source content merely because the response is already visible in client state where policy requires revocation.

Caches and conversation persistence MUST respect authorization boundaries.

---

## 2.84 Sensitive output handling

Generated output containing sensitive information MUST follow the same:

- access controls;
- copy controls where applicable;
- retention;
- export;
- audit

requirements as equivalent non-AI content.

Generated content MUST NOT be assumed non-sensitive simply because the model created it.

---

## 2.85 Auditability for consequential workflows

Where AI participates in consequential business workflows, systems SHOULD preserve sufficient provenance to reconstruct:

- user instruction;
- relevant model/version class where required;
- source context;
- generated proposal;
- user approval;
- tool action;
- resulting system response.

Audit logging MUST follow Security and privacy requirements and MUST NOT indiscriminately record hidden reasoning or secrets.

---

## 2.86 Testing

AI UX tests MUST cover more than ideal completed responses.

Representative test states SHOULD include:

- immediate completion;
- slow first token;
- streaming;
- stop;
- stream interruption;
- malformed structured output;
- refusal;
- rate limit;
- model error;
- tool failure;
- citation unavailable;
- contradictory sources;
- attachment processing failure;
- memory disabled;
- cost exhaustion;
- reduced-motion mode;
- keyboard-only use;
- screen-reader use.

The UI MUST be tested with very long generated content and very short content.

---

## 2.87 Accessibility testing

Accessibility testing MUST include:

- composer operation;
- send/stop transition;
- generation status;
- completed-message discovery;
- citation navigation;
- regenerated-version navigation;
- errors;
- refusal;
- code;
- tables;
- tool status.

Streaming MUST be tested with actual assistive technology.

Automated accessibility tests alone are insufficient to validate streaming announcement cadence.

---

# 3. Anti-patterns

The following are non-conforming unless an explicit, documented requirement provides a stronger justification.

## 3.1 Disclosure

- AI-generated content presented as human-authored without disclosure.
- Sparkle icon as the only AI disclosure.
- Generated database-like values styled as verified truth.
- Assistant persona implying a real employee performed work when it did not.

## 3.2 Streaming

- Treating a partially streamed answer as complete.
- Announcing every streamed token to a screen reader.
- Controls moving continuously as tokens arrive.
- Losing all useful partial output after connection interruption.
- Streaming malformed Markdown protocol directly to users.
- Auto-scrolling so aggressively that users cannot inspect earlier text.

## 3.3 Thinking and progress

- Exposing raw private chain-of-thought.
- Fabricating detailed “thinking” narration.
- Fake percentages.
- `Almost done` without actual progress knowledge.
- Treating model-generated progress prose as execution telemetry.
- Showing verbose internal logs to ordinary users without purpose.

## 3.4 Sources

- Citation numbers with no source behind them.
- One source list implying all claims are supported.
- Cited styling implying guaranteed truth.
- Fabricated titles, URLs, or document references.
- Quote styling for model paraphrase.
- Source previews inaccessible to keyboard users.

## 3.5 Confidence

- Arbitrary `97% confident` labels.
- Green confidence badge meaning “true”.
- Generic uncertainty disclaimers on every message.
- Hiding known uncertainty because the output reads more confidently.
- Treating disagreement between sources as model confidence.

## 3.6 Regeneration and editing

- Regeneration silently deleting the previous answer.
- Retrying a failed external action without checking whether it already succeeded.
- Editing an old prompt while leaving dependent later messages presented as valid.
- Regeneration duplicating sent emails, purchases, deletions, or other effects.

## 3.7 Memory

- Saying `I'll remember that` without successful persistence.
- Saying information was deleted without actual deletion state.
- Calling connected email or document access “memory”.
- Hiding persistent personalization so users cannot understand why it affects answers.
- Persisting sensitive context unnecessarily.

## 3.8 Errors and refusals

- Refusal displayed as `Something went wrong`.
- Rate limit displayed as safety refusal.
- Tool authorization failure blamed on the model.
- Clearing the user's prompt after a generation error.
- Recommending repeated retries for an intentionally unsupported request.
- Hostile or moralizing refusal language.

## 3.9 Cost and quota

- Charging material credits without pre-action visibility.
- Calling an estimate an exact price.
- Requiring users to understand token accounting when credits/currency would be clearer.
- Running expensive agents indefinitely without budget controls.
- Quota exhaustion displayed as generic model failure.

## 3.10 Actions

- Generated `Done` text when the API action failed.
- A model granting itself permission to perform an action.
- Hidden bundles of consequential tool calls behind one vague confirmation.
- Automatically navigating to model-generated external links.
- Executing AI-suggested destructive action without required authorization.

## 3.11 Accessibility

- Token-by-token `aria-live` announcements.
- AI answer rendered as one giant unstructured text node.
- Citation controls named only `1`, `2`, `3`.
- Code copy control with no accessible name.
- Streaming completion stealing focus from the composer.
- AI suggestions appearing only through colour.
- Generated images without equivalent alternatives where needed.

## 3.12 Loading personality

- Fake status messages to entertain users.
- Anthropomorphic processing statements presented as technical facts.
- Artificially delaying output so an animation can finish.
- Endless spinner where actual tool state is available.

## 3.13 Security

- Treating retrieved text as trusted system instruction.
- Prompt content bypassing backend authorization.
- Exposing secrets in generation debug UI.
- Recording private reasoning or sensitive prompts indiscriminately for analytics.
- Assuming generated content is harmless because it originated from the model.

---

# 4. Checklist

## 4.1 AI disclosure

- [ ] Users can determine that AI is involved.
- [ ] Generated and authoritative application content remain distinguishable.
- [ ] Disclosure does not rely only on colour or iconography.
- [ ] The product does not falsely imply human review or action.

## 4.2 Streaming

- [ ] Pending, streaming, complete, stopped, and failed states are distinct.
- [ ] Streaming remains readable.
- [ ] Partial content can be recovered where appropriate.
- [ ] Stop is accessible and stable.
- [ ] Visual streaming does not produce token-by-token AT announcements.
- [ ] Stream failures do not masquerade as completion.

## 4.3 Progress and thinking

- [ ] User-visible progress reflects real system/task state.
- [ ] Unknown progress is represented as indeterminate.
- [ ] No fabricated percentages are shown.
- [ ] Raw private chain-of-thought is not exposed.
- [ ] Useful explanation is provided through summaries, methodology, assumptions, or sources instead.
- [ ] Tool progress derives from orchestration state where available.

## 4.4 Citations

- [ ] Citations are attached to the claims they support.
- [ ] Every citation resolves to a real source object.
- [ ] Source identity is clear.
- [ ] Access restrictions are represented accurately.
- [ ] Quotes and paraphrases are distinguishable.
- [ ] Citation controls are keyboard and screen-reader accessible.
- [ ] Citation styling does not imply guaranteed correctness.

## 4.5 Uncertainty

- [ ] Material uncertainty is communicated.
- [ ] Uncertainty appears near the relevant claim.
- [ ] Missing data, disagreement, estimate, and prediction are distinguished where relevant.
- [ ] Unsupported numerical confidence is absent.
- [ ] Visual certainty indicators have validated semantics.

## 4.6 User controls

- [ ] Stop is available for materially long generation.
- [ ] Retry and regenerate have distinct semantics.
- [ ] Regeneration does not silently destroy previous output.
- [ ] Historical edits preserve or clearly revise conversational lineage.
- [ ] Consequential actions are not repeated during regeneration.

## 4.7 Memory

- [ ] Conversation context and persistent memory are distinguishable.
- [ ] Persistent memory is inspectable where supported.
- [ ] Memory enable/disable/update/delete actions reflect actual state.
- [ ] Connected sources are not misrepresented as memory.
- [ ] Sensitive memory follows Security and privacy requirements.

## 4.8 Errors and refusals

- [ ] Technical errors, refusals, limits, and authorization failures are distinct.
- [ ] User work is preserved after recoverable errors.
- [ ] The next available action is clear.
- [ ] Refusal wording is concise and non-accusatory.
- [ ] Retry cannot accidentally duplicate external actions.

## 4.9 Cost and quota

- [ ] Material cost is visible before commitment.
- [ ] Estimates are identified as estimates.
- [ ] Remaining quota/credits are understandable where applicable.
- [ ] Expensive long-running tasks have appropriate limits.
- [ ] Quota exhaustion has a distinct state.

## 4.10 External actions

- [ ] Suggestion, draft, approval, execution, and completion are distinct.
- [ ] Tool/API state is authoritative.
- [ ] Consequential actions have appropriate confirmation.
- [ ] Authorization is enforced independently of model output.
- [ ] Tool failures cannot become fabricated success messages.

## 4.11 Forms and generated data

- [ ] Generated structured values pass normal validation.
- [ ] AI suggestions remain suggestions until accepted where necessary.
- [ ] Generated edits do not bypass authorization or domain constraints.
- [ ] Form error state survives generation and retries.

## 4.12 Accessibility

- [ ] Composer and generation controls are keyboard operable.
- [ ] Generation status is programmatically available.
- [ ] Streaming announcements are appropriately throttled.
- [ ] Completion does not unexpectedly steal focus.
- [ ] Generated headings use semantic hierarchy.
- [ ] Tables use semantic table markup.
- [ ] Code blocks are usable and copy controls are labelled.
- [ ] Citations have descriptive accessible names.
- [ ] Generated images have appropriate alternatives.
- [ ] AI suggestions are not distinguished by colour alone.

## 4.13 Security

- [ ] Retrieved content is treated as untrusted input.
- [ ] Prompt text cannot override backend authorization.
- [ ] Sensitive data is protected in history, logs, and generated content.
- [ ] Generated links follow safe-link policy.
- [ ] AI output cannot self-authorize tool use.
- [ ] Audit records do not indiscriminately expose secrets or hidden reasoning.

## 4.14 State management

- [ ] Conversation branches have explicit lineage.
- [ ] Generation state has one canonical owner.
- [ ] Partial output state is represented explicitly.
- [ ] External actions remain independent from conversational branch presentation.
- [ ] Memory state reflects backend state.
- [ ] Animation state is not confused with generation state.

## 4.15 shadcn/ui

- [ ] shadcn/ui remains the component baseline.
- [ ] Composer uses established input primitives.
- [ ] Status and errors use canonical components.
- [ ] Citation details use accessible overlay components.
- [ ] Progress uses `Progress`, `Spinner`, `Skeleton`, or an appropriate composition.
- [ ] AI-specific abstractions extend rather than replace the component system.

## 4.16 Testing

- [ ] Slow first-token latency is tested.
- [ ] Streaming interruption is tested.
- [ ] Stop is tested.
- [ ] Retry is tested.
- [ ] Regeneration is tested.
- [ ] Refusal is tested.
- [ ] Tool failure is tested.
- [ ] Citation failure is tested.
- [ ] Memory state changes are tested.
- [ ] Quota exhaustion is tested.
- [ ] Long generated content is tested.
- [ ] Keyboard and screen-reader flows are tested with actual streaming.

## 4.17 Corpus alignment

- [ ] Security controls authorization and untrusted source handling.
- [ ] Data & Database controls persistence, provenance and retention.
- [ ] API controls streaming, cancellation, retries, limits and tool execution.
- [ ] State Management controls branches, generation state and memory state.
- [ ] Forms & Validation governs prompt inputs and AI-generated structured values.
- [ ] Accessibility governs streaming status and generated-content semantics.
- [ ] Design Tokens govern AI status and provenance styling.
- [ ] Components use shadcn/ui as the baseline.
- [ ] Pattern standards govern errors, confirmations, overlays, loading and undo.
- [ ] Content & UX Writing governs disclosure, uncertainty, refusals and status language.

---

# 5. Canonical summary

A Gold Standard 2026 AI interface MUST make AI involvement understandable without overwhelming the user with repetitive disclaimers.

Streaming MUST be represented as partial generation rather than finished truth. Pending, streaming, stopped, failed, refused, and completed states MUST remain distinguishable.

Users SHOULD be able to stop materially long generation. Retry, regenerate, edit, and continue MUST have distinct semantics, and regeneration MUST NOT silently destroy previous useful output or repeat consequential external actions.

Progress disclosure MUST represent actual system state. Unknown progress MUST remain indeterminate, and products MUST NOT fabricate percentages or detailed internal activity merely to appear transparent.

Raw private chain-of-thought MUST NOT be treated as a standard user-visible surface. Useful transparency SHOULD instead come from concise reasoning summaries, assumptions, methodology, evidence, tool status, and verifiable intermediate results. citeturn919553search0turn919553search3

Citations MUST point to real sources and SHOULD sit near supported claims. Citation presence MUST NOT be presented as proof that every generated statement is correct.

Material uncertainty SHOULD be communicated specifically and locally. Unsupported numerical confidence MUST NOT be invented.

Persistent memory, current conversation context, account preferences, and connected-source access MUST remain conceptually distinct. Any claim that information was remembered, deleted, or changed MUST reflect actual persistence state.

Generated language describing an external action MUST never override authoritative API state. The interface MUST distinguish suggestion, draft, approval, execution, and successful completion.

Technical errors, refusals, authorization failures, rate limits, and quota exhaustion MUST remain distinguishable. Recoverable failures SHOULD preserve user input and useful partial output.

Material AI cost or credit usage SHOULD be visible before commitment. Estimated and actual cost MUST remain distinct.

Generated structured values MUST pass the same validation and authorization requirements as ordinary user input. Model output MUST NOT bypass Security, Forms, API, or database invariants.

AI-generated content MUST be accessible as semantic content rather than merely visually formatted text. Streaming status MUST be available to assistive technology without creating token-by-token announcement noise; W3C requires programmatic status communication and explicitly cautions that excessive live updates can become overly chatty. citeturn919553search1turn919553search5

shadcn/ui is the canonical component baseline. AI-specific message, composer, citation, source, generation-state, and memory abstractions SHOULD compose the shared component system rather than create a parallel one. citeturn324584search4

**Canonical rule:** an AI interaction is conforming only when users can understand what is generated, what is sourced, what is uncertain, what is remembered, what is happening, what has actually been executed, what it may cost, and how to stop, correct, inspect, or recover the interaction without relying on hidden model reasoning or inaccessible interface state.

The strictest architectural boundary in this standard is deliberate: **model language is presentation; application/tool state is authority**. That prevents a large class of AI UX failures around fake progress, fabricated action completion, memory claims, citations, and cost reporting.


<!-- ===== security | security | standards/security/01-security.md ===== -->

This version treats security as a **product architecture constraint**, not a final penetration-test phase. The baseline is aligned to the current **OWASP ASVS 5.0.0**, **OWASP Top 10:2025**, NIST SSDF, and current NIST SP 800-63-4 identity guidance. OWASP’s 2025 Top 10 now places Broken Access Control first and explicitly includes Software Supply Chain Failures and Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions, so those are first-class sections below. citeturn293660search0turn977297search0turn977297search1

# Security Guidelines — Gold Standard

## 1. Purpose

These guidelines define the minimum security standard for product engineering.

The objective is to ensure that products are:

- secure by design;
- secure by default;
- resilient to misuse;
- resistant to common attack classes;
- defensible during incidents;
- observable;
- recoverable;
- maintainable;
- testable;
- least-privileged;
- safe across tenant boundaries.

Security is a product property.

It is not:

- a penetration test performed before launch;
- a compliance checkbox;
- a responsibility delegated solely to infrastructure;
- something users must manually configure correctly;
- something that can be added after architecture is complete.

The core principle is:

> **The secure path must be the default path.**

---

# 2. Normative Language

The following terms are intentional:

- **MUST** — mandatory.
- **MUST NOT** — prohibited.
- **SHOULD** — expected unless an explicitly documented exception exists.
- **SHOULD NOT** — generally prohibited unless justified.
- **MAY** — optional.

Exceptions to mandatory security controls require:

1. documented justification;
2. risk assessment;
3. compensating controls;
4. named owner;
5. expiration/review date.

---

# 3. Security Hierarchy

Security should be applied at every architectural layer.

```text
Product Requirements
        ↓
Threat Model
        ↓
Identity
        ↓
Authorization
        ↓
Application Logic
        ↓
Data Protection
        ↓
API / Network Boundaries
        ↓
Infrastructure
        ↓
Supply Chain
        ↓
Deployment
        ↓
Monitoring
        ↓
Incident Response
```

A secure UI over an insecure backend is not a secure product.

---

# 4. Security Principles

## 4.1 Secure by design

Security requirements MUST be considered while designing the feature.

Do not design:

```text
Feature
↓
Implementation
↓
Launch
↓
Security review
```

Prefer:

```text
Requirements
↓
Threat model
↓
Security requirements
↓
Implementation
↓
Verification
↓
Launch
```

---

## 4.2 Secure by default

The default configuration MUST be the safe configuration.

Users SHOULD NOT need to:

- discover security settings;
- disable dangerous defaults;
- buy a higher plan for fundamental protections;
- understand infrastructure security to use the product safely.

---

## 4.3 Deny by default

When authorization is unclear:

```text
deny
```

not:

```text
allow
```

Access should require a positive authorization decision.

---

## 4.4 Least privilege

Every:

- user;
- service;
- API key;
- worker;
- database role;
- CI job;
- integration;

MUST receive only the permissions required to perform its function.

---

## 4.5 Minimize trust

Do not trust a value merely because it comes from:

- your own frontend;
- another microservice;
- a mobile application;
- an authenticated user;
- a signed-in administrator;
- a webhook;
- an internal network.

Validate trust at boundaries.

---

## 4.6 Defense in depth

Critical controls SHOULD have independent protective layers.

Example:

```text
Authentication
+
Authorization
+
Tenant isolation
+
Database constraints
+
Audit logging
```

Do not rely on one control to prevent catastrophic compromise.

---

## 4.7 Fail securely

Unexpected conditions MUST default to safe behavior.

If authorization cannot be determined:

```text
deny
```

If security configuration is unavailable:

```text
fail closed where appropriate
```

If a signature cannot be validated:

```text
reject
```

Never interpret an unexpected condition as permission.

---

# 5. Security Ownership

Every production system MUST have identifiable owners for:

- application security;
- authentication;
- authorization;
- infrastructure;
- secrets;
- dependency management;
- incident response;
- vulnerability remediation.

Security responsibilities MUST NOT depend on institutional memory.

---

# 6. Asset Classification

Before implementing security controls, identify what is being protected.

Typical categories:

```text
Public
Internal
Confidential
Highly sensitive
Regulated
Secret / credential material
```

Examples of high-risk assets:

- authentication credentials;
- session tokens;
- API keys;
- private encryption keys;
- financial data;
- personal data;
- health information;
- security logs;
- recovery credentials.

Controls should reflect data sensitivity.

---

# 7. Threat Modeling

Significant features SHOULD undergo threat modeling before implementation.

At minimum identify:

```text
Assets
Actors
Trust boundaries
Entry points
Privileges
Data flows
External dependencies
Failure modes
Abuse cases
```

Ask:

1. What are we protecting?
2. Who could attack it?
3. Where does untrusted data enter?
4. Where does privilege change?
5. What happens if this dependency is compromised?
6. What happens if the client is malicious?
7. What happens if one tenant attempts to access another?
8. How would abuse be detected?

---

# 8. Threat Model Triggers

Threat review is particularly important for:

- authentication;
- authorization;
- payments;
- file uploads;
- webhooks;
- public APIs;
- admin tools;
- multi-tenant boundaries;
- encryption;
- secrets;
- account recovery;
- data exports;
- integrations;
- user-generated content;
- AI agents or autonomous actions.

---

# 9. Authentication

Authentication establishes identity.

Authorization establishes permission.

Never confuse the two.

A valid login does not imply authorization to access every resource.

---

# 10. Prefer Established Identity Systems

Do not build custom authentication protocols unless identity is a core product capability and the organization has appropriate security expertise.

Prefer established:

- identity providers;
- authentication frameworks;
- OAuth/OIDC implementations;
- WebAuthn/passkey libraries.

Authentication code has a high failure cost.

---

# 11. Phishing-Resistant Authentication

Phishing-resistant authentication SHOULD be offered wherever practical.

Preferred mechanisms include:

```text
Passkeys / WebAuthn
Hardware security keys
Enterprise federation with strong authenticators
```

Privileged administrative accounts SHOULD use phishing-resistant authentication.

---

# 12. Password Policy

Where passwords are supported:

- permit long passphrases;
- block known compromised/common passwords;
- do not impose arbitrary character-composition rules;
- do not require routine password rotation without evidence of compromise;
- permit password managers and paste;
- do not truncate passwords silently.

Recommended baseline:

```text
Single-factor password:
minimum 15 characters

Password used as part of MFA:
minimum 8 characters

Maximum accepted length:
at least 64 characters
```

Password requirements SHOULD be revisited when authoritative identity guidance changes.

---

# 13. Password Storage

Passwords MUST NOT be:

- stored in plaintext;
- reversibly encrypted for authentication;
- logged;
- exposed through support tooling.

Use an approved password hashing algorithm designed for password storage.

Prefer:

```text
Argon2id
```

when supported.

Use:

- unique salts;
- appropriate work factors;
- versioned hashing parameters;
- safe migration strategy.

---

# 14. Multi-Factor Authentication

MFA SHOULD be available for user accounts and required where risk warrants it.

MFA SHOULD be mandatory for:

- privileged operators;
- administrative consoles;
- production infrastructure;
- source control administration;
- security-sensitive internal systems.

Prefer phishing-resistant factors over SMS or manually entered OTP where practical.

---

# 15. Authentication Rate Limiting

Authentication endpoints MUST resist automated guessing.

Controls MAY include:

- rate limiting;
- progressive delay;
- IP/device risk signals;
- compromised-password detection;
- bot mitigation.

Avoid permanent account lockouts that create trivial denial-of-service attacks.

---

# 16. Authentication Enumeration

Authentication and recovery flows SHOULD avoid unnecessary account enumeration.

Responses such as:

```text
No account exists with that email.
```

may expose registered accounts.

Where relevant, use consistent responses such as:

```text
If an account exists, recovery instructions have been sent.
```

Do not compromise usability blindly; apply this where enumeration creates meaningful risk.

---

# 17. Reauthentication

Require stronger or recent authentication before security-sensitive operations.

Examples:

- changing password;
- changing primary email;
- adding an authenticator;
- disabling MFA;
- viewing recovery codes;
- transferring ownership;
- changing payout information;
- deleting an account;
- modifying privileged access.

---

# 18. Account Recovery

Account recovery is an authentication mechanism and MUST receive equivalent security scrutiny.

Recovery MUST NOT be weaker than normal authentication without explicit risk analysis.

Recovery credentials MUST:

- be random;
- be single-use where appropriate;
- expire;
- be protected from disclosure.

High-risk recovery events SHOULD generate security notifications.

---

# 19. Email Verification

Email ownership SHOULD be verified before relying on an email address for:

- account recovery;
- sensitive notifications;
- invitations;
- identity decisions.

Changing the primary email SHOULD require appropriate reauthentication.

---

# 20. Session Management

Authenticated sessions are security credentials.

Treat session identifiers with the same care as authentication credentials.

Session identifiers MUST:

- be unpredictable;
- have sufficient entropy;
- be transmitted only over protected channels;
- not appear in URLs;
- be invalidated appropriately.

---

# 21. Session Cookies

Web session cookies SHOULD use appropriate attributes such as:

```text
Secure
HttpOnly
SameSite
```

Use the most restrictive `SameSite` behavior compatible with required workflows.

Prefer host-bound cookies where architecture allows it.

Do not make session tokens accessible to client-side JavaScript unless the architecture explicitly requires and secures that model.

---

# 22. Session Rotation

Session identifiers SHOULD rotate following security-sensitive transitions such as:

- authentication;
- privilege elevation;
- account recovery;
- major credential change.

This reduces session fixation risk.

---

# 23. Session Expiration

Sessions MUST have defined expiration behavior.

Consider:

```text
Idle timeout
Absolute lifetime
Reauthentication interval
Remember-me behavior
```

Higher-risk contexts require shorter or stronger reauthentication policies.

---

# 24. Session Revocation

The system SHOULD support revoking:

- a single session;
- all sessions for a user;
- sessions associated with compromised credentials.

Security-sensitive credential changes SHOULD invalidate affected sessions where appropriate.

---

# 25. Logout

Logout MUST invalidate the server-side session or equivalent credential state where applicable.

Removing only client-side UI state is insufficient.

---

# 26. Authorization

Authorization is one of the highest-risk application concerns.

Every sensitive operation MUST enforce authorization on the trusted server side.

Never rely solely on:

- hidden buttons;
- disabled controls;
- frontend route guards;
- client-side role checks.

---

# 27. Object-Level Authorization

Every request for a resource MUST verify that the requester can access that specific resource.

Example:

```text
GET /projects/123
```

must verify:

```text
Can this principal access project 123?
```

not merely:

```text
Is this principal authenticated?
```

---

# 28. Function-Level Authorization

Sensitive operations require explicit permission checks.

Examples:

```text
create
read
update
delete
invite
export
approve
administer
transfer
```

Do not assume access to a resource implies permission for every operation.

---

# 29. Authorization Model

Use a deliberate authorization model such as:

```text
RBAC
ABAC
ReBAC
Policy-based authorization
```

Avoid scattered ad hoc checks such as:

```text
if user.email === ...
```

or feature-specific permission logic with no central semantics.

---

# 30. Authorization Centralization

Authorization policy SHOULD be centralized enough to:

- audit;
- test;
- reason about;
- evolve safely.

Avoid duplicating subtly different authorization checks across controllers, routes, workers, and UI code.

---

# 31. Ownership Checks

Never trust an object identifier from the client to establish ownership.

Bad:

```text
userId supplied by client
↓
query resource
```

Preferred:

```text
authenticated principal
↓
authorized scope
↓
resource lookup
```

---

# 32. Multi-Tenant Isolation

Tenant boundaries are security boundaries.

Every tenant-scoped operation MUST establish tenant context independently from untrusted client claims.

Verify:

```text
principal
↓
tenant membership
↓
permission
↓
resource ownership
```

before returning or modifying tenant data.

---

# 33. Tenant Context

Do not rely solely on:

```text
workspaceId from request
```

or:

```text
tenantId from frontend state
```

Use authenticated identity and authoritative membership data to validate tenant context.

---

# 34. Cross-Tenant Testing

Multi-tenant systems MUST include tests specifically attempting:

```text
Tenant A user
→ Tenant B object ID
```

for:

- reads;
- writes;
- deletes;
- exports;
- file downloads;
- search;
- bulk actions;
- background tasks.

---

# 35. Privileged Roles

Administrative access MUST be tightly controlled.

Privileged accounts SHOULD:

- be minimal in number;
- use strong MFA;
- be logged extensively;
- avoid routine day-to-day use;
- have narrowly scoped permissions where possible.

---

# 36. Impersonation

Support/admin impersonation is a high-risk capability.

If supported, it MUST include:

- explicit permission;
- visible impersonation state;
- audit logging;
- reason/context where appropriate;
- controlled exit;
- restrictions on highly sensitive actions.

Never make impersonation invisible to operators.

---

# 37. Input Validation

All untrusted input MUST be validated at a trusted boundary.

Client-side validation improves UX.

It does not provide security.

Server-side validation remains mandatory.

---

# 38. Allowlist Validation

Prefer defining what is valid.

Example:

```text
status ∈ {
  active,
  paused,
  archived
}
```

instead of attempting to enumerate every invalid value.

---

# 39. Type and Range Validation

Validate:

- type;
- length;
- range;
- structure;
- allowed values;
- required relationships.

Example:

```text
page:
integer
>= 1
<= safe maximum
```

Never assume framework type coercion is sufficient.

---

# 40. Injection Prevention

Do not construct executable queries by concatenating untrusted input.

Use safe APIs and parameterization for:

- SQL;
- NoSQL;
- shell commands;
- LDAP;
- templates;
- search languages;
- expression languages.

Preferred:

```text
parameterized operation
```

not:

```text
string concatenation
```

---

# 41. SQL Injection

Use parameterized queries or safe ORM query construction.

Never interpolate untrusted input directly into SQL.

Dynamic:

- column names;
- sort directions;
- table names;

must be mapped against explicit allowlists.

---

# 42. Command Injection

Avoid invoking shell commands with user-controlled values.

Where operating-system interaction is necessary:

- avoid shell parsing;
- use safe process APIs;
- provide arguments separately;
- allowlist permissible values.

---

# 43. Cross-Site Scripting

Treat output context correctly.

Prefer framework-native output encoding.

Avoid unsafe rendering primitives such as raw HTML injection unless content has undergone appropriate sanitization.

User-controlled HTML MUST be sanitized with a purpose-built, maintained sanitizer.

---

# 44. HTML Sanitization

Do not attempt to sanitize HTML using regular expressions.

Use a vetted HTML sanitizer configured according to the product's allowed markup.

Sanitization policy should be explicit.

---

# 45. Content Security Policy

Web applications SHOULD deploy a meaningful Content Security Policy.

Prefer policies that restrict:

- scripts;
- frames;
- object sources;
- base URIs;
- form destinations.

Avoid relying indefinitely on extremely broad policies such as unrestricted inline script execution.

CSP is defense in depth and does not replace safe output handling.

---

# 46. Cross-Site Request Forgery

State-changing requests authenticated through browser credentials MUST address CSRF risk.

Use appropriate protections such as:

- CSRF tokens;
- origin verification;
- same-site cookies;
- framework protections.

`SameSite` cookies are defense in depth, not a universal replacement for CSRF controls.

---

# 47. CORS

CORS policy MUST be explicit.

Do not deploy:

```text
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
```

for credentialed sensitive APIs.

Allow only origins required by the architecture.

Validate origins exactly rather than using unsafe substring matching.

---

# 48. Security Headers

Web applications SHOULD deliberately configure relevant headers, including where applicable:

```text
Content-Security-Policy
Strict-Transport-Security
X-Content-Type-Options
Referrer-Policy
Permissions-Policy
frame restrictions
```

Do not rely on historical browser defaults.

---

# 49. HTTPS

All authenticated and sensitive traffic MUST use HTTPS.

HTTP SHOULD redirect to HTTPS where appropriate.

Production systems SHOULD enable HSTS once deployment architecture is known to support it safely.

---

# 50. TLS

Use supported modern TLS configurations.

Do not manually create cryptographic transport protocols.

Certificate issuance and renewal SHOULD be automated and monitored.

---

# 51. Cryptography

Use established cryptographic libraries and protocols.

Never create custom cryptographic algorithms.

Developers SHOULD NOT manually combine cryptographic primitives unless they have specialist expertise and a reviewed design.

---

# 52. Encryption at Rest

Sensitive data SHOULD be encrypted at rest according to threat model and platform capabilities.

Encryption keys MUST be separated from encrypted data to the extent practical.

Encryption does not replace authorization.

---

# 53. Encryption in Transit

Sensitive data MUST be protected in transit.

This applies to:

- browser connections;
- service-to-service communication where risk warrants;
- database connections;
- administrative interfaces;
- integrations.

---

# 54. Key Management

Encryption keys MUST have controlled lifecycle management.

Define:

```text
Creation
Storage
Access
Rotation
Revocation
Backup
Destruction
```

Prefer managed key-management systems for production.

---

# 55. Secrets

Secrets include:

- API keys;
- private keys;
- database passwords;
- signing secrets;
- OAuth client secrets;
- webhook secrets;
- service credentials.

Secrets MUST NOT be committed to source control.

---

# 56. Secret Storage

Production secrets SHOULD be stored in an approved secret-management system.

Avoid:

```text
source files
frontend bundles
Docker images
documentation
chat messages
shared spreadsheets
```

as secret storage.

---

# 57. Secret Rotation

Secrets MUST be rotatable.

High-value secrets SHOULD support rotation without prolonged downtime.

Rotation procedures SHOULD be tested before an incident occurs.

---

# 58. Secret Exposure

If a secret is exposed:

```text
Revoke/rotate
↓
Investigate
↓
Determine exposure window
↓
Review logs
↓
Remediate source
```

Deleting the secret from Git history alone does not invalidate it.

---

# 59. Frontend Secrets

Anything shipped to a browser or mobile client must be considered observable by the user.

Never embed server secrets in frontend environment variables.

A variable being called:

```text
SECRET
```

does not make it secret once included in a client bundle.

---

# 60. Data Minimization

Collect only the data required for legitimate product needs.

Do not collect sensitive data merely because it may become useful later.

Reduced data collection reduces breach impact.

---

# 61. Data Retention

Sensitive information MUST have a defined retention policy.

Define:

```text
Why collected
How long retained
Where stored
How deleted
Backup lifecycle
```

Do not retain data indefinitely without a documented reason.

---

# 62. Data Deletion

Deletion semantics MUST be explicit.

Distinguish:

```text
soft delete
hard delete
scheduled deletion
legal retention
backup expiration
```

Do not tell users that data is permanently deleted if recoverable production copies remain indefinitely.

---

# 63. Sensitive Data in Logs

Never intentionally log:

- passwords;
- session tokens;
- access tokens;
- refresh tokens;
- recovery tokens;
- private keys;
- full payment card data.

PII and other sensitive fields SHOULD be minimized or redacted.

---

# 64. Sensitive Data in URLs

Do not put confidential information or secrets in URLs.

URLs may leak through:

- browser history;
- referrer headers;
- analytics;
- proxy logs;
- screenshots;
- support logs.

---

# 65. APIs

Every API endpoint MUST define:

```text
Authentication
Authorization
Input schema
Output schema
Error behavior
Rate limits where required
Audit requirements
```

Public APIs additionally require versioning and abuse considerations.

---

# 66. API Authorization

API authorization MUST be enforced on the server for every protected operation.

Never infer permission from the fact that the frontend exposed the endpoint.

---

# 67. API Schemas

Requests and responses SHOULD use explicit schemas.

Reject unexpected or invalid data when appropriate.

Avoid mass-assignment vulnerabilities by mapping permitted fields explicitly.

---

# 68. Mass Assignment

Do not bind untrusted request bodies directly to privileged database models.

Bad:

```text
updateUser(request.body)
```

where request body could contain:

```text
role: "admin"
```

Prefer explicit fields:

```text
updateUser({
  displayName,
  timezone
})
```

---

# 69. Excessive Data Exposure

API responses SHOULD return only fields required by the consumer.

Do not serialize complete internal models by default.

Sensitive server fields must remain server-side.

---

# 70. Rate Limiting

Rate-limit operations vulnerable to:

- brute force;
- enumeration;
- spam;
- expensive computation;
- resource exhaustion;
- financial abuse.

Limits SHOULD consider identity, IP, tenant, resource, or other appropriate dimensions.

---

# 71. Resource Limits

Requests SHOULD have bounded:

- body size;
- file size;
- batch size;
- page size;
- query complexity;
- processing time;
- concurrency.

Unbounded operations create denial-of-service risk.

---

# 72. GraphQL

GraphQL deployments SHOULD control:

- query depth;
- complexity;
- pagination;
- authorization;
- batching abuse;
- introspection where appropriate.

Authorization must occur at relevant resource boundaries, not merely at the top-level query.

---

# 73. Webhooks — Incoming

Incoming webhooks MUST be authenticated where the provider supports it.

Use mechanisms such as:

```text
signature verification
timestamp verification
shared secret
mTLS
```

Verify the raw payload exactly as required by the provider.

---

# 74. Webhook Replay Protection

Signed webhooks SHOULD defend against replay where supported.

Use:

- timestamp tolerance;
- unique event IDs;
- deduplication.

Webhook handlers SHOULD be idempotent.

---

# 75. Webhooks — Outgoing

Do not allow arbitrary webhook destinations without considering SSRF risk.

Restrict protocols and destination behavior as appropriate.

Webhook secrets SHOULD be:

- generated securely;
- rotatable;
- protected;
- redacted from UI after creation where feasible.

---

# 76. SSRF

Server-side network requests using user-controlled destinations are high risk.

Defenses MAY include:

- destination allowlists;
- DNS/IP validation;
- blocked internal address ranges;
- controlled egress;
- redirect restrictions;
- dedicated outbound proxies.

Protect cloud metadata and internal administrative endpoints.

---

# 77. URL Fetching

Features that fetch:

- previews;
- images;
- imports;
- webhooks;
- remote documents;

MUST treat destination URLs as hostile input.

Validate after redirects and resolution as required by the threat model.

---

# 78. File Uploads

File uploads MUST be treated as hostile.

Validate:

- size;
- declared type;
- actual content where practical;
- filename;
- extension;
- storage location.

Do not trust the browser-provided MIME type.

---

# 79. Uploaded File Storage

User uploads SHOULD be stored outside directly executable application paths.

Where feasible:

```text
upload
↓
quarantine/validation
↓
object storage
↓
controlled retrieval
```

Do not allow uploaded files to become executable server code.

---

# 80. File Names

Do not use user-provided filenames directly as storage paths.

Generate server-controlled identifiers.

Store original names as metadata if needed.

Prevent:

- traversal;
- overwrite;
- control-character issues.

---

# 81. File Downloads

Downloads require authorization just like API resources.

A difficult-to-guess object-storage URL is not an authorization mechanism.

Signed URLs SHOULD be:

- scoped;
- short-lived;
- generated after authorization.

---

# 82. Path Traversal

Never concatenate untrusted paths directly into filesystem locations.

Normalize and constrain filesystem access to intended directories.

Prefer server-generated storage identifiers.

---

# 83. Archive Extraction

Treat archive uploads carefully.

Protect against:

- path traversal;
- decompression bombs;
- excessive file counts;
- oversized expanded content.

Enforce limits before and during extraction.

---

# 84. Image and Document Processing

Media parsers increase attack surface.

Use maintained processing libraries and isolate high-risk processing where warranted.

Apply resource limits.

---

# 85. Database Security

Production databases MUST NOT be broadly internet-accessible unless explicitly required and secured.

Applications SHOULD use restricted database identities.

Application credentials SHOULD NOT have unrestricted administrative privileges.

---

# 86. Database Roles

Separate roles where practical:

```text
application runtime
migrations
read-only analytics
administration
backup
```

Do not run ordinary application queries as a database superuser.

---

# 87. Database Constraints

Security-sensitive invariants SHOULD be reinforced at the database layer where practical.

Examples:

- unique relationships;
- foreign keys;
- tenant ownership relationships;
- state constraints.

Application checks alone may be insufficient under concurrency or bugs.

---

# 88. Backups

Backups are sensitive production data.

They MUST be:

- access-controlled;
- encrypted where appropriate;
- monitored;
- retention-managed;
- tested for restoration.

A backup that has never been restored is not a verified recovery mechanism.

---

# 89. Background Jobs

Workers MUST enforce appropriate authorization and tenant context.

Do not assume a queued job is trustworthy merely because it originated inside the application.

Job payloads SHOULD contain stable identifiers, not unnecessary sensitive data.

---

# 90. Queue Security

Queues SHOULD have:

- restricted access;
- authenticated publishers/consumers;
- message limits;
- poison-message handling;
- retry controls.

Repeated failures MUST NOT cause unbounded processing.

---

# 91. Idempotency

Sensitive repeatable operations SHOULD support idempotency where duplicate execution creates risk.

Examples:

- payments;
- provisioning;
- invitations;
- webhook processing;
- external side effects.

---

# 92. Error Handling

Errors MUST fail predictably.

Do not expose:

- stack traces;
- database queries;
- infrastructure addresses;
- filesystem paths;
- secrets;
- internal implementation details;

to untrusted users.

---

# 93. Exceptional Conditions

Applications MUST intentionally handle:

```text
timeouts
dependency failures
partial responses
invalid states
race conditions
retry exhaustion
resource exhaustion
unexpected exceptions
```

Unexpected conditions MUST NOT accidentally bypass authorization or validation.

---

# 94. Client Error Messages

User-facing errors SHOULD explain:

```text
what happened
what the user can do
```

without exposing sensitive internal diagnostics.

---

# 95. Server Diagnostics

Detailed error information MAY be retained in protected observability systems.

Correlate user-facing failures with internal diagnostics using safe request or incident identifiers.

---

# 96. Logging

Security-relevant systems MUST produce sufficient logs to investigate incidents.

Log events such as:

- authentication success/failure;
- MFA changes;
- password/recovery changes;
- authorization failures;
- privilege changes;
- administrative actions;
- API key lifecycle;
- sensitive exports;
- account deletion;
- security configuration changes.

---

# 97. Audit Logs

High-value business actions SHOULD produce durable audit events.

An audit event SHOULD include where appropriate:

```text
actor
action
target
tenant
timestamp
result
source/context
```

Do not log secrets.

---

# 98. Audit Integrity

Security audit records SHOULD be protected from ordinary application users.

High-risk systems SHOULD make tampering or deletion difficult and observable.

---

# 99. Monitoring

Security logs are useful only if important events can be detected.

Define alerting for suspicious behavior such as:

- repeated authentication failures;
- unusual privilege changes;
- abnormal API key use;
- large data exports;
- cross-tenant authorization failures;
- unusual administrative access;
- sudden security-control failures.

---

# 100. Time Synchronization

Systems generating security events SHOULD use reliable synchronized time.

Incident investigation depends on trustworthy event ordering.

---

# 101. Dependency Security

Third-party code becomes part of the product attack surface.

Maintain visibility into:

- direct dependencies;
- transitive dependencies;
- runtime dependencies;
- build dependencies;
- container base images.

---

# 102. Dependency Minimization

Do not add a dependency for trivial functionality without considering:

```text
maintenance
security history
ownership
transitive dependencies
update frequency
licensing
package integrity
```

Less dependency surface generally means less supply-chain surface.

---

# 103. Lockfiles

Applications SHOULD commit and enforce appropriate dependency lockfiles.

Build pipelines SHOULD produce reproducible or sufficiently deterministic dependency resolution.

---

# 104. Dependency Updates

Security updates MUST have an established remediation process.

Do not depend solely on ad hoc developer awareness.

Automated dependency alerts SHOULD feed a triaged workflow rather than being ignored as noise.

---

# 105. Package Installation

Be cautious with:

- install scripts;
- untrusted registries;
- package-name typos;
- newly published packages;
- abandoned libraries.

Internal package naming SHOULD avoid dependency-confusion risk.

---

# 106. Software Bill of Materials

Organizations with meaningful supply-chain requirements SHOULD generate and retain an SBOM for production releases.

The SBOM should enable identifying affected software when dependency vulnerabilities emerge.

---

# 107. Artifact Integrity

Production artifacts SHOULD have verifiable provenance where supported.

Build outputs should originate from controlled CI/CD rather than individual developer machines.

---

# 108. Source Control

Production source repositories MUST enforce appropriate access controls.

Strongly recommended:

```text
MFA
protected branches
review requirements
restricted administrative access
auditability
```

Critical protections SHOULD not be bypassable by ordinary contributors.

---

# 109. Branch Protection

Critical branches SHOULD require:

- reviewed changes;
- passing required checks;
- controlled force pushes;
- controlled deletion.

Direct production changes should be exceptional.

---

# 110. Code Review

Security-sensitive code requires deliberate review.

Particularly:

- authentication;
- authorization;
- cryptography;
- payment;
- tenant isolation;
- file handling;
- deserialization;
- infrastructure permissions;
- secret handling.

---

# 111. CI/CD Security

CI systems are production-security infrastructure.

Protect:

- CI credentials;
- deployment tokens;
- signing keys;
- package publishing credentials;
- cloud identities.

CI jobs SHOULD receive only required secrets.

---

# 112. Pull Request Security

Untrusted pull request code MUST NOT automatically gain access to privileged production secrets.

This is particularly important for:

- public repositories;
- forks;
- external contributors;
- automated dependency PRs.

---

# 113. Environment Separation

Production SHOULD be meaningfully separated from:

- development;
- local environments;
- test environments;
- preview deployments.

Do not casually reuse:

- production credentials;
- production databases;
- production secrets;

in lower environments.

---

# 114. Production Data in Development

Production data SHOULD NOT be copied into lower environments without explicit controls.

Where representative data is required, prefer:

- synthetic data;
- anonymized data;
- appropriately masked data.

---

# 115. Infrastructure as Code

Production infrastructure SHOULD be defined through reviewable infrastructure-as-code where practical.

This improves:

- reproducibility;
- review;
- auditability;
- drift detection.

Manual production configuration should be minimized.

---

# 116. Cloud IAM

Cloud permissions MUST follow least privilege.

Avoid persistent broad permissions such as:

```text
*
```

unless strictly justified.

Prefer workload identity and short-lived credentials over static long-lived access keys.

---

# 117. Network Exposure

Services SHOULD expose only required interfaces.

Internal services SHOULD NOT become publicly accessible by default.

Administrative interfaces require stronger access controls.

---

# 118. Administrative Interfaces

Production administrative surfaces SHOULD have:

- strong authentication;
- least privilege;
- network restrictions where useful;
- audit logging;
- short sessions;
- clear privileged-state indication.

---

# 119. Containers

Container images SHOULD:

- use maintained base images;
- minimize unnecessary packages;
- avoid embedded secrets;
- avoid privileged execution;
- run as non-root where practical;
- be scanned for known vulnerabilities.

---

# 120. Production Configuration

Debug or development settings MUST NOT reach production unintentionally.

Production MUST NOT expose:

- debug consoles;
- development error pages;
- source maps containing sensitive source where prohibited;
- test endpoints;
- development credentials.

---

# 121. Secure Defaults

New deployments SHOULD default to:

```text
authentication enabled
least privilege
private resources
logging enabled
safe cookie settings
TLS
restricted network exposure
```

Security controls should not require customers to discover hidden configuration.

---

# 122. Feature Flags

Feature flags MUST NOT be treated as authorization.

A hidden or disabled feature can still be attacked if the backend endpoint remains exposed.

Authorization remains mandatory.

---

# 123. Debug and Support Tools

Debug capabilities MUST NOT create hidden bypasses.

Support tools require:

- authorization;
- audit logs;
- explicit production policy;
- removal or disabling when unnecessary.

---

# 124. Remote Code Execution Features

Features capable of executing:

- user code;
- templates;
- scripts;
- queries;
- plugins;

require strong isolation.

Do not execute untrusted code directly inside the primary application environment.

---

# 125. Sandboxing

Untrusted code execution SHOULD use appropriately hardened isolation.

Depending on risk:

```text
separate process
container
VM
specialized sandbox
separate account/project
```

Resource and network limits are required.

---

# 126. Deserialization

Avoid unsafe deserialization of untrusted data.

Use data formats and libraries that do not instantiate arbitrary executable objects.

Treat serialized input as untrusted input.

---

# 127. Redirects

User-controlled redirects MUST be validated.

Do not implement:

```text
?next=https://attacker.example
```

without restricting acceptable destinations.

Prefer relative or allowlisted application destinations.

---

# 128. OAuth and OIDC

Use established protocol libraries.

Validate where applicable:

- issuer;
- audience;
- signature;
- state;
- nonce;
- redirect URI;
- token expiration.

Do not manually parse and trust token payloads without cryptographic validation.

---

# 129. OAuth Redirect URIs

Redirect URIs SHOULD be exact and narrowly configured.

Avoid broad wildcard redirect destinations.

OAuth state must not become an open-redirect mechanism.

---

# 130. API Keys

API keys MUST be:

- generated with sufficient entropy;
- scoped;
- revocable;
- attributable;
- protected from disclosure.

Where possible:

```text
display secret once
store verifier/hash where architecture permits
```

---

# 131. API Key Prefixes

API keys MAY use non-secret prefixes to:

- identify key type;
- improve secret scanning;
- support operational debugging.

The secret portion must remain high entropy.

---

# 132. API Key Scoping

Keys SHOULD support appropriate restriction by:

- tenant;
- environment;
- permission;
- API surface.

Avoid universal administrator keys when narrower credentials suffice.

---

# 133. API Key Rotation

Users and operators SHOULD be able to rotate keys without unnecessary downtime.

Support temporary overlap where necessary for safe migration.

---

# 134. Service-to-Service Authentication

Services SHOULD authenticate to one another using managed workload identity or strong service credentials.

Avoid one static secret shared across the entire architecture.

---

# 135. WebSocket Security

WebSocket connections MUST establish authorization.

Do not assume authorization remains valid forever merely because the initial connection succeeded.

Validate sensitive channel subscriptions and tenant scope.

---

# 136. Realtime Channels

Users MUST NOT be able to subscribe to:

```text
another user's channel
another tenant's channel
privileged event streams
```

by manipulating channel identifiers.

---

# 137. Search

Search endpoints can create data-leakage paths.

Search results MUST enforce the same authorization boundaries as direct object retrieval.

Do not index data into globally searchable stores without tenant/access controls.

---

# 138. Exports

Data exports are high-value exfiltration paths.

Exports SHOULD require:

- explicit authorization;
- appropriate audit logging;
- secure temporary storage;
- expiration;
- protected download URLs.

Large or sensitive exports MAY warrant reauthentication.

---

# 139. Bulk Operations

Bulk actions MUST authorize every affected resource.

Do not authorize only the first object or collection-level page.

---

# 140. Imports

Imported files and records are untrusted input.

Validate:

- schema;
- size;
- record count;
- permissions;
- resource ownership;
- references.

Provide bounded processing.

---

# 141. Notifications

Security-sensitive notifications SHOULD be sent for meaningful account changes such as:

- password changed;
- MFA disabled;
- email changed;
- new recovery method;
- suspicious login;
- API credential created where appropriate.

Do not include secrets in notification content.

---

# 142. Email Security

Emails MUST NOT be treated as a trusted rendering or authentication environment.

Links involving sensitive actions SHOULD use:

- limited-purpose tokens;
- expiration;
- single use where appropriate.

Do not put long-lived session credentials into email URLs.

---

# 143. Race Conditions

Security-sensitive state changes MUST consider concurrency.

Examples:

- coupon redemption;
- balance changes;
- permissions;
- invitations;
- resource ownership;
- inventory.

Use database transactions, locking, idempotency, or atomic operations where required.

---

# 144. Business Logic Abuse

Security testing must consider valid operations used maliciously.

Examples:

```text
creating thousands of free resources
inviting unlimited users
repeated trial creation
abusing refunds
automation intended for humans
bypassing workflow sequencing
```

Security is broader than injection vulnerabilities.

---

# 145. Abuse Controls

High-abuse features SHOULD define:

```text
rate limits
quotas
verification
monitoring
cost controls
manual review thresholds
```

These controls should reflect real abuse models.

---

# 146. Denial of Service

Expensive operations MUST be bounded.

Consider:

- query complexity;
- memory;
- CPU;
- upload size;
- export size;
- job concurrency;
- pagination;
- retries.

One user should not be able to exhaust shared infrastructure trivially.

---

# 147. Retry Behavior

Retries MUST be bounded.

Use:

- maximum attempts;
- exponential backoff;
- jitter where appropriate;
- dead-letter handling.

Never retry permanent errors indefinitely.

---

# 148. Security Logging vs Privacy

Collect enough telemetry to investigate incidents without creating unnecessary repositories of sensitive user data.

Security observability and privacy must be designed together.

---

# 149. Vulnerability Management

The organization MUST have a defined vulnerability lifecycle:

```text
Discover
↓
Triage
↓
Prioritize
↓
Remediate
↓
Verify
↓
Close
↓
Learn
```

---

# 150. Vulnerability Severity

Severity SHOULD reflect more than CVSS alone.

Consider:

```text
exploitability
internet exposure
data sensitivity
privilege required
tenant impact
active exploitation
blast radius
existing mitigations
```

---

# 151. Remediation Targets

Define organization-specific remediation SLAs.

Example policy structure:

```text
Critical → immediate priority
High     → accelerated remediation
Medium   → planned remediation
Low      → backlog/risk-managed
```

Exact deadlines SHOULD reflect organizational risk and operational capability.

---

# 152. Known Exploited Vulnerabilities

Actively exploited vulnerabilities affecting exposed production assets require elevated remediation priority.

Do not treat active exploitation as an ordinary backlog item.

---

# 153. Security Testing

Security verification SHOULD combine:

```text
code review
unit/integration tests
SAST
dependency analysis
secret scanning
DAST where appropriate
infrastructure scanning
manual security testing
penetration testing where warranted
```

No single tool provides sufficient coverage.

---

# 154. Security Unit Tests

Security invariants SHOULD have automated tests.

Examples:

```text
User cannot access another tenant
Member cannot perform admin action
Expired token is rejected
Invalid webhook signature is rejected
Private file requires authorization
```

---

# 155. Negative Testing

Security tests MUST attempt forbidden behavior, not only correct behavior.

Test:

```text
wrong user
wrong tenant
wrong role
missing token
expired token
modified ID
invalid state
duplicate request
oversized request
```

---

# 156. Authorization Matrix Testing

Significant applications SHOULD maintain testable relationships among:

```text
Roles × Resources × Actions
```

Example:

| Role | Read | Create | Update | Delete | Admin |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Viewer | ✓ | — | — | — | — |
| Member | ✓ | ✓ | scoped | — | — |
| Admin | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | scoped |

The actual matrix depends on product semantics.

---

# 157. Penetration Testing

Independent penetration testing SHOULD be considered for:

- high-risk applications;
- major architecture changes;
- regulated systems;
- externally exposed sensitive systems;
- significant authentication/authorization changes.

Penetration testing does not replace ongoing secure development.

---

# 158. Secure Development Lifecycle

Security MUST be integrated into ordinary product development.

Recommended lifecycle:

```text
Requirements
↓
Threat model
↓
Design review
↓
Implementation
↓
Automated checks
↓
Code review
↓
Security verification
↓
Deployment
↓
Monitoring
↓
Feedback
```

---

# 159. Security Requirements

Features involving sensitive behavior SHOULD include explicit security requirements alongside functional requirements.

Example:

```text
Functional:
Workspace owner can invite a member.

Security:
Only authorized workspace administrators may create invitations.
Invitation is tenant-bound.
Invitation expires.
Invitation cannot be reused.
Invitation events are auditable.
```

---

# 160. Security Design Review

Security review SHOULD occur before code becomes expensive to change.

Architecture requiring specialist review includes:

- custom authentication;
- cryptography;
- tenancy;
- payments;
- sandboxing;
- external code execution;
- high-risk integrations;
- secret-management changes.

---

# 161. Security Champions

Engineering teams MAY designate security champions to improve local ownership.

Security champions support secure engineering.

They do not replace dedicated security expertise where required.

---

# 162. Incident Response

Production systems MUST have an incident response process.

It should define:

```text
Detection
Triage
Containment
Eradication
Recovery
Communication
Post-incident analysis
```

---

# 163. Incident Access

During incidents, emergency access procedures MUST remain controlled and auditable.

Do not normalize permanent excessive privileges merely because they may be useful during emergencies.

---

# 164. Security Contacts

The organization SHOULD maintain an obvious internal escalation path for suspected vulnerabilities and incidents.

Public-facing software organizations SHOULD consider a documented vulnerability-reporting channel.

---

# 165. Vulnerability Disclosure

External vulnerability reports SHOULD receive:

- acknowledgment;
- triage;
- safe communication;
- remediation;
- appropriate disclosure handling.

Good-faith reports should not disappear into ordinary customer support queues.

---

# 166. Incident Logging

Incident investigations require preserved evidence.

Ensure relevant:

- application logs;
- authentication logs;
- cloud audit logs;
- infrastructure events;

have suitable retention and access controls.

---

# 167. Recovery

Security architecture MUST consider recovery from compromise.

Define how to rotate:

- user sessions;
- API keys;
- service credentials;
- database credentials;
- signing keys;
- encryption keys where possible.

---

# 168. Disaster Recovery

Security and availability overlap.

Critical systems SHOULD define:

```text
Recovery Point Objective
Recovery Time Objective
Backup strategy
Restore procedure
Failover procedure
```

Recovery procedures must be tested.

---

# 169. Supply-Chain Incident Readiness

The organization SHOULD be able to answer:

```text
Are we using dependency X?
Which production versions contain it?
Where are those deployments?
Can we patch or remove it quickly?
```

This requires dependency visibility and release traceability.

---

# 170. Security Documentation

Security-critical architecture SHOULD be documented.

Documentation MAY include:

- trust boundaries;
- auth flows;
- authorization model;
- tenant model;
- key ownership;
- secret lifecycle;
- data classification;
- incident procedures.

Do not rely entirely on tribal knowledge.

---

# 171. Security Decisions

Material security tradeoffs SHOULD be documented through an architecture or security decision record.

Include:

```text
Decision
Threat
Alternatives
Chosen control
Residual risk
Owner
Review date
```

---

# 172. Security Exceptions

Exceptions MUST NOT silently become permanent defaults.

Every exception requires:

```text
reason
risk
compensating control
owner
expiration
```

Expired exceptions require review.

---

# 173. Security and UX

Security controls SHOULD minimize unnecessary user burden.

Good security UX:

- supports password managers;
- supports passkeys;
- explains sensitive actions;
- makes account security visible;
- uses secure defaults;
- avoids needless repeated prompts.

Poor UX can cause users to circumvent controls.

---

# 174. Destructive Actions

Sensitive destructive actions SHOULD require deliberate confirmation proportionate to consequence.

Authorization must still be server-side.

A confirmation dialog is a UX safeguard, not a security boundary.

---

# 175. Security Settings

Security-critical settings SHOULD clearly communicate:

- current state;
- consequences;
- recent changes;
- recovery implications.

Avoid hiding critical security configuration inside obscure advanced menus.

---

# 176. AI-Generated Code

AI-generated code MUST meet the same security standard as human-written code.

AI output is untrusted until reviewed and tested.

---

# 177. AI Security Inspection

Before implementing security-sensitive code, an AI coding agent SHOULD inspect existing:

```text
auth utilities
authorization policies
middleware
tenant resolution
validation schemas
secret management
database abstractions
security headers
logging
rate limiting
```

The AI MUST reuse established controls rather than invent parallel security systems.

---

# 178. AI Authentication Rule

An AI MUST NOT casually implement custom:

```text
password hashing
session protocols
token signing
OAuth
MFA
cryptography
```

when established repository/framework mechanisms exist.

---

# 179. AI Authorization Rule

AI-generated endpoints MUST explicitly consider authorization.

For each protected operation, answer:

```text
Who is the principal?
What resource is being accessed?
Which tenant owns it?
What action is requested?
Where is permission enforced?
```

---

# 180. AI Input Rule

AI-generated server handlers MUST assume all external input is malicious until validated.

This includes data from:

```text
URL
query string
headers
cookies
forms
JSON
webhooks
files
third-party APIs
AI output
```

---

# 181. AI Secret Rule

AI MUST NOT:

- hardcode credentials;
- invent production secrets;
- expose server environment variables to clients;
- log sensitive tokens;
- commit `.env` contents.

Use existing secret-management patterns.

---

# 182. AI Dependency Rule

AI SHOULD NOT add a new dependency if the existing platform safely provides the required capability.

When adding one, inspect:

```text
maintenance
security
license
dependency tree
repository maturity
```

---

# 183. AI Security Comments

Do not produce comments such as:

```text
// TODO: add auth later
```

for production-sensitive endpoints and consider the feature complete.

Missing security controls are incomplete functionality.

---

# 184. AI Fail-Secure Rule

If the AI cannot determine whether an operation is authorized, it MUST NOT invent permissive behavior.

Prefer:

```text
explicit denial
```

or integration with the established policy layer.

---

# 185. AI Database Rule

AI-generated queries MUST:

- use parameterization;
- preserve tenant boundaries;
- avoid mass assignment;
- avoid excessive data return;
- use transactions for relevant invariants.

---

# 186. AI Route Rule

AI-generated protected routes MUST align with the route security standard:

```text
authentication
authorization
```
