# 147. Dashboard Units

Every graph should have clear:

```text
unit
legend
title
```

---

# 148. Dashboard Axes

Avoid misleading y-axis scaling where it distorts operational interpretation.

---

# 149. Dual Axes

Use dual-axis graphs sparingly.

They can create misleading apparent relationships.

---

# 150. Dashboard Noise

Do not display dozens of irrelevant metrics simply because they are available.

---

# 151. Dashboard Ownership

Critical dashboards MUST have an owner.

---

# 152. Dashboard as Code

Dashboard definitions SHOULD be version-controlled where platform tooling supports it.

---

# 153. Dashboard Review

Changes to critical dashboards/alerts SHOULD receive code/review discipline similar to other operational configuration.

---

# 154. SLIs

A Service Level Indicator measures an aspect of service behavior that matters to users.

---

# 155. SLI Examples

Useful SLIs may include:

```text
availability
request success
latency
freshness
durability
correctness
```

depending on the service.

---

# 156. User-Centric SLIs

Prefer indicators close to actual user outcomes.

Example:

```text
successful checkout requests
/
valid checkout attempts
```

rather than:

```text
server process is running
```

---

# 157. Availability SLI

Availability SHOULD represent usable service success, not merely host uptime.

---

# 158. Latency SLI

Latency SLIs SHOULD identify which requests count as sufficiently fast.

---

# 159. Freshness SLI

Data pipelines/search/indexes may require freshness indicators.

Example:

```text
percentage of documents indexed within target delay
```

---

# 160. Durability SLI

Systems managing critical stored data MAY require durability/error-loss objectives.

---

# 161. Correctness SLI

Where technically measurable, correctness can be a meaningful SLI.

Do not claim it if the metric cannot actually detect incorrect output.

---

# 162. SLOs

A Service Level Objective defines the target level for an SLI over a defined window.

---

# 163. SLO Example

Conceptually:

```text
99.9% of valid API requests succeed
over rolling 30 days
```

---

# 164. SLO Window

Every SLO requires a time window.

Examples:

```text
7 days
28 days
30 days
calendar month
```

Use one organization convention where practical.

---

# 165. SLO Scope

Specify:

```text
service
operation population
excluded traffic
measurement source
```

clearly.

---

# 166. SLO Denominator

Be explicit about what counts in the denominator.

Ambiguous denominators create meaningless SLOs.

---

# 167. Valid Requests

Do not penalize service availability for clearly invalid client requests unless the product definition intentionally treats them as service failures.

---

# 168. User-Caused Errors

Typical:

```text
400
401
403
```

should not automatically count as server availability failures.

The exact SLI classification depends on product semantics.

---

# 169. Server Errors

Unexpected:

```text
5xx
timeouts
invalid output
```

are typical service failures.

---

# 170. SLO Target Selection

SLO targets should reflect:

```text
user need
business need
architecture
cost
```

not prestige.

---

# 171. Five Nines Is Not Automatically Better

Higher SLOs can dramatically increase:

```text
engineering cost
operational complexity
infrastructure cost
```

Choose justified targets.

---

# 172. SLO Must Be Achievable

An SLO above the reliability of an unavoidable dependency requires architectural compensation.

---

# 173. SLO ≠ SLA

Distinguish:

```text
SLI
→ measurement

SLO
→ internal/operational target

SLA
→ contractual commitment/consequence
```

---

# 174. Error Budget

The error budget represents how much unreliability the SLO permits.

---

# 175. Error Budget Purpose

Error budgets help balance:

```text
reliability
delivery velocity
```

using measurable service health.

---

# 176. Error Budget Policy

Critical services SHOULD define what happens when error-budget consumption becomes excessive.

Potential responses:

```text
investigate
pause risky rollout
prioritize reliability
reduce change velocity
```

---

# 177. Error Budget Is Not Permission to Fail Deliberately

It represents tolerated reliability variance, not a goal to consume fully.

---

# 178. Burn Rate

Alerting SHOULD consider the rate at which the error budget is being consumed.

---

# 179. Fast Burn

Fast burn indicates severe degradation capable of exhausting budget rapidly.

It deserves fast response.

---

# 180. Slow Burn

Slow sustained degradation may require investigation without immediate paging.

---

# 181. Multi-Window Burn Alerts

Mature SLO alerting SHOULD consider multiple windows to distinguish:

```text
severe short incident
```

from:

```text
persistent lower-rate degradation
```

---

# 182. SLO Dashboard

Critical services SHOULD expose:

```text
current SLI
SLO target
error-budget remaining
burn rate
```

---

# 183. SLO Review

Review SLOs periodically.

An SLO that:

```text
never matters
always passes trivially
always fails
```

may be poorly designed.

---

# 184. Alerting

Alerts exist to trigger human or automated action.

If nobody needs to act:

> It should probably not page.

---

# 185. Alert Types

Distinguish:

```text
Page
Ticket
Notification
Dashboard-only signal
```

---

# 186. Paging

Pages are for urgent conditions requiring timely human intervention.

---

# 187. Ticket Alerts

Nonurgent actionable issues MAY create tickets/work items.

---

# 188. Informational Notifications

Informational events SHOULD not use the same channel/severity as incidents.

---

# 189. Symptom-Based Alerts

Prefer alerting on:

```text
user-visible symptoms
SLO impact
```

over internal causes alone.

---

# 190. Cause Alerts

Cause-based alerts may supplement user-impact alerts when early intervention reliably prevents impact.

---

# 191. CPU Alert Anti-Pattern

Avoid paging simply because:

```text
CPU > 80%
```

if there is no evidence of service impact or imminent capacity failure.

---

# 192. Alert Actionability

Every alert SHOULD answer:

```text
What is wrong?
What is affected?
How urgent is it?
Where do I investigate?
```

---

# 193. Alert Runbook

Critical alerts SHOULD link to a runbook.

---

# 194. Alert Owner

Every alert MUST have an owner/team.

---

# 195. No Orphan Alerts

An alert routed to:

```text
nobody
old team
unmonitored channel
```

is worse than no alert because it creates false confidence.

---

# 196. Alert Threshold

Thresholds SHOULD derive from:

```text
SLO
baseline
capacity limit
known failure condition
```

rather than arbitrary values.

---

# 197. Static Thresholds

Static thresholds work for predictable limits.

---

# 198. Dynamic/Anomaly Detection

Anomaly detection MAY supplement fixed thresholds for highly variable signals.

Do not assume machine-detected anomalies are automatically actionable.

---

# 199. Alert Duration

Require conditions to persist for a suitable duration when brief spikes are harmless.

---

# 200. Immediate Alerts

Some events require immediate alerting regardless of duration.

Examples:

```text
break-glass account used
critical signing key compromised
mass data deletion detected
```

---

# 201. Alert Deduplication

Related symptoms SHOULD be grouped/deduplicated where possible.

---

# 202. Alert Storm

One underlying outage should not generate:

```text
500 independent pages
```

for every downstream symptom.

---

# 203. Dependency Alerting

When a shared dependency fails, alert routing should identify the likely shared cause.

---

# 204. Alert Suppression

Temporary alert suppression MAY be appropriate during planned maintenance.

It must be:

```text
scoped
time-bounded
auditable
```

---

# 205. Never Disable Alerts Permanently to Stop Noise

Fix:

```text
threshold
signal
routing
instrumentation
```

instead.

---

# 206. Alert Quality

Track alert quality where useful.

Potential measurements:

```text
actionable percentage
false-positive rate
pages per incident
```

---

# 207. Alert Fatigue

Too many low-value alerts reduce response quality to real incidents.

---

# 208. Error Monitoring

Unexpected application exceptions SHOULD flow into a centralized error-monitoring system.

---

# 209. Error Grouping

Error monitoring SHOULD group equivalent failures rather than produce one issue per request.

---

# 210. Error Fingerprint

Grouping SHOULD rely on stable technical characteristics.

Do not group solely by raw message when messages contain dynamic values.

---

# 211. Release Association

Errors SHOULD be associated with:

```text
release/version
environment
service
```

---

# 212. First Seen

Error tooling SHOULD expose:

```text
first seen
last seen
frequency
affected releases
```

where platform supports it.

---

# 213. Regression Detection

Previously resolved errors that reappear after deployment SHOULD be detectable.

---

# 214. Error Volume

A single exception can matter, but volume/rate provides additional prioritization.

---

# 215. User Impact

Where privacy allows, error monitoring MAY estimate:

```text
affected sessions
affected requests
affected tenants
```

without recording sensitive identity unnecessarily.

---

# 216. Source Maps

Frontend error monitoring SHOULD use securely managed source maps where this materially improves diagnosis.

---

# 217. Source Map Exposure

Do not expose source maps publicly when organizational/security policy requires private upload/storage.

---

# 218. Error Context

Useful context can include:

```text
route
browser
release
trace
request
feature flag
```

where safe.

---

# 219. Breadcrumbs

Error-monitoring breadcrumbs MAY provide preceding operational context.

Do not collect sensitive form values or private content casually.

---

# 220. Handled Errors

Do not report every expected handled error into exception monitoring.

---

# 221. Unexpected Client Errors

Unexpected browser exceptions SHOULD be monitored for major user-facing applications.

---

# 222. Promise/Rejection Monitoring

Unhandled asynchronous client/server failures SHOULD be visible through the runtime/platform error pipeline.

---

# 223. Audit Logs

Audit logging is distinct from ordinary operational logging.

---

# 224. Audit Purpose

Audit logs answer:

```text
Who did what
To which resource
When
In which tenant/context
With what result
```

---

# 225. Audit Events

Typical auditable actions include:

```text
role change
permission change
member removal
API key creation/revocation
data export
ownership transfer
impersonation
security-setting changes
high-impact deletion
```

---

# 226. Audit Actor

Every audit event SHOULD identify the true actor.

---

# 227. Subject

If actor acts on behalf of another identity, record both.

Example:

```text
support_admin
acting_as
customer_user
```

---

# 228. Audit Target

Identify affected:

```text
resource
tenant
object type
```

where applicable.

---

# 229. Audit Result

Record:

```text
attempted/succeeded/failed
```

where useful.

---

# 230. Audit Timestamp

Audit events require trustworthy timestamps.

---

# 231. Audit Reason

High-risk administrative actions MAY require a reason/ticket identifier.

---

# 232. Audit Before/After

Selected configuration changes MAY record safe before/after representations.

Do not copy secrets into audit logs.

---

# 233. Audit Immutability

Audit trails SHOULD be protected against unauthorized:

```text
modification
deletion
```

---

# 234. Audit Access

Access to audit data MUST itself be restricted and, where appropriate, audited.

---

# 235. Audit Retention

Audit retention is governed separately from ordinary debug log retention.

Consider:

```text
security
compliance
legal
privacy
contractual
```

requirements.

---

# 236. Audit Availability

Users/tenant administrators MAY receive access to appropriate tenant audit history.

Platform-internal fields should remain protected.

---

# 237. Audit vs Security Logs

Audit logs and security-detection logs overlap but have distinct purposes.

Do not force everything into one undifferentiated stream.

---

# 238. Security Logging

Security-sensitive applications SHOULD log meaningful events such as:

```text
authentication changes
authorization failures where suspicious
credential creation/revocation
security policy changes
unexpected validation anomalies
```

according to Security standards.

---

# 239. Security Signal Noise

Do not make every routine 403 a critical security alert.

Context and volume matter.

---

# 240. Tamper Protection

Critical security/audit logs should be protected against tampering in transit and at rest.

---

# 241. Central Collection

Production telemetry SHOULD be centrally searchable or queryable.

Local server files alone are insufficient in ephemeral/distributed systems.

---

# 242. Telemetry Pipeline

Canonical flow:

```text
Application/Infrastructure
↓
Telemetry SDK/Agent
↓
Collector/Pipeline
↓
Processing/Redaction/Sampling
↓
Backend Storage
↓
Dashboards/Alerts/Investigation
```

---

# 243. Collector

A telemetry collector/gateway MAY centralize:

```text
export
redaction
sampling
routing
enrichment
```

---

# 244. Collector High Availability

If telemetry is operationally critical, collector infrastructure SHOULD be sufficiently resilient.

---

# 245. Telemetry Failure Must Not Take Product Down

Routine observability export failure MUST NOT normally make the business operation fail.

---

# 246. Telemetry Backpressure

Telemetry pipelines must have bounded:

```text
queues
memory
disk buffering
```

so an exporter outage cannot exhaust the application.

---

# 247. Drop Policy

If telemetry must be dropped during overload, prioritize retaining:

```text
errors
critical security events
audit data
```

according to architecture.

Audit data requiring guaranteed durability may require a separate pipeline.

---

# 248. Export Timeout

Telemetry export calls require bounded timeouts.

---

# 249. Async Export

Application request paths SHOULD NOT synchronously wait on remote telemetry storage.

---

# 250. Batch Export

Use batching where supported to reduce export overhead.

---

# 251. Shutdown Flush

Applications SHOULD attempt bounded flushing of important buffered telemetry during graceful shutdown.

---

# 252. Telemetry Health

Monitor the observability system itself.

Examples:

```text
dropped spans
export failures
collector queue
ingestion errors
```

---

# 253. Missing Telemetry

A silent absence of data may itself represent a failure.

---

# 254. Heartbeats

Critical scheduled/infrequent systems MAY emit heartbeat/success signals to detect absence.

---

# 255. Cardinality Governance

Cardinality is an explicit operational/cost concern.

Every telemetry review SHOULD consider it.

---

# 256. Cardinality Budget

Large systems SHOULD establish telemetry cardinality budgets or practical guardrails.

---

# 257. Attribute Allowlist

For high-volume signals, use approved attribute sets rather than arbitrary context dumping.

---

# 258. Dynamic Attribute Names

Never generate telemetry field names dynamically from user/resource input.

Values may be dynamic within controlled semantics; schema should remain stable.

---

# 259. Cost Governance

Observability has real infrastructure cost.

Track cost by:

```text
signal
service
team
retention
```

where useful.

---

# 260. Telemetry Volume

Measure:

```text
logs/day
metric series count
spans/sec
trace retention
```

for major systems.

---

# 261. Cost Optimization Order

Prefer:

```text
remove useless telemetry
↓
reduce cardinality
↓
sample
↓
shorten retention
↓
compress/archive
```

before sacrificing critical visibility.

---

# 262. Cost vs Incident Capability

Do not eliminate the telemetry required to diagnose critical incidents merely to reduce storage cost.

---

# 263. Debug Logs

Verbose debugging SHOULD be disabled by default in production unless specifically justified.

---

# 264. Temporary Debug Logging

Temporary production diagnostics MAY be enabled when:

```text
scoped
time-limited
reviewed
safe
```

---

# 265. Debug Logging Expiry

Temporary verbose instrumentation MUST have an explicit removal/expiry path.

---

# 266. Dynamic Log Levels

If runtime log-level adjustment exists, it must be:

```text
authorized
auditable
bounded
```

---

# 267. Production Debugging Principle

Production debugging MUST prioritize:

```text
Safety
Read-only observation
Minimal blast radius
Auditability
Reversibility
```

---

# 268. Observe Before Mutating

Production investigation order:

```text
Dashboard
↓
Metrics
↓
Traces
↓
Logs
↓
Safe read-only queries
↓
Controlled intervention
```

---

# 269. No Debugging by Random Mutation

Do not modify production data/configuration merely to see what happens.

---

# 270. No Ad Hoc Print Debugging

Do not ship uncontrolled:

```text
console.log(...)
```

containing arbitrary production objects or secrets.

Use structured controlled telemetry.

---

# 271. Production Shell Access

Direct shell access to production SHOULD be minimized.

Prefer managed operational tooling.

---

# 272. Named Access

Production debugging access MUST use identifiable individual accounts.

Shared credentials are prohibited.

---

# 273. Least Privilege

Engineers receive only the production access required for their role.

---

# 274. Just-in-Time Access

Sensitive production access SHOULD be temporary/JIT where organizational infrastructure supports it.

---

# 275. Break-Glass Access

Emergency high-privilege access must be:

```text
rare
strongly authenticated
audited
alerted
reviewed
```

---

# 276. Production Database Access

Direct production DB access SHOULD be restricted.

Use:

```text
read replicas
controlled query tools
admin tooling
```

where practical.

---

# 277. Read-Only First

Investigations SHOULD begin with read-only access.

---

# 278. Production Queries

Ad hoc production queries MUST consider:

```text
full scans
locks
CPU
replica impact
sensitive output
```

---

# 279. Query Limits

Operational query tools SHOULD apply:

```text
timeouts
row limits
read-only constraints
```

where practical.

---

# 280. Sensitive Data During Debugging

Operational necessity does not authorize unrestricted viewing of customer data.

Data-access policies still apply.

---

# 281. No Production Data Copying

Do not download production datasets to personal machines for debugging without explicit authorized process.

---

# 282. Screenshots

Incident screenshots can contain sensitive information.

Treat them according to data-handling policy.

---

# 283. Temporary Scripts

Emergency production scripts require:

```text
review where practical
dry-run
scope
audit
rollback/recovery plan
```

---

# 284. One-Off Data Fix

A data repair should preferably become:

```text
version-controlled script
migration
admin operation
```

rather than an unrecorded console command.

---

# 285. Dry Run

High-impact repair tooling SHOULD offer dry-run/preview where practical.

---

# 286. Data Repair Audit

Record:

```text
actor
reason
affected scope
time
result
```

for consequential production repair.

---

# 287. Feature Flags During Incident

Feature flags MAY disable problematic functionality quickly.

Changes must be:

```text
authorized
auditable
reversible
```

---

# 288. Kill Switch

Critical integrations/features MAY require operational kill switches.

They should have explicit observability.

---

# 289. Incident Debugging

During incidents, preserve:

```text
timeline
hypotheses
changes
observations
```

rather than relying on memory.

---

# 290. Correlate Changes

Investigation SHOULD examine:

```text
deployments
config changes
feature flags
traffic changes
dependency incidents
```

near onset.

---

# 291. Change Events

Operationally significant changes SHOULD produce deploy/configuration events that can be overlaid on telemetry.

---

# 292. Production Sampling Changes

Sampling changes during an incident may be useful.

They must consider:

```text
cost
performance
privacy
```

and be reverted afterward.

---

# 293. Production Debug Headers

Internal diagnostic headers/endpoints MUST NOT expose sensitive information to arbitrary users.

---

# 294. Debug Endpoints

Production debug endpoints should be absent or strongly restricted.

---

# 295. Profiling Production

Production profiling MAY be performed using low-overhead approved tooling.

Do not attach invasive debuggers casually to critical processes.

---

# 296. Heap Dumps

Heap/core dumps can contain:

```text
secrets
PII
credentials
```

Treat them as highly sensitive artifacts.

---

# 297. Incident Artifact Retention

Incident telemetry/artifacts should follow defined security and retention rules.

---

# 298. Dashboard During Incident

Incident responders SHOULD have a known service dashboard rather than creating every query from scratch.

---

# 299. Runbooks

Alerts for critical services SHOULD reference runbooks.

---

# 300. Runbook Structure

Useful runbook:

```text
Meaning of alert
Likely causes
Initial checks
Dashboard links
Safe remediation
Escalation
Recovery verification
```

---

# 301. Observability and Incident Response

Observability should make it possible to answer:

```text
When did impact start?
Who is affected?
How severe is it?
Which component is failing?
What changed?
Is mitigation working?
Has recovery completed?
```

---

# 302. Recovery Verification

Do not close an incident simply because an error disappeared.

Verify:

```text
SLIs recovered
backlog draining
dependency healthy
error rate normal
reconciliation complete
```

---

# 303. Post-Incident Review

After meaningful incidents, identify telemetry gaps.

Ask:

```text
What did we wish we could see?
Which alert was late/noisy?
Which correlation was missing?
```

---

# 304. Observability Improvement

Incident action items MAY include:

```text
new metric
better trace attribute
new dashboard
alert correction
additional audit event
```

when they close a real diagnostic gap.

---

# 305. Synthetic Monitoring

Critical public workflows MAY use synthetic monitoring.

Examples:

```text
login availability
checkout probe
public API health
```

---

# 306. Synthetic Monitoring Is External

Synthetic monitoring SHOULD execute from outside the application boundary where the objective is end-user availability.

---

# 307. Synthetic Accounts

Use dedicated controlled test accounts/tenants.

Do not use real customer identities.

---

# 308. Synthetic Side Effects

Avoid uncontrolled:

```text
payments
emails
customer notifications
```

from synthetic monitoring.

---

# 309. Health Endpoints

Health endpoints should expose what orchestration needs—not a complete internal diagnostic report.

---

# 310. Liveness

Liveness answers:

```text
Should this process be restarted?
```

---

# 311. Readiness

Readiness answers:

```text
Can this instance safely receive traffic?
```

---

# 312. Health Privacy

Health endpoints MUST NOT expose:

```text
connection strings
secrets
database topology
stack traces
```

publicly.

---

# 313. Frontend Error Correlation

Where possible, frontend error reports SHOULD correlate to backend request/trace identifiers.

---

# 314. API Correlation

API responses MAY expose a safe request ID for support/debugging.

---

# 315. Database Correlation

Database spans/query fingerprints SHOULD correlate with originating requests where tracing support exists.

---

# 316. Queue Correlation

Job/message processing SHOULD include durable operation/message identity plus trace linkage where appropriate.

---

# 317. Webhook Correlation

Webhook processing SHOULD retain:

```text
provider event ID
internal request/trace
processing result
```

without logging signature secrets.

---

# 318. Idempotency Correlation

High-impact writes MAY record a safe hashed/reference form of idempotency identity where needed for investigation.

Do not expose reusable credentials.

---

# 319. Authentication Observability

Authentication systems SHOULD monitor:

```text
login success
login failure
MFA challenges
recovery activity
session revocation
```

at appropriate aggregate levels.

---

# 320. Authorization Observability

Monitor unusual:

```text
access denials
cross-tenant attempts
privilege changes
```

according to security requirements.

---

# 321. Security vs Operational Dashboards

Security detection may require separate dashboards/access from general service operations.

---

# 322. Payment Observability

Payment workflows SHOULD expose states such as:

```text
attempted
provider accepted
confirmed
failed
unknown
reconciled
```

where architecture supports them.

---

# 323. Unknown Financial Outcome

Unknown payment outcomes require high-quality tracing/reconciliation visibility.

Do not infer failure merely because the request timed out.

---

# 324. AI Observability

AI-backed functionality requires additional telemetry.

Potential signals:

```text
model/provider
latency
token/usage volume
tool invocation
failure type
fallback
cost
```

subject to privacy/security policy.

---

# 325. AI Prompt Logging

Do not automatically log full user prompts or model responses.

They may contain:

```text
PII
secrets
confidential business content
```

---

# 326. AI Content Telemetry

Prefer metadata such as:

```text
model
token counts
latency
outcome
safe operation IDs
```

unless content capture is explicitly approved.

---

# 327. AI Tool Calls

Privileged AI tool actions SHOULD be auditable.

---

# 328. AI Cost

AI features SHOULD monitor cost-related usage where financially material.

---

# 329. AI Fallback

Record when:

```text
fallback model
fallback provider
```

is used so quality/availability behavior can be analyzed.

---

# 330. AI Safety Events

Security/safety-relevant events MAY require a separate controlled telemetry path.

---

# 331. Multi-Tenant Observability

Tenant identity may be useful for diagnosis but can create:

```text
cardinality
privacy
access-control
```

problems.

Use deliberately.

---

# 332. Tenant Dashboards

Per-tenant operational views MAY be appropriate for enterprise support.

Prefer queryable logs/traces rather than unbounded per-tenant metric series at large scale.

---

# 333. No Cross-Tenant Telemetry Exposure

Customer-facing observability must never expose another tenant's data.

---

# 334. Customer Observability

Enterprise products MAY expose:

```text
audit history
usage
API logs
webhook delivery history
```

with strict tenant authorization.

---

# 335. Support Diagnostics

Support tools SHOULD expose curated diagnostics rather than granting unrestricted access to internal logging systems.

---

# 336. Observability Security

Telemetry platforms are sensitive systems.

They may contain:

```text
architecture
identifiers
errors
customer metadata
security events
```

---

# 337. Telemetry Access

Use:

```text
SSO
MFA
RBAC
least privilege
```

for observability platforms.

---

# 338. Telemetry Export Security

Use encrypted transport when exporting telemetry across untrusted networks.

---

# 339. Telemetry Storage

Protect stored telemetry according to its data classification.

---

# 340. Telemetry Access Audit

Sensitive log/audit-system access SHOULD itself be auditable.

---

# 341. Telemetry Injection

Do not allow untrusted external callers to fabricate trusted internal security/audit telemetry.

---

# 342. Source Trust

Telemetry from less-trusted systems must be treated accordingly.

Do not assume all reported metadata is trustworthy.

---

# 343. Metric Spoofing

Security decisions SHOULD NOT rely exclusively on unauthenticated client-provided telemetry.

---

# 344. Client Analytics ≠ Security Evidence

Browser telemetry can be modified by the user.

It may inform diagnostics, not authoritative security decisions.

---

# 345. Telemetry Availability

Loss of observability should itself trigger investigation for critical systems.

Running blind is an operational risk.

---

# 346. Observability Degraded Mode

If telemetry backend is down:

```text
product continues where safe
local buffering bounded
operators notified
```

---

# 347. Audit Durability

Audit events requiring compliance durability may need stronger guarantees than ordinary application logs.

---

# 348. Testing Instrumentation

Important telemetry SHOULD be tested where practical.

---

# 349. Structured Log Tests

Test critical log/event schema without tightly coupling every test to exact prose.

---

# 350. Metric Tests

Verify critical counters/histograms are emitted with bounded labels and correct semantics.

---

# 351. Trace Tests

Integration tests MAY verify meaningful spans/context propagation for critical cross-service workflows.

---

# 352. Audit Tests

Security-sensitive actions SHOULD verify expected audit records.

---

# 353. Redaction Tests

Test that:

```text
tokens
passwords
sensitive fields
```

do not appear in telemetry.

---

# 354. Cardinality Tests

Static/CI rules MAY detect obvious dynamic-label mistakes.

---

# 355. Dashboard Testing

Dashboard/query definitions SHOULD be validated automatically where platform tooling supports it.

---

# 356. Alert Testing

Alerts SHOULD be tested/simulated before relying on them.

---

# 357. Page Delivery Test

Critical paging paths SHOULD periodically verify that notifications reach the expected on-call target.

---

# 358. Runbook Testing

Runbooks SHOULD be exercised during:

```text
incidents
game days
failure drills
```

so obsolete procedures are discovered.

---

# 359. SLO Validation

Verify SLI queries represent actual intended user populations.

A mathematically correct query can still measure the wrong thing.

---

# 360. Telemetry Development Environment

Developers SHOULD be able to inspect relevant logs/traces locally or in development environments without needing production access.

---

# 361. Local Traceability

Complex distributed applications SHOULD provide a practical local/development telemetry workflow.

---

# 362. Production Parity

Telemetry schemas SHOULD remain broadly consistent across environments so debugging knowledge transfers.

---

# 363. Environment-Specific Volume

Log levels/sample rates MAY differ between environments.

Schema semantics should not.

---

# 364. Documentation

Every critical service SHOULD document:

```text
dashboards
SLOs
alerts
runbooks
log/trace query basics
ownership
```

---

# 365. Service Catalog Integration

The service catalog SHOULD link:

```text
owner
repository
dashboard
SLO
alerts
runbook
dependencies
```

where platform maturity supports it.

---

# 366. Observability Review Trigger

Review instrumentation when introducing:

```text
new service
new dependency
critical workflow
queue
payment flow
authentication flow
multi-tenant boundary
AI provider
```

---

# 367. Telemetry Schema Governance

Shared telemetry fields SHOULD have documented ownership.

Do not create duplicate fields with overlapping semantics.

---

# 368. Deprecating Telemetry

When changing metric/log/attribute names:

```text
update dashboards
update alerts
update runbooks
update queries
```

before removing old data.

---

# 369. Observability Backward Compatibility

Telemetry may have operational consumers just like APIs.

Treat important signal changes deliberately.

---

# 370. Production Debugging Checklist

Before investigating:

```text
□ Confirm user impact
□ Confirm environment/service
□ Check recent deployments
□ Check SLO/burn
□ Check dependencies
□ Find trace/request example
□ Inspect correlated logs
□ Prefer read-only investigation
□ Avoid sensitive-data exposure
□ Record interventions
```

---

# 371. Structured Logging Checklist

```text
□ Stable schema
□ Timestamp
□ Severity
□ Event name
□ Service/environment
□ Request/trace correlation
□ Error type when relevant
□ No secrets
□ PII minimized
□ No dynamic field names
□ Volume appropriate
```

---

# 372. Metrics Checklist

```text
□ Metric answers operational question
□ Correct instrument type
□ Unit explicit
□ Labels bounded
□ Cardinality estimated
□ No IDs/secrets
□ Histogram used for distributions
□ Dashboard/alert consumer known
□ Retention/cost acceptable
```

---

# 373. Tracing Checklist

```text
□ Meaningful root span
□ Stable span names
□ Context propagated
□ Critical dependencies instrumented
□ Error state correct
□ Sensitive attributes excluded
□ Sampling policy defined
□ Trace-to-log correlation works
```

---

# 374. Dashboard Checklist

```text
□ User/service outcome visible first
□ Traffic visible
□ Error visible
□ Latency visible
□ Saturation visible
□ Dependencies visible
□ Deployment markers
□ Units/labels clear
□ Drill-down possible
□ Owner known
```

---

# 375. Alert Checklist

```text
□ Actionable
□ Owner/on-call known
□ User impact understood
□ Severity appropriate
□ Threshold justified
□ Duration justified
□ Deduplication considered
□ Runbook linked
□ Tested
```

---

# 376. SLO Checklist

```text
□ User-relevant SLI
□ Population defined
□ Success criteria defined
□ Measurement source defined
□ Window defined
□ Target defined
□ Error budget calculable
□ Burn-rate visibility
□ Policy for excessive burn
□ Reviewed periodically
```

---

# 377. Audit Logging Checklist

```text
□ Actor
□ Subject where different
□ Action
□ Target
□ Tenant
□ Timestamp
□ Result
□ No secrets
□ Integrity protected
□ Access controlled
□ Retention defined
```

---

# 378. Error Monitoring Checklist

```text
□ Centralized collection
□ Production environment
□ Release association
□ Useful grouping
□ Stack/source context
□ Trace/request correlation
□ Sensitive data redacted
□ Regression detection
□ Ownership/routing
```

---

# 379. External Dependency Checklist

```text
□ Dependency name
□ Request rate
□ Latency
□ Errors
□ Timeouts
□ Rate limits
□ Circuit state where used
□ Trace spans
□ Alerting
□ Runbook for critical dependency
```

---

# 380. Queue Observability Checklist

```text
□ Queue depth
□ Oldest-message age
□ Processing throughput
□ Processing latency
□ Retry rate
□ Failure rate
□ DLQ depth
□ Stuck jobs
□ Worker saturation
```

---

# 381. Observability Definition of Done — Feature

A significant feature is not production-ready until:

```text
✓ Success/failure outcomes measurable
✓ Unexpected errors observable
✓ Relevant structured logs exist
✓ Metrics exist where aggregate behavior matters
✓ Trace propagation preserved
✓ Sensitive data excluded
✓ Operational owner known
✓ Critical alerts/dashboards updated
✓ Audit events added where required
```

---

# 382. Definition of Done — Service

A production service is observability-ready when:

```text
✓ Canonical service identity
✓ Structured logging
✓ Request correlation
✓ RED/service metrics
✓ Relevant infrastructure saturation metrics
✓ Distributed tracing where justified
✓ Overview dashboard
✓ Error monitoring
✓ Critical dependency monitoring
✓ Alerts
✓ Runbooks
✓ SLOs where service criticality warrants them
✓ Telemetry retention/access defined
```

---

# 383. Definition of Done — Critical Workflow

Critical workflows additionally require:

```text
✓ User-outcome metric
✓ Failure taxonomy
✓ End-to-end traceability
✓ Dependency visibility
✓ SLI/SLO where applicable
✓ SLO burn alerting
✓ Safe incident diagnostics
✓ Recovery verification metric
```

---

# 384. Observability Anti-Patterns

Avoid:

```text
console.log(object)
```

as production observability architecture.

Avoid:

```text
plain text only
```

when structured logging is available.

Avoid:

```text
"something failed"
```

with no error type/context.

Avoid:

```text
every request body logged
```

Avoid:

```text
Authorization header logged
```

Avoid:

```text
email address as metric label
```

Avoid:

```text
request ID as metric label
```

Avoid:

```text
raw URL path as metric dimension
```

Avoid:

```text
average latency only
```

Avoid:

```text
CPU dashboard = service health
```

Avoid:

```text
500 graphs on one dashboard
```

Avoid:

```text
page on every exception
```

Avoid:

```text
alert with no owner
```

Avoid:

```text
alert with no action
```

Avoid:

```text
alert threshold copied from another service
```

Avoid:

```text
SLO = 99.99%
```

because it sounds impressive.

Avoid:

```text
server running = availability
```

Avoid:

```text
audit trail mixed into disposable debug logs
```

Avoid:

```text
trace every function
```

Avoid:

```text
100% trace sampling forever
```

without cost justification.

Avoid:

```text
production issue
→ SSH
→ random commands
```

Avoid:

```text
production debugging
→ full DB dump to laptop
```

Avoid:

```text
turn off alert because noisy
```

without fixing the signal.

Avoid:

```text
observability exporter unavailable
→ product request fails
```

Avoid:

```text
collect everything forever
```

as retention policy.

---

# 385. AI Observability Rules

AI coding agents MUST inspect existing observability conventions before adding instrumentation.

Inspect:

```text
logging library
metric naming
tracing
OpenTelemetry setup
error monitoring
audit mechanism
```

---

# 386. AI Structured Logging Rule

AI MUST use structured fields rather than interpolating all context into a message string.

---

# 387. AI Secret Rule

AI MUST NOT log:

```text
passwords
tokens
cookies
API-key secrets
OTP
private keys
```

---

# 388. AI PII Rule

AI SHOULD minimize personal information in telemetry.

It MUST NOT add user-content logging simply to make debugging easier.

---

# 389. AI Metric Rule

Before adding a metric, AI should answer:

```text
What question does this metric answer?
```

---

# 390. AI Cardinality Rule

Before adding a metric label, AI MUST evaluate whether values are bounded.

Never add:

```text
userId
requestId
email
raw URL
```

as ordinary metric dimensions.

---

# 391. AI Trace Rule

AI SHOULD add spans around meaningful external/long-running operations where existing auto-instrumentation does not already cover them.

---

# 392. AI Duplicate Instrumentation Rule

AI MUST inspect existing auto-instrumentation before adding manual duplicate spans/metrics.

---

# 393. AI Correlation Rule

New server request/background-job code SHOULD preserve canonical trace/correlation context.

---

# 394. AI Error Rule

Unexpected errors SHOULD include enough safe context to diagnose and should flow into the canonical error-monitoring path.

---

# 395. AI Expected-Error Rule

AI MUST NOT send routine validation/domain errors to exception monitoring indiscriminately.

---

# 396. AI Audit Rule

When introducing privileged actions, AI SHOULD consider whether an audit event is required.

---

# 397. AI Dashboard Rule

A new critical service/flow is incomplete if its health cannot be seen from existing or updated dashboards.

---

# 398. AI Alert Rule

AI MUST NOT create paging alerts without:

```text
actionability
owner
severity
runbook/recovery context
```

---

# 399. AI SLO Rule

AI MUST NOT invent reliability percentages arbitrarily.

SLOs must reflect user/business requirements and measurable SLIs.

---

# 400. AI Production-Debugging Rule

AI MUST prefer:

```text
telemetry
read-only analysis
controlled tooling
```

over invasive production mutation.

---

# 401. AI Temporary-Debug Rule

Temporary production debugging instrumentation requires:

```text
scope
redaction
expiration/removal
```

---

# 402. AI Query Rule

AI MUST NOT recommend unbounded production database queries for investigation.

---

# 403. AI Telemetry-Cost Rule

AI SHOULD consider cardinality, volume, retention, and sampling before introducing high-volume instrumentation.

---

# 404. AI OpenTelemetry Rule

Where the system uses OpenTelemetry, AI SHOULD use established semantic conventions instead of inventing parallel attribute naming.

---

# 405. AI Gold Rule

When uncertain:

```text
User impact
>
Correct signal semantics
>
Correlation
>
Actionability
>
Diagnostic detail
>
Telemetry volume
```

---

# 406. Golden Observability Rules

**1. Production systems are designed to be observable.**

**2. Logs, metrics, and traces solve different problems and should correlate.**

**3. Use standardized telemetry conventions before inventing new ones.**

**4. Every service has a stable identity.**

**5. Every meaningful signal identifies environment and release where useful.**

**6. Production logs are structured.**

**7. Structured logging means stable schema, not merely JSON.**

**8. Machine behavior never depends on parsing log prose.**

**9. Secrets never enter telemetry.**

**10. PII is minimized.**

**11. Expected errors do not flood exception monitoring.**

**12. Unexpected errors retain useful diagnostic context.**

**13. Metrics use explicit units and appropriate instrument semantics.**

**14. Metric cardinality is controlled deliberately.**

**15. User IDs, request IDs, trace IDs, and raw URLs do not belong in ordinary metric labels.**

**16. Latency is measured as a distribution, not only an average.**

**17. Request-driven services observe rate, errors, and duration.**

**18. Resource systems observe utilization, saturation, and errors where relevant.**

**19. Distributed traces use stable low-cardinality operation names.**

**20. Trace context propagates through meaningful service boundaries.**

**21. Trace/log correlation works.**

**22. Sampling is an explicit architecture decision.**

**23. Dashboards begin with user/service outcomes.**

**24. Alerts are actionable.**

**25. Every alert has an owner.**

**26. Pages are reserved for urgent human-actionable conditions.**

**27. Alert on user impact/SLO burn before arbitrary infrastructure numbers where practical.**

**28. SLOs measure user-relevant service behavior.**

**29. SLO targets are justified, not chosen for prestige.**

**30. Error budgets inform reliability decisions.**

**31. Audit logs are distinct from ordinary debug logs.**

**32. Privileged actions are auditable.**

**33. Audit data is protected from unauthorized change/access.**

**34. Production debugging begins read-only.**

**35. Production changes during investigation are controlled, auditable, and reversible.**

**36. Direct production data access is minimized.**

**37. Telemetry exporter failure does not normally break the product.**

**38. Observability infrastructure is itself monitored.**

**39. Telemetry cost, retention, and cardinality are governed.**

**40. If an incident cannot be diagnosed from available signals, observability is incomplete.**

---

# 407. Canonical Observability Standard

The organizational standard is:

> **Production systems emit correlated, structured, privacy-conscious telemetry across logs, metrics, traces, error monitoring, and audit events. OpenTelemetry-compatible data models and semantic conventions are preferred where supported so telemetry remains consistent across services and vendors. Services expose stable identity, deployment version, environment, request/trace context, and meaningful operation semantics without including credentials or unnecessary personal information.**

> **Logs represent structured events and diagnostic context; metrics represent bounded aggregate measurements; traces represent causal distributed operations. Metrics maintain explicit units and controlled cardinality, traces use stable operation names and propagated context, and unexpected errors preserve sufficient diagnostic information without exposing internal details to users. Telemetry is sampled, retained, and stored according to diagnostic value, privacy, security, and cost rather than collected indefinitely.**

> **Critical services maintain dashboards centered on user-visible outcomes, traffic, errors, latency, saturation, dependency health, and relevant changes. Alerts exist only when a person or automated process can take useful action, are routed to an explicit owner, and include sufficient context and runbooks for response. Service Level Indicators represent user-relevant service behavior, Service Level Objectives define justified reliability targets over explicit windows, and error-budget consumption guides reliability response and change decisions.**

> **Security-sensitive and privileged actions produce protected audit trails distinct from disposable operational logs. Production debugging begins with telemetry and read-only investigation; privileged production access, data repairs, configuration changes, kill switches, and temporary diagnostics are tightly scoped, attributable, auditable, and reversible. Observability failure must not normally cause business-operation failure, but loss of critical telemetry is itself monitored as an operational risk.**

A production-grade observable system should make it easy to answer:

```text
Are users succeeding right now?
How many users/requests are affected?
When did degradation begin?
Was there a deployment or configuration change?
Which operation is failing?
Which dependency is slow?
What is the p95/p99 latency?
Are resources saturated?
What is the trace for a failed request?
Which logs correspond to that trace?
What error type occurred?
Is this a regression?
What is the service's SLO?
How quickly is the error budget burning?
Should someone be paged?
Who owns the alert?
What runbook should they use?
Who performed this privileged action?
Can we investigate without modifying production?
How do we know recovery is complete?
```

If those questions cannot be answered reliably, the system is not yet observability-ready.

Two governance distinctions are especially important. OpenTelemetry recommends structured logs with a **consistent schema**, and its model supports direct log/trace correlation through `TraceId` and `SpanId`; merely outputting arbitrary JSON does not by itself make logging well structured. citeturn217442search6turn217442search8 OWASP likewise recommends consistent application logging but warns that operational, security, transaction, and audit trails can have different purposes and may appropriately remain separate; it also calls for protection against unauthorized access, modification, deletion, and over-retention. citeturn217442search0

In the master hierarchy, I would now place it as:

**Architecture → Framework → Security → Authentication & Authorization → Data & Database → API → Routes → State Management → Design Tokens → Layouts → Facade → Components → Forms & Validation → Accessibility → Error Handling & Resilience → Testing → Performance → Observability → Infrastructure & Deployment → Documentation → Governance.**


<!-- ===== configuration-environment | operations | standards/operations/02-configuration-environment.md ===== -->

This standard treats **configuration as a deploy/runtime contract**, **secrets as a separate security class**, and **environments as isolated deployment contexts rather than branches of application logic**.

# Configuration & Environment Guidelines — Gold Standard

## 1. Purpose

These guidelines define the canonical standard for:

- application configuration;
- local development;
- test environments;
- preview environments;
- development environments;
- staging;
- production;
- environment variables;
- `.env` files;
- runtime configuration;
- build-time configuration;
- configuration validation;
- secrets;
- credentials;
- secret managers;
- feature flags;
- environment parity;
- configuration ownership;
- configuration promotion;
- CI/CD configuration;
- infrastructure configuration;
- emergency configuration changes.

The objective is to ensure configuration is:

```text
Explicit
Validated
Secure
Owned
Auditable
Environment-aware
Reproducible
Easy to operate
Difficult to misuse
```

The core principle is:

> **Code defines behavior. Configuration selects approved behavior for a deployment. Secrets authorize access. These concerns must remain distinct.**

---

# 2. Normative Language

- **MUST** — mandatory.
- **MUST NOT** — prohibited.
- **SHOULD** — expected unless a documented exception exists.
- **SHOULD NOT** — generally avoided unless justified.
- **MAY** — optional.

Exceptions SHOULD document:

```text
Reason
Affected environment
Security impact
Operational impact
Owner
Expiry/review date
```

---

# 3. Configuration Definition

Configuration is information that can legitimately vary between deployments without changing application code.

Examples:

```text
DATABASE_URL
PUBLIC_APP_URL
EMAIL_PROVIDER_REGION
LOG_LEVEL
QUEUE_NAME
PAYMENT_PROVIDER_MODE
```

---

# 4. Configuration vs Code

A value belongs in configuration when:

```text
same application code
+
different deployment
→
different value
```

A value belongs in code when it expresses stable application behavior.

---

# 5. Code Example

Good code-owned constant:

```text
MAX_PROJECT_NAME_LENGTH = 120
```

if this is a stable product rule.

Potential configuration:

```text
UPLOAD_BUCKET
```

because it changes between deployments.

---

# 6. Do Not Externalize Everything

Not every constant should become an environment variable.

Excessive external configuration creates:

- hidden behavior;
- deployment complexity;
- weak discoverability;
- testing explosion.

Prefer code unless legitimate deploy-time variability exists.

---

# 7. Configuration Categories

The canonical configuration categories are:

```text
Static code configuration
Deployment configuration
Runtime configuration
Secret configuration
Feature configuration
Infrastructure configuration
User/product settings
```

---

# 8. Static Code Configuration

Static application behavior that does not vary by deployment belongs in version-controlled code.

Examples:

```text
route definitions
domain invariants
component defaults
supported file types
```

---

# 9. Deployment Configuration

Deployment configuration varies between deployed instances.

Examples:

```text
database host
public hostname
storage bucket
provider endpoint
```

---

# 10. Runtime Configuration

Runtime configuration may change without rebuilding the application.

Examples may include:

```text
operational kill switch
runtime feature rollout
rate limit
```

when architecture explicitly supports dynamic updates.

---

# 11. Secret Configuration

Secrets include:

```text
passwords
API keys
private keys
signing secrets
database credentials
OAuth client secrets
encryption keys
```

Secrets require stronger handling than ordinary configuration.

---

# 12. Feature Configuration

Feature flags control:

```text
availability
rollout
experimentation
operational disablement
```

They require dedicated lifecycle governance.

---

# 13. Infrastructure Configuration

Infrastructure configuration includes:

```text
CPU/memory
autoscaling
network
load balancer
regions
storage class
```

and SHOULD generally be managed through Infrastructure as Code.

---

# 14. User/Product Settings

User-editable application settings are not deployment environment variables.

Examples:

```text
workspace timezone
notification preferences
branding
```

belong in application data/configuration systems.

---

# 15. Environment Model

Canonical deployment environments are conceptually:

```text
Local
Test
Preview
Development / Integration
Staging
Production
```

Not every project needs every environment.

---

# 16. Environment Purpose

Each environment MUST have a defined purpose.

Do not create environments because:

```text
"every company has staging"
```

Create them when they provide meaningful isolation or verification.

---

# 17. Local Environment

Local exists for developer iteration.

Goals:

```text
fast startup
safe experimentation
reasonable production similarity
independence
```

---

# 18. Local Must Be Safe

Local development MUST NOT require production:

```text
credentials
databases
customer data
queues
storage
```

for ordinary engineering work.

---

# 19. Test Environment

Test environments exist for automated verification.

They SHOULD be:

```text
isolated
repeatable
disposable
deterministic
```

---

# 20. Preview Environment

Preview environments provide deployment-like verification for a branch/change.

They SHOULD be ephemeral where practical.

---

# 21. Preview Isolation

Preview deployments MUST NOT share mutable production resources.

---

# 22. Preview Credentials

Preview credentials must have:

```text
limited privileges
non-production scope
automatic expiry where practical
```

---

# 23. Development Environment

Shared development/integration environments MAY support:

```text
cross-service integration
QA
internal demonstrations
```

They MUST NOT be treated as production.

---

# 24. Staging Environment

Staging exists to validate production-like behavior before production.

It SHOULD resemble production in architecture where this provides real verification value.

---

# 25. Production Environment

Production serves real users/business operations.

It requires the strongest:

```text
access controls
change controls
secret handling
observability
auditability
```

---

# 26. Environment Separation

Production MUST be isolated from non-production where compromise or accidental modification could affect users.

Isolation SHOULD include applicable:

```text
accounts/projects
credentials
databases
buckets
queues
networks
domains
```

---

# 27. Separate Credentials

Each environment MUST use its own credentials.

Never use:

```text
same production API key
```

for staging, preview, or local development.

---

# 28. Separate Databases

Production and non-production databases MUST be separate.

---

# 29. Separate Storage

Production object storage SHOULD be separate from non-production storage.

---

# 30. Separate Queues

Production queues/topics SHOULD be separate from non-production.

---

# 31. Separate External Provider Modes

Use:

```text
sandbox
test mode
development account
```

for external providers when available.

---

# 32. Environment Naming

Environment names SHOULD be stable and consistent.

Canonical examples:

```text
local
test
development
staging
production
```

---

# 33. Avoid Environment Synonyms

Do not inconsistently use:

```text
prod
production
prd
live
```

through different systems for the same concept.

Pick one canonical identifier.

---

# 34. Production Name

Recommended canonical machine identifier:

```text
production
```

---

# 35. Environment Is Not Feature Logic

Avoid code such as:

```ts
if (environment === "production") {
  enableBusinessFeature();
}
```

for ordinary product behavior.

Use explicit configuration/feature flags.

---

# 36. Environment Checks

Environment checks are appropriate for true environment-specific behavior such as:

```text
development tooling
test isolation
production debugging restrictions
```

---

# 37. Avoid Environment Explosion

Do not encode configuration into dozens of named environment categories.

Prefer independent explicit config values.

---

# 38. Orthogonal Configuration

Configuration values SHOULD be independently controllable.

Prefer:

```text
EMAIL_ENABLED=false
PAYMENTS_MODE=sandbox
```

over an overloaded:

```text
ENVIRONMENT=qa-eu-special
```

that implicitly controls everything.

---

# 39. Environment Parity

Environment parity means:

> Important production characteristics should be represented in pre-production environments closely enough to expose meaningful defects.

---

# 40. Parity Is Not Identity

Staging does not need production scale.

Example:

```text
Production
20 app instances

Staging
2 app instances
```

may still have useful architectural parity.

---

# 41. Parity Priorities

Prioritize parity for:

```text
runtime version
database engine/version
deployment mechanism
migration process
network assumptions
authentication integration
build artifact
```

---

# 42. Same Artifact Principle

Production SHOULD deploy the same immutable application artifact that was tested earlier.

Prefer:

```text
Build once
↓
Test artifact
↓
Promote artifact
↓
Deploy production
```

---

# 43. Do Not Rebuild for Production

Avoid:

```text
build staging artifact
↓
test
↓
rebuild from source for production
```

when avoidable.

The production build may differ from the tested artifact.

---

# 44. Environment-Specific Configuration Injection

Prefer:

```text
same artifact
+
environment-specific configuration
```

over separate source builds.

---

# 45. Runtime Version Parity

Local/CI/staging SHOULD use the supported production runtime version.

Examples:

```text
Node
Python
Java
PostgreSQL
```

---

# 46. Database Engine Parity

If production uses PostgreSQL:

```text
SQLite in tests
```

is not sufficient verification for database-specific behavior.

---

# 47. Service Parity

Mocking may be appropriate locally, but integration/staging SHOULD exercise real classes of dependencies where their behavior matters.

---

# 48. Configuration Source of Truth

Each configuration item MUST have one authoritative source.

Avoid competing values in:

```text
.env
CI variables
Terraform
deployment YAML
runtime admin UI
```

without precedence rules.

---

# 49. Configuration Precedence

If multiple configuration sources exist, precedence MUST be documented.

Example:

```text
runtime secret manager
>
deployment environment
>
safe default
```

Do not leave precedence to framework accident.

---

# 50. Recommended Precedence Simplicity

Prefer as few configuration layers as possible.

Every additional layer increases ambiguity.

---

# 51. Configuration Registry

Significant applications SHOULD maintain a configuration registry/catalog.

Each item SHOULD document:

```text
Name
Purpose
Type
Required?
Default
Secret?
Scope
Owner
Example
Validation
Restart/reload behavior
```

---

# 52. Configuration Naming

Environment/config variables SHOULD use:

```text
UPPER_SNAKE_CASE
```

unless platform convention requires otherwise.

---

# 53. Name for Meaning

Prefer:

```text
DATABASE_POOL_MAX
```

over:

```text
MAX
```

---

# 54. Boolean Naming

Boolean configuration SHOULD communicate positive meaning.

Prefer:

```text
EMAIL_SENDING_ENABLED
```

over:

```text
DISABLE_EMAIL_SENDING
```

when practical.

---

# 55. Units in Names

Include units where ambiguity exists.

Prefer:

```text
REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS
CACHE_TTL_SECONDS
MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES
```

---

# 56. Configuration Names Are Contracts

Renaming a production environment variable can break deployment.

Treat important config names as external contracts.

---

# 57. Typed Configuration

Configuration MUST be parsed into typed application values.

Do not use raw strings throughout the application.

---

# 58. Boolean Parsing

Bad:

```ts
Boolean(process.env.FEATURE_ENABLED)
```

because:

```text
"false"
```

is truthy in many languages.

Use explicit parsing.

---

# 59. Number Parsing

Validate:

```text
integer
range
unit
```

not merely that a string can be converted.

---

# 60. URL Parsing

URL configuration SHOULD be parsed/validated structurally.

---

# 61. Enum Configuration

Bounded configuration SHOULD use explicit enum validation.

Example:

```text
LOG_LEVEL:
debug
info
warn
error
```

---

# 62. Unknown Values

Unknown enum/config values MUST fail validation rather than silently map to a fallback.

---

# 63. Configuration Schema

Every production application SHOULD define one canonical configuration schema.

---

# 64. Configuration Schema Responsibilities

The schema SHOULD define:

```text
name
type
required/optional
default
validation
secret classification where useful
```

---

# 65. Validate at Startup

Required configuration MUST be validated during application startup.

---

# 66. Fail Fast

Invalid critical configuration SHOULD cause the process to fail before serving traffic.

Bad:

```text
app starts
↓
first customer request
↓
DATABASE_URL undefined
```

---

# 67. Clear Startup Errors

Configuration validation errors should clearly identify:

```text
which config is invalid
expected format
```

without printing secret values.

---

# 68. Missing Config

Prefer:

```text
PAYMENT_PROVIDER_KEY is required.
```

not:

```text
Configuration error.
```

---

# 69. Secret Validation Error

Do not output:

```text
Invalid token: sk_live_...
```

Instead:

```text
PAYMENT_API_KEY is invalid or unavailable.
```

---

# 70. No Silent Defaults for Critical Config

Do not silently default:

```text
AUTH_REQUIRED=false
TLS_VERIFY=false
```

when configuration is missing.

Security-sensitive config MUST have safe behavior.

---

# 71. Safe Defaults

Defaults SHOULD be:

```text
secure
predictable
low-risk
```

---

# 72. Required vs Default

Critical external configuration SHOULD often be required rather than defaulted.

Example:

```text
DATABASE_URL
```

normally has no production default.

---

# 73. Development Defaults

Safe development defaults MAY exist.

They must not accidentally become production behavior.

---

# 74. Production Validation

The application SHOULD explicitly prevent unsafe development defaults in production.

---

# 75. Example

Invalid:

```text
production
+
EMAIL_PROVIDER=console
```

if real email delivery is mandatory.

Configuration validation can reject this combination.

---

# 76. Cross-Field Validation

Configuration schemas SHOULD support invariants between fields.

Example:

```text
TLS_ENABLED=true
→ TLS_CERTIFICATE required
```

---

# 77. Conditional Configuration

Conditional requirements SHOULD remain explicit.

---

# 78. Dead Configuration

Unused configuration SHOULD be removed.

Do not leave mysterious variables indefinitely.

---

# 79. Configuration Discovery

Developers should be able to determine required configuration without searching the entire source tree.

---

# 80. `.env` Purpose

`.env` files MAY be used as a developer convenience for local environment variables.

They are not a secrets-management platform.

---

# 81. `.env.example`

Repositories SHOULD provide:

```text
.env.example
```

or equivalent documentation containing:

```text
variable names
safe example values
comments where useful
```

---

# 82. Never Put Real Secrets in `.env.example`

Example files MUST contain only safe placeholders.

Good:

```text
PAYMENT_API_KEY=replace_me
```

---

# 83. `.env` Git Ignore

Local secret-containing `.env` files MUST be excluded from version control.

---

# 84. Explicit Ignore Patterns

Repositories SHOULD explicitly ignore applicable variants such as:

```text
.env
.env.local
.env.*.local
```

according to framework conventions.

---

# 85. Beware `.env.production`

A filename containing:

```text
production
```

does not make it safe.

Do not commit production credentials to source control.

---

# 86. Local Secret Provisioning

Local development secrets SHOULD come from:

```text
developer secret manager
approved CLI
local ignored file
short-lived identity
```

according to platform maturity.

---

# 87. `.env` Permissions

Local `.env` files containing secrets SHOULD have appropriately restrictive filesystem access where supported.

---

# 88. `.env` Duplication

Avoid many inconsistent local files such as:

```text
.env
.env.dev
.env.development
.env.local
.env.user
.env.override
```

without documented precedence.

---

# 89. Framework Loading Rules

Document framework-specific `.env` loading precedence.

Do not rely on developer memory.

---

# 90. Environment Variables

Environment variables are suitable for many simple deployment configuration values.

They are not automatically secure.

---

# 91. Environment Variables Are Strings

Treat them as untrusted string input until validated.

---

# 92. Secret Environment Variables

Environment variables MAY carry secrets when platform architecture requires it, but stronger secret injection mechanisms SHOULD be preferred where practical.

---

# 93. Environment Variable Exposure

Secrets in environment variables may leak through:

```text
process inspection
crash dumps
debug output
child processes
diagnostic tooling
```

depending on platform.

---

# 94. Build-Time Environment Variables

Build-time configuration is embedded during build.

Examples:

```text
PUBLIC_API_ORIGIN
PUBLIC_ANALYTICS_ID
```

depending on framework architecture.

---

# 95. Build-Time Values Are Frozen

Changing a build-time value generally requires a rebuild.

Do not pretend it is runtime configuration.

---

# 96. Runtime Configuration

Runtime config is read by the running deployment.

Changing it may require:

```text
restart
reload
```

depending on platform.

---

# 97. Build-Time vs Runtime Must Be Documented

Every important config value SHOULD identify:

```text
build_time
runtime
dynamic_runtime
```

semantics.

---

# 98. Public Configuration

Frontend/browser configuration is public.

Any value delivered to browser JavaScript MUST be treated as visible to users.

---

# 99. Public Prefixes

Frameworks often use conventions such as:

```text
PUBLIC_
NEXT_PUBLIC_
VITE_
```

Treat such variables as intentionally exposed.

---

# 100. Never Put Secrets in Browser Config

No:

```text
database password
private API key
OAuth client secret
signing key
```

may be exposed to client bundles.

---

# 101. Browser Build Inspection

Assume users can inspect:

```text
JavaScript
source maps
network
HTML
```

Do not rely on obscurity.

---

# 102. Secret Definition

A secret is any value whose disclosure could allow unauthorized:

```text
access
identity impersonation
data decryption
privilege
signing
```

or other sensitive capability.

---

# 103. Common Secrets

Examples:

```text
database passwords
API keys
private signing keys
TLS private keys
OAuth client secrets
webhook signing secrets
```

---

# 104. Not Every Configuration Value Is Secret

Examples typically nonsecret:

```text
region
public hostname
queue name
log level
```

Do not force ordinary config through secret storage unnecessarily.

---

# 105. Secret Management Platform

Production secrets SHOULD be stored in an approved secret-management system.

---

# 106. Secret Manager Capabilities

Preferred capabilities include:

```text
encryption
access policy
audit
rotation
versioning
runtime delivery
```

---

# 107. No Hardcoded Secrets

Secrets MUST NOT be committed into:

```text
source code
Dockerfile
container image
Terraform variable defaults
documentation
tests
fixtures
```

---

# 108. Secret Scanning

Source repositories and CI SHOULD run secret scanning.

---

# 109. Secret Leak Response

A committed secret is considered exposed even if:

```text
commit was deleted
branch was removed
```

Rotate/revoke it.

---

# 110. Git History

Removing a secret from the current file does not erase it from Git history.

---

# 111. Secret Rotation

All long-lived secrets SHOULD support rotation.

---

# 112. Rotation Without Downtime

Where practical, support:

```text
new credential
↓
overlap
↓
deployment update
↓
old credential revoke
```

---

# 113. Secret Versioning

Secret stores SHOULD support versions so deployments can migrate safely.

---

# 114. Secret Expiration

Prefer short-lived credentials where platform capabilities permit.

---

# 115. Workload Identity

Prefer:

```text
workload identity
managed identity
federated identity
```

over static credentials when available.

---

# 116. Human vs Workload Credentials

Do not use personal developer credentials for production application workloads.

---

# 117. Environment-Specific Secrets

Production and staging secrets MUST be different.

---

# 118. Secret Naming

Secret identifiers SHOULD communicate:

```text
service
purpose
environment
```

without embedding the secret itself.

---

# 119. Secret Scope

A secret should grant only the minimum required permissions.

---

# 120. Shared Secrets

Avoid one secret shared across many unrelated services.

Shared credentials increase blast radius and reduce attribution.

---

# 121. Secret Ownership

Every important secret SHOULD have:

```text
owner
purpose
consumer
rotation policy
```

---

# 122. Secret Inventory

Maintain an inventory of important production credentials.

---

# 123. Secret Access

Secret-manager access MUST follow least privilege.

---

# 124. Developer Secret Access

Developers SHOULD NOT need routine read access to production application secrets.

---

# 125. CI Secret Access

CI jobs receive only secrets required for that workflow.

---

# 126. Pull Request Safety

Untrusted pull requests/forks MUST NOT automatically receive production secrets.

---

# 127. CI Logging

Pipeline logs MUST NOT expose secret values.

---

# 128. Shell Tracing

Avoid:

```text
set -x
```

or equivalent debugging when it could print credentials.

---

# 129. Secret Masking

CI secret masking is defense in depth.

It does not make arbitrary secret printing acceptable.

---

# 130. Secret Files

Secrets MAY be injected as temporary files when supported.

File permissions and cleanup must be controlled.

---

# 131. Mounted Secrets

Mounted secret files can be preferable to environment variables for some workloads.

The application SHOULD read them through a clear secret abstraction if needed.

---

# 132. Container Images

Container images MUST NOT contain environment-specific secrets.

---

# 133. Docker Build Arguments

Build args are not safe secret storage.

Do not pass production secrets into image builds unless using dedicated secure build-secret mechanisms.

---

# 134. Kubernetes ConfigMaps

Non-confidential deployment configuration MAY use ConfigMaps or equivalent configuration resources.

---

# 135. ConfigMap Is Not Secret Storage

Confidential values MUST NOT be treated as safe merely because they are stored in a configuration object.

---

# 136. Kubernetes Secrets

Kubernetes Secrets MAY store confidential deployment data, but their existence alone does not guarantee sufficient protection.

Cluster:

```text
encryption
RBAC
namespace isolation
secret-store integration
```

must still be considered.

---

# 137. Immutable Config

Critical deployment config MAY use immutable/versioned resources to reduce accidental mutation.

---

# 138. Configuration Changes Are Deployments

A configuration change can be as consequential as a code change.

Treat high-impact configuration changes with equivalent review discipline.

---

# 139. Configuration-as-Code

Non-secret infrastructure/deployment configuration SHOULD be version-controlled where practical.

---

# 140. Benefits of Configuration-as-Code

This provides:

```text
review
history
reproducibility
rollback
ownership
```

---

# 141. Secret Values Are Not Configuration-as-Code

Version-control the:

```text
secret reference
secret identifier
access policy
```

not plaintext secret contents.

---

# 142. Configuration Review

Changes to production configuration SHOULD be reviewed.

---

# 143. High-Risk Configuration

Examples requiring stronger review:

```text
authentication bypass
authorization policy
network allowlist
payment provider
retention
encryption
rate limits
```

---

# 144. Change History

Production configuration changes SHOULD be auditable.

---

# 145. Actor

Audit should identify:

```text
who changed
what
when
environment
```

for important production config.

---

# 146. Reason

High-impact manual changes SHOULD record:

```text
ticket
incident
reason
```

where operational process supports it.

---

# 147. Config Diff

Operators SHOULD be able to inspect the effective difference before applying a production change.

---

# 148. Dry Run

Infrastructure/config tooling SHOULD offer:

```text
plan
preview
dry-run
```

where feasible.

---

# 149. Automatic Deployment

Normal production config changes SHOULD flow through approved delivery automation.

Avoid console-click configuration drift.

---

# 150. Emergency Changes

Emergency manual configuration changes MAY be allowed during incidents.

They MUST be:

```text
scoped
authorized
audited
reversible
```

---

# 151. Reconcile Emergency Changes

After the incident, any manual production change MUST be reconciled into the canonical configuration source or reverted.

---

# 152. Configuration Drift

Configuration drift means actual deployed config differs from intended/configured state.

---

# 153. Drift Detection

Infrastructure/platform tooling SHOULD detect important drift.

---

# 154. Drift Is a Defect

Persistent undocumented drift undermines:

```text
reproducibility
disaster recovery
incident diagnosis
```

---

# 155. Configuration Promotion

Configuration SHOULD be promoted deliberately across environments.

Do not blindly copy all staging values to production.

---

# 156. Promotion Pattern

Conceptually:

```text
Same config schema
+
environment-specific values
```

rather than:

```text
copy staging config wholesale
```

---

# 157. Production-Specific Values

Expected differences include:

```text
hostnames
credentials
resource capacity
provider account
regions
```

---

# 158. Staging Is Not Source of Production Truth

Production configuration has its own governed values.

Staging merely validates configuration shape and behavior.

---

# 159. Environment Parity Check

CI/CD SHOULD verify required config keys exist across applicable deployment definitions.

---

# 160. Configuration Migration

Changing configuration contracts requires migration planning.

Example:

```text
OLD_API_URL
→
SERVICE_BASE_URL
```

---

# 161. Config Rename

Safe sequence:

```text
support new + old
↓
deploy
↓
update environment
↓
verify
↓
remove old support
```

when zero-downtime compatibility is needed.

---

# 162. Config Deprecation

Deprecated variables SHOULD have:

```text
replacement
warning
removal date/version
```

---

# 163. Unknown Configuration

Applications MAY warn/fail on unknown environment variables within their owned namespace where this helps detect typos.

---

# 164. Typo Example

```text
DATABASE_POOL_MXA=20
```

should not silently appear to work.

---

# 165. Configuration Documentation

Every required production config item MUST be documented.

---

# 166. Example Values

Documentation SHOULD include safe examples.

---

# 167. Secret Documentation

Document:

```text
secret purpose
source
required permissions
```

not the value.

---

# 168. Config Ownership

Every major configuration namespace SHOULD have an owner.

Example:

```text
DATABASE_*
→ Platform/Data team

AUTH_*
→ Identity team
```

according to organization.

---

# 169. Ownership Questions

For every important config ask:

```text
Who defines it?
Who can change it?
Who reviews changes?
Who responds if it breaks?
```

---

# 170. Product vs Platform Ownership

Feature teams should not casually modify platform-level settings.

Platform teams should not independently change domain semantics.

---

# 171. Config Change Blast Radius

Before changing configuration determine:

```text
single instance?
service?
region?
all production?
all tenants?
```

---

# 172. Canary Configuration

High-risk dynamic configuration MAY be rolled out gradually.

---

# 173. Regional Rollout

Configuration MAY be applied region-by-region where architecture supports this.

---

# 174. Tenant-Specific Config

Tenant-specific behavior usually belongs in product configuration/data, not environment variables.

---

# 175. Avoid Per-Tenant Environment Variables

Bad:

```text
TENANT_123_FEATURE_ENABLED=true
TENANT_456_FEATURE_ENABLED=false
```

Use a governed product/feature configuration system.

---

# 176. Feature Flags

Feature flags are temporary or operational controls over specific behavior.

---

# 177. Feature Flag Categories

Canonical categories:

```text
Release flag
Experiment flag
Operational flag
Permission/entitlement-adjacent flag
Kill switch
```

---

# 178. Release Flag

Used for progressive delivery of incomplete/new functionality.

---

# 179. Experiment Flag

Used to assign product experiments.

Experiment semantics follow Analytics Guidelines.

---

# 180. Operational Flag

Controls behavior for operational reasons.

Example:

```text
disable expensive recommendation service
```

---

# 181. Kill Switch

A kill switch can rapidly disable risky functionality.

---

# 182. Feature Flag ≠ Authorization

Feature flags MUST NOT replace server-side authorization.

Bad:

```text
if feature_enabled:
   allow_admin_action
```

without permission validation.

---

# 183. Feature Flag ≠ Entitlement by Default

Commercial entitlement should have an authoritative entitlement model.

A feature flag may participate in rollout but should not become accidental billing logic.

---

# 184. Flag Naming

Feature flags SHOULD use stable descriptive names.

Example:

```text
projects_new_editor
```

---

# 185. Avoid Negated Flags

Prefer:

```text
new_checkout_enabled
```

over:

```text
disable_old_checkout
```

when practical.

---

# 186. Flag Metadata

Every flag SHOULD have:

```text
owner
purpose
type
created date
expected removal
safe default
```

---

# 187. Flag Defaults

Feature flag defaults must be explicitly defined.

---

# 188. Remote Flag Failure

If the remote feature-flag service is unavailable, the application MUST have safe fallback behavior.

---

# 189. Security Flag Default

Security-sensitive flags SHOULD fail conservatively.

---

# 190. Optional Feature Default

Optional enhancements MAY safely default off.

---

# 191. Cached Flags

Remote flags MAY use cached last-known values where appropriate.

Freshness semantics must be understood.

---

# 192. Flag Evaluation Location

Critical server behavior should evaluate flags on trusted servers.

Client flags control presentation, not security.

---

# 193. User-Targeted Flags

Targeting rules may use:

```text
account
region
cohort
plan
```

where permitted.

Avoid unnecessary PII.

---

# 194. Flag Consistency

Determine whether one operation requires consistent evaluation.

Do not let the same user receive:

```text
old behavior
new behavior
old behavior
```

during one transactional workflow unexpectedly.

---

# 195. Flag Snapshot

Long-running operations MAY capture the flag version/decision at start.

---

# 196. Flag Analytics

Important experiment/release exposure SHOULD follow Analytics Guidelines.

---

# 197. Flag Lifecycle

Canonical lifecycle:

```text
Create
↓
Roll out
↓
100% stable
↓
Remove conditional
↓
Delete flag
```

---

# 198. Flag Debt

Flags are not permanent architecture.

Temporary release flags MUST be removed after rollout.

---

# 199. Flag Expiry

Temporary flags SHOULD have an expiry/review date.

---

# 200. Flag Cleanup

Removing a flag includes:

```text
remove branches
remove tests for obsolete path
remove dashboard/config
remove flag definition
```

---

# 201. Long-Lived Flags

Long-lived configuration should graduate into a proper product/runtime configuration mechanism when appropriate.

---

# 202. Flag Count

Large numbers of interacting flags create combinatorial state explosion.

Keep active flag count controlled.

---

# 203. Flag Dependency

Avoid flag logic such as:

```text
A && !B || (C && D)
```

across features.

Complex flag dependencies require redesign.

---

# 204. Flag Testing

Critical flags SHOULD test:

```text
off
on
```

and migration coexistence where needed.

---

# 205. Dynamic Runtime Configuration

Dynamic configuration changes without deployment require stronger governance because they bypass normal artifact promotion.

---

# 206. Dynamic Config Use Cases

Appropriate examples:

```text
rate limits
operational thresholds
kill switches
runtime capacity settings
```

---

# 207. Dynamic Config Schema

Dynamic config MUST be validated using the same rigor as startup config.

---

# 208. Dynamic Config Update

Invalid dynamic values MUST NOT replace the last valid configuration.

---

# 209. Last Known Good

Dynamic config systems SHOULD retain:

```text
last known good
```

values where appropriate.

---

# 210. Atomic Config Updates

Related values SHOULD update atomically when inconsistent intermediate states would be unsafe.

---

# 211. Configuration Version

Dynamic config SHOULD have version/revision identity.

---

# 212. Config Rollback

Operators SHOULD be able to restore a previous valid version.

---

# 213. Config Propagation
