Know whether changes propagate:

```text
instantly
eventually
on restart
```

---

# 214. Propagation Monitoring

Critical dynamic configuration SHOULD expose rollout state.

---

# 215. Inconsistent Instances

If different instances can temporarily run different config versions, determine whether the application can tolerate it.

---

# 216. Configuration Cache

Runtime config MAY be cached.

Define:

```text
TTL
refresh
failure
last-known-good
```

behavior.

---

# 217. Config Service Outage

Applications SHOULD NOT depend synchronously on a remote config service for every request.

Use cached/evaluated configuration where architecture allows.

---

# 218. Startup Config Dependency

If required config cannot be loaded safely:

```text
fail readiness/startup
```

rather than guessing values.

---

# 219. Configuration Security

Configuration can alter security posture.

Examples:

```text
CORS
cookie mode
TLS
authorization
debugging
```

must receive security review.

---

# 220. Debug Mode

Production MUST NOT run general development/debug mode.

---

# 221. Debug Endpoints

Development-only debugging endpoints MUST be disabled or strongly restricted in production.

---

# 222. Verbose Errors

Production configuration MUST NOT expose stack traces/debug details to untrusted users.

---

# 223. TLS Verification

Never introduce:

```text
TLS_VERIFY=false
```

as an ordinary production workaround.

---

# 224. Insecure Production Overrides

Dangerous configuration overrides SHOULD be explicitly prohibited by production validation.

---

# 225. CORS Configuration

CORS origins MUST be explicit and environment-specific.

Avoid:

```text
*
```

for credentialed production applications.

---

# 226. Hostname Configuration

Public/canonical URLs MUST match the deployment environment.

They affect:

```text
links
OAuth redirects
cookies
metadata
webhooks
```

---

# 227. Cookie Configuration

Production cookies should use appropriate:

```text
Secure
SameSite
domain
```

configuration.

Do not derive sensitive cookie behavior from loosely defined environment checks.

---

# 228. Authentication Callback URLs

OAuth/OIDC callback URLs SHOULD be explicit per deployment.

Never allow arbitrary wildcard behavior to simplify environment configuration.

---

# 229. Webhook Endpoints

Provider webhook configuration is environment-specific.

Test and production endpoints must be separate.

---

# 230. Email Configuration

Non-production environments SHOULD prevent accidental real-user email delivery.

---

# 231. Safe Email Defaults

Strategies include:

```text
email sandbox
allowlist
sink
provider test mode
```

---

# 232. SMS/Push Safety

The same applies to:

```text
SMS
push
phone calls
```

during testing.

---

# 233. Payment Safety

Non-production environments MUST use provider test/sandbox payment facilities.

---

# 234. Production Data in Non-Production

Configuration MUST NOT point local/staging applications at production datasets under normal workflows.

---

# 235. Read-Only Production Connections

Exceptional production read access requires explicit controlled tooling, not a developer changing:

```text
DATABASE_URL
```

locally.

---

# 236. Environment Banner

Administrative/non-production interfaces MAY visibly identify the current environment.

Example:

```text
STAGING
```

to reduce operator mistakes.

---

# 237. Production Confirmation

High-risk operational tooling MAY require additional confirmation when operating against production.

---

# 238. CLI Environment Safety

Operational CLIs SHOULD make the selected environment explicit.

---

# 239. Dangerous CLI Defaults

Never default destructive operational commands to production.

---

# 240. Production Explicitness

Prefer:

```text
--environment production
```

for dangerous operations rather than implicit production targeting.

---

# 241. CI/CD Configuration

CI configuration SHOULD be version-controlled.

---

# 242. CI Environment Separation

CI jobs should have explicit environments such as:

```text
test
preview
staging
production
```

with different permissions.

---

# 243. Protected Production Deployment

Production deployment jobs SHOULD require protected branches/workflows and appropriate authorization.

---

# 244. Environment Protection

CI/CD platforms SHOULD use environment protection capabilities where available.

---

# 245. Production Secret Access

Only production deployment/runtime jobs should access production deployment secrets.

---

# 246. Build Jobs

Ordinary build/test jobs SHOULD NOT receive production secrets.

---

# 247. Build Reproducibility

Build output SHOULD depend on:

```text
source
lockfile
toolchain
declared build configuration
```

not undocumented developer state.

---

# 248. Build-Time Public Variables

Build pipelines SHOULD explicitly document which values become part of public frontend bundles.

---

# 249. Artifact Metadata

Build artifacts SHOULD record:

```text
version
commit
build ID
```

for observability/debugging.

---

# 250. Deployment Config Audit

A production deployment SHOULD make it possible to identify:

```text
artifact version
config revision
secret references
feature-state revision where relevant
```

---

# 251. Config Snapshot

Critical deployments MAY persist a non-secret snapshot/hash of effective config for later diagnosis.

---

# 252. Never Snapshot Secret Values into Logs

Configuration diagnostics should show:

```text
PAYMENT_API_KEY=<configured>
```

not the value.

---

# 253. Effective Config Debugging

Applications MAY expose an authenticated internal diagnostic view showing:

```text
config key
source
effective nonsecret value
secret presence
```

without exposing credentials.

---

# 254. Config Redaction

Config-dump tooling MUST redact secrets by classification, not by hoping names contain:

```text
PASSWORD
SECRET
```

only.

---

# 255. Configuration Testing

Configuration behavior MUST be tested.

---

# 256. Schema Tests

Test that required production configuration fails appropriately when missing.

---

# 257. Type Tests

Test parsing of:

```text
boolean
integer
URL
enum
duration
```

where configuration libraries do not already guarantee it.

---

# 258. Unsafe Value Tests

Security-sensitive config should test rejection of unsafe combinations.

---

# 259. Environment Matrix Tests

Avoid testing every theoretical combination.

Test supported meaningful environment/config modes.

---

# 260. Feature Flag Tests

Test both flag branches while both are supported.

---

# 261. Flag Removal Tests

After rollout cleanup, remove tests for obsolete behavior.

---

# 262. Secrets Tests

Tests should verify applications can consume secret references without exposing values.

---

# 263. Secret Redaction Tests

Verify secret values do not appear in:

```text
logs
errors
diagnostics
telemetry
```

---

# 264. CI Tests

CI SHOULD verify `.env.example` or configuration documentation remains aligned with the actual schema where practical.

---

# 265. Environment Contract Test

Deployments MAY validate required configuration before rollout.

---

# 266. Preflight Validation

A deployment preflight SHOULD detect:

```text
missing config
invalid secret reference
invalid hostname
unsupported enum
```

before replacing healthy instances.

---

# 267. Readiness

An instance MUST NOT become ready if required runtime configuration is invalid.

---

# 268. Partial Rollout

If new instances fail config validation:

```text
retain healthy previous deployment
```

according to deployment strategy.

---

# 269. Config Rollback Test

Critical config systems SHOULD periodically verify rollback/recovery procedures.

---

# 270. Disaster Recovery

Disaster recovery MUST include restoration of:

```text
configuration
secret references
feature configuration
```

not only databases.

---

# 271. Secret Recovery

Backup/recovery plans should account for secret-management infrastructure.

---

# 272. Do Not Backup Secrets Casually

Secret backups require encryption and access controls equivalent to or stronger than live secrets.

---

# 273. Infrastructure Rebuild

Infrastructure-as-code plus managed configuration SHOULD allow rebuilding an environment without relying on undocumented manual settings.

---

# 274. Environment Bootstrap

A new environment SHOULD be creatable through documented automation.

---

# 275. Snowflake Environments

Avoid environments dependent on years of unrecorded manual changes.

---

# 276. Environment Teardown

Ephemeral environments SHOULD support automated cleanup.

---

# 277. Preview Cleanup

Delete:

```text
database
bucket
DNS
secrets
queues
```

associated with expired preview environments where applicable.

---

# 278. Orphan Resources

Configuration/environment automation SHOULD identify stale resources.

---

# 279. Cost Governance

Environment configuration controls resource cost.

Non-production SHOULD use appropriately smaller capacity when production-scale resources are unnecessary.

---

# 280. Cost vs Parity

Do not destroy useful architecture parity purely to save small amounts of cost.

Optimize responsibly.

---

# 281. Data Residency

Environment configuration MUST preserve applicable region/residency requirements.

---

# 282. Region Configuration

Region selection is high-impact configuration.

Changes require architectural review.

---

# 283. Time Zone Configuration

Server infrastructure SHOULD generally operate using UTC.

Business timezone belongs in explicit product/domain configuration.

---

# 284. Locale Configuration

Default locale MAY be deployment/product config.

User locale remains user state.

---

# 285. Clock Configuration

Do not depend on manually configured host time.

Infrastructure should provide synchronized system clocks.

---

# 286. Rate-Limit Configuration

Rate limits MAY be runtime configuration.

They require:

```text
safe bounds
owner
observability
rollback
```

---

# 287. Timeout Configuration

Timeouts SHOULD have:

```text
units
minimum
maximum
```

validation.

---

# 288. Retry Configuration

Retry counts/backoff may be configurable but SHOULD have safe limits.

Never allow:

```text
RETRY_COUNT=999999
```

without validation.

---

# 289. Connection Pool Configuration

Database pool sizing should be bounded relative to deployment/database capacity.

---

# 290. Memory/CPU Configuration

Infrastructure resource limits SHOULD be version-controlled and reviewed.

---

# 291. Configuration Coupling

Avoid hidden dependencies such as:

```text
if REGION=us
then PAYMENTS_MODE automatically becomes live
```

unless explicitly modeled.

---

# 292. Explicit Beats Magical

Prefer:

```text
PAYMENTS_MODE=test
```

over deriving it from unrelated environment naming.

---

# 293. Config Composability

Independent config should remain orthogonal where possible.

---

# 294. Config Explosion

If one feature requires 20 environment variables, review whether configuration architecture is too fragmented.

---

# 295. Structured Config

For complex structured configuration, a validated configuration file/service MAY be preferable to dozens of flat variables.

---

# 296. Structured Config Security

Do not commit secret values simply because the format is YAML/JSON.

---

# 297. Configuration Files

Version-controlled configuration files are suitable for non-secret declarative settings.

---

# 298. Config File Schema

Structured config files SHOULD have schema validation.

---

# 299. Unsupported Fields

Unknown critical config-file fields SHOULD fail or warn explicitly.

---

# 300. Comments

Configuration documentation/comments should explain:

```text
why
units
constraints
```

rather than restating the name.

---

# 301. Configuration Defaults in Code

Defaults SHOULD be declared centrally with the configuration schema.

Avoid defaults scattered across consumers.

---

# 302. One Parse Point

Environment/raw configuration should be parsed once near application startup.

Application modules consume typed configuration.

---

# 303. Good Architecture

```text
Raw environment
↓
Configuration parser
↓
Validated typed Config
↓
Application
```

---

# 304. Bad Architecture

```text
Feature A → process.env.X
Feature B → process.env.X
Feature C → process.env.Y
```

throughout the codebase.

---

# 305. Dependency Injection

Typed configuration MAY be injected into modules/services to improve:

```text
testing
clarity
dependency ownership
```

---

# 306. Server/Client Config Boundary

Maintain separate typed models for:

```text
server configuration
public client configuration
```

where applicable.

---

# 307. Public Config Allowlist

Only explicitly approved keys may cross into client-side configuration.

---

# 308. Config Serialization

Do not serialize the entire server config object to clients.

---

# 309. Environment Detection

Prefer canonical platform environment identity.

Do not infer production from:

```text
hostname contains "prod"
```

---

# 310. Hostname Is Not Environment Authority

Domains can change.

Explicit deployment metadata is safer.

---

# 311. Config Observability

Applications SHOULD expose safe signals about configuration state.

Examples:

```text
config revision
feature flag revision
secret version/reference
```

without secret values.

---

# 312. Configuration Change Metrics

High-risk runtime config systems MAY monitor:

```text
change rate
failed evaluations
propagation lag
```

---

# 313. Configuration Alerts

Alert when:

```text
required dynamic config unavailable
critical config invalid
secret near expiry
configuration drift detected
```

where action is required.

---

# 314. Secret Expiry Alerting

Certificates/credentials with expiry SHOULD alert sufficiently before expiration.

---

# 315. Secret Rotation Monitoring

Operators should know whether new versions have been adopted by workloads before revoking old versions.

---

# 316. Feature Flag Monitoring

Monitor rollout distribution and failures for critical flags.

---

# 317. Production Config Dashboard

Critical platforms MAY provide an operational view showing:

```text
deployment
config revision
feature changes
secret health
```

without revealing values.

---

# 318. Incident Investigation

During an incident inspect:

```text
recent deployments
config changes
secret rotation
feature flag changes
```

early.

---

# 319. Config Changes as Change Events

Observability SHOULD capture production config-change markers.

---

# 320. Configuration Incident

A misconfiguration causing user impact is a production incident just like a bad code deployment.

---

# 321. Rollback

Every high-impact config change should have a known rollback path.

---

# 322. Last Known Good Config

Dynamic systems SHOULD preserve previous known-good versions.

---

# 323. Configuration Freeze

During severe incidents or critical business periods, organizations MAY temporarily restrict nonessential config changes.

---

# 324. Change Freeze Does Not Replace Review

Routine review discipline still applies.

---

# 325. Configuration Access Control

Who can:

```text
read
write
approve
deploy
```

configuration should be deliberately controlled.

---

# 326. Read vs Write

Production configuration read access does not automatically imply write access.

---

# 327. Secret Read vs Use

Prefer architectures where workloads can use secrets without humans routinely retrieving plaintext values.

---

# 328. Four-Eyes Review

High-risk configuration changes MAY require approval by another authorized person.

---

# 329. Break-Glass Config Changes

Emergency privileges should follow Security and Authentication standards.

---

# 330. Audit Administrative Access

Sensitive config/secret-management systems SHOULD record administrative actions.

---

# 331. Production Console Access

Direct cloud/provider console changes SHOULD be restricted.

Prefer managed pipelines/IaC.

---

# 332. Console Changes

Where manual console changes occur, reconcile them into source-controlled configuration.

---

# 333. Config Review Checklist

Before adding configuration:

```text
□ Does this legitimately vary by deployment?
□ Could this remain code?
□ Is it secret?
□ What is its type?
□ What is its unit?
□ Is it required?
□ What is its safe default?
□ Who owns it?
□ Build-time or runtime?
□ Does changing it require restart?
□ What happens if invalid?
□ Is documentation updated?
```

---

# 334. Environment Checklist

```text
□ Purpose defined
□ Production isolated
□ Database isolated
□ Storage isolated
□ Credentials isolated
□ Provider modes isolated
□ Runtime versions aligned
□ Deployment mechanism aligned
□ Data policy appropriate
□ Access controls appropriate
```

---

# 335. `.env` Checklist

```text
□ Local use only where appropriate
□ Ignored from Git
□ .env.example exists
□ No real secrets in example
□ Loading precedence documented
□ Variables validated by application
□ Production does not depend on checked-in .env secrets
```

---

# 336. Secret Management Checklist

```text
□ Secret manager used
□ No source-code secret
□ Environment-specific
□ Least privilege
□ Owner
□ Consumer known
□ Rotation possible
□ Expiry monitored
□ Audit available
□ CI exposure minimized
□ Redaction tested
□ Revocation process known
```

---

# 337. Feature Flag Checklist

```text
□ Clear purpose
□ Correct category
□ Owner
□ Safe default
□ Server/client evaluation defined
□ Security not delegated to flag
□ Failure behavior defined
□ On/off tested
□ Rollout observed
□ Expiry/removal defined
```

---

# 338. Dynamic Config Checklist

```text
□ Schema validated
□ Bounds validated
□ Versioned
□ Owner
□ Change audited
□ Propagation understood
□ Last-known-good behavior
□ Rollback available
□ Outage behavior defined
□ Metrics/alerts present where critical
```

---

# 339. Production Change Checklist

```text
□ Exact environment confirmed
□ Change reviewed
□ Diff understood
□ Blast radius understood
□ Secrets not exposed
□ Rollback available
□ Monitoring ready
□ Change recorded
□ Post-change verification completed
```

---

# 340. Environment Parity Checklist

```text
□ Same application artifact model
□ Same runtime family/version
□ Same DB engine where behavior matters
□ Same migration mechanism
□ Same config schema
□ Same auth architecture
□ Same deployment mechanism
□ Intentional differences documented
```

---

# 341. CI/CD Configuration Checklist

```text
□ Pipeline version-controlled
□ Production environment protected
□ Non-prod jobs lack prod secrets
□ Fork/PR secrets protected
□ Artifact reproducible
□ Config validated before deployment
□ Artifact/version identifiable
□ Config changes auditable
```

---

# 342. Definition of Done — New Configuration

A new configuration item is complete when:

```text
✓ Need for external config justified
✓ Canonical name chosen
✓ Type defined
✓ Validation implemented
✓ Safe default/required status defined
✓ Secret classification known
✓ Owner assigned
✓ Build/runtime semantics defined
✓ Example/documentation added
✓ Failure behavior tested
✓ Production deployment updated
```

---

# 343. Definition of Done — New Environment

A new environment is production-worthy when:

```text
✓ Purpose documented
✓ Isolation defined
✓ Identity/accounts isolated
✓ Secrets isolated
✓ Datastores isolated
✓ Deployment automated
✓ Configuration validated
✓ Monitoring available
✓ Cleanup/lifecycle defined
✓ Access ownership established
```

---

# 344. Definition of Done — New Feature Flag

```text
✓ Purpose/type documented
✓ Owner assigned
✓ Safe default defined
✓ Evaluation location defined
✓ Rollout plan defined
✓ Failure behavior defined
✓ Tests cover active branches
✓ Analytics/observability considered
✓ Cleanup date/condition defined
```

---

# 345. Definition of Done — Secret

```text
✓ Secret is not in source
✓ Stored in approved system
✓ Access least-privileged
✓ Production/non-prod separated
✓ Rotation supported
✓ Expiry monitored where applicable
✓ Logs/redaction safe
✓ Consumer documented
✓ Revocation procedure exists
```

---

# 346. Configuration Anti-Patterns

Avoid:

```text
if NODE_ENV === "production"
  enableFeature()
```

for ordinary product features.

Avoid:

```text
SECRET="abc123"
```

in source control.

Avoid:

```text
.env.production
```

committed with credentials.

Avoid:

```text
same DATABASE_URL
```

for staging and production.

Avoid:

```text
same API key
```

for local and production.

Avoid:

```text
process.env.*
```

throughout the application.

Avoid:

```text
Boolean(process.env.FLAG)
```

without explicit parsing.

Avoid:

```text
missing value
→ silently assume insecure default
```

Avoid:

```text
environment name controls ten unrelated behaviors
```

Avoid:

```text
production config edited directly in console forever
```

Avoid:

```text
manual emergency change never reconciled
```

Avoid:

```text
staging = production database with different frontend
```

Avoid:

```text
production secret available to every CI job
```

Avoid:

```text
secret value printed to troubleshoot
```

Avoid:

```text
feature flag = authorization
```

Avoid:

```text
release flag left forever
```

Avoid:

```text
hundreds of interacting flags
```

Avoid:

```text
remote config required synchronously for every request
```

Avoid:

```text
invalid runtime config replaces working config
```

Avoid:

```text
config changed
no audit
no rollback
```

Avoid:

```text
staging build tested
production rebuilt differently
```

Avoid:

```text
local development requires production credentials
```

Avoid:

```text
browser env variable treated as secret
```

Avoid:

```text
Kubernetes Secret exists
therefore secret is secure
```

Avoid:

```text
ConfigMap containing credentials
```

Avoid:

```text
configuration files nobody owns
```

Avoid:

```text
unknown configuration variables ignored forever
```

Avoid:

```text
production debugging mode enabled temporarily
and never disabled
```

---

# 347. AI Configuration Rules

AI coding agents MUST inspect the existing configuration schema before adding new configuration.

---

# 348. AI Code-vs-Config Rule

Before adding an environment variable, AI MUST ask conceptually:

```text
Does this genuinely vary between deployments?
```

If not, keep it in code.

---

# 349. AI Search-Before-Create Rule

AI SHOULD search for an existing:

```text
config key
configuration object
feature flag
secret reference
```

before creating another.

---

# 350. AI Typed-Config Rule

AI MUST use the canonical typed/validated configuration layer.

It MUST NOT scatter direct environment access across features.

---

# 351. AI Fail-Fast Rule

Required invalid configuration MUST fail startup clearly.

---

# 352. AI Safe-Default Rule

AI MUST NOT invent insecure defaults for missing security-sensitive config.

---

# 353. AI Secret Rule

AI MUST NOT place credentials in:

```text
source
.env.example
tests
Dockerfile
frontend config
documentation
```

---

# 354. AI Public-Config Rule

AI MUST treat any browser-delivered environment/config value as public.

---

# 355. AI `.env` Rule

AI MAY use ignored local `.env` files for developer convenience but MUST NOT treat them as production secret management.

---

# 356. AI Feature-Flag Rule

AI MUST NOT use feature flags as authorization.

---

# 357. AI Flag-Lifecycle Rule

When creating a temporary release flag, AI SHOULD define its cleanup condition.

---

# 358. AI Environment Rule

AI MUST NOT add production-specific business behavior through environment-name checks if an explicit feature/config value is more appropriate.

---

# 359. AI Database Rule

AI MUST NOT point local/test/staging configuration to production databases as a shortcut.

---

# 360. AI Provider Rule

AI SHOULD use provider sandbox/test modes in non-production.

---

# 361. AI Logging Rule

AI MUST NOT print the complete configuration object if it may contain secrets.

---

# 362. AI CI Rule

AI MUST NOT expose production secrets to generic PR/test workflows.

---

# 363. AI Container Rule

AI MUST NOT bake runtime credentials into container images.

---

# 364. AI Kubernetes Rule

AI MUST distinguish nonsecret ConfigMap-style configuration from secret material.

---

# 365. AI Dynamic-Config Rule

When implementing dynamic configuration, AI MUST define:

```text
validation
versioning
failure behavior
last-known-good behavior
rollback
```

---

# 366. AI Config-Migration Rule

AI SHOULD maintain backward compatibility during config-key migrations when rolling deployment requires it.

---

# 367. AI Observability Rule

High-impact runtime config/flag changes SHOULD remain observable and auditable.

---

# 368. AI Ownership Rule

New high-impact configuration SHOULD have an explicit owner documented in the appropriate registry.

---

# 369. AI Gold Rule

When uncertain:

```text
Code-owned stable behavior
>
Explicit typed configuration
>
Runtime dynamic configuration
>
Feature flag
>
Environment-name magic
```

and for credentials:

```text
Workload identity
>
Short-lived managed secret
>
Long-lived managed secret
>
Local environment secret
>
Hardcoded secret
```

---

# 370. Golden Configuration & Environment Rules

**1. Code defines behavior; configuration selects deployment-specific behavior.**

**2. Do not externalize values that do not need deployment variability.**

**3. Configuration, secrets, feature flags, and user settings are different concepts.**

**4. Production and non-production are isolated.**

**5. Production credentials are never reused in local, test, preview, or staging.**

**6. Production data is not an ordinary development dependency.**

**7. Use the same application artifact across promotion stages where practical.**

**8. Important runtime and database versions remain reasonably production-parallel.**

**9. Every configuration key has one authoritative source.**

**10. Configuration precedence is explicit.**

**11. Parse raw configuration once into a typed validated model.**

**12. Environment variables are untrusted strings until validated.**

**13. Critical invalid configuration fails fast.**

**14. Security-sensitive settings never silently fall back to insecure defaults.**

**15. `.env` is a local-development convenience, not a production secret manager.**

**16. `.env.example` contains names and safe examples, never real secrets.**

**17. Secrets never enter source control or immutable application artifacts.**

**18. Production secrets live in an approved secret-management system.**

**19. Prefer short-lived workload identity over static credentials where possible.**

**20. Secrets are environment-specific, least-privileged, rotatable, and owned.**

**21. CI jobs receive only the secrets they actually require.**

**22. Untrusted pull requests never receive production secrets.**

**23. Browser configuration is public.**

**24. Build-time and runtime configuration are explicitly distinguished.**

**25. Configuration changes are treated as production changes.**

**26. Important production config changes are reviewed and auditable.**

**27. Manual emergency changes are reconciled or reverted.**

**28. Configuration drift is detected and removed.**

**29. Feature flags do not replace authorization.**

**30. Feature flags have an owner, safe default, and lifecycle.**

**31. Temporary rollout flags are removed after rollout.**

**32. Dynamic configuration validates new values before activation.**

**33. Invalid dynamic config never replaces the last known good configuration.**

**34. Remote configuration outages have defined safe behavior.**

**35. Environment checks are reserved for genuine environment semantics.**

**36. External provider test/sandbox modes are used outside production.**

**37. Non-production notification systems cannot accidentally contact real customers.**

**38. Configuration and secret health are observable without revealing secret values.**

**39. Disaster recovery includes configuration and secret dependencies, not only data.**

**40. An environment should be reproducible from declared automation rather than undocumented manual state.**

---

# 371. Canonical Configuration & Environment Standard

The organizational standard is:

> **Application behavior is divided deliberately between stable code and deployment-specific configuration. Values vary by deployment only where real operational variability exists; stable domain rules remain version-controlled code. Raw configuration is read through one canonical layer, validated into typed values before the application becomes ready, and consumed through explicit configuration interfaces rather than scattered environment-variable access. Invalid critical configuration fails fast, while security-sensitive configuration uses conservative defaults or requires explicit values.**

> **Local, test, preview, development, staging, and production environments exist only for defined purposes and remain appropriately isolated. Production databases, storage, queues, credentials, customer data, provider accounts, and other sensitive resources are not reused as ordinary non-production dependencies. Important production characteristics—runtime, database technology, deployment mechanism, migrations, configuration schema, and application artifact—remain sufficiently parallel across pre-production environments to provide meaningful verification. The preferred promotion model builds an immutable artifact once and deploys that same artifact with environment-specific configuration.**

> **Secrets are not ordinary configuration. Production secrets are stored in approved secret-management infrastructure, separated by environment, restricted through least privilege, rotated and revoked through known workflows, prevented from entering source control, images, logs, frontend bundles, documentation, and untrusted CI jobs, and replaced with short-lived workload identities where practical. `.env` files are a local-development convenience only and never constitute the production secret-management architecture.**

> **Feature flags and dynamic configuration are governed operational systems. Flags have explicit purpose, type, owner, safe default, targeting semantics, failure behavior, tests, and removal lifecycle; they never substitute for authorization or authoritative entitlement. Dynamic configuration is typed, bounded, versioned, auditable, rollback-capable, and does not replace a known-good value until validation succeeds. Remote configuration failure has a defined safe operating mode.**

> **Production configuration changes receive engineering discipline comparable to code changes: ownership, review, audit history, blast-radius assessment, rollout, monitoring, and rollback. Non-secret deployment and infrastructure configuration is version-controlled where practical; emergency manual changes are temporary and reconciled into the canonical source of truth. Configuration drift, expired credentials, missing values, invalid configuration, unsafe environment combinations, and failed propagation are detectable operational conditions.**

A production-grade configuration architecture should make it easy to answer:

```text
What configuration does this application require?
Which values are stable code rather than config?
Which configuration varies by deployment?
Which values are secrets?
Which values are exposed to the browser?
Which values are build-time?
Which are runtime?
Which can change dynamically?
What validates each value?
What happens if it is missing?
What happens if it is malformed?
What is the safe default?
Who owns it?
Where is its source of truth?
Which environments define it?
How are production and staging isolated?
How is a secret rotated?
Can CI expose the secret?
Which feature flags are temporary?
When will each flag be removed?
How are config changes audited?
How do we roll back?
Can an environment be rebuilt from declared automation?
```

If those questions cannot be answered, configuration is acting as hidden application logic rather than a controlled deployment contract.

The foundational distinction is consistent with the Twelve-Factor configuration principle: deployment-varying configuration should remain separate from application code, and independent config values scale better than encoding many behaviors into named environment groups. citeturn349383search0

For secrets, the stronger rule above deliberately goes beyond “put it in an environment variable.” OWASP recommends centralized secret management, tight access control, auditing and rotation, and specifically notes that environment variables can leak through processes, logs or dumps; short-lived/managed credentials should be preferred where the platform supports them. citeturn349383search1 Kubernetes makes the same distinction operationally: ConfigMaps are for **non-confidential** configuration, while Secrets are intended for confidential values—but Kubernetes also warns that Secret objects still require encryption-at-rest and least-privilege RBAC rather than being assumed secure automatically. citeturn349383search2turn349383search3

In the master hierarchy, this sits naturally after Privacy/Data Governance and before dependency/repository/delivery concerns:

**… → Observability → Analytics → Privacy & Data Governance → Configuration & Environments → Dependencies → Git & Repository → CI/CD → Infrastructure & Deployment → Backup & Disaster Recovery → Documentation → Governance.**


<!-- ===== deployment-infrastructure | operations | standards/operations/03-deployment-infrastructure.md ===== -->

The standard below uses a vendor-neutral baseline. AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure all frame well-architected cloud workloads around broadly the same concerns: **reliability, security, operational excellence, performance, and cost efficiency**, with AWS and Google additionally making sustainability explicit. citeturn865016search7turn865016search9turn865016search0

# Deployment & Infrastructure Guidelines — Gold Standard

## 1. Purpose

These guidelines define the canonical organizational standard for:

- cloud architecture;
- infrastructure topology;
- cloud accounts/projects/subscriptions;
- compute selection;
- virtual machines;
- containers;
- container orchestration;
- Kubernetes;
- serverless;
- managed application platforms;
- runtime selection;
- availability zones;
- regions;
- multi-region architecture;
- scaling;
- load balancing;
- DNS;
- TLS;
- CDN;
- edge infrastructure;
- queues;
- event infrastructure;
- object storage;
- block/file storage;
- infrastructure as code;
- IAM;
- workload identity;
- network boundaries;
- ingress;
- egress;
- private networking;
- firewalls;
- service connectivity;
- secrets integration;
- infrastructure observability;
- reliability;
- capacity;
- cost governance;
- production access;
- infrastructure lifecycle.

The objective is to create infrastructure that is:

```text
Secure
Reliable
Scalable
Observable
Reproducible
Recoverable
Cost-conscious
Operable
Replaceable
Appropriately simple
```

The core principle is:

> **Infrastructure should provide the minimum reliable platform required by the workload, expressed through reproducible automation, protected by identity and network controls, and designed to fail predictably rather than depend on manual intervention.**

---

# 2. Normative Language

- **MUST** — mandatory.
- **MUST NOT** — prohibited.
- **SHOULD** — expected unless a documented reason exists.
- **SHOULD NOT** — generally avoided unless justified.
- **MAY** — optional.

Infrastructure exceptions SHOULD document:

```text
Reason
Workload
Security impact
Reliability impact
Cost impact
Compensating controls
Owner
Review/expiry date
```

---

# 3. Infrastructure Is Architecture

Infrastructure decisions affect:

```text
Availability
Failure domains
Latency
Security
Data residency
Scaling
Cost
Deployment
Recovery
Operations
```

They are architectural decisions, not merely deployment details.

---

# 4. Infrastructure Follows Requirements

Choose infrastructure after establishing:

```text
Workload characteristics
Traffic
Data model
Reliability target
Latency target
Security requirements
Residency requirements
Recovery requirements
Cost constraints
Operational capability
```

Do not begin with:

```text
We should use Kubernetes.
```

---

# 5. Workload First

Canonical decision order:

```text
Product requirement
↓
Quality attributes / SLO
↓
Workload characteristics
↓
Failure model
↓
Deployment topology
↓
Infrastructure technology
```

---

# 6. Simplest Viable Infrastructure

Prefer the simplest infrastructure capable of satisfying the required:

```text
Security
Reliability
Performance
Scale
Operations
```

Do not build for hypothetical scale without evidence.

---

# 7. Managed Services First

Managed services SHOULD be preferred when they:

```text
reduce operational burden
provide acceptable control
meet security requirements
meet reliability requirements
meet cost requirements
```

---

# 8. Managed Does Not Mean Responsibility-Free

A managed service reduces responsibility for some layers.

The organization still owns:

```text
configuration
identity
data
network access
backup policy
capacity
application behavior
cost
```

---

# 9. Responsibility Model

For every infrastructure service, understand who owns:

```text
Hardware
Operating system
Runtime
Patching
Availability
Backups
Encryption
IAM
Application
Data
```

Do not assume the cloud provider owns all of them.

---

# 10. Platform Complexity Ladder

Prefer approximately:

```text
Managed SaaS / managed service
↓
Managed application platform
↓
Managed containers / serverless containers
↓
Managed Kubernetes
↓
Self-managed orchestration
↓
Raw VMs
↓
Bare metal
```

when each lower layer provides no necessary advantage.

This is a heuristic, not a mandatory ordering.

---

# 11. Do Not Introduce Kubernetes by Default

Kubernetes is justified when its orchestration capabilities solve real needs such as:

```text
many containerized workloads
standardized workload scheduling
advanced rollout requirements
portable deployment abstractions
platform engineering
complex resource orchestration
```

A small web application does not require Kubernetes merely to be production-grade.

---

# 12. Serverless Is Not Automatically Simpler

Serverless can reduce infrastructure management but introduce:

```text
runtime constraints
cold starts
execution limits
vendor coupling
observability differences
cost characteristics
```

Evaluate the workload.

---

# 13. Infrastructure Ownership

Every production workload MUST have an owning team.

Ownership includes:

```text
deployment
capacity
cost
security
observability
incident response
lifecycle
```

---

# 14. Platform Ownership

Shared infrastructure SHOULD have an accountable platform owner.

Examples:

```text
network
cluster
CI deployment layer
shared ingress
DNS
identity platform
```

---

# 15. Application vs Platform Responsibility

Responsibilities MUST be clear.

Example:

```text
Platform team
→ cluster, ingress, node lifecycle

Application team
→ workload config, resources, probes, scaling policy
```

---

# 16. Cloud Account Hierarchy

Cloud resources SHOULD be organized using the provider's account/project/subscription hierarchy.

Separate:

```text
production
non-production
security
shared infrastructure
```

according to scale and risk.

---

# 17. Production Isolation

Production SHOULD use a distinct cloud account/project/subscription from development where provider architecture allows it.

---

# 18. Account Is a Strong Boundary

Cloud account/project boundaries SHOULD be used for important separation such as:

```text
IAM
billing
quotas
audit
resource policy
```

---

# 19. Do Not Put Everything in One Cloud Account

A single unrestricted account for:

```text
dev
staging
production
security
experiments
```

creates unnecessary blast radius.

---

# 20. Account Naming

Use predictable naming.

Example:

```text
company-product-prod
company-product-staging
company-shared-security
```

according to provider conventions.

---

# 21. Environment Isolation

Infrastructure follows Configuration & Environment Guidelines.

Production and non-production MUST NOT unintentionally share:

```text
credentials
mutable databases
queues
buckets
private networks
customer notification endpoints
```

---

# 22. Cloud Regions

A region is a major geographic deployment location.

Region selection MUST be deliberate.

---

# 23. Region Selection Criteria

Consider:

```text
user latency
data residency
service availability
price
regulatory requirements
disaster risk
dependency proximity
organizational support
```

---

# 24. Default Region

An organization SHOULD establish preferred regions where possible.

This reduces arbitrary infrastructure diversity.

---

# 25. Region Availability

Do not select a region without verifying required services/features exist there.

---

# 26. Region Pricing

Cloud pricing can differ by region.

Cost differences MAY influence selection after security/residency/latency constraints.

---

# 27. Region Proximity

Place latency-sensitive compute near:

```text
primary users
authoritative databases
critical dependencies
```

where possible.

---

# 28. Availability Zones

Production workloads requiring meaningful availability SHOULD use multiple independent availability zones where the provider architecture supports them.

---

# 29. Zone Failure

A zone failure SHOULD NOT necessarily take down the entire critical service.

---

# 30. Multi-Zone Compute

Stateless critical application instances SHOULD normally span at least two failure zones.

---

# 31. Zone-Aware Data

Stateful managed services SHOULD use appropriate multi-zone resilience based on their availability/recovery requirements.

---

# 32. Multi-Zone Cost

Do not add zone redundancy without understanding:

```text
replication cost
cross-zone network cost
capacity
consistency
```

---

# 33. Multi-Region

Multi-region architecture is NOT the default.

It introduces major complexity in:

```text
data replication
consistency
routing
deployment
observability
failover
cost
testing
```

---

# 34. Multi-Region Justification

Use multi-region only when required by:

```text
regional disaster tolerance
latency
residency
business continuity
very high availability targets
```

---

# 35. Active-Active

Active-active multi-region means multiple regions serve production traffic simultaneously.

It requires deliberate:

```text
data consistency
routing
conflict resolution
failure handling
```

architecture.

---

# 36. Active-Passive

Active-passive may provide simpler disaster recovery when continuous multi-region traffic is unnecessary.

---

# 37. Multi-Region Data Is the Hard Part

Do not design multi-region compute without solving:

```text
source of truth
write ownership
replication
failover
consistency
```

for data.

---

# 38. Region Failover

Regional failover MUST be tested if it is part of the reliability claim.

A diagram is not a recovery mechanism.

---

# 39. DNS Failover

DNS MAY participate in failover but has:

```text
TTL
resolver caching
propagation
```

limitations.

Do not assume DNS switching is instantaneous.

---

# 40. Runtime Selection

Choose runtime based on:

```text
application needs
team capability
security support
performance
ecosystem
deployment model
operability
```

---

# 41. Supported Runtime

Production MUST use supported runtime versions receiving security maintenance.

---

# 42. Runtime Standardization

Organizations SHOULD maintain a small approved set of runtimes.

Example categories:

```text
Node.js
Python
JVM
Go
.NET
```

according to actual needs.

---

# 43. Avoid Runtime Proliferation

Do not introduce a new language/runtime for a small service unless the benefit outweighs:

```text
tooling
security
hiring
observability
deployment
maintenance
```

cost.

---

# 44. Runtime Ownership

Every runtime ecosystem requires an owner responsible for:

```text
supported versions
base images
security updates
tooling
deprecation
```

---

# 45. Runtime EOL

Applications MUST migrate before or promptly after runtime end-of-support according to risk policy.

---

# 46. VM Selection

Virtual machines MAY be appropriate for:

```text
legacy applications
special kernel needs
licensed software
special hardware
stateful systems
```

where higher-level managed compute is unsuitable.

---

# 47. VM Images

Production VMs SHOULD originate from:

```text
approved base image
versioned build process
patched image
```

rather than ad hoc manually configured hosts.

---

# 48. Immutable VM Pattern

Prefer replacing instances from a new image rather than repeatedly modifying running hosts manually.

---

# 49. Configuration Management

Where mutable VMs remain necessary, configuration management MUST be automated and version-controlled.

---

# 50. No Snowflake Servers

A server that cannot be recreated from documented automation is infrastructure debt.

---

# 51. SSH Access

Routine production operations SHOULD NOT require SSH access to application servers.

---

# 52. Break-Glass SSH

Emergency shell access MAY exist but MUST be:

```text
strongly authenticated
individually attributable
time-bounded where practical
audited
```

---

# 53. Containers

Containers package the application and runtime dependencies into a deployable artifact.

---

# 54. Container Image Principle

Container images SHOULD be:

```text
immutable
minimal
reproducible
versioned
scanned
```

---

# 55. Image Registry

Production images MUST be stored in an approved registry.

---

# 56. Immutable Image Identity

Production deployments SHOULD use immutable:

```text
digest
```

or equivalent artifact identity.

Do not rely solely on:

```text
latest
```

---

# 57. Base Images

Use approved maintained base images.

---

# 58. Base Image Pinning

Base images SHOULD be pinned sufficiently to provide reproducible builds and intentional updates.

---

# 59. Base Image Updates

Base images MUST receive security updates through regular rebuilds.

---

# 60. Small Images

Prefer minimal production images where practical.

Benefits include reduced:

```text
attack surface
download time
storage
```

---

# 61. Minimal Does Not Mean Unusable

Do not remove tooling required for:

```text
runtime correctness
TLS certificates
internationalization
```

merely to achieve smaller image size.

---

# 62. Multi-Stage Builds

Use multi-stage builds where they reduce production image contents.

---

# 63. Build Toolchain

Compilers/package managers SHOULD generally remain outside the final runtime image unless required.

---

# 64. Non-Root Containers

Application containers SHOULD run as a non-root user unless privileged execution is explicitly required.

---

# 65. Privileged Containers

Privileged containers MUST be exceptional and security-reviewed.

---

# 66. Container Capabilities

Drop unnecessary operating-system capabilities.

---

# 67. Read-Only Filesystem

Use a read-only root filesystem where the application supports it.

Writable state should be explicit.

---

# 68. Temporary Files

Applications requiring temporary disk SHOULD use explicitly provisioned temporary storage.

---

# 69. Container Secrets

Secrets MUST NOT be baked into images.

---

# 70. Image Layers

Deleting a secret in a later Docker layer does not necessarily remove it from earlier layers.

Never introduce it into the build context/image history.

---

# 71. Docker Build Context

Keep build context narrow.

Use ignore files to exclude:

```text
.git
.env
local credentials
large irrelevant files
```

---

# 72. Image Labels

Images SHOULD expose useful metadata such as:

```text
source revision
version
build identity
```

where appropriate.

---

# 73. Container Scanning

Production images SHOULD be scanned for known vulnerabilities according to Security Guidelines.

---

# 74. Image Signing / Provenance

Critical images SHOULD follow CI/CD artifact provenance/signing policy.

---

# 75. Container Runtime Resources

Containers MUST have deliberate CPU/memory sizing in orchestrated environments.

---

# 76. Resource Requests

Resource requests SHOULD represent expected scheduling requirements.

---

# 77. Resource Limits

Limits SHOULD be applied where they improve isolation and prevent runaway consumption.

They MUST be calibrated rather than copied blindly.

---

# 78. CPU Limits

CPU limits may throttle workloads.

Use based on workload characteristics and platform policy.

---

# 79. Memory Limits

Memory limits protect nodes but may terminate processes exceeding their allocation.

Applications MUST tolerate/process this correctly.

---

# 80. Resource Sizing

Sizing SHOULD derive from:

```text
measurement
load testing
production observation
```

rather than guesses alone.

---

# 81. Headroom

Critical workloads need sufficient headroom for:

```text
traffic spikes
instance loss
deployments
```

---

# 82. Container Health

Distinguish:

```text
startup
readiness
liveness
```

health semantics.

---

# 83. Startup Health

Startup checks answer:

> Has the application completed initialization?

---

# 84. Readiness

Readiness answers:

> Can this instance receive traffic or work right now?

---

# 85. Liveness

Liveness answers:

> Is this process stuck in a way where restart is likely to help?

---

# 86. Do Not Conflate Readiness and Liveness

A temporary downstream outage may justify:

```text
not ready
```

without justifying:

```text
restart application forever
```

---

# 87. Liveness Caution

Aggressive liveness checks can amplify incidents by repeatedly restarting healthy-but-overloaded workloads.

---

# 88. Health Checks Must Be Cheap

Health endpoints MUST NOT execute expensive queries on every probe.

---

# 89. Startup Dependency

Long startup processes SHOULD use startup/readiness semantics instead of excessively delayed liveness checks.

---

# 90. Graceful Shutdown

Application workloads MUST support graceful termination where requests/jobs can be in flight.

---

# 91. Termination Flow

Conceptually:

```text
Receive termination
↓
Stop accepting new work
↓
Drain in-flight work
↓
Flush bounded telemetry
↓
Exit before deadline
```

---

# 92. Termination Timeout

Shutdown MUST remain bounded.

Do not wait indefinitely.

---

# 93. Load Balancer Draining

Instances SHOULD be removed from traffic before process termination.

---

# 94. Long-Lived Connections

Applications using:

```text
WebSockets
SSE
long polling
```

need deliberate connection-draining behavior.

---

# 95. Kubernetes

If Kubernetes is used, it is infrastructure—not the application architecture.

Applications SHOULD remain understandable independently of cluster implementation details.

---

# 96. Managed Kubernetes

Prefer managed control planes unless self-management is materially justified.

---

# 97. Cluster Count

Do not create clusters casually.

Clusters introduce:

```text
control plane
upgrades
networking
security
capacity
observability
```

overhead.

---

# 98. Cluster Boundary

A Kubernetes cluster can be a useful blast-radius boundary but is not automatically a complete security boundary.

---

# 99. Namespace

Namespaces provide organization and policy scope.

They MUST NOT be treated as sufficient isolation without:

```text
RBAC
network policy
workload identity
resource policy
```

---

# 100. Kubernetes RBAC

Use least-privilege Kubernetes RBAC.

---

# 101. Cluster Admin

Cluster-admin access MUST be tightly restricted.

---

# 102. Workload Identity in Kubernetes

Pods SHOULD use workload/service identity rather than embedded long-lived cloud keys.

---

# 103. Service Accounts

Use dedicated service accounts for workloads.

Avoid one shared highly privileged identity.

---

# 104. Pod Security

Workloads SHOULD use restrictive security contexts.

Examples:

```text
non-root
no privilege escalation
minimal capabilities
read-only filesystem where possible
```

---

# 105. Host Namespace Access

Avoid:

```text
hostNetwork
hostPID
hostIPC
```

unless explicitly required.

---

# 106. Host Path

Host filesystem mounts require security review.

---

# 107. Resource Quotas

Shared clusters SHOULD use quotas/limits to prevent one workload from exhausting shared capacity.

---

# 108. Limit Ranges

Platform policies MAY establish default resource ranges.

Defaults do not replace workload-specific sizing.

---

# 109. Pod Disruption

Critical workloads SHOULD define disruption behavior that permits safe node maintenance without destroying availability.

---

# 110. Replica Count

Critical stateless workloads SHOULD normally have multiple replicas when availability objectives require it.

---

# 111. One Replica

A single replica is a single workload failure point.

It may still be acceptable for low-criticality applications.

---

# 112. Anti-Affinity / Topology

Critical replicas SHOULD be distributed across relevant failure domains where platform support and scale justify it.

---

# 113. Node Pools

Separate node pools MAY be appropriate for:

```text
GPU
high-memory
trusted workloads
special architectures
```

---

# 114. Node Lifecycle

Cluster nodes MUST have an upgrade/replacement strategy.

---

# 115. Kubernetes Version Support

Clusters SHOULD remain within provider/project-supported Kubernetes release windows.

---

# 116. Cluster Upgrades

Cluster upgrades require routine testing and should not become rare high-risk projects.

---

# 117. Custom Operators

Do not introduce a Kubernetes operator unless the lifecycle problem genuinely requires controller-style automation.

---

# 118. CRD Governance

Custom Resource Definitions become platform APIs.

They require:

```text
ownership
versioning
upgrade policy
```

---

# 119. Service Mesh

A service mesh MAY be justified for:

```text
service identity
mTLS
traffic policy
deep observability
```

at sufficient scale.

---

# 120. Service Mesh Is Not Default

Do not introduce a mesh simply because services communicate over a network.

Its complexity must be justified.

---

# 121. Compute Scaling

Scaling strategy MUST reflect workload behavior.

---

# 122. Vertical Scaling

Vertical scaling increases resources available to an instance.

It is simple but bounded.

---

# 123. Horizontal Scaling

Horizontal scaling adds workload instances.

It generally requires:

```text
statelessness
shared/external state
safe concurrency
```

---

# 124. Stateless Application Tier

Web/API tiers SHOULD remain stateless where practical.

Store durable/shared state in appropriate state systems.

---

# 125. Local Memory

Do not assume requests from one user always return to the same instance.

---

# 126. Sticky Sessions

Sticky sessions MAY be used when needed but SHOULD NOT compensate for avoidable stateful application architecture.

---

# 127. Autoscaling

Autoscaling SHOULD use metrics that represent actual resource/workload pressure.

---

# 128. CPU Autoscaling

CPU MAY be an appropriate signal for CPU-bound workloads.

It is not universally correct.

---

# 129. Queue-Based Autoscaling

Worker fleets SHOULD consider signals such as:

```text
queue depth
oldest message age
processing latency
```

---

# 130. Request-Based Scaling

Request rate/concurrency MAY be more appropriate than CPU for I/O-heavy services.

---

# 131. Scale-Up Delay

Scaling is not instantaneous.

Capacity planning must account for:

```text
instance startup
container pull
application warmup
```

---

# 132. Minimum Capacity

Critical services SHOULD maintain minimum capacity sufficient for baseline traffic and failure tolerance.

---

# 133. Maximum Capacity

Autoscaling MUST have maximum limits to constrain:

```text
runaway cost
dependency overload
```

---

# 134. Scaling One Layer Can Break Another

Increasing application replicas can overload:

```text
database
connection pool
downstream API
queue
```

Scaling must consider the complete system.

---

# 135. Database Connections

Instance scaling plans MUST account for database connection limits.

---

# 136. Connection Pool Budget

Conceptually:

```text
maximum instances
×
max connections per instance
≤
safe DB capacity
```

with appropriate headroom.

---

# 137. Load Testing

Scaling assumptions SHOULD be validated through load/performance testing.

---

# 138. Capacity Planning

Critical services SHOULD understand:

```text
normal demand
peak demand
growth
failure capacity
quota limits
```

---

# 139. Quotas

Cloud provider quotas are capacity constraints.

Critical services MUST monitor/request adequate quotas before demand requires them.

---

# 140. Load Balancing

Load balancers distribute traffic across healthy service instances.

---

# 141. Managed Load Balancers

Managed load balancing SHOULD be preferred unless specialized behavior requires otherwise.

---

# 142. Health-Based Routing

Load balancers MUST stop sending normal traffic to instances that are not ready.

---

# 143. Layer 4 vs Layer 7

Choose the simplest load-balancing layer that provides required:

```text
routing
TLS
protocol
observability
```

behavior.

---

# 144. TLS Termination

TLS MAY terminate at:

```text
edge
load balancer
application
```

depending on trust architecture.

---

# 145. Internal Encryption

Sensitive internal service communication SHOULD use encrypted transport where threat model/policy requires it.

---

# 146. End-to-End TLS

Use end-to-end encryption when intermediate network boundaries cannot be trusted or policy requires it.

---

# 147. Load Balancer Timeout

Configure connection/request timeouts according to application protocols.

Avoid provider defaults without review for long-running operations.

---

# 148. Upload Timeout

Large upload workflows may require different timeout architecture from normal API requests.

---

# 149. Idle Timeout

Long-lived connections need compatible load-balancer idle timeouts.

---

# 150. Connection Draining

Load balancers SHOULD support graceful backend draining during deployments.

---

# 151. Algorithms

Default load-balancing algorithms are usually sufficient.

Use specialized algorithms only when measured workload characteristics justify them.

---

# 152. Internal Load Balancers

Services not intended for public access SHOULD use private/internal exposure where practical.

---

# 153. Internet Exposure

Only services intentionally designed for public access should receive public endpoints.

---

# 154. DNS

DNS configuration is production infrastructure.

It MUST be versioned/controlled where practical.

---

# 155. DNS Ownership

Every production domain SHOULD have explicit ownership.

---

# 156. DNS TTL

Choose TTLs deliberately.

Lower TTL:

```text
faster changes
more DNS traffic
```

Higher TTL:

```text
better caching
slower failover/change
```

---

# 157. DNS Changes

High-impact DNS changes require review and rollback planning.

---

# 158. Domain Renewal

Production domains MUST have controlled:

```text
ownership
renewal
MFA
```

to prevent accidental expiration or takeover.

---

# 159. DNS Security

Registrar/DNS provider accounts require strong authentication and restricted access.

---

# 160. TLS Certificates

Production endpoints MUST use valid TLS certificates.

---

# 161. Certificate Automation

Certificate issuance and renewal SHOULD be automated.

---

# 162. Certificate Expiry

Certificate expiry MUST be monitored before expiration.

---

# 163. Private Keys

TLS private keys are Restricted secrets.

---

# 164. CDN

CDNs SHOULD be used when they materially improve:

```text
latency
origin load
availability
bandwidth efficiency
```

---

# 165. CDN Content

Good CDN candidates include:

```text
static assets
public images
downloads
cacheable responses
```

according to content semantics.

---

# 166. CDN Is a Cache

Every CDN decision requires an explicit cache policy.

---

# 167. Private Data

Do not cache personalized/private content publicly.

---

# 168. Cache-Control

Applications SHOULD use correct HTTP caching semantics rather than relying solely on provider-specific CDN rules.

---

# 169. CDN Cache Key

Cache keys must contain all dimensions affecting the response.

Examples:

```text
path
approved query params
locale
content encoding
```

where relevant.

---

# 170. Authorization and CDN

Authenticated responses require particular care.

Do not accidentally serve User A's response to User B.

---

# 171. CDN Query Parameters

Ignore irrelevant tracking parameters where safe to improve cache efficiency.

Do not ignore parameters that alter content.

---

# 172. Cache Invalidation

CDN invalidation should be:

```text
deliberate
bounded
rare where versioned asset URLs can solve it
```

---

# 173. Fingerprinted Assets

Static assets SHOULD use content-hashed/fingerprinted names where supported.

This enables long cache lifetimes.

---

# 174. CDN Origin Protection

Origins SHOULD be protected from arbitrary bypass when security/architecture requires edge controls to apply.

---

# 175. Edge Functions

Edge compute MAY reduce latency for suitable lightweight tasks.

It SHOULD NOT become an uncontrolled second application architecture.

---

# 176. Edge Runtime Constraints

Understand:

```text
runtime APIs
execution time
storage
network
observability
region behavior
```

before choosing edge compute.

---

# 177. WAF

A web application firewall MAY provide defense in depth for internet-facing workloads.

It does not replace secure application code.

---

# 178. WAF Rules

WAF rules SHOULD be tested to avoid blocking legitimate traffic.

---

# 179. DDoS Protection

Internet-facing critical services SHOULD use provider/platform DDoS protections appropriate to risk.

---

# 180. Rate Limiting

Rate limiting SHOULD be enforced at the most useful boundary:

```text
edge
gateway
application
```

or combination.

---

# 181. Network Architecture

Network design SHOULD minimize unnecessary reachable paths.

---

# 182. Network Boundary Principle

A network boundary is a defense-in-depth control.

It MUST NOT be treated as the sole authorization mechanism.

---

# 183. Zero Trust Principle

Do not grant implicit application trust simply because traffic originated from:

```text
private network
VPN
same VPC
same cluster
```

---

# 184. Identity-Based Access

Service access SHOULD increasingly rely on:

```text
workload identity
authentication
authorization
```

in addition to network boundaries.

---

# 185. VPC / Virtual Network

Production workloads SHOULD use deliberately designed virtual network boundaries.

---

# 186. Public Subnets

Only resources requiring direct public connectivity SHOULD reside behind public ingress paths.

---

# 187. Private Compute

Application/database infrastructure SHOULD generally use private addressing where direct internet access is unnecessary.

---

# 188. Internet Egress

Outbound internet access SHOULD be intentional.

---

# 189. Default Egress

Sensitive environments SHOULD consider restricting arbitrary outbound traffic.

---

# 190. Egress Allowlisting

High-assurance workloads MAY restrict egress to approved destinations.

---

# 191. Egress Proxy/Gateway

Central egress controls MAY improve:

```text
policy
logging
IP stability
```

for suitable environments.

---

# 192. NAT

NAT is a connectivity mechanism.

It is not a security boundary by itself.

---

# 193. Private Endpoints

Use private provider-service endpoints where they materially reduce unnecessary public network exposure.

---

# 194. Security Groups / Firewalls

Firewall rules MUST follow least-access principles.

---

# 195. `0.0.0.0/0`

Broad inbound access MUST be justified.

It is appropriate only for intentionally public services/ports.

---

# 196. Administrative Ports

Administrative interfaces MUST NOT be publicly exposed without strong controlled access.

---

# 197. Bastion Hosts

Traditional bastions MAY be used where required but SHOULD be replaced with identity-aware managed access where practical.

---

# 198. VPN

VPN access alone MUST NOT imply application authorization.

---

# 199. Service-to-Service Networking

Internal services SHOULD expose only required:

```text
ports
protocols
callers
```

where platform support allows.

---

# 200. Network Policy

Container orchestration environments SHOULD use network policy where meaningful isolation is required.

---

# 201. Deny-by-Default Networking

High-assurance environments SHOULD consider:

```text
default deny
+
explicit allow
```

network policy.

---

# 202. Network Segmentation

Segment environments/workloads where it reduces blast radius.

Do not create segmentation so complex that operators cannot understand it.

---

# 203. Service Discovery

Service discovery SHOULD use canonical platform mechanisms.

Do not hardcode ephemeral instance IP addresses.

---

# 204. Internal DNS

Stable service names SHOULD resolve to dynamic instances through managed discovery.

---

# 205. Service Ports

Service ports SHOULD be standardized/documented where practical.

---

# 206. IAM

Identity and Access Management is the primary control plane for cloud authorization.

---

# 207. Human Identity

Humans MUST use individual identities.

No shared cloud-admin accounts.

---

# 208. SSO

Cloud administrative access SHOULD use centralized SSO.

---

# 209. MFA

Privileged human cloud access MUST use strong MFA.

---

# 210. Root / Owner Accounts

Cloud root/owner identities MUST be highly restricted.

They SHOULD NOT be used for routine operations.

---

# 211. Root Credentials

Root/recovery credentials MUST be:

```text
strongly protected
rarely used
monitored
```

---

# 212. Least Privilege

Grant only:

```text
required actions
required resources
required duration
```

---

# 213. Role-Based Access

Use roles/groups rather than attaching one-off permissions to individual users where practical.

---

# 214. Temporary Privilege

High privilege SHOULD be:

```text
just in time
time bounded
audited
```

where platform capability allows.

---

# 215. Workload Identity

Applications SHOULD authenticate to cloud services through workload identity rather than embedded static credentials.

---

# 216. No Cloud Keys in Source

Cloud API keys/secret access keys MUST NOT appear in:

```text
source
images
configuration repositories
```

---

# 217. Service Identity

Each meaningful service SHOULD have a distinct workload identity.

---

# 218. Shared Service Accounts

Avoid one service account for all applications.

---

# 219. Permission Blast Radius

Compromise of one workload identity SHOULD NOT grant control over unrelated workloads.

---

# 220. Read vs Write IAM

Separate read and write permissions where operationally meaningful.

---

# 221. Resource-Scoped IAM

Prefer resource-scoped permissions over account-wide permissions.

---

# 222. Wildcard Permissions

Permissions like:

```text
*
```

require strong justification and SHOULD be avoided.

---

# 223. IAM Conditions

Use contextual conditions where they materially improve least privilege.

Examples:

```text
resource tags
environment
service identity
```

---

# 224. IAM as Code

IAM policy SHOULD be managed as code where practical.

---

# 225. IAM Review

High-risk IAM changes require review.

---

# 226. IAM Access Review

Privileged human access SHOULD be reviewed periodically.

---

# 227. Dormant Access

Remove access that is no longer needed.

---

# 228. Break-Glass Access

Emergency cloud administration MUST be:

```text
rare
MFA protected
individually attributable
alerted
reviewed
```

---

# 229. IAM Audit Logs

Cloud identity and administrative actions MUST be auditable.

---

# 230. Control Plane Logs

Important production cloud control-plane audit logs SHOULD be enabled and retained appropriately.

---

# 231. Log Protection

Security/audit logs require controlled access and retention.

---

# 232. Infrastructure as Code

Production infrastructure SHOULD be represented through Infrastructure as Code wherever practical.

---

# 233. IaC Is Source

IaC definitions are production code.

They require:

```text
version control
review
testing
ownership
```

---

# 234. IaC Tools

Use a small approved toolset.

Examples may include declarative cloud-native tools or Terraform/OpenTofu-style systems.

The standard is the practice, not one product.

---

# 235. No ClickOps as Normal Architecture

Routine production infrastructure SHOULD NOT depend on undocumented manual console creation.

---

# 236. IaC Plan

Infrastructure changes SHOULD produce a plan/diff before application.

---

# 237. Plan Review

Review changes for:

```text
creation
modification
replacement
deletion
IAM
network
data
```

impact.

---

# 238. Destructive Changes

Destructive infrastructure changes MUST be clearly visible before approval.

---

# 239. IaC Apply

Production IaC SHOULD be applied through controlled CI/CD workflows.

---

# 240. Local Production Apply

Routine:

```text
terraform apply
```

or equivalent from developer laptops against production SHOULD be prohibited.

---

# 241. IaC Identity

IaC automation must use least-privilege workload identity.

---

# 242. IaC State

IaC state is sensitive production data.

It may contain:

```text
resource IDs
configuration
occasionally sensitive values
```

---

# 243. Remote State

Shared production infrastructure SHOULD use controlled remote state or equivalent backend.

---

# 244. State Encryption

Infrastructure state SHOULD be encrypted at rest and in transit.

---

# 245. State Access

State access MUST be restricted.

---

# 246. State Locking

Concurrent writes to shared state MUST be prevented.

---

# 247. State Backup

Critical IaC state requires recoverability.

---

# 248. Secrets in State

Avoid designs that unnecessarily persist plaintext secret values in state.

---

# 249. IaC Modules

Shared IaC modules SHOULD follow Reusability Guidelines.

---

# 250. Module Boundaries

Modules should represent stable infrastructure capabilities rather than wrappers around every single resource.

---

# 251. Module Versioning

Shared infrastructure modules require controlled versioning.

---

# 252. Module Updates

Do not silently force every workload onto changed infrastructure semantics.

---

# 253. IaC Validation

CI SHOULD perform:

```text
formatting
syntax validation
policy checks
security scanning
plan generation
```

as applicable.

---

# 254. Policy as Code

Organizations MAY enforce infrastructure policy automatically.

Examples:

```text
no public database
encryption required
approved regions
required tags
```

---

# 255. Policy Exceptions

Infrastructure-policy exemptions require:

```text
reason
owner
scope
review/expiry
```

---

# 256. Drift

Infrastructure drift means live resources differ from declared infrastructure.

---

# 257. Drift Detection

Important production infrastructure SHOULD be checked for drift.

---

# 258. Manual Emergency Changes

Emergency console changes MAY occur.

They MUST be:

```text
audited
documented
reconciled to IaC
or reverted
```

---

# 259. Import Existing Resources

Existing manually created resources SHOULD be imported or otherwise brought under declared management where practical.

---

# 260. Do Not Recreate Dangerous Resources Blindly

Adopting IaC MUST NOT accidentally destroy critical existing resources.

Import/adoption plans require care.

---

# 261. Immutable Infrastructure

Prefer replacement over uncontrolled mutation where practical.

---

# 262. Resource Naming

Resource names SHOULD be:

```text
predictable
stable
environment-aware
```

according to provider constraints.

---

# 263. Resource IDs

Do not depend unnecessarily on human-readable resource names when provider-assigned stable IDs exist.

---

# 264. Infrastructure Tags / Labels

Resources SHOULD include canonical metadata such as:

```text
environment
service
owner
cost center/product
managed-by
```

where provider support permits.

---

# 265. Tags Are Governance Data

Tagging supports:

```text
cost
ownership
inventory
automation
security
```

and should be enforced consistently.

---

# 266. Sensitive Tags

Do not place secrets or sensitive customer data in cloud resource tags.

---

# 267. Object Storage

Object storage SHOULD be used for durable blobs such as:

```text
uploads
images
exports
backups
artifacts
```

when appropriate.

---

# 268. Object Storage Is Not Database Replacement

Do not use object storage for transactional mutable records merely to avoid a database unless workload semantics justify it.

---

# 269. Bucket Access

Buckets/containers MUST be private by default.

---

# 270. Public Objects

Public access requires deliberate design.

Prefer scoped public delivery through:

```text
CDN
signed URL
approved public bucket
```

depending on requirements.

---

# 271. Block Public Access

Provider-level public-access prevention SHOULD be enabled for storage expected to remain private.

---

# 272. Storage IAM

Use workload identity and least privilege for object storage.

---

# 273. Object Encryption

Sensitive object storage MUST use appropriate encryption.

---

# 274. Object Keys

Object names/keys SHOULD NOT contain unnecessary sensitive data.

---

# 275. Signed URLs

Signed URLs SHOULD be:

```text
short-lived
scope-limited
HTTPS
```

for private object sharing.

---

# 276. Upload URLs

Direct browser-to-storage upload MAY reduce application bandwidth.

It requires:

```text
scoped key/path
size constraints
type validation
expiry
post-upload verification
```

---

# 277. Uploaded Content Is Untrusted

Uploading to cloud storage does not make content safe.

Follow File & Media Security rules.

---

# 278. Object Lifecycle

Storage lifecycle policies SHOULD automatically handle:

```text
expiry
archival
tiering
deletion
```

where applicable.

---

# 279. Object Versioning

Versioning MAY protect against accidental overwrite/delete.

It increases storage and retention complexity.

---

# 280. Object Retention

Object lifecycle MUST align with Privacy/Data Governance retention policies.

---

# 281. Replication

Cross-region object replication should exist only when:

```text
recovery
latency
residency
```

requirements justify it.

---

# 282. Storage Events

Object-created/deleted events MAY trigger asynchronous processing.

Consumers must tolerate duplicate/out-of-order delivery where the provider semantics permit it.

---

# 283. File Storage

Shared file systems MAY be appropriate for workloads requiring POSIX/shared file semantics.

Do not choose them for applications that naturally fit object storage.

---

# 284. Block Storage

Block storage should remain attached to workloads that genuinely require filesystem/block semantics.

---

# 285. Ephemeral Disk

Containers/VMs MUST NOT treat ephemeral local disk as durable state.

---

# 286. Queue Infrastructure

Queues decouple producers from asynchronous consumers.

---

# 287. Queue Justification

Use a queue when:

```text
work is asynchronous
load must be buffered
producer/consumer should decouple
retries are required
```

Do not introduce one merely because distributed systems often use queues.

---

# 288. Durable Queues

Business-critical asynchronous work SHOULD use durable managed queues where appropriate.

---

# 289. Delivery Semantics

Understand whether infrastructure provides:

```text
at-most-once
at-least-once
ordered subsets
```

semantics.

---

# 290. At-Least-Once Default Mindset

Consumers SHOULD generally be designed idempotently because duplicate delivery is common in durable messaging systems.

---

# 291. Message ID

Important messages SHOULD have stable identity where deduplication/tracing requires it.

---

# 292. Visibility / Lease Timeout

Queue visibility/lease timeout MUST exceed normal job processing duration with appropriate renewal semantics for long tasks.

---

# 293. Retry

Retries MUST use bounded:

```text
attempts
backoff
jitter
```

according to Error Handling Guidelines.

---

# 294. Dead-Letter Queue

Poison/failed messages SHOULD have a defined dead-letter policy where the queue system supports it.

---

# 295. DLQ Is Not Disposal

Messages reaching a DLQ require:

```text
monitoring
ownership
inspection
replay/disposition
```

---

# 296. Queue Depth

Observe:

```text
queue depth
oldest message age
processing rate
failure rate
DLQ depth
```

---

# 297. Queue Autoscaling

Worker scaling SHOULD prioritize queue pressure and age rather than CPU alone where appropriate.

---

# 298. Backpressure

Systems MUST have a plan when producers exceed consumer capacity.

---

# 299. Unbounded Queue

An infinitely growing queue is not resilience.

It is delayed failure.

---

# 300. Queue Message Size

Keep queue messages reasonably small.

For large payloads:

```text
store object
send reference
```

when appropriate.

---

# 301. Message Secrets

Do not place long-lived credentials in queue payloads.

---

# 302. PII in Queues

Queue contents are data stores and follow Privacy/Data Governance rules.

---

# 303. Queue Encryption

Sensitive messaging SHOULD use provider-supported encryption and restricted access.

---

# 304. Queue Identity

Producer and consumer SHOULD have distinct permissions.

---

# 305. Publish vs Consume

A producer often needs:

```text
send
```

not:

```text
receive/delete/administer
```

permissions.

---

# 306. Events vs Queues

Use:

```text
queue
```

for work distribution.

Use:

```text
event/pub-sub
```

for notifying independent interested consumers.

Do not conflate semantics.

---

# 307. Event Infrastructure

Event systems require:

```text
schema
versioning
ownership
ordering assumptions
idempotency
```

according to Architecture/API Guidelines.

---

# 308. Infrastructure Databases

Database infrastructure follows Data & Database Guidelines.

Deployment architecture still owns:

```text
network placement
availability
compute class
backup integration
IAM
capacity
```

---

# 309. Managed Database Default

Managed database platforms SHOULD generally be preferred unless self-management is specifically justified.

---

# 310. Database Public Exposure

Production databases SHOULD NOT be directly internet-accessible unless a specialized architecture requires it.

---

# 311. Database Network Access

Only approved application/admin paths should reach the database.

---

# 312. Database Authentication

Prefer managed identity/tokenized access where database/provider support makes it practical.

---

# 313. Database TLS

Application/database traffic SHOULD use secure transport.

---

# 314. Read Replicas

Read replicas MAY address:

```text
read scaling
analytics isolation
regional reads
```

but introduce replication lag semantics.

---

# 315. Cache Infrastructure

Caches follow Caching Guidelines.

Infrastructure must still govern:

```text
network
memory
availability
persistence
encryption
```

---

# 316. Cache Is Disposable by Default

Application correctness SHOULD NOT rely on a cache as the only authoritative copy unless the technology is explicitly being used as a durable datastore.

---

# 317. Cache Failure

Loss of ordinary cache SHOULD degrade performance, not corrupt authoritative data.

---

# 318. Secrets Management

Production secrets MUST use the approved secret-management architecture.

---

# 319. Cloud Secret Manager

Managed secret/key management SHOULD be preferred over plaintext environment/config stores for production secrets.

---

# 320. Runtime Secret Delivery

Applications SHOULD retrieve or receive secrets without developers needing plaintext production access.

---

# 321. Secret Rotation

Infrastructure must support secret rotation with minimal downtime where practical.

---

# 322. Key Management

Encryption keys SHOULD use managed key-management infrastructure appropriate to sensitivity.

---

# 323. Customer-Managed Keys
